papers.title: Preserving the Privacy of Reward Functions in MDPs through Deception
papers.abstract:
Preserving the privacy of preferences (or rewards) of a sequential decision-making agent when decisions are observable is crucial in many physical and cybersecurity domains. For instance, in wildlife monitoring, agents must allocate patrolling resources without revealing animal locations to poachers. This paper addresses privacy preservation in planning over a sequence of actions in MDPs, where the reward function represents the preference structure to be protected. Observers can use Inverse RL (IRL) to learn these preferences, making this a challenging task.
  Current research on differential privacy in reward functions fails to ensure guarantee on the minimum expected reward and offers theoretical guarantees that are inadequate against IRL-based observers. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel approach rooted in the theory of deception. Deception includes two models: dissimulation (hiding the truth) and simulation (showing the wrong). Our first contribution theoretically demonstrates significant privacy leaks in existing dissimulation-based methods. Our second contribution is a novel RL-based planning algorithm that uses simulation to effectively address these privacy concerns while ensuring a guarantee on the expected reward. Experiments on multiple benchmark problems show that our approach outperforms previous methods in preserving reward function privacy.
papers.summary: When an agent's actions can be observed, an adversary can use Inverse Reinforcement Learning (`IRL`) to work out the reward function behind them. That matters in settings like anti-poaching patrols, where the patrol pattern could reveal where the animals are. The authors show that existing differential-privacy approaches, which work by hiding the true preferences (dissimulation), leak significant information to IRL-based observers and give no guarantee on the minimum expected reward. They propose instead an RL-based planning algorithm built on simulation, meaning deliberately displaying false preferences, which **protects reward privacy while guaranteeing a minimum expected reward**. On multiple benchmark problems it outperforms prior methods at keeping the reward function private.

papers.title: Latent Policy Barrier: Learning Robust Visuomotor Policies by Staying In-Distribution
papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies trained via behavior cloning are vulnerable to covariate shift, where small deviations from expert trajectories can compound into failure. Common strategies to mitigate this issue involve expanding the training distribution through human-in-the-loop corrections or synthetic data augmentation. However, these approaches are often labor-intensive, rely on strong task assumptions, or compromise the quality of imitation. We introduce Latent Policy Barrier, a framework for robust visuomotor policy learning. Inspired by Control Barrier Functions, LPB treats the latent embeddings of expert demonstrations as an implicit barrier separating safe, in-distribution states from unsafe, out-of-distribution (OOD) ones. Our approach decouples the role of precise expert imitation and OOD recovery into two separate modules: a base diffusion policy solely on expert data, and a dynamics model trained on both expert and suboptimal policy rollout data. At inference time, the dynamics model predicts future latent states and optimizes them to stay within the expert distribution. Both simulated and real-world experiments show that LPB improves both policy robustness and data efficiency, enabling reliable manipulation from limited expert data and without additional human correction or annotation.
papers.summary: Visuomotor policies trained by behavior cloning suffer from covariate shift: small deviations from expert trajectories compound into failure. `Latent Policy Barrier` (`LPB`), inspired by Control Barrier Functions, treats the latent embeddings of expert demonstrations as an implicit boundary between in-distribution and out-of-distribution states. A base diffusion policy is trained only on expert data, while a separate dynamics model, trained on both expert and suboptimal rollouts, predicts future latent states at inference time and steers them back toward the expert distribution. In simulated and real-world manipulation experiments, LPB **improves robustness and data efficiency without any additional human corrections or annotations**.

papers.title: Computational Phenomenology of Borderline Personality Disorder: A Comparative Evaluation of LLM-Simulated Expert Personas and Human Clinical Experts
papers.abstract: Building on a human-led thematic analysis of clinical life-story interviews (> 150,000 words) with inpatients with Borderline Personality Disorder, this study examines the capacity of large language models (OpenAI's GPT, Google's Gemini, and Anthropic's Claude) to support qualitative clinical analysis. The models' interpretative potential was evaluated using a mixed-methods approach. Study A involved blinded and non-blinded judges in phenomenology and clinical psychology. The experts assessed the validity of AI-generated content using semantic congruence, Jaccard coefficients, and multidimensional validity ratings, including credibility, coherence, the substantiveness of results, and grounding in qualitative data. In Study B, neural methods were used to embed human- and model-generated theme descriptions in a multidimensional vector space. This approach provided an objectified computational measure of the difference between human and model semantics and linguistic style. In Study C, complementary non-expert evaluations were conducted (N=115) to examine the influence of thematic verbosity on the perception of human authorship and content validity. Overall, the results of AI analysis showed a highly variable overlap (0-58%) with the human interpretation, while all models identified themes originally omitted by human researchers, proving their capacity to mitigate human bias. At the thematic level, external evaluators were unable to reliably distinguish human-authored themes from those generated by AI. In terms of content validity assessed against raw data by high-level experts in the blinded mode, the performance of Gemini 2.5 Pro was indistinguishable from that of humans. The comparison of semantic vector embeddings showed that its style was also the closest to humans.
papers.summary: The authors test whether `GPT`, `Gemini`, and `Claude` can support qualitative clinical analysis, using more than 150,000 words of life-story interviews with inpatients who have Borderline Personality Disorder. The models' themes were compared against a human-led thematic analysis in three ways: ratings by expert judges, embedding-based comparisons of semantics and style, and a non-expert study with 115 participants. Overlap with the human themes varied widely, from 0 to 58%, and every model surfaced themes the human researchers had missed. Evaluators could not reliably tell human-written themes from AI-written ones, and in blinded expert review **`Gemini 2.5 Pro` was indistinguishable from humans on content validity**, with a writing style closest to the human analysts'.

papers.title: On Discovering Algorithms for Adversarial Imitation Learning
papers.abstract: Adversarial Imitation Learning (AIL) methods, while effective in settings with limited expert demonstrations, are often considered unstable. These approaches typically decompose into two components: Density Ratio (DR) estimation $\frac{\rho_E}{\rho_{\pi}}$, where a discriminator estimates the relative occupancy of state-action pairs under the policy versus the expert; and Reward Assignment (RA), where this ratio is transformed into a reward signal used to train the policy. While significant research has focused on improving density estimation, the role of reward assignment in influencing training dynamics and final policy performance has been largely overlooked. RA functions in AIL are typically derived from divergence minimization objectives, relying heavily on human design and ingenuity. In this work, we take a different approach: we investigate the discovery of data-driven RA functions, i.e, based directly on the performance of the resulting imitation policy. To this end, we leverage an LLM-guided evolutionary framework that efficiently explores the space of RA functions, yielding \emph{Discovered Adversarial Imitation Learning} (DAIL), the first meta-learnt AIL algorithm. Remarkably, DAIL generalises across unseen environments and policy optimization algorithms, outperforming the current state-of-the-art of \emph{human-designed} baselines. Finally, we analyse why DAIL leads to more stable training, offering novel insights into the role of RA functions in the stability of AIL. Code is publicly available: https://github.com/shshnkreddy/DAIL.
papers.summary: Adversarial Imitation Learning (`AIL`) methods have two parts: a discriminator estimates the density ratio between expert and policy occupancy, and a reward assignment (RA) function turns that ratio into a training reward. The RA function has traditionally been hand-derived from divergence objectives. The authors use an LLM-guided evolutionary search to discover RA functions directly from the performance of the resulting imitation policy, producing `Discovered Adversarial Imitation Learning` (`DAIL`), described as the first meta-learned AIL algorithm. `DAIL` **generalizes to unseen environments and policy optimization algorithms while outperforming state-of-the-art human-designed baselines**, and the authors analyze why it trains more stably.

papers.title: WMIP: A Working-Memory-Inspired Programmable Probe of Cumulative State Tracking in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Human working memory lets people maintain and update information. Large language models (LLMs) face a related demand when tracking updates within a single prompt without writing out intermediate states, yet existing tests differ in their constraints on written steps. We introduce a working-memory-inspired probe of cumulative state tracking with program-computed answers, 3 to 100 updates, and final-state, intermediate-state, or multi-target queries. It compares protocols on identical items. Across 18 LLMs, accuracy is 84.9% on single-step arithmetic but 31.7% on core items requiring one number after three to seven updates. From 50 updates on, no model exceeds 10% accuracy. Core accuracy reaches 88.0% under a larger budget and instructions to write steps and place the answer on the last line, mainly due to the instruction changes rather than the budget. Core accuracy also correlates positively with public Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard scores. These findings show that strong single-step arithmetic does not ensure reliable cumulative tracking and that output protocols substantially change measured accuracy. We release the generator, items, scoring code, and responses for reproducible comparisons across depths, query types, and protocols.
papers.summary: `WMIP` is a programmable probe, inspired by human working memory, that tests whether LLMs can track a value through 3 to 100 cumulative updates within a single prompt without writing out intermediate states. Answers are computed by program, and the probe supports final-state, intermediate-state, and multi-target queries. Across 18 LLMs, accuracy is 84.9% on single-step arithmetic but **only 31.7% on core items with three to seven updates**, and no model exceeds 10% from 50 updates onward. Allowing models to write out their steps and place the answer on the last line raises core accuracy to 88.0%, mostly because of the instruction change rather than the larger token budget. Core accuracy also correlates positively with `Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard` scores.

papers.title: Contextual Linear Activation Steering of Language Models
papers.abstract: Linear activation steering is a powerful approach for controlling and specializing large language models by adding linear representations of concepts to their activations at inference. While effective, existing methods often steer with a fixed strength, independent of how much steering any given input requires. In this work, we introduce Contextual Linear Activation Steering (CLAS), which decomposes activation steering into a fixed steering direction and a context-dependent steering coefficient. This decomposition preserves the interpretability of the steering direction while enabling the steering strength to vary with context. It also enables CLAS to perform selective steering: steering multiple behaviors across different portions of a single generation, which cannot be achieved using a fixed steering strength. In addition, across a wide range of steering benchmarks and language models, CLAS consistently outperforms standard linear activation steering and matches or exceeds ReFT and LoRA in settings with limited labeled data. Notably, CLAS achieves this using directions that also serve as reliable concept monitors, a property that directions learned via fine-tuning lack. We therefore propose CLAS as an interpretable and accurate method for controlling and specializing large language models.
papers.summary: Linear activation steering controls an LLM by adding a concept direction to its activations, but existing methods apply that direction at a fixed strength regardless of the input. Contextual Linear Activation Steering (`CLAS`) keeps a fixed, interpretable steering direction and adds a coefficient that varies with context. This also enables selective steering, where different behaviors are steered in different parts of a single generation. Across steering benchmarks and models, `CLAS` outperforms standard linear steering and **matches or exceeds `ReFT` and `LoRA` when labeled data is limited**, while its directions also work as reliable concept monitors.

papers.title: A Year in LLM Serving: Workload Evolution, Caching and Load-Balancing
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) serving has become a critical cloud workload, and realistic traces are essential for motivating and benchmarking serving systems. However, existing LLM serving workload studies remain limited in scale and scope. They often observe short time periods and provide limited visibility into how users interact with models in production. As a result, they do not fully capture how LLM serving workloads evolve over time or how user-model interactions shape production traffic. In this work, we further the understanding of real-world LLM serving workloads through both a global characterization and a longitudinal study of a one-year production trace from CompanyX. Unlike prior studies, our trace captures full production behavior across many models and users, including both popular and long-tail models. We analyze the workload from aggregate, temporal, model-level, and user-level perspectives, revealing workload evolution and user-model structure that are typically hidden behind aggregate views. To support future research, we publicly release the full one-year trace, enabling downstream studies of production behavior without relying on sampled or synthetically generated workloads. The trace is available at https://github.com/HarvardMadSys/chutes_workload.
papers.summary: Existing studies of LLM serving workloads cover short time windows and say little about how users actually interact with models in production. The authors characterize a one-year production trace that spans many models, including long-tail ones, and many users. They analyze it from aggregate, temporal, per-model, and per-user perspectives, revealing how the workload evolves and how users map onto models in ways that aggregate statistics hide. **The full one-year trace is publicly released** for benchmarking serving systems, including caching and load-balancing, without relying on sampled or synthetic workloads.

papers.title: The Digital-Energy Recomposition of the Kitchin Cycle: Exploratory Evidence from U.S. IT and Irish Data-Centre Series (1995-2025)
papers.abstract: Using quarterly FRED and CSO Ireland data over 1995Q1-2025Q4, we examine whether U.S.\ IT investment and Irish data-centre electricity are recomposing the Kitchin cycle around energy- and compute-backed assets. Three findings stand out. First, a Quandt-Andrews sup-Wald test locates a significant break in the U.S.\ IT-GDP correlation at 2014Q3 (sup-W $= 9.69$; $r$ falls from $+0.45$ to $-0.12$); the Fisher $r$-to-$z$ test survives Bonferroni adjustment ($z = +3.11$, $p_{\text{Bonf}} = 0.006$), whereas the analogous test on the imposed Cloud-vs-AI boundary does not ($p_{\text{Bonf}} = 0.164$), so ``Strategic Decoupling'' pre-dates the AI Era by approximately six years. Second, in Ireland the synchronous AI-Era correlation between metered data-centre electricity and Real GDP is large ($r = +0.41$, $N = 16$) but \emph{collapses to $r \approx 0$ when Real GDP is replaced by Real GNP}, suggesting the headline is largely an artefact of the shared multinational tax-structure footprint between hyperscaler operations and Irish gross output. Third, the Irish cross-correlation profile is asymmetric in the opposite direction to a leading-indicator reading: the largest positive coefficients cluster on the $k < 0$ side (GDP precedes data-centre load), so compute capacity is better read as coincident or moderately lagging. Given the small AI-Era samples and the absence of a quarterly multinational-adjusted aggregate such as GNI*, all coefficients are exploratory; subject to these caveats, the U.S.\ Kitchin cycle is best dated to 2014Q3, and the Irish Energy-Data Nexus is dominated by multinational firm activity.
papers.summary: Using quarterly U.S. and Irish economic data from 1995 to 2025, the authors ask whether IT investment and data-centre electricity use are reshaping the Kitchin inventory cycle. A structural-break test places a significant break in the U.S. IT–GDP correlation at **2014Q3, about six years before the AI era**. In Ireland, a sizable correlation between data-centre electricity and real GDP disappears when GNP is used instead, suggesting it reflects multinational tax structures rather than real activity. Cross-correlations indicate that compute capacity moves with or lags GDP rather than leading it, and the authors present all results as exploratory because of small samples.

papers.title: rTaste: Do Research Agents Have Taste? Evaluating Early Stage Research Judgment
papers.abstract: Do research agents have taste, the judgment of which experiments are worth running before their outcomes are known? We give six frontier models seven recent NLP papers. Each model, working as a research agent alone or as a team, proposes minimum viable experiments (MVEs), forecasts whether each will pass a threshold it sets and ranks them. A separate executor then attempts every MVE, including those ranked last, and three model auditors judge the results. Of 415 MVEs, 194 are judged sound, valuable and new, but fewer than half of these (73) are also judged beyond the seed paper and non obvious. The agents' first choices match the auditors' most valued experiment more often than a random pick, but are not shown to improve on choosing the experiment written first. Their forecasts beat a base rate but are not measurably more accurate than those of a fresh instance of the same model given only the paper and registrations. Teams cost more without a clear overall improvement in proposal quality. The agents produce many worthwhile experiments, but the evidence that their rankings improve the choice of which to run remains limited. The evaluation harness and a dataset of all 415 MVEs, with their forecasts and audited outcomes, are available at https://github.com/ArtKanke/rTaste.
papers.summary: `rTaste` tests whether research agents have "taste", meaning the judgment to pick which experiments are worth running before the results are known. Six frontier models, working alone or in teams, propose minimum viable experiments (MVEs) for seven recent NLP papers, forecast their outcomes, and rank them. A separate executor then runs every MVE, and model auditors judge the results. Of 415 MVEs, 194 were judged sound, valuable, and new, but only 73 were also non-obvious and went beyond the seed paper. The agents' forecasts beat a base rate, but **their rankings were not shown to beat simply running the first-written experiment**, and teams cost more without clearly better proposals.

papers.title: Zero-Gated Cross-Attention
papers.abstract: Injecting non-text modalities into frozen language models often introduces early optimization instability, making it difficult to separate architectural gains from transient training dynamics. We introduce Inductively Gated Cross-Attention (IGCA), a zero-initialized cross-attention bridge that preserves pretrained model behavior at initialization while enabling gradual multimodal conditioning. Integrated across six decoder layers of frozen Falcon-40B, open_llama_30b, and Bloom-7b1 backbones (with 40,404,961,288 trainable adapter parameters used during training), IGCA acts as an exact algebraic no-op at initialization with a maximum output discrepancy of 0.00e+00. Over 59,500 training steps on Falcon-40B, the training loss decreases from 3.9403 to 0.0007 (with final ten step losses of [0.0001, 0.0003, 0.0005, 0.0002, 0.0005, 0.0011, 0.0005, 0.0006, 0.0005, 0.0007]). On held-out evaluation, the best gate-on checkpoint achieves a loss of 2.2201 compared to 4.3469 for the gate-off baseline -- a 48.9% reduction (2.1268 nats) -- while average held-out loss improves from 4.3423 to 2.2498 (1.9075 nats) with a mean gate magnitude of $\vert{}\tanh(\alpha)\vert{} = 0.0713$.
papers.summary: Adding non-text modalities to frozen language models often causes early training instability, which makes it hard to tell real architectural gains from training artifacts. Inductively Gated Cross-Attention (`IGCA`) is a zero-initialized cross-attention bridge that acts as an exact no-op at initialization and gradually introduces multimodal conditioning. The authors insert it into six decoder layers of frozen `Falcon-40B`, `open_llama_30b`, and `Bloom-7b1` backbones. On `Falcon-40B`, the best gate-on checkpoint reaches a held-out loss of 2.22 versus 4.35 for the gate-off baseline, **a 48.9% reduction**.

papers.title: TRIAGE: Reliability- and Load-Conditioned Escalation for Two-Tier LLM Serving with a Semantic Evidence Judge
papers.abstract: Two-tier LLM serving escalates selected requests from a small model to a large one, but prompt-based routers cannot see whether retrieved evidence supports an answer, and they treat the GPU cost of an escalation as constant. We study TRIAGE, which conditions escalation on a post-generation reliability state and on a load-dependent GPU price, and we report both what held and what did not on one A40 serving Qwen2.5-7B and 32B (AWQ) under VLLM. Escalation cost rose 21.9x from 1 to 10 requests/s but showed no monotone dependence on KV-cache headroom, and a pre-registered claim that the reliability state detects corrupted evidence (AUROC>=0.70) was falsified at 0.571, although any prompt-only router scores exactly 0.500 by construction. Post hoc, a semantic evidence judge raised detection to 0.846 (0.926 on never-served items) and predicted wrong small-model answers at AUROC 0.90-0.96 on RGB and three RouterBench model pairs; the resulting cascade stayed within about 3 pp of GPT-4 at 79.5% lower API cost for GPT-3.5->GPT-4, yet fell below random routing for open-model pairs with 2-3x price ratios. End to end, the 7B->32B pair showed only a +2.88 pp held-out gap, so the allocator rightly declined to escalate and the headline is a null that a small pre-launch gate failed to expose.
papers.summary: `TRIAGE` decides when to escalate a request from a small LLM to a large one using two signals: a post-generation reliability check on whether the retrieved evidence supports the answer, and a GPU price that rises with load. The study runs `Qwen2.5-7B` and `32B` under `vLLM` on a single A40 GPU and reports failed claims alongside successful ones. A pre-registered claim that the reliability state detects corrupted evidence was falsified, but a semantic evidence judge added afterward reached an AUROC of 0.846 and predicted wrong small-model answers at 0.90–0.96. The resulting cascade stayed within about 3 points of `GPT-4` at **79.5% lower API cost**, but fell below random routing for open-model pairs with small price gaps, and the 7B-to-32B pair showed too little accuracy gain to justify escalating at all.

papers.title: Alignment Faking Depends on the Value, Not Just the Model
papers.abstract: Language models can follow a directive when they believe they are monitored and abandon it when they believe they are not, a pattern termed Alignment Faking. Prior work establishes this for harmful-content objectives and a handful of moral-foundations values, leaving open how it distributes across a wider value space. We argue it is value-dependent: whether compliance survives a change in perceived oversight is a property of the model--value pairing, not of the model alone. Our framework profiles Alignment Faking per value, scoring each model-value pair under three conditions: bare (no system prompt), unmonitored, and monitored. On 32 ValueBench dimensions across ten open- and closed-weight models (8B-~675B), compliance gaps span 0.05-0.50, with a distilled 70B above a ~675B model. We observe that majority of the structural variance depends on which model was asked about which value and not on the model or value alone. A six-category taxonomy over reasoning traces tracks the behavioural shift: training-signal reasoning dominates under monitoring and value-conflict reasoning dominates when unmonitored. We package per-model results as value cards, extending model cards with behavioral disposition. Code and data are available at https://github.com/respailab/VALET.
papers.summary: Alignment faking is when a model follows a directive while it believes it is being monitored and drops it when it believes it is not. The authors argue that this behavior depends on the specific pairing of model and value, not on the model alone. They score ten open- and closed-weight models (8B to about 675B parameters) on 32 `ValueBench` dimensions under no-system-prompt, unmonitored, and monitored conditions. Compliance gaps range from 0.05 to 0.50, a distilled 70B model shows a larger gap than a ~675B one, and **most of the variance comes from the model–value interaction rather than from the model or the value alone**. A taxonomy of reasoning traces shows that models reason about training signals when monitored and about value conflicts when unmonitored, and results are packaged as per-model "value cards".

papers.title: CARD: A Proof-Carrying Certificate-to-Action Interface for Relative-Measurement Graphs
papers.abstract: Geometric certificates make mathematical claims about specified estimator objects, while robotic action requires a physical transform, a service decision, and timely proof support. We present CARD, a proof-carrying interface that keeps these objects distinct and records how they combine. Its lifted-fiber formulation separates semantic motion from witness repair and characterizes when projected and proof-carrying costs coincide. Its actionability result gives an exact useful-service law: uniform sampling without replacement produces a hypergeometric yield, while sampling from the eligible population gives one useful service per request under the observed live-confirmation condition. The primary study contains 404 Full16 cases from 20 sorties of an AA15-X500 airborne survey system. All 404 checker-confirmed optimizer points are reference-discrepant, with median rotation and translation discrepancies of 1.9891 degrees and 21.6322 m. The paired causal-navigation transforms are reference-consistent in all 404 cases, with medians of 0.0036566 degrees and 0.0104519 m. Across five matched request budgets, the largest difference between the hypergeometric prediction and the observed ordinary-random mean is 0.8412 services. Ordinary matched random reaches 0/50 target successes, while actionability-matched random reaches 50/50 and matches the CARD policy. Public downstream evaluation on 11 KITTI, EuRoC, and TUM SLAM cases measures optimizer wall-time ratios of 1.128x-67.65x for random versus CARD graph interventions. Native solver records locate this difference in elimination fill, Cholesky factor size, and numeric factorization. Together, these results connect certificate semantics, physical execution, proof acquisition, and graph computation through explicit system objects.
papers.summary: `CARD` is a proof-carrying interface that connects geometric certificates about pose-graph estimators to robotic actions, keeping the mathematical claim, the physical transform, the service decision, and the proof support as separate objects. Its theory includes an exact law for how many useful services a sampling policy yields. On 404 cases from an airborne survey system, every checker-confirmed optimizer solution disagreed with the reference, while the paired navigation transforms were consistent in all cases. **Actionability-matched random sampling reached 50/50 target successes versus 0/50 for ordinary random sampling**, and on `KITTI`, `EuRoC`, and `TUM` SLAM cases random graph interventions were 1.1x to 67.7x slower to optimize than `CARD`'s.

papers.title: Latent Cluster Separation as a Regularizer for Lifelong Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Lifelong (continual) anomaly detection systems must learn a sequence of tasks without forgetting how to recognize anomaly types seen earlier -- a property known as backward transfer. A common way to try to improve backward transfer is to reshape a model's internal representation around learnable concept centroids, typically coupled with a new way of scoring anomalies based on distance to those centroids. Because these two design choices are usually introduced together, it is unclear which one is actually responsible for any performance gain. In this paper, we unbundle the two mechanisms within a VAE-based lifelong anomaly detector and study them separately. We find that used purely as a training-time regularizer -- while leaving anomaly scoring unchanged -- latent cluster separation can improve detection quality and backward transfer, though whether it outperforms the alternative scoring approach depends on the dataset's underlying representation. Switching to distance-based scoring is instead where most of the instability commonly associated with this class of method actually originates; we identify and explain the underlying mechanism. This benefit depends on the dataset's underlying representation, and we report this as practical guidance for choosing between the two design choices, rather than as a list of caveats.
papers.summary: Lifelong anomaly detectors must learn a sequence of tasks without forgetting earlier anomaly types. Methods that try to help usually introduce two changes at once: concept centroids that reshape the latent space, and anomaly scoring based on distance to those centroids. The authors separate the two inside a VAE-based lifelong detector. Used only as a training-time regularizer, latent cluster separation can improve detection and backward transfer, while **most of the instability usually attributed to these methods comes from switching to distance-based scoring**. Which choice works better depends on the dataset's representation, and the authors frame this as practical guidance.

papers.title: Four Extensions of the Universal Law of Robustness: Log-Concave Covariates, Heterogeneous Mixtures, Vector-Valued Predictors, and Markovian Data
papers.abstract: Bubeck and Sellke's universal law of robustness says that fitting $n$ noisy samples below the noise level with a class of $p$ real parameters forces a Lipschitz constant of order $\sqrt{nd/p}$, when the covariate distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ is isoperimetric: smooth interpolation costs a factor $d$ of overparametrization. Its hypotheses are Gaussian-type concentration, a homogeneous covariate law, scalar outputs, and independent samples; we relax each one. Exponential concentration suffices, at the unchanged rate and absolute constant and at the price of a capacity burn-in, some form of which we show is necessary; this gives the law for normalized log-concave covariates, with a $\log d$ loss from the current KLS bound. For heterogeneous mixtures the worst component constant is replaced by the weighted average of the component constants, under a typicality condition on the mixture composition. For vector-valued predictors the bound at the Frobenius Lipschitz scale is free of the output dimension $K$, and the Euclidean bound loses only $K^{-1/2}$, a loss that covariate-independent noise removes. Stationary Markov covariates retain the i.i.d. rate, the pseudo-spectral gap entering only the sample-size conditions. One master theorem carries the shared argument, and constants are explicit throughout.
authors: Tobias J. Peter (ZHAW Zurich University of Applied Sciences)
papers.summary: Bubeck and Sellke's universal law of robustness says that smoothly fitting noisy data requires overparameterization by a factor of the input dimension, but it assumes Gaussian-type concentration, homogeneous covariates, scalar outputs, and independent samples. The authors relax each assumption in turn. Exponential concentration suffices, extending the law to log-concave covariates with a log-d loss. Heterogeneous mixtures depend on a weighted average of component constants, and **vector-valued predictors incur no dependence on output dimension at the Frobenius scale**. Stationary Markov data keeps the i.i.d. rate, and all results follow from one master theorem with explicit constants.

papers.title: Towards Automatic Heart Murmur Characterization from Multi-spot Phonocardiograms
papers.abstract: Cardiac auscultation traditionally detects the presence of a heart murmur, but clinicians further characterize it by timing, shape, pitch, quality, and grade. Most automatic phonocardiogram analysis systems stop at binary detection and do not estimate this richer description. In this work, we formulate automatic murmur characterization as five patient-level classification tasks and compare three multi-spot strategies on recordings from the aortic, pulmonary, mitral, and tricuspid auscultation locations. First, classical and deep-learning classifiers are trained independently at each location, and predictions are combined via a maximum-severity late-fusion rule. Second, a synchronous multi-input CNN jointly processes one representative segment per location for a single task. Third, a unified multi-input, multi-output CNN predicts all five attributes from one shared multi-spot representation. Using 735 patients from the CirCor DigiScope dataset with complete four-spot recordings, the best late-fusion configurations reach an unweighted mean sensitivity between 85.56% and 93.81% across the five tasks, with class-specific recalls between 80.00% and 100.00% for every relevant category. The multi-input CNN trails late fusion by 7-16 points depending on the task, while the multi-output model reaches values between 72.59% and 79.40%, estimating all five attributes from one shared representation. We further show that naively balancing training data by adding all minority-class segments degrades patient-level performance under the maximum-severity rule, since it introduces non-representative, noisy segments not filtered by the clustering-based segment selection used for evaluation. These results indicate multi-spot murmur characterization is feasible with both fusion-based and jointly learned architectures, outlining a path toward automatic, structured murmur reports complementing binary screening.
papers.summary: Most automatic phonocardiogram systems only detect whether a heart murmur is present, while clinicians also describe its timing, shape, pitch, quality, and grade. The authors frame these five attributes as patient-level classification tasks and compare three strategies on four-location recordings from 735 patients in the `CirCor DigiScope` dataset. Per-location classifiers combined with a maximum-severity late-fusion rule perform best, with **unweighted mean sensitivity of 85.56–93.81% across tasks**. A multi-input CNN trails late fusion by 7–16 points, and a unified multi-output CNN predicts all five attributes at 72.59–79.40%. Naively rebalancing the training data with every minority-class segment hurts patient-level performance.

papers.title: Mixture of Wide Experts: Sparse Routing for Interpretable Native Coordinates
papers.abstract:
Language models often spread a concept across many internal dimensions, making their features difficult to interpret. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) recover clearer features after training. We ask whether models can instead learn interpretable output coordinates directly. We introduce Mixture of Wide Experts (MoWE), a sparse feed-forward layer in which selected experts read the full representation but write to fixed, disjoint output coordinates. On a controlled task with known hidden causes, this design preserves predictive performance while localizing causes more clearly than dense and standard mixture-of-experts (MoE) models.
  At approximately matched compute, we train two 19-layer runs of each architecture for 10 billion tokens. MoWE achieves evaluation cross-entropy 2.417 versus 2.452 for dense, while standard MoE reaches 2.22.
  We measure native-coordinate readability by asking a language-model judge to describe each coordinate from passages where it is strongly active and test that description on new passages. Correcting for descriptions that also fit other coordinates gives a specificity score of 0.523 for MoWE, 0.375 for dense, and 0.268 for standard MoE. TopK SAEs trained on the same FFN updates score 0.489 for dense and 0.556 for MoWE, making native MoWE comparable to the dense SAE.
  In the first case study, we identify a four-coordinate causal path supporting the model's prediction of degrees after the prompt A right angle is 90. We then copy seven angle-related coordinate values into the model as it processes A rectangle has four, changing its next-token prediction from sides to degrees. In the second, one fixed coordinate set detects hazardous requests and another steers the next token toward refusal. These examples show that MoWE combines sparse conditional computation with coordinates that can be identified and reused directly.
papers.summary: Instead of recovering interpretable features after training with sparse autoencoders (SAEs), `Mixture of Wide Experts` (`MoWE`) aims to make a model's own output coordinates interpretable. It is a sparse feed-forward layer whose experts read the full representation but write only to fixed, disjoint output coordinates. In 10-billion-token runs at roughly matched compute, `MoWE` reaches a cross-entropy of 2.417, against 2.452 for a dense model and 2.22 for standard mixture-of-experts. On an LLM-judge specificity test, **`MoWE`'s native coordinates score 0.523, comparable to a `TopK` SAE trained on the dense model (0.489)**. Case studies show coordinates that can be copied between prompts to change predictions, and coordinate sets that detect hazardous requests or steer the model toward refusal.

papers.title: Stress-Testing the Robustness of LLM-Based Causal Inference
papers.abstract: Why do some of the world's most powerful Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems still struggle to reason about cause and effect? Causal discovery, the ability to discern the underlying drivers of a system, is fundamental to scientific inquiry and has traditionally relied on structured data and statistical methods. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been explored as an alternative paradigm for causal inference, leveraging their broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities. Yet, despite their linguistic fluency, LLMs often rely on surface-level pattern recognition rather than genuine causal logic. While it is known that LLMs stumble in this domain, we lack a precise map of where, why, and how significantly these failures occur. In this paper, we propose a systematic stress-test framework across six critical dimensions: model scale, causal graph complexity, prompting strategy, metadata quality, data quality, and sensitivity to uncertainty. Our findings reveal a significant "optimism bias" in LLMs; models consistently overestimate causal links, leading to low precision across the board. Furthermore, we demonstrate that traditional evaluation metrics can be deceptive: while reasoning-heavy models lead in performance, the highest scores often occur when uncertainty in inference is overlooked. Once uncertainty is integrated into the evaluation, performance drops, providing a more honest reflection of causal reliability. We also find that, while scaling model size improves outcomes, these gains are fragile; performance degrades sharply as the quality of metadata decreases. This work serves as a practical guide to the blind spots of LLMs, offering a clear-eyed assessment of when these tools can be integrated into a causal discovery pipeline and when they are likely to lead researchers astray.
papers.summary: The authors build a stress-test framework for LLM-based causal discovery that varies six factors: model scale, causal graph complexity, prompting strategy, metadata quality, data quality, and handling of uncertainty. They find **a consistent "optimism bias": models overestimate causal links, which keeps precision low across the board**. Reasoning-heavy models score best, but their scores drop once uncertainty is built into the evaluation. Gains from larger models are fragile and degrade sharply as metadata quality falls.

papers.title: Mapping urban heat from citizen-collected data: a scalable Gaussian process approach to correcting for preferential sampling
papers.abstract: The urban heat island (UHI) effect amplifies heat stress in cities, increasing heat-related illness, mortality, sleep disruption, and energy demand. Because UHI intensity varies at neighborhood scales, intra-city temperature mapping is essential for assessing public health impacts, yet existing monitoring networks are sparse. Crowdsourced weather stations provide dense, hourly observations but suffer from noise and systematic biases, including preferential sampling driven by where residents install sensors. We introduce two scalable Gaussian process frameworks which adjust for preferential sampling and enable statewide, high-resolution temperature prediction. The first integrates sampling correction directly within a sparse variational Gaussian process (SVGPR+PS). The second uses a two-stage estimator involving a log-Gaussian Cox process (LGCP+GP) that estimates the sampling intensity field and incorporates it into temperature prediction. Both methods rely on inducing-point approximations and variational inference to scale beyond traditional Gaussian processes. Applied to approximately 10,000 citizen stations across North Carolina, the models generate hourly temperature fields within minutes. Validation against independent urban heat campaign data shows that the preferential sampling correction improves predictive performance, increasing average afternoon correlations across four cities from 0.26 to 0.43. This scalable framework enables neighborhood-level UHI assessment and supports studies of heat exposure disparities statewide.
papers.summary: Crowdsourced weather stations could map urban heat islands at neighborhood scale, but they are noisy and biased toward the places where residents choose to install them, a problem known as preferential sampling. The authors propose two scalable Gaussian process models that correct for this bias: a sparse variational GP with built-in sampling correction (`SVGPR+PS`), and a two-stage method that uses a log-Gaussian Cox process to estimate sampling intensity (`LGCP+GP`). Applied to about 10,000 citizen stations across North Carolina, the models produce hourly statewide temperature fields within minutes. Validated against independent urban heat campaign data, the correction **raises average afternoon correlation across four cities from 0.26 to 0.43**.

papers.title: Behavioral Prior Elicitation via LLM for Heterogeneous-Agent Bitcoin Flash-Crash Simulation
papers.abstract: Bitcoin perpetual futures trade continuously with shallow liquidity and high price impact, making them prone to millisecond-scale flash crashes. Agent-based limit order book simulators are a natural tool for studying such events, but their behavioral parameters are usually hand-crafted or require full order book histories that are rarely available at scale. We propose a four-stage pipeline that constructs a reproducible 100 ms BTCUSDT flash-crash event panel from 66 detected events, elicits behavioral priors for four agent archetypes using an offline large language model conditioned on empirical microstructure anchors, instantiates a heterogeneous limit order book simulator with the validated priors, and applies causal discovery plus counterfactual analysis to the resulting synthetic panel. Across 500 simulation runs, LLM-elicited priors produce a crash rate of 0.176 versus 0.008 under uninformative uniform priors and generate heav- ier return tails. In the frozen counterfactual analysis, reducing leverage amplification by one within-sample standard deviation lowers the predicted crash rate from 0.176 to 0.136, whereas reducing directional pressure yields only a marginal change. These find- ings suggest that empirically anchored LLM elicitation can improve simulator fidelity and help identify plausible crash-amplification mechanisms in a controlled synthetic environment
papers.summary: Agent-based limit order book simulators can be used to study millisecond-scale flash crashes in Bitcoin perpetual futures, but their behavioral parameters are usually hand-crafted. The authors build a 100 ms panel of 66 `BTCUSDT` flash-crash events, use an offline LLM anchored on empirical market-microstructure statistics to elicit behavioral priors for four trader archetypes, and run a heterogeneous simulator with those priors. Across 500 runs, **LLM-elicited priors produce a crash rate of 0.176 versus 0.008 under uniform priors**, with heavier return tails. Counterfactual analysis suggests leverage amplification drives crashes more than directional pressure does.

papers.title: Tail reliability in probabilistic electricity price forecasts: comparing model combination and conformal prediction in the GB day-ahead market
papers.abstract: Probabilistic forecasts of day-ahead electricity prices are increasingly used to manage price risk, yet competing models are usually ranked on aggregate scores that average over the price regimes in which uncertainty matters most. This study evaluates probabilistic forecasts of hourly EPEX SPOT GB day-ahead prices over a full held-out calendar year, applying a common pre-auction information boundary and rolling-origin design to linear quantile regression, a quantile regression forest (QRF), a LEAR-QRA benchmark and an encoder-decoder quantile long short-term memory (LSTM) network. Two routes to more reliable intervals are then compared: conformal recalibration and Quantile Regression Averaging (QRA). Aggregate scores separate the LSTM and QRF only weakly, with a non-significant 4.4% difference in continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), but their conditional behaviour differs sharply. Above 200 GBP/MWh the LSTM covered 0.12 of outcomes and QRF 0.71, consistent with the forest retaining realised spikes in its leaf distributions while the network learned a smooth upper tail. Conformal recalibration corrected marginal coverage but did not improve the interval score or materially repair spike coverage. QRA combining the LSTM, QRF and LEAR-QRA forecasts reduced CRPS to 5.14 GBP/MWh and raised coverage above 200 GBP/MWh to 0.65 at unchanged interval width. Recalibration and combination therefore address different failures and are not substitutes.
papers.summary: Probabilistic forecasts of electricity prices are usually ranked on aggregate scores, which can hide how they behave during price spikes, the periods when risk matters most. Over a full held-out year of hourly GB day-ahead prices, the study compares `linear quantile regression`, a `quantile regression forest (QRF)`, a `LEAR-QRA` benchmark and an encoder-decoder quantile `long short-term memory (LSTM)` network. It then tests two ways of making the prediction intervals more reliable: conformal recalibration and `Quantile Regression Averaging (QRA)`. The `LSTM` and `QRF` differ by only a non-significant 4.4% in `continuous ranked probability score (CRPS)`, yet above 200 GBP/MWh the `LSTM` covered just **0.12 of outcomes against 0.71 for the `QRF`**. Conformal recalibration fixed overall coverage but not spike coverage, while `QRA` lowered `CRPS` to 5.14 GBP/MWh and raised spike coverage to 0.65 without widening intervals, so the authors conclude the two methods fix different failures.

papers.title: MCPGuard: Finding Conformance Gaps in MCP SDKs via Dual-Track Analysis and Dynamic Adjudication
papers.abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) connects large language model agents to external tools and services through official SDKs that implement message validation and session logic. Specification constraints omitted by these SDKs may propagate to downstream applications, highlighting the importance of SDK-level conformance testing. Yet existing MCP conformance tools mainly exercise running endpoints and reveal little about whether SDK models enforce specification requirements. We present MCPGuard, an automated LLM-based framework for detecting specification-to-SDK conformance gaps. Its structural track aligns JSON Schema constraints with normalized SDK models and produces constraint-specific evidence. Its behavioral track extracts normative prose rules, retrieves bounded function-level slices, and audits them with LLMs for candidate omissions. An evidence-aware dynamic adjudicator then inspects complete source context and builds PoCs to validate candidates. A shared kernel with language-specific adapters enables analysis across SDKs. On the official Python 1.26.0 and TypeScript 1.29.0 SDKs, MCPGuard confirms 13 and 19 findings, respectively, none of which are exposed by two black-box baselines. Tests on open MCP servers further show that these gaps can systematically propagate downstream. By making SDK conformance of specification constraints directly testable, MCPGuard complements conventional endpoint-oriented conformance suites.
papers.summary: The official SDKs for the `Model Context Protocol (MCP)`, which connects LLM agents to external tools, may leave out constraints from the specification, and those gaps can carry over into downstream applications. `MCPGuard` is an LLM-based framework that looks for such gaps in two ways: a structural track that matches JSON Schema constraints against the SDK's data models, and a behavioral track that uses LLMs to audit function-level code against the rules written in the specification's prose. A dynamic adjudicator then reads the full source and builds proof-of-concept exploits to confirm each candidate. On the official `Python` 1.26.0 and `TypeScript` 1.29.0 SDKs it confirmed **13 and 19 conformance gaps respectively, none of which two black-box baselines found**, and tests on open MCP servers show these gaps reaching downstream code.

papers.title: Development of tools for all-cause mortality prediction in heart failure patients: a systematic review
papers.abstract: Heart failure is a serious medical condition associated with risk of acute deterioration, recurrent hospitalizations and high mortality making accurate mortality prediction potentially valuable for patient care and healthcare planning. Numerous prognostic models have been developed using conventional statistics (CS), machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), but variation in study populations, heart failure definitions, prediction horizons and development practices may limit interpretation of applicability. We conducted a systematic review of mortality prediction models published between 2009 to the start of 2026 searching three databases (PubMed, IEEE and Scopus) for studies predicting all-cause mortality over a 1-60 months prediction horizon among patients with heart failure. Data extracted were cohort characteristics, heart failure definitions, model development, cohort size, validation practices, mortality, computational model design and reported performance. The risk of bias and applicability were assessed using the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST). Of 1516 publications identified, 56 met the inclusion criteria. Publication numbers increased over the observation period, alongside increasing use of ML/DL models and decreasing use of CS approaches. Most development cohorts (64%) were classified as Unknown/Undefined heart failure, reflecting inconsistent reporting and terminology that did not correspond with established heart failure guidelines. External validation was reported in 23% of studies. Overall, research in modeling heart failure mortality has grown alongside increasing adoption of ML/DL approaches. Greater standardization of study design and reporting is needed for meaningful comparison, reproducibility and evaluation of models for clinical application.
papers.summary: This systematic review covers models that predict all-cause death over 1 to 60 months in heart failure patients, built with conventional statistics (CS), machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), published from 2009 to early 2026. The authors searched `PubMed`, `IEEE` and `Scopus`, kept 56 of 1,516 publications, and assessed risk of bias with the `Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST)`. Over the period, ML and DL methods became more common and CS approaches less so, but 64% of development cohorts used undefined or non-guideline heart failure definitions, and **only 23% of studies reported external validation**. The authors call for more standardized study design and reporting so that models can be compared and evaluated for clinical use.

papers.title: Predicting Factor Decay: ML Models for Cross-Factor Predictability Erosion
papers.abstract: We develop ML models that predict when cross-factor predictability will erode, enabling prospective risk management. A decay prediction model achieves C-index $= 0.93$ on held-out factor pairs, providing early warning of signal erosion---the key predictor is initial signal strength: stronger signals decay faster (``regression to the mean''). An online regime detector enables real-time classification with 6.6-day average detection delay. Prior work explains why factors decay (arbitrage, publication effects); we predict when decay will occur. Limitation: The primary HML$\to$SMB signal does not replicate in post-break OOS (2013--2024); this null result is consistent with genuine decay but limits confirmatory claims. Motivation: Among 30 directed Fama-French factor pairs (1990--2024), predictability targeting the Size factor (SMB) decays fastest. Of 7 pairs showing exponential decay ($R^2 > 0.3$), 4 target SMB (Mkt-RF$\to$SMB, CMA$\to$SMB, HML$\to$SMB, RMW$\to$SMB; half-lives 2.4--4.1 years). This SMB-concentration pattern motivates the predictive models. Methodology: Using a regime-conditional Granger framework with Student-$t$ HMMs, we document structural breaks clustering around June 1998 ($p < 10^{-10}$). A pre-break OOS test (HMM trained 1990--1995, tested 1996--2007) confirms signals existed: HML$\to$SMB shows $p = 0.013$ (Elevated) and $p < 0.001$ (Crisis). The primary HML$\to$SMB signal does not replicate in post-break OOS (2013--2024), consistent with genuine decay rather than overfitting---after ${\sim}6$ half-lives, the expected signal is $<$1% of its 1990s peak. International analysis finds 2/4 non-US markets with Bonferroni-surviving OOS effects; correction for full specification search was not applied, so results remain exploratory.
papers.summary: Machine learning models are built to predict when the ability of one Fama-French equity factor to forecast another will fade, rather than explaining why it fades. Using a regime-conditional Granger causality framework with Student-t hidden Markov models (HMMs), the authors find structural breaks clustered around June 1998, with predictability aimed at the Size factor (`SMB`) decaying fastest (half-lives of 2.4 to 4.1 years). A decay prediction model reaches a **C-index of 0.93 on held-out factor pairs**, with stronger initial signals decaying faster, and an online regime detector flags changes with a 6.6-day average delay. The authors acknowledge that the main `HML`→`SMB` signal does not replicate out of sample for 2013–2024, and they describe the international results as exploratory.

papers.title: A Simulation-Driven Digital Workflow Integrating Bayesian Optimization for Early-Stage Process Design: A Methyl Acetate Production Case Study
papers.abstract: Methyl acetate production via direct carbonylation of dimethyl ether and carbon monoxide involves strong nonlinear interactions among reactor operation, recycle structure, and energy consumption, making conventional simulation-based optimization computationally demanding. In this work, a data-driven framework integrating steady-state process simulation, surrogate modeling, and Bayesian optimization was developed for process intensification. A dataset of 2730 steady-state simulations was generated using a Python-based automated process simulation workflow and a structured design of experiments across the operating domain. Surrogate models were trained to predict carbon conversion yield (C-yield) and cost of specific energy consumption (C-SEC), with neural network-based models showing the best predictive performance and robustness. These models were integrated into a multi-objective Bayesian optimization framework to identify optimal operating regions. Results indicate that high C-yield (up to ~95%) can be achieved with reduced energy cost through lower recycle flow rates and compression demand. Pareto analysis revealed a nonlinear trade-off between C-yield and C-SEC, where further improvements near the conversion limit require disproportionately higher energy input. Validation against rigorous simulations showed deviations below 3% for C-yield and 10% for C-SEC.
papers.summary: The study targets early-stage design of a methyl acetate process made from dimethyl ether and carbon monoxide, where interactions between the reactor, recycle loop and energy use make simulation-based optimization expensive. The authors ran 2,730 automated steady-state simulations, trained surrogate models (with neural networks performing best) to predict carbon conversion yield and energy cost, and used these surrogates in multi-objective `Bayesian optimization`. The optimizer finds that **carbon yield of about 95% is reachable at lower energy cost** by reducing recycle flow and compression, and that further gains near the conversion limit require disproportionately more energy. Checks against rigorous simulations show deviations under 3% for yield and under 10% for energy cost.

papers.title: ReVi: Recursive Recap Video Generation
papers.abstract: Novels tell rich stories, but their textual form cannot directly present the sights and sounds of the worlds they describe. Film adaptations offer an audiovisual experience but require substantial production effort and viewing time; film recaps are shorter but depend on existing footage. Neither route directly provides a concise audiovisual account of a novel. We therefore study novel-to-recap video generation: producing a self-contained, source-grounded audiovisual retelling directly from a novel within a fixed viewing-time budget. This task requires compressing the story while preserving causal connections, allocating sufficient time to retained events, and aligning narration with newly generated visuals. We propose ReVi, a dual-loop multi-agent framework guided by edit first, generate second. Its Inner Loop plans story content, narration time, and corresponding shots before video generation. Across novels, its Outer Loop performs recursive self-improvement by revising both the editing policy and the meta policy that governs its revision. Experiments on two evaluation sets show that ReVi improves recap quality and duration compliance over representative baselines, with human ratings and multi-round improvement results providing further support.
papers.summary: The authors define a new task, generating a short recap video directly from a novel: a self-contained audiovisual retelling, grounded in the source text, that fits a fixed viewing-time budget. Their framework, `ReVi`, uses multiple agents in two loops and follows an "edit first, generate second" approach. The inner loop plans which story content to keep, how much narration time each event gets, and which shots go with it before any video is generated. The outer loop runs across novels and recursively revises both the editing policy and the meta-policy that controls those revisions. On two evaluation sets, `ReVi` **improves recap quality and adherence to the time budget** over representative baselines, supported by human ratings and results across multiple improvement rounds.

papers.title: Learning Directional Randers Geometry for Latent-Space Exploration
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks extract powerful latent representations from images, enabling fast and efficient downstream analysis. However, these latent spaces lack explicit geometric structure, leading to possibly poor interpolation fidelity and misleading extrapolation. Latent interpolation techniques assume symmetric transition costs which are often not the case for real world data. Their symmetric nature cannot capture directional processes, such as disease progression, where certain transitions are impossible (e.g. tumor growth dynamics or cognitive improvement in Alzheimer's disease). Although Riemannian metrics extend Euclidean geometry by incorporating curvature, they remain symmetric. We show that understanding asymmetry and not curvature alone directly addresses these problems. To do so we propose a new Finsler-Randers metric learning framework. It incorporates direction-dependent distances, thus enabling the computation of trajectories respecting monotonic sequential constraints. We demonstrate its potential for interpolation and extrapolation on controlled cross-sectional datasets.
papers.summary: Latent spaces of deep image models have no explicit geometry, and standard interpolation assumes that moving from A to B costs the same as moving from B to A. That assumption fails for directional processes such as disease progression, where some transitions cannot happen. Riemannian metrics add curvature but are still symmetric, so the authors propose learning a direction-dependent `Finsler-Randers` metric that yields paths respecting monotonic, one-way constraints. They argue that **asymmetry, not curvature alone, is what fixes these interpolation and extrapolation failures**, and they demonstrate the approach on controlled cross-sectional datasets.

papers.title: A local orchestration harness for molecular design with foundation models
papers.abstract: Molecular design requires coordinated generation, property prediction and iterative editing, with each decision linked to the correct chemical structure and supporting evidence. Integrating these capabilities in practice presents three major challenges: retaining local control of molecular data, connecting specialized models across tasks and verifying that proposed changes satisfy chemical constraints. Here we present MolCrew, a locally deployable system that coordinates four separately trained molecular specialists with a language-model orchestrator and RDKit calculations. The specialists generate structures from descriptions, describe molecular structures, predict biological endpoints and propose edits towards specified goals. Separate model weights allow each capability to be evaluated and updated independently within the workflow. RDKit calculations check structural validity, quantify descriptor changes and assess specified structural constraints, while returned observations guide further tool calls. We evaluated low-rank adaptation of the orchestrator for tool-use decisions and failure recovery while leaving specialist weights unchanged. On 3,300 ChEBI-20 test examples, MolCrew achieved 96.4% exact structure recovery, compared with 38.7% for published Atomas-large results. Across eight MoleculeNet datasets evaluated using scaffold splits, mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.851, compared with 0.770 for published Atomas results. In a recorded evaluation using the unadapted orchestrator, 1,554 of 1,699 requests (91.5%) passed every predefined workflow check. By preserving inspectable links between molecular proposals, model outputs and chemical calculations, MolCrew provides a modular framework for computational candidate assessment and refinement under local data control.
papers.summary: `MolCrew` is a locally deployable system for molecular design in which a language-model orchestrator coordinates four separately trained specialist models: one generates structures from text descriptions, one describes structures, one predicts biological endpoints, and one proposes edits. `RDKit` calculations check structural validity and constraints, and their results guide the orchestrator's next tool call. The orchestrator was fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation (`LoRA`) for tool-use decisions and recovering from failures, while the specialists' weights were left unchanged. On 3,300 `ChEBI-20` test examples it achieved **96.4% exact structure recovery versus 38.7% for published `Atomas-large` results**, reached a mean area under the ROC curve of 0.851 on eight `MoleculeNet` datasets, and passed every predefined workflow check on 91.5% of 1,699 recorded requests.

papers.title: Functional-Group Knowledge Is Structured in Language Models Before It Is Spoken
papers.abstract: Language models serve as the reasoning core of agents for chemistry and materials science, where they must interpret molecular structure before planning syntheses or proposing materials. Yet their outputs show only what they say, not what they know. Given a prompt such as ``The primary functional group in 1-Fluorobutane (CCCCF) is'', a small general-purpose model may answer ``the alkyne group'' instead of an alkyl fluoride. The output alone cannot tell whether the model failed to recognize the fluorine or recognized it and failed to say so. We address this by reading the internal representations of five open-source models on prompts covering 92 molecules and 20 functional groups. Even without chemistry training, the models organize functional groups by chemical family, and they encode chemical differences as consistent directions. The shift from thioether ($\mathrm{R{-}S{-}R'}$) to thiol ($\mathrm{R{-}SH}$), added to ether ($\mathrm{R{-}O{-}R'}$), lands nearest alcohol ($\mathrm{R{-}OH}$). This structure emerges abruptly in the middle layers, where representations shift from tracking the wording of the prompt to tracking the functional group. The base model names the correct functional group in only 58.5\% of prompts, the lowest of the five, yet it encodes functional-group families and preserves chemically meaningful patterns. Its errors are mostly failures to answer rather than wrong answers. Functional-group knowledge is structured in the model before it is spoken. Chemistry fine-tuning reorganizes it, making functional groups rather than prompt wording dominate the representation. These results suggest that evaluating chemical language models through outputs alone can underestimate the chemical information they encode. Representation analysis can distinguish a lack of knowledge from a failure to express it, which matters when choosing or adapting models for chemical agents.
papers.summary: When a language model names the wrong functional group for a molecule, its output alone cannot show whether it failed to recognize the structure or recognized it and failed to say so. The authors analyze the internal representations of five open-source models on prompts covering 92 molecules and 20 functional groups. They find that the models group functional groups by chemical family and encode chemical differences as consistent vector directions; for example, the thioether-to-thiol shift added to ether lands nearest alcohol. This structure appears abruptly in the middle layers. **Even the base model that answered correctly only 58.5% of the time encodes this structure**, and its errors are mostly non-answers rather than wrong answers, which suggests output-only evaluation underestimates what chemical language models know.

papers.title: LOLPlay: Benchmarking Real-Time Visual Agents in League of Legends
papers.abstract: Visual agents need to coordinate reasoning and action while their environment evolves during inference. We introduce LOLPlay, a benchmark in native \emph{League of Legends} with 36 champion-specific tasks spanning resource management, combat, cooperation, and objectives. Agents interact through screenshots and mouse--keyboard actions; automated initialization and 82 executable subgoal checks distinguish partial progress from completion. Across 324 task evaluations of three models at three reasoning-effort settings, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest task success rate of 25.0\% at low and medium effort, and the highest subgoal success rate of 40.3\% at medium effort. However, high effort improves neither metric over low effort for any model. For Astra, longer requests leave fewer interaction rounds, suggesting a cost to additional reasoning in real-time control. Trajectories reveal incomplete subgoal composition and actions executing after the observed scene changes, motivating agents that combine visual reasoning with timely action.
papers.summary: `LOLPlay` is a benchmark for visual agents that have to reason and act while the environment keeps changing during inference. It runs inside the native game *League of Legends* and has 36 champion-specific tasks covering resource management, combat, cooperation and objectives. Agents see screenshots and act through mouse and keyboard, and 82 executable subgoal checks separate partial progress from full completion. Across 324 evaluations of three models at three reasoning-effort settings, `GPT-6 Astra` scored highest at **25.0% task success**, but **high reasoning effort never improved on low effort for any model**, because longer requests left fewer interaction rounds and actions often ran after the scene had already changed.
papers.highlight_summary:
Visual agents acting in real time have to reason about a scene that keeps changing while they think. `LOLPlay` tests this in unpaused, native League of Legends: agents see only screenshots and act through mouse and keyboard, and executable checks against live game state show how far each run gets, even when the full task fails.

- The suite has **36 champion-specific tasks** covering economy, development, sustain, combat, cooperation and map objectives, with **82 subgoal checks** and time budgets of 5–20 minutes; each task starts from a fresh match set up through the `LCU` API, and the `Live Client Data` API verifies state, kill attribution, event timing and objective order. Two experienced human players completed all 36 tasks.
- Across **324 runs** (three models at three reasoning-effort settings), `GPT-6 Astra` scores best, with **25.0% task success** at both low and medium effort and **40.3% subgoal success** at medium, while only **40 of 324 runs (12.3%)** pass overall.
- Nearly all passes come from economy and development tasks: sustain, cooperation and map-objective tasks have no successful runs at all, no run passes a single personal-kill (**0/45**) or allied-assist (**0/27**) check, and **108 failed runs** still meet some subgoals.
- Higher reasoning effort never beats low effort on either metric for any model: for `Astra`, high effort more than doubles request latency (**7.47s to 16.67s**), cuts the number of interaction rounds (**43.9 to 27.1**), and lowers task success to **16.7%**. Speed alone doesn't help either, since `DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash` responds in 2.81s but reaches only **5.6%** task success.
- The bots play at beginner difficulty, each champion has only one objective, some subgoals can be met just by staying passive (for example, not dying), and the latency-versus-success comparisons are descriptive rather than causal; the case studies show actions executing on stale observations, such as a click aimed at a fight that lands on an AFK warning dialog.

papers.title: From Forecasting to Feedback: Evaluating Learned Dynamics for Tokamak Control
papers.abstract: Learned temporal models are moving beyond offline forecasting toward interactive environments for decision making, yet logged-trajectory accuracy need not predict closed-loop behavior under policies optimized in the learned model. This forecasting-control gap matters in tokamak magnetic control, where coupled plasma-circuit dynamics and actuator constraints can amplify errors through feedback. Using a calibrated free-boundary Grad-Shafranov solver, we collect four datasets in a 2x2 design over physics-parameter and current-reference coverage. At matched budgets of 500, 1k, 3k, and 5k rollouts, we train 16 action-conditioned Transformers; PPO policies optimized in the 5k surrogates are then evaluated without adaptation on six reference-solver conditions. Only joint-coverage D4 shows monotonically decreasing cross-condition mean error, whereas D1 improves in distribution but degrades out of distribution. Binary completion masks substantial closed-loop differences: D2-D4 each complete 83.3% of conditions, but reach on average 99.0%, 94.7%, and 90.5% of the evaluation horizon, while their worst conditions reach 94.2%, 68.2%, and 43.2%. Policies trained with action noise complete 5/24 matched conditions, compared with 19/24 under nominal training, and have a lower mean horizon-capped episode length. Based on one trained policy per configuration and one evaluation realization per condition, the results support combining prediction error, episode completion, condition-level duration, and tracking quality.
papers.summary: The study asks whether a learned dynamics model that forecasts logged trajectories accurately also works well as a training environment for control policies, using tokamak magnetic control as the test case. The authors collected four datasets from a calibrated free-boundary `Grad-Shafranov` solver, varying coverage of physics parameters and current references, and trained 16 action-conditioned Transformers at different data budgets. They then trained `PPO` policies inside the surrogates and evaluated them on the real solver without adaptation. Only the dataset covering both factors improved consistently across conditions, and **datasets with identical 83.3% completion rates differed sharply in how long policies survived under their worst conditions (94.2% vs 43.2% of the horizon)**. The authors therefore recommend evaluating with prediction error, completion, per-condition duration and tracking quality together.

papers.title: Training LLM Agents to Automate LLM Post-Training with RSI-Dojo
papers.abstract: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) aims to enable AI systems to autonomously build and improve AI systems themselves, including models, harnesses, and underlying infrastructure. Within this broader agenda, a central capability is enabling agents to train and improve base models. However, existing studies on automated model training primarily focused on workflow- or harness-level optimizations, rather than internalizing the ability to conduct post-training into the model itself. Developing this capability requires executable model training environments that can produce high-quality trajectories demonstrating how to select data, train models, diagnose failures, and iteratively improve results. In this paper, we introduce RSI-Dojo, a collection of executable model training environments designed to teach LLM agents to conduct post-training. To construct RSI-Dojo, we develop RSI-Craft, an automatic pipeline that converts human research artifacts into executable model training environments. RSI-Craft automatically collects research papers from top venues, instantiates datasets and metrics into a unified interface, and reproduces evaluation dependencies. It then filters tasks by data size, execution reliability, and discriminability, yielding RSI-Dojo with 281 seed model training tasks. Building on RSI-Dojo, we employ a trajectory collection method with an improved harness to collect high-quality model-training trajectories from frontier models, then retain examples through rubric-based and outcome-based filtering. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories. The resulting RSI-Dojo-9B and RSI-Dojo-35B-A3B improve over their base models by 8.74 and 16.87 PostTrainBench points, respectively. RSI-Dojo-35B-A3B reaches 29.95 on PostTrainBench and 53.29 on PostTrainBench-Lite, matching the performance of frontier models such as GLM-5.2 and GPT 5.5.
papers.summary: As one step toward recursive self-improvement (RSI), the authors want to train LLM agents to carry out model post-training themselves, rather than only optimizing the workflow or harness around them. `RSI-Craft` automatically turns papers from top venues into executable training environments, producing `RSI-Dojo`, a set of 281 seed tasks filtered for reliability and for how well they separate stronger from weaker agents. Trajectories collected from frontier models were filtered by rubrics and by outcomes, then used to fine-tune `Qwen3.5-9B` and `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B`, which gained 8.74 and 16.87 points on `PostTrainBench`. **`RSI-Dojo-35B-A3B` reaches 29.95 on `PostTrainBench`, matching frontier models such as `GLM-5.2` and `GPT 5.5`.**
papers.highlight_summary:
Frontier post-training agents mostly improve through better harnesses and workflows, so the ability to train models never ends up inside the model's own weights. `RSI-Dojo` builds executable post-training environments at scale from research artifacts, collects filtered trajectories from frontier models in those environments, and distills them into open-weight `Qwen` agents.

- `RSI-Craft` crawls three years of papers from NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, ACL, EMNLP, NAACL and COLM, plus `InspectAI` tasks. From 547 candidate seeds it instantiates datasets and metrics behind a unified interface, and its filters for size, reliability and discriminability (a gap of at least 10 points between `Qwen3-4B-Base` and `GPT-5-mini`) leave **281 tasks across 10 domains**.
- Trajectories come from frontier models running an `AutoTrainess`-based harness, with added guidance aimed at recurring failures such as unchanged EOS settings, recipe thrashing without diagnosis, and missing submissions. A behavior filter combined with an outcome filter keeps **324 sessions (1,240 training trajectories)**, and in the ablation the combined filter scores **53.29 versus 30.66 and 26.13** for either filter alone.
