- `RSI-Dojo-35B-A3B` rises from 13.08 to **29.95 on `PostTrainBench`** (+16.87) and from 5.80 to **53.29 on `PostTrainBench-Lite`**, edging out `GLM-5.2` (29.52) and `GPT-5.5` (27.80) under the authors' own evaluation. `RSI-Dojo-9B` gains +8.74 to reach 16.46.
- Fine-tuning also makes runs more reliable: the 35B model completes a training run in **28/28 settings (up from 15)** and achieves 34.86% effective iterations, compared with about 20% for the GPT models. `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` still leads overall at 36.36 with a 48.51% iteration efficiency.
- The evaluation ran on a weaker GPU than the official benchmark requires, without `web_search`, and with pre-downloaded datasets. The model is weak on `AIME 2025` and `Arena-Hard`, because math rollouts rarely improved and teacher-distillation trajectories were absent, and the trained agent is never used to train its own successor.

papers.title: All Paths All at Once: A Quantum Monte Carlo and Neural Committor Approach to Reaction Pathway Search
papers.abstract: Locating competing reaction pathways is difficult when potential-energy gradients are unavailable. Here we present tReax\_expedition, an energy-only approach combining coupled Monte Carlo exploration, stochastic quench labelling and restrained continuation. Exploration identifies connected states, while continuation resolves candidate channels and records sampled chain maxima. Single-search benchmarks on three two-dimensional potentials recovered an intermediate and competing routes without transition-state guesses. For eight of nine gas-phase reactions on GFN2-xTB, sampled chain maxima differed from independently refined saddle energies by less than 0.76~kJ\,mol$^{-1}$. Alanine dipeptide instead revealed incomplete conformational relaxation, showing that route connectivity can persist despite structural and energetic errors. Neural committor learning and local straddling-pair sampling connect the resulting paths to transition-region sampling, although molecular shooting diagnostics indicate limited committor calibration. These results show how energy-only exploration and continuation recover candidate pathways, while distinguishing route connectivity from geometric localization, barrier resolution and finite-temperature transition statistics.
papers.summary: Finding competing chemical reaction pathways is hard when potential-energy gradients are unavailable. `tReax_expedition` uses energy evaluations only: it combines coupled Monte Carlo exploration, stochastic quench labelling to identify connected states, and restrained continuation to resolve candidate pathways. On GFN2-xTB gas-phase reactions, **the highest energies it sampled along each path were within 0.76 kJ/mol of independently refined saddle-point energies for eight of nine reactions**. Alanine dipeptide exposed incomplete conformational relaxation, and neural committor learning showed limited calibration, so the authors separate correctly finding a route from accurately locating its geometry and barrier.

papers.title: A Compact Formula-Aware Spreadsheet Abstraction for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to assist spreadsheet users with tasks such as spreadsheet model construction, formula generation, and data analysis, yet their interaction with real-world spreadsheets remains limited by the mismatch between the structure of spreadsheets and the sequential textual representations typically provided to LLMs. We propose a compact formula-aware spreadsheet abstraction that represents large homogeneous ranges through their positions, types, R1C1 formula patterns, and selected boundary values. An efficient algorithm detects and structures these ranges before a textual serialization is supplied to an LLM. The abstraction is provided to the LLM before detailed spreadsheet content is submitted, improving the accuracy and efficiency of spreadsheet processing while reducing token consumption. We evaluate the method on 50 spreadsheet-query cases. The evaluation shows that the abstraction alone was sufficient to answer some queries. When additional spreadsheet content is required, the abstraction reduces the amount of data that must be submitted to the LLM, thereby reducing token consumption. The abstraction layer also improves the reliability and accuracy of spreadsheet processing. We conclude by discussing further techniques for combining spreadsheet static analysis with artificial intelligence to improve the reliability, accuracy, and efficiency of AI assisted spreadsheet tasks.
papers.summary: LLMs handle real spreadsheets poorly because a spreadsheet's two-dimensional structure does not map well onto sequential text. The proposed abstraction summarizes large uniform ranges by their position, data type, `R1C1` formula pattern and selected boundary values, and an efficient algorithm detects these ranges before the summary is sent to the LLM ahead of any detailed cell content. On 50 spreadsheet-query cases, **the abstraction alone was enough to answer some queries**, and for the rest it reduced how much data had to be sent, cutting token use while improving reliability and accuracy.

papers.title: Unsatz: Evaluating Scientific Discovery Without a Given Ansatz
papers.abstract: Before a scientist fits any parameter, they must decide what the model contains: which quantities exist, which are hidden, how they interact, and how they are measured. Physicists call such a trial form an ansatz. Benchmarks for automated equation discovery mostly supply it, by fixing the variables, a library of candidate terms, or a law to be modified. We introduce Unsatz, a benchmark in which an LLM agent must construct the ansatz itself. Each task is a simulated system, generated from a private seed as a program in a small modeling language: ordinary, delay, or partial differential equations, discrete maps, static and causal models, or stochastic processes, possibly with hidden states, distorted sensors, and uninformative measurement channels. The agent buys experiments within a budget, writes candidate programs in the same language, obtains their coefficients from the benchmark's fitter, and is scored only on how its final program predicts experiments it never saw: conditions outside the range it could explore, interventions, and longer runs. Across 80 systems in 20 domains, nine language models solve between 21% and 60%. On 44 of these systems, classical equation-discovery methods almost never succeed, although the same data usually suffice once the true equations are given with unknown coefficients; the difficulty lies in finding the structure, not in estimating it. Because mechanisms recur across systems, we also give agents the program they discovered for a related system; it helped only when the new system shared the mechanism and the first investigation had succeeded. Stronger agents make fewer unscientific errors; beyond these, agents find which variables a system has but not how they act, and prefer revisions that lower the training error to revisions that predict better.
papers.summary: Most benchmarks for automated equation discovery give the solver a predefined model form (an ansatz), such as fixed variables or a library of candidate terms. `Unsatz` instead requires an LLM agent to build that structure itself. Each task is a simulated system generated as a program, which can involve differential equations, discrete maps, causal models or stochastic processes, sometimes with hidden states or distorted sensors. The agent buys experiments within a budget, writes candidate programs, and is scored on how well its final program predicts held-out extrapolations and interventions. Across 80 systems, **nine language models solve between 21% and 60%**, while classical equation-discovery methods almost never succeed on the 44 systems where they were tried, even though the data usually suffice once the true structure is given. The authors also observe that agents identify a system's variables but not how they interact, and prefer revisions that lower training error over revisions that predict better.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Functional Tucker Method with RKHS Factors for Sparse Spatiotemporal Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Reconstructing physical dynamics from fixed sparse sensors and missing frames is a fundamental challenge in scientific research. Sparsity leaves large regions of the field unconstrained, making the inverse problem ill-posed: a model may fit the observed sensors while producing inaccurate off-sensor structures or unreliable predictions between support frames. To this end, we propose PhysFTM---a physics-informed functional Tucker model that parameterizes the Tucker mode factors in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs) and incorporates PDE constraints through finite-difference residuals evaluated at off-sensor collocation points. These residuals provide additional physical information in regions without direct observational supervision. PhysFTM first reconstructs continuous spatial fields at support frames via an alternating minimization scheme, optimizing the Tucker core tensor and the RKHS-based factors separately. To enable missing-frame reconstruction, PhysFTM constructs a continuous trajectory in Tucker-core space, which is decoded by the learned spatial RKHS-FTM representation to recover the full spatiotemporal field. Experiments on Allen--Cahn, Navier--Stokes, three-dimensional Heat equations, and a three-dimensional gridded Copernicus ocean reanalysis demonstrate accurate 2D/3D reconstruction under two missing-frame protocols. Code is available at https://github.com/liusirzzz/PhysFTM.
papers.summary: Reconstructing physical fields from a few fixed sensors with missing time frames is ill-posed, because a model can fit the sensor readings while getting the unobserved regions wrong. `PhysFTM` is a functional Tucker tensor model whose factors live in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs), with PDE constraints enforced through finite-difference residuals at points that have no sensors. It reconstructs spatial fields at the observed frames by alternating minimization, then fills in missing frames by building a continuous trajectory in the Tucker core space. Experiments on `Allen–Cahn`, `Navier–Stokes`, 3D heat equations and `Copernicus` ocean reanalysis data show **accurate 2D and 3D reconstruction under two missing-frame protocols**.

papers.title: NepTTS-Bench: Native-Speaker Benchmarking and NepaliMOS for Nepali Text-to-Speech
papers.abstract: Nepali TTS has reached a point where multiple systems are available, but there is no shared evaluation to compare them. NepTTS-Bench was created to address what existing automated and manual evaluation systems lack for Nepali TTS. A controlled benchmark with phonological grounding which contains 205 sentences (77 minimal pairs targeting aspiration, retroflex/dental contrasts, nasalization, gemination, and schwa deletion) which is rated by 180 speakers. There are 6,962 ratings for 10 TTS configurations and two human references. Along with this 7 ASR systems were evaluated for round-trip CER. SCOREQ was also run as an automated baseline. The key finding is that automated evaluation like SCOREQ prefers proprietary systems like ElevenLabs but native listeners prefer Piper. This is contributed by the fact that most of the systems not properly tuned for Nepali tend to show Hindi phonological behaviour and our minimal pairs are designed to surface such contrasts. We also present NepaliMOS predictor which is fine tuned on collected ratings. NepaliMOS achieves system-level rho = 0.90 on the dense panel but drops to utterance-level rho = 0.43 under leave-one-system-out evaluation. This is statistically significant and confirms that NepaliMOS captures genuine signal but cross-provider transfer is limited. A human calibration is recommended for new systems for which we release a Python evaluation package for practitioners to run the benchmark against new systems.
papers.summary: Several Nepali text-to-speech (TTS) systems exist, but there has been no shared way to compare them. `NepTTS-Bench` provides 205 sentences, including 77 minimal pairs that target Nepali-specific sound contrasts such as aspiration, retroflex versus dental consonants, and schwa deletion, along with 6,962 ratings from 180 native speakers covering 10 TTS configurations. **The automated metric `SCOREQ` favors proprietary systems like `ElevenLabs`, while native listeners prefer `Piper`**, largely because systems not tuned for Nepali carry over Hindi pronunciation patterns. A fine-tuned `NepaliMOS` predictor reaches a system-level correlation of 0.90, but this drops to 0.43 at the utterance level on systems held out from training, so the authors recommend human calibration for new systems.

papers.title: Counterexample-driven autonomous research with application to excess radiated energy in a Z-pinch
papers.abstract: Recent breakthroughs in artificial-intelligence-assisted mathematics show that open-ended machine search can outperform human mathematicians, yet transferring this paradigm to physics requires refactoring the research workflow. We introduce Simjecture, an open-source framework in which language-model agents pursue human-defined physical conjectures. The framework tackles two central challenges in this transfer: first, because physics is empirical and no model is final, it structures inquiry around counterexample-driven falsification and prospective hypothesis repair; second, because physical theories must interact with the real world, it uses computational physics as an executable testbed while separating the qualification of numerical instruments from scientific claim review so solvers and diagnostics can be adapted within a recorded investigation. We apply the framework in an 82.6 h investigation to tackle the long-standing problem of radiated energy exceeding the imploding-shell kinetic energy in a Z-pinch. The investigation reveals competing effects of energy conversion, retention, and release timing. Stronger coherent helical deformation increases resistive conversion while reducing radiation and increasing retained energy. A broader trailing-plasma profile delays the later radiation maximum and recovers much of its early bolometric deficit, with a spectral response that changes during the pulse. These results provide new insight into energy conversion in high-energy-density plasma physics and demonstrate a new paradigm for physics research.
papers.summary: `Simjecture` is an open-source framework in which language-model agents investigate physical conjectures that humans define, adapting the open-ended search used in AI-assisted mathematics to physics. Inquiry is organized around finding counterexamples and then repairing the hypothesis. Computational physics simulations serve as the executable testbed, and checking that the numerical tools are trustworthy is kept separate from reviewing the scientific claims. In an **82.6-hour autonomous investigation** of why Z-pinch plasmas radiate more energy than the imploding shell's kinetic energy, the agents found competing effects: stronger helical deformation increases resistive conversion while reducing radiation, and a broader trailing-plasma profile delays the later radiation peak.

papers.title: EMBERS: Empirically Motivated Robustness Testing of Deep Research Systems via Defect-Guided Fuzzing
papers.abstract: Deep Research (DR) systems extend large language models into autonomous agents that decompose complex information needs, iteratively search the web, and synthesize evidence to answer challenging questions. However, their multi-stage execution may introduce robustness risks, as variations in user questions or intermediate search inputs may propagate across research stages and lead to incorrect answers. Existing evaluations focus on task-solving capabilities or robustness against external evidence disturbances, leaving intrinsic weaknesses in DR execution insufficiently explored. Thus, we conduct an empirical study of 1,932 execution trajectories from three representative DR systems and identify nine recurring defect categories across subquestion formulation, online search, and final reasoning. Guided by these findings, we propose EMBERS, an empirically motivated, defect-guided fuzzing framework for robustness testing of DR systems. Starting from correctly answered seed questions, EMBERS generates stage-targeted test inputs using defect-guided mutation, web-search-assisted fidelity assurance, and diversity-aware seed maintenance. Experiments across 16 framework--model--dataset settings show that EMBERS achieves 3.21 times the failure-discovery throughput of the strongest baseline under identical testing budgets. Human and LLM-assisted evaluations demonstrate that most generated inputs preserve the original information need and necessary contextual constraints. Moreover, model fine-tuning experiments show consistent-answer performance improvement, highlighting their value for robustness testing and model improvement.
papers.summary: Deep Research (DR) systems are LLM agents that break questions into subquestions, search the web, and combine the evidence into an answer, and small variations in inputs at any stage can push them to a wrong answer. An empirical study of 1,932 execution trajectories from three DR systems identifies nine recurring defect categories across subquestion formulation, search and final reasoning. Building on these defects, `EMBERS` fuzzes correctly answered seed questions with stage-targeted mutations, uses web search to check that mutated inputs keep their meaning, and maintains a diverse seed pool. Across 16 settings it achieves **3.21 times the failure-discovery throughput of the strongest baseline** at the same budget, and fine-tuning on the generated inputs makes model answers more consistent.

papers.title: Does the Trust Boundary Hold over Time? A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Receiver-Directed Federated Learning
papers.abstract: In receiver-directed federated learning, each site draws a trust boundary. For every source and model component it judges, on its own data, whether the transfer helps (admit), harms (reject) or cannot yet be told (abstain). We ask whether this boundary holds over hundreds of rounds. Our benchmark has a federation of thirteen semi-synthetic sites, an exact oracle for every evaluated transfer, paired seeds, an attack protocol, fourteen methods over 600 rounds and Qwen3-1.7B LoRA sites over 500. The answer depends on which boundary is measured. Across 20 paired CPU seeds, a gate judging against a fixed reference better identified transfers useful relative to the site's starting model. Yet it admitted 29% of transfers harmful to the model the site now has. A gate judging against the current model admitted 2% of harmful transfers on that target in the CPU tier, but missed many transfers useful to the starting model. Two short propositions explain these distinct failures. We also evaluate a held out audit that leaves gate verdicts intact. After training, it decides whether each final model is deployed or the site falls back to local training, and reports admissions that have gone stale. With independent audit data its guarantees hold after any training history. At 600 rounds the audit deployed 65 to 72% of models, none with negative benefit on its target, and kept 98% of the gain. No stale report had the wrong sign in our runs. With 20,000 audit observations, a variance-adaptive bound found 99% of stale transfers that cost at least 0.01 in log loss. A common-target Qwen3 comparison on 60 selected transfers shows the same tension over 100 rounds. With 38% adversarial sites, FedFomo and CS-Gate were the only evaluated methods with positive mean gain in every honest group.
papers.summary: In receiver-directed federated learning, each site decides for every incoming transfer whether to admit it, reject it, or abstain. The benchmark tests whether those decisions stay correct over hundreds of rounds, using 13 semi-synthetic sites with an exact oracle, 14 methods run for 600 rounds, and `Qwen3-1.7B` `LoRA` sites. A gate that judges transfers against a fixed reference admitted 29% of transfers that harmed the site's current model, while a gate that judges against the current model admitted only 2% but missed many useful ones. A held-out audit applied after training **deployed 65–72% of models with none harming their target while keeping 98% of the gain**. With 38% adversarial sites, only `FedFomo` and `CS-Gate` had positive mean gain in every honest group.

papers.title: From Logs to Faults: Reference-Free Fault Localization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Pipelines
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines are widely used for domain-specific question answering, yet locating faults remains manual and time-consuming. Fault localization is challenging because RAG pipelines consist of interdependent stages, where faults can propagate downstream, masking their origin, or remain undetected even when the final answer is correct. Existing evaluation approaches often focus on individual stages and rely on reference answers or code instrumentation. We present RAGLog, which detects and localizes faults across RAG stages using execution logs, without requiring reference answers or code instrumentation. RAGLog transforms heterogeneous API logs into a common RAG schema and combines rule-based, embedding-based, and LLM-based checks to identify faulty stages. We introduce a live fault injector and RAGLog Faults, a dataset of 3,134 runs from five RAG pipelines with stage-level fault labels. With Claude Haiku 5.5, RAGLog achieves a pooled F1 score of 0.73 on runs with naturally occurring faults, outperforming Claude Code (0.58) and Codex (0.52), and comparable effectiveness on runs with injected faults (0.84 versus 0.80 and 0.82, respectively). It analyzes runs in approximately five seconds at US\$0.005 each, with overall lower cost and latency than agent baselines. RAGLog is available as an open-source tool for debugging, evaluating, and monitoring RAG pipelines.
papers.summary: Finding where a fault starts in a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline is hard: errors can spread to later stages and hide their origin, or stay invisible even when the final answer is correct. `RAGLog` locates faulty stages from execution logs alone, with no reference answers or code instrumentation. It converts different API logs into a shared RAG schema and then applies rule-based, embedding-based and LLM-based checks. The authors also release a live fault injector and the `RAGLog Faults` dataset of 3,134 labeled runs from five pipelines. Using `Claude Haiku 5.5`, `RAGLog` reaches **a pooled F1 of 0.73 on naturally occurring faults, compared with 0.58 for `Claude Code` and 0.52 for `Codex`**, at about five seconds and US$0.005 per run.

papers.title: DualClusterNet: Personalized Pattern-Space Composition for Next-POI Recommendation
papers.abstract: Next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation supports personalized place discovery on location-based Web platforms. Mobility routines can recur across users while being realized at different places and adapted to individual preferences. We present DualClusterNet, a causal sequential recommender that composes two population-shared prototype dictionaries. At each observed prefix, soft routers retrieve pattern and spatial mixtures; a factorized multiplicative interaction couples them, feature-wise affine modulation adapts the shared representation, and a separate user-conditioned branch with an additive--projective gate retains individual variation. The prediction head combines this representation with a learned first-order transition term and ranks the complete training POI vocabulary. We evaluate on NYC and TKY using a training-only vocabulary and an original-final-target protocol that neither bridges unknown POIs nor substitutes earlier targets. The available single-seed results show competitive full-candidate ranking, while controlled analyses support the contribution of the compositional and personalized branches. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DualClusterNet-F4EE/.
papers.summary: Next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation has to capture mobility routines that many users share but carry out at different places and with personal preferences. `DualClusterNet` is a causal sequential recommender that combines two population-shared prototype dictionaries, one for behavior patterns and one for spatial patterns, using soft routers and a factorized multiplicative interaction. A separate user-conditioned branch with a gate keeps individual variation, and a learned first-order transition term feeds the ranking over the full POI vocabulary. On the `NYC` and `TKY` datasets, under a strict training-only vocabulary protocol, **single-seed results show competitive full-candidate ranking**, and ablations support the value of the compositional and personalized branches.

papers.title: Auditing a Model-Hub Benchmark: Data Quality, Training Budgets, and Side Information in HuggingBench
papers.abstract: Benchmarks built from model hubs combine interaction data, knowledge graphs (KGs) and resource documentation, but valid files do not ensure that these artifacts describe the same objects. Treating the release as a data product, we audit HuggingBench (SIGIR 2025), a benchmark for recommending Hugging Face resources, through data validation, a replication of its eleven recommendation methods and controlled experiments with three training seeds. In three of its four external KGs, the files pass key and range checks but violate the item-entity identity constraint on which KG recommenders rely. Correcting this join improves every KG-based method in every seed, by up to 73% in mean Recall@10, and consistently reverses ten of 27 comparisons between KG configurations. The protocol matters as well: the 100-epoch budget ends before early stopping in seven to eight of 29 validation-selected settings, and 21 of 23 such setting-seed pairs improve with a longer budget. The released item text, which no reported method uses, is the strongest signal: closed-form linear models with text and the item graph exceed the best reported Recall@10 by 18% while fitting in minutes on a CPU. Checks of other recommendation releases show that individually valid releases of one dataset can use incompatible identifiers. We release corrected files, mappings, validators and logs, and derive practices for preserving identity and provenance across the artifacts of benchmarks and model lakes.
papers.summary: The authors audit `HuggingBench`, a SIGIR 2025 benchmark for recommending Hugging Face resources, by validating its data, replicating its eleven methods and running controlled experiments over three seeds. In three of its four external knowledge graphs (KGs), the files pass basic checks but map items to the wrong entities. Fixing this join improves every KG-based method by up to 73% in mean Recall@10 and reverses ten of 27 configuration comparisons. The 100-epoch training budget also cuts off several settings before early stopping. The item text, which no reported method uses, turns out to be the strongest signal: **closed-form linear models using text and the item graph beat the best reported Recall@10 by 18% while training in minutes on a CPU**.

papers.title: Learning to read residual images for single-pixel photography
papers.abstract: Continuous video scales in cost with camera count, resolution and recording duration, yet many monitoring tasks seek events rather than complete images and can operate on a compact single-pixel measurement stream. Recovering a chosen interval as video is then desirable, but at 0.24\% of the pixel count the scene correlation image looks like noise and per-clip optimization takes minutes. Correlating the residual of an estimate with the coding patterns nevertheless gives a residual image, the gradient of a centered measurement loss. Lifted through a pretrained video decoder, its agreement with the true error exceeds that of control decoders. Video-latent inversion (VLI) then outperforms frame-wise image-latent reconstruction at 1{,}000 bucket values. Measurement-Gradient-Conditioned Video Flow (MGV-Flow), trained once to read the lifted residual image with preceding frames, reconstructs five frames in 1.55\,s at 22.9\,dB median PSNR, against 398\,s and 18.1\,dB for VLI, with the largest gains in high-motion scenes. Directional fidelity ranks 30 coding configurations and selects one needing a third fewer bucket values. On a physical system, MGV-Flow outperforms per-frame reconstruction without retraining. A sliding window over the bucket-value stream yields 3.2 frames per second on one RTX~4090 and, in theory, 20 frames per second on a data-centre accelerator. Demonstrations are available at https://cavedweller509.github.io/MGV-Flow.
papers.summary: Single-pixel cameras record a compact measurement stream that is cheap to store, but turning a chosen interval back into video is slow, and at 0.24% of the pixel count the raw correlation image looks like noise. The authors correlate the residual of a current estimate with the coding patterns to get a residual image, which is the gradient of the measurement loss. They show that a pretrained video decoder lifts this image into a useful error signal. `MGV-Flow` is trained once to read this lifted residual together with the preceding frames, and **reconstructs five frames in 1.55 s at 22.9 dB median PSNR, versus 398 s and 18.1 dB for per-clip video-latent inversion**. It also works on a physical system without retraining and runs at 3.2 frames per second on one `RTX 4090`.

papers.title: Complete Donor-Set Guidance for Frozen Diffusion Docking Models
papers.abstract: Metalloprotein docking requires a ligand pose to satisfy both global pocket fit and the identity and geometry of metal-coordinating atoms. General-purpose diffusion docking models do not explicitly condition generation on externally specified complete ligand donor sets, and their predicted poses can exhibit incorrect metal-donor relationships. Metal-aware models address coordination during training and generation; here we ask whether external donor information can correct already-trained general-purpose models without retraining. We propose Complete-Identity Contract Guidance (CICG), which applies a supplied complete donor set through translation, rotation, and torsion updates, and Historical Contract Transfer (HCT), which supplies donor identities from earlier complexes at compatible receptor sites. We compare HCT with trajectory-local controls retaining the historical donor count with or without elemental composition. On 86 assessable HCT-covered queries, HCT-guided CICG increases frozen-confidence-selected joint success from 21.5% to 36.6% on SurfDock and from 25.0% to 34.9% on DiffDock-L. The joint criterion requires correct global ligand placement, complete native donor recovery, coordination geometry, preserved stereochemistry, and absence of fatal receptor clashes. Composition-matched guidance reaches 33.14% and 34.30%, leaving the additional benefit of fixed historical membership unresolved. Our results therefore support donor-set guidance as a conditional correction for frozen docking models, while identifying donor-source reliability and physical-quality preservation as the main barriers to broader use.
papers.summary: General-purpose diffusion docking models often get metal–donor relationships wrong when they dock ligands into metalloproteins. `Complete-Identity Contract Guidance` (`CICG`) steers frozen, already-trained docking models toward a supplied complete donor set through translation, rotation and torsion updates, with no retraining. `Historical Contract Transfer` (`HCT`) supplies those donor identities from earlier complexes at compatible receptor sites. On 86 covered queries, **HCT-guided CICG raises joint success from 21.5% to 36.6% on `SurfDock` and from 25.0% to 34.9% on `DiffDock-L`**. However, guidance that only matches the donors' elemental composition does almost as well, so the extra benefit of using the exact historical donor set remains unresolved.

papers.title: Minimal Superior Penalties: Characterising and Calibrating Decision-Aware Proper Scoring Rules
papers.abstract: Training a classifier means letting a validation metric decide which model is kept and when training stops. A natural requirement on that metric is superiority: every correctly classified forecast should score better than every incorrectly classified one, however close the underlying probabilities are. Neither the Brier score nor the logarithmic score satisfies this on its own. We show that superiority is governed by the separation between two endpoints -- the supremum of the score on correct predictions and the infimum on incorrect predictions -- and derive both in closed form for each score. Their difference is the infimal penalty, the greatest lower bound on the penalty needed to restore superiority. Prior work restores superiority with a penalty calibrated from the first endpoint alone; for the Brier base, our infimal penalty is smaller than that published penalty by a factor ranging from 4.00 at three classes to 2.11 at twenty. We further embed the published and infimal penalties in a one-parameter family and show that, under a single-valued tie convention, every member of the family is strictly proper. In a pre-specified two-dataset case study, mean selected-model macro-F1 rises with the penalty in the reported ten-class regimes, though not distinguishably from noise once seed/selection-mode nesting is accounted for; a fifth regime at forty-seven classes does not reproduce even this descriptive pattern. The intended no-superiority baseline is algebraically a rescaling of the family under test, so the experiment cannot attribute the observed pattern specifically to superiority. When superiority itself is the objective, any penalty strictly above the infimal value suffices; choosing a larger penalty is a separate calibration trade-off rather than a requirement for the guarantee.
papers.summary: When a validation metric is used to pick models, one natural requirement is superiority: every correctly classified forecast should score better than every incorrect one. Neither the Brier score nor the logarithmic score guarantees this on its own. The authors derive closed-form endpoints that govern superiority and the smallest penalty, called the infimal penalty, that restores it. For the Brier score, **this penalty is 2.11 to 4.00 times smaller than the previously published one**, and every member of a one-parameter family spanning the two remains strictly proper. In a case study, model selection improvements could not be distinguished from noise, and the authors note that the experimental design cannot attribute any effect specifically to superiority.

papers.title: HyVox: Rethinking Low-Power Voice Intelligence towards Neuromorphic-von Neumann Edge Computing
papers.abstract: We present HyVox, a hybrid neuromorphic--von Neumann system for low-energy open-set speaker identification under tight energy budgets. HyVox splits the workload at the speaker embedding. A neuromorphic processor embeds the speech with sparse, event-driven computation, and a von Neumann microcontroller holds the speaker gallery and makes every decision: it scores queries by cosine similarity, rejects unknown speakers, and enrolls new users by writing a prototype, with no weight update. On the neuromorphic processor, a hierarchical temporal abstraction (HTA) SNN backbone learns a synaptic time constant per leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron, allocating 832 neurons across fast, medium, and slow timescales. A 32-neuron spiking embedding extractor (SEE), pretrained on episodes that each enroll new speakers and reject outsiders, turns the backbone output into an embedding for speakers unseen in training; its 32 spike counts are the only interface between the two processors. To fit the chip's synapse and integer budgets, we compress the backbone 6.5x to 29.0k synapses, train it for integer bit-shift dynamics, and fine-tune it with chip-accurate spiking training (CAST). CAST trains through a differentiable replica of the chip's integer neuron update, derived from its cycle-accurate simulator, so that gradient descent optimizes the exact weights and thresholds the chip runs; it doubles the top-1 accuracy of the mapped backbone on unseen speakers. On 20 Common Voice households of unseen speakers, HyVox reaches 99.6\% top-1 and 5.5\% rejection EER with 2 members and 94.9\% and 13.2\% with 20, and the network deployed on the neuromorphic chip matches its trained model. Each inference on a 3-s window takes 0.96 s and 1.63 mJ of dynamic energy, 42\% lower latency than the fastest embedded ANN baseline and 13.5x less dynamic and 5.8x less total energy than the most energy-efficient one.
papers.summary: `HyVox` performs low-energy open-set speaker identification by splitting work between a neuromorphic chip and a conventional (von Neumann) microcontroller. A spiking neural network (SNN) backbone on the chip turns speech into a 32-spike-count embedding, and the microcontroller scores speakers by cosine similarity, rejects unknown voices and enrolls new users without any weight update. To fit the chip's limits, the backbone is compressed 6.5x and fine-tuned with chip-accurate spiking training (`CAST`), which trains through a differentiable replica of the chip's integer neuron update and doubles accuracy on unseen speakers. On `Common Voice` households, the system reaches 99.6% top-1 accuracy with 2 members and 94.9% with 20, using **1.63 mJ of dynamic energy per 3-second window, 13.5x less than the most efficient embedded neural-network baseline**.

papers.title: SSPE: Robust Sequential Staypoint Extraction in Degraded Trajectory Data
papers.abstract: Extracting semantically meaningful staypoints from raw trajectory streams is a foundational prerequisite for mobility analytics. However, real-world trajectory data is frequently degraded by severe spatial noise and protracted temporal dropouts. Classic threshold-based extraction methods, such as the widely adopted sliding-window algorithm, are highly sensitive to these anomalies, routinely fracturing continuous stationary episodes into disjointed fragments. To overcome this limitation, we propose the Sequential Staypoint Extraction (SSPE) algorithm. SSPE employs a resilient, state-driven architecture that replaces static spatial anchors with a dynamic centroid and introduces an $n$-step lookahead heuristic to structurally tolerate transient coordinate drift. Concurrently, it utilizes temporal bridging mechanisms to prevent artificial fragmentation during prolonged signal loss. Since optimal extraction parameters vary significantly across datasets, we further introduce a fully unsupervised, consensus-based parameter estimation framework. This framework derives baseline statistical scales directly from the raw trajectory data and identifies the optimal parameter configuration by maximizing structural agreement, thereby eliminating the reliance on annotated ground truth. We evaluate SSPE on the ExtraSensory dataset, a real-world mobility corpus with manually verified ground-truth staypoints, against the sliding-window implementation of Trackintel, one of the most widely adopted extraction baselines in the field. Empirical results demonstrate that SSPE achieves superior accuracy, yielding higher F1-scores while simultaneously improving computational efficiency over this standard.
papers.summary: Real-world GPS trajectories are noisy and full of signal gaps, which cause standard threshold-based methods to split one continuous stay into several fragments. `SSPE` is a state-driven staypoint extraction algorithm that tracks a moving centroid, looks a few steps ahead to tolerate brief coordinate drift, and bridges long signal losses. It also includes an unsupervised method for choosing parameters, which picks the configuration that maximizes structural agreement without needing labeled data. On the `ExtraSensory` dataset, **`SSPE` achieves higher F1 scores and faster runtime than the sliding-window method in `Trackintel`**.

papers.title: RATSIFT: Resolution-Adaptive Transformer for Solar Irradiance Forecasting and Temporal Downscaling
papers.abstract: Accurate forecasting and temporal downscaling of solar irradiance is critical for reliable renewable energy integration and grid management. Traditional methods often struggle to capture rapid irradiance variability. In this work, we develop a Transformer-based architecture for simultaneous forecasting and temporal downscaling. The model takes input data at arbitrary resolutions and generates outputs at any resolutions represented within the training data, leveraging both global and local contextual information. To improve training efficiency, a genetic algorithm-based optimization framework is implemented to identify suitable model hyperparameters, while reducing the computational cost of exhaustive grid search. The effectiveness of the proposed model is shown by analyzing real data in Dallas, Texas. The proposed model achieved root mean square error (RMSE) values of 28.785, 29.544, 30.157, 32.132~W/m\(^2\) for 15-, 30-, 60-minute, and irregularly spaced global input and producing forecast at 5-minutes resolution, respectively. Furthermore, this model produced reliable uncertainty estimates, exhibiting wider prediction intervals for high-resolution inputs during volatile solar conditions, whereas coarser-resolution inputs result in narrower intervals and significantly lower training time and computational cost. Our approach provides a scalable and efficient framework for multi-resolution solar irradiance forecasting and temporal downscaling, suitable for practical energy forecasting and grid management applications.
papers.summary: `RATSIFT` is a Transformer that forecasts solar irradiance and downscales it in time at the same step. It accepts input at any resolution, including irregular spacing, and produces output at any resolution seen in training. Hyperparameters are chosen with a genetic algorithm instead of an exhaustive grid search. On data from Dallas, Texas, **5-minute forecasts reach RMSE between 28.8 and 32.1 W/m² for 15-, 30-, 60-minute and irregular inputs**. Prediction intervals widen during volatile conditions when the inputs are high-resolution.

papers.title: Reasoning is topologically simple
papers.abstract: We formulate and investigate the hypothesis that reasoning text has simpler co-occurrence topology than non-reasoning text, and that higher-quality reasoning has simpler co-occurrence topology than lower-quality reasoning. We discuss and test applications to AI safety and AI evaluation.
papers.summary: The authors propose that reasoning text has **simpler word co-occurrence topology than non-reasoning text, and that better reasoning is simpler still**, and they test this hypothesis. They also discuss and evaluate possible uses of the measure for AI safety and for evaluating AI systems.

papers.title: EvoMemState: Evolving Memory State for Personal Agents
papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to provide continuous personalized assistance by retaining user information across interactions. Existing systems support this process through fact extraction, organization, updating, and retrieval, but largely maintain memories as independent facts. This fact-centric paradigm may overlook how new facts update, constrain, or conflict with earlier ones, while leaving their applicability, role, and priority for the current request implicit. In this paper, we introduce EvoMemState, a state-centric framework that augments persistent facts with two complementary states: Relational States that capture how facts remain valid and relate to one another as memory evolves, and a Reasoning State that determines how these facts should be applied to the current request. Specifically, EvoMemState consists of three key components: (i) Ontology-Guided Memory State Induction extracts Persistent Facts and constructs Relational States that maintain their validity, scope, and evolving relations. (ii) RL-Based State Evolution internalizes memory-use experience into a policy through reinforcement learning to generate a request-specific Reasoning State. (iii) State-Aware Reasoning then combines the relevant facts with their Relational States and the generated Reasoning State to guide the personal agent. Extensive experiments on long-term dialogue and memory-use benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing memory systems in retrieval completeness and memory-grounded response accuracy. Our code and implementation details are available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/EvoMemState.git.
papers.summary: Long-term memory systems for LLM agents usually store user facts as independent items, without tracking how new facts update or conflict with old ones or how they apply to the current request. `EvoMemState` adds two kinds of state to stored facts. Relational States, built by ontology-guided extraction, track each fact's validity, scope and changing relations. A Reasoning State, generated per request by a policy trained with reinforcement learning, decides how the facts should be applied. On long-term dialogue and memory-use benchmarks, the framework **consistently improves retrieval completeness and the accuracy of memory-grounded responses over existing memory systems**.

papers.title: CaRe-KT: Continuity-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning for Knowledge Tracing
papers.abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) estimates learners' evolving knowledge states from interaction histories to support adaptive learning. Retrieval-augmented KT improves these estimates using cross-learner behavioral evidence, but existing approaches typically separate evidence retrieval from downstream prediction. This creates a retrieval-inference alignment gap because evidence relevance varies with the learner's evolving state and prediction context. We propose CaRe-KT, a query-adaptive framework that maintains relevance continuity between evidence acquisition and inference without equating retrieval relevance with predictive utility. CaRe-KT introduces an Evidence-Graph Cache (EGC) that combines persistent question-level relational compatibility with interaction-level temporal validity to construct query-specific evidence subgraphs. Historical learning trajectories retrieved through these subgraphs are encoded alongside the target learner's history in a shared representation space using outcome-supervised contrastive learning. An attention mechanism combines acquisition relevance with learned query-evidence compatibility, allowing relevance to inform, rather than determine, each trajectory's predictive influence. Experiments across five benchmarks show that CaRe-KT outperforms strong KT baselines and remains robust under sparse-history and cold-start conditions. These findings support relevance continuity as a design principle for retrieval-augmented knowledge tracing.
papers.summary: Knowledge tracing (KT) estimates what a learner knows from their interaction history. Retrieval-augmented KT methods usually retrieve evidence from other learners separately from the prediction step, so relevance at retrieval time can drift from what actually matters for the prediction. `CaRe-KT` builds query-specific evidence subgraphs with an `Evidence-Graph Cache` that combines question-level relationships with how recent each interaction is. It encodes the retrieved trajectories with outcome-supervised contrastive learning and uses attention so that retrieval relevance informs, but does not fix, each trajectory's influence. On five benchmarks, **`CaRe-KT` beats strong KT baselines and stays robust when histories are sparse or learners are new**.

papers.title: Enhancing Stock Market Information Retrieval with Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has been widely applied in financial domains, enabling automated analysis and retrieval of stock market information. However, traditional NLP-based systems often struggle with maintaining contextual accuracy and generating relevant responses in dynamic financial environments. To address these challenges, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models have emerged as a powerful solution, combining retrieval-based methods with generative capabilities to enhance response quality. In this study, we present a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system designed to generate responses related to stock market information. The system integrates retrieval-based and generative approaches to enhance the accuracy and relevance of financial text generation. To evaluate its effectiveness, we employ the ROUGE metric, specifically ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L, to measure lexical and structural similarity between generated and reference texts. Experimental results on a dataset of 100 stock market-related queries demonstrate high ROUGE scores, indicating strong alignment with reference documents. Additionally, we assess latency to evaluate the system responsiveness, achieving an average response time of 1.16 seconds. These findings confirm that our RAG model is capable of providing accurate and timely stock market insights, making it a promising approach for financial information retrieval.
papers.summary: The authors build a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system that answers questions about stock market information by combining document retrieval with text generation. They measure answer quality with `ROUGE-1`, `ROUGE-2` and `ROUGE-L` against reference texts on 100 stock-market queries. They report **high ROUGE scores and an average response time of 1.16 seconds**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Large language models (LLMs) hallucinate and go stale in fast-moving financial settings, so the authors build a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) question-answering system over Vietnamese stock-market news from `VnExpress`. It grounds `Gemini-1.5-Flash` answers in documents fetched by a hybrid dense-plus-keyword retriever.

- The pipeline segments Vietnamese text and removes stop words, embeds each document with multilingual `LaBSE`, and stores the vectors in a `FAISS` index; a query first pulls nearest neighbours by L2 distance, then `BM25` re-ranks them before the top results go into a structured prompt.
- On **100 queries**, the generated answers score very close to the reference texts on ROUGE F-measure: **ROUGE-1 0.9555**, **ROUGE-2 0.9314**, and **ROUGE-L 0.9436**.
- Average latency is **1.16 s** per query, ranging from 0.92 s to 2.46 s.
- The knowledge base is only **30 news articles** across four topic categories, and the paper never says how the queries or reference answers were made, so the near-ceiling ROUGE scores may mostly show the model copying retrieved text.
- There are no baselines (for example, no-RAG, dense-only, or BM25-only), no ablations, and no measures of factuality or retrieval quality, and the method description has inconsistencies, such as naming both `Underthesea` and `Jieba` as the tokenizer.

papers.title: LoRA-Patch: Defending Against Backdoored LoRA Adapters via Directional Steering
papers.abstract: Third-party LoRA adapters introduce serious backdoor risks: malicious adapters can maintain normal task performance while embedding hidden, trigger-activated behaviors, making them difficult to detect through standard utility evaluations. Existing removal-based defenses typically sanitize backdoored models by updating, pruning, distilling, or mixing model parameters. However, these approaches are misaligned with adapter-based deployment, where the trusted base model is expected to remain frozen. In this work, we propose LoRA-Patch, a lightweight backdoor defense tailored to LoRA adapters. Our key insight is that backdoor injection distorts the directional geometry of a poisoned adapter relative to its trusted base model. Building on this insight, LoRA-Patch suppresses trigger-activated behaviors by realigning adapter directions through layer-wise steering, without modifying the base model weights. Extensive experiments across five backdoor attacks and three models show that LoRA-Patch effectively mitigates trigger-activated backdoors, outperforming existing baselines while preserving benign task performance. Moreover, LoRA-Patch is computationally efficient, constructing patches within 20 seconds across all evaluated models and adapters. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/FOXVEDA/LoRA-Patch.
papers.summary: Third-party LoRA adapters can carry hidden backdoors that activate on a trigger while normal task performance stays intact. Existing defenses edit, prune or distill model parameters, which does not fit deployments where the trusted base model must stay frozen. `LoRA-Patch` builds on the observation that backdoor injection distorts the directional geometry of an adapter relative to its base model, and suppresses triggered behavior by realigning adapter directions with layer-wise steering. Across five backdoor attacks and three models, it **outperforms existing defenses while preserving benign task performance, and builds each patch in under 20 seconds**.

papers.title: The Web Doesn't Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise for empowering search agents to tackle complex information-seeking tasks. However, since acquiring external information necessitates web search, these agents are highly susceptible to various adversarial attacks (e.g., malicious information injection or stealthy context manipulation). Existing attack strategies inevitably rely on static and human-crafted templates, failing to emulate the dynamic and complex nature of real-world threats. In this paper, we propose an adversarial self-evolution framework that integrates bi-level optimization between the attacker's strategy evolution and the defender's adaptive mitigation, to expose the vulnerabilities of search agents. Specifically, we introduce the Contrastive Rollout Evolutionary Optimization (CREO) method to drive the directional evolution of the attack strategy population via contrastive evolutionary signals. To provide a stable environment for this continuous evolution, we further construct a controlled sandbox and design fine-grained metrics to quantify internal vulnerabilities. Extensive experiments across various multi-hop QA benchmarks and frontier LLMs demonstrate that the proposed framework yields attack efficacy superior to static baselines, underscoring the urgent need to develop more robust defense frameworks.
papers.summary: LLM-based search agents depend on web content, which makes them vulnerable to injected or manipulated information. Existing attacks mostly rely on static, hand-written templates. The authors propose an adversarial self-evolution framework that uses bi-level optimization: attack strategies evolve while a defender adapts its mitigations. The attack side is driven by `Contrastive Rollout Evolutionary Optimization` (`CREO`), and experiments run in a controlled sandbox with fine-grained vulnerability metrics. Across multi-hop QA benchmarks and frontier LLMs, **the evolved attacks are more effective than static baselines**.

papers.title: Honest Small Decision Models for Finance: Scale, Specialization Collapse, and Mixed-Corpus Remediation
papers.abstract: Financial workflows need fast, calibrated, auditable decisions, not just generated text. We train System-1 decision models, small language models fine-tuned to answer typed questions (choice/score/noul) with a probability in a single forward pass, across two model families (K2-Horizon and Qwen3.5/3.8) and nine rungs from 0.8B to 32B parameters, using one frozen LoRA recipe on a public decision benchmark and two new finance corpora: a programmatic-gold policy corpus (rule-reading with exact labels) and a reality-labeled outcome corpus (19,640 realized forward-return questions in walk-forward splits, plus a sealed 2026 test of 1,360 questions). Narrow fine-tuning costs general decision competence 9-45 percentage points, a data-mixture effect that shrinks with model scale and is associated with narrow-gradient volume. On reality-labeled questions, every trained rung from 0.8B to 32B lands at the horizon-conditioned prior baseline (accuracy 0.37-0.38, no detectable conditional edge under our controls); the models respond with flat, well-calibrated probabilities that track per-horizon base rates: naturally honest uncertainty, with a mid-scale calibration sweet spot (ECE 0.026 at 2B, degrading to 0.043-0.044 at 9-32B under prior drift). A mixed-corpus remediation carries all competencies in one adapter at modest cost: it matches or slightly exceeds the generalist specialist on the public benchmark while holding the policy ceiling and near-specialist outcome calibration, yielding a deployable artifact with per-domain temperature regimes and a band-dispatch escalation analysis: sharp, dispatchable bands where rules determine answers; flat, review-routing bands where reality does not.
papers.summary: The authors fine-tune small language models from 0.8B to 32B parameters, from the `K2-Horizon` and `Qwen` families, to answer typed financial decision questions with a probability in a single forward pass, using one fixed LoRA recipe. Narrow fine-tuning costs 9 to 45 percentage points of general decision ability, a loss that shrinks as models get larger. On questions labeled by real forward stock returns, **every model from 0.8B to 32B lands at the prior baseline (accuracy 0.37–0.38) with no detectable predictive edge**, but its probabilities stay well calibrated to base rates. Training on a mixed corpus keeps all the competencies in one adapter at modest cost and produces a deployable model that separates rule-determined questions from ones that should be sent to human review.

papers.title: Language Models Can Benefit from Domain-Specific Inductive Biases
papers.abstract: Language models are typically trained with a single choice of architecture on diverse domains and data sources. Modern transformers have been extensively refined for such general-purpose learning, but are they equally effective across different subsets of the pretraining data? We investigate this question by training small language models from scratch on representative subsets of pretraining data such as web text, code, and mathematics. We introduce variants of transformers in which standard activation functions are replaced with learned splines tuned on specific datasets, providing a simple way to modify their inductive biases. Using a mix-and-match of architectures and datasets, we evaluate cross-domain transfer, i.e. how well does an architecture tuned for one domain perform on data from another? We find that the tuned transformer variants improve training efficiency or generalization on all seven of our tested datasets, but the gains are often domain-specific. For example, architectures tuned on a natural language dataset such as FineWeb perform well on TinyStories, whereas those tuned on mathematics perform poorly on natural language. We identify several mechanisms underlying these improvements, including wider loss basins and more abundant "lottery tickets". Our results show that different subsets of pretraining data can benefit from different learning mechanisms, highlighting a limitation of the prevailing trend towards a small set of general-purpose architectures and optimizers. This points to an opportunity to improve data efficiency by developing domain-specific learning strategies that retain the ability to train general-purpose models.
papers.summary: The authors ask whether standard transformer architectures work equally well on every part of the pretraining data. They train small language models from scratch on web text, code and math, replacing standard activation functions with learned splines tuned to each dataset. **The tuned variants improve training efficiency or generalization on all seven datasets**, but the gains are often domain-specific: variants tuned on `FineWeb` transfer well to `TinyStories`, while math-tuned variants do poorly on natural language. The authors trace the gains to mechanisms such as wider loss basins and more abundant "lottery tickets", and argue that domain-specific learning strategies could improve data efficiency.

papers.title: JevBreak: Your Model, Their Decision
papers.abstract: Restricting what a model can say is often mistaken for restricting an attacker's influence over its decision. An attacker can add text to the evidence and steer the model toward a wrong answer that still belongs to the allowed set. We evaluate seven decision models spanning hosted APIs, open-weight models and an encoder on 16 tasks in seven domains from Decision Bench, targeting every wrong option across 240 text examples (990 targets per model). We present Slot Attack, a black-box attack designed for decision models that appends text assembled from named components to steer predictions toward an attacker-selected incorrect option. The method relies solely on returned label probabilities, achieves success rates of 32--99\% on initially correct decisions, and identifies the effective component combinations with a median of 17--72 queries per successful attack. Accuracy and confidence do not reliably reveal this vulnerability. Models with near-identical accuracy on the sampled tasks differ by about 20\%age points in attack success. We demonstrate that an attacker can force not just one wrong answer but every available one: on about 20\% of correct decisions for the JEV models, 77\% for gpt-6-luna and 98\% for GLiNER2.5; a confidence threshold does not reliably screen the attack out. A fixed answer set constrains a decision's form, not its source; robustness must be measured per model, per task and per version rather than assumed from output format.
papers.summary: Limiting a model's output to a fixed set of labels does not stop an attacker from steering which label it picks. `Slot Attack` is a black-box attack that appends text built from named components to the input evidence, pushing decision models toward an attacker-chosen wrong option using only the returned label probabilities. Across seven models and 16 tasks from `Decision Bench`, it **succeeds on 32–99% of initially correct decisions**, needing a median of 17 to 72 queries. Models with nearly identical accuracy differ by about 20 percentage points in vulnerability, and confidence thresholds do not reliably filter out the attack.

papers.title: The role of injected noise in diffusion model generalization
papers.abstract: Diffusion models trained on distinct datasets can produce highly similar samples when prompted with the same noise input, suggesting that they learn a generalized data distribution. We investigate the role of noise injected during the sampling process, and show that it plays an important role in making or breaking this strong generalization effect. Based on this finding we investigate the robustness of sample similarity to changes in the injected noise, and find that its impact is largest in the sampling regime where broad structure already exists but the precise identity of the sample is not yet determined.
papers.summary: Diffusion models trained on different datasets can produce very similar samples from the same noise input, which suggests they learn a general data distribution. The authors study the noise injected during sampling and show that **it plays a key role in creating or breaking this generalization effect**. Sample similarity is most sensitive to changes in injected noise at the stage of sampling when the broad structure already exists but the sample's exact identity is not yet set.

papers.title: VagueBench: Benchmarking the Robustness of Embodied Agents on Ambient Context Illusions
papers.abstract: Embodied agents are increasingly deployed in open-world environments, yet current robustness evaluations remain biased toward hazardous instructions and jailbreak vulnerabilities. A more fundamental issue is largely overlooked: agents are rarely tested under semantically sufficient but contextually minimal instructions (i.e., common in real-world human communication), where auxiliary contextual cues are absent. For the first, we identify a novel phenomenon termed Ambient Context Illusion, where agents fail to execute tasks correctly when non-essential contextual details are omitted, despite unchanged task semantics. To systematically study this, we establish VagueBench, a benchmark built upon the AI2-THOR interactive simulation environment for the evaluation of context dependency in embodied agents. We systematically consider key semantic components of instructions (entities, procedures, constraints, and prior knowledge) and derive a unified taxonomy with four categories and nine subtypes to reduce auxiliary information. VagueBench contains 1,303 instruction pairs across diverse indoor environments, constructed via a human-agent co-generation framework that integrates semantic redundancy estimation, taxonomy-guided transformation, and rigorous semantic-invariance verification. Through extensive evaluation on 6 state-of-the-art embodied agents, we observe significant degradation on VagueBench in both task performance and executability (relatively -19.65% in task success rate and relatively +54.10% in empty plan rate) revealing a strong reliance on auxiliary linguistic signals rather than core task semantics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this phenomenon persists in real-world robotic systems, where it can lead to incorrect decisions and potential safety risks.
papers.summary: Embodied agents are rarely tested on short instructions that have the full meaning but leave out the extra context people often omit. The authors call the resulting failures Ambient Context Illusion: agents fail when non-essential details are removed even though the task itself is unchanged. `VagueBench`, built on the `AI2-THOR` simulator, contains 1,303 instruction pairs created with a nine-subtype taxonomy for removing context and checked to preserve meaning. Across six state-of-the-art embodied agents, the reduced instructions cause **a relative 19.65% drop in task success and a 54.10% relative increase in empty plans**, and the effect also appears on real robots.

papers.title: Quantifying out-of-distribution data severity with Wasserstein distances: benchmarking large language models for alloy property prediction
papers.abstract: As general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs), such as Gemini and DeepSeek, exhibit increasingly advanced reasoning capabilities, a critical question arises: how do their property prediction abilities compare to those of domain-specific pretrained materials models? In this study, we evaluate predictions for Ti, steels, high-entropy alloy (HEA) and Al, demonstrating that general-purpose LLMs surprisingly outperform SteelBERT, MatSciBERT, and SciBERT. To further enhance performance, we introduce a hybrid approach that utilizes numerical priors from a prior model, such as CatBoost or SteelBERT, to guide the general LLMs (Deepseek V3.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash). By inputting these initial estimates from a prior model as prompts, the LLM acts as a reasoning corrector, achieving accuracy superior to the prior model and "unguided mode". Furthermore, we investigate the impact of data strategy using a similarity-based metric, revealing that data quality dominates quantity; using merely 5% of high-similarity reference data of training set as input yields performance similar to the results of using 100% of training set. Additionally, the LLMs demonstrate excellent uncertainty calibration, where self-reported "high" confidence strongly correlates with minimal deviation from ground truth. Our findings suggest that synergizing general-purpose LLMs with prior model numerical baselines and high-quality data curation creates a cost-effective and accurate paradigm for materials discovery, reducing the need for expensive domain-specific pretraining.
papers.summary: General-purpose large language models (LLMs) are compared with domain-specific pretrained materials models at predicting properties of titanium alloys, steels, high-entropy alloys (HEA) and aluminum alloys. `Gemini` and `DeepSeek` models outperform `SteelBERT`, `MatSciBERT` and `SciBERT`. A hybrid mode feeds numerical estimates from a prior model such as `CatBoost` or `SteelBERT` into the prompt, so the LLM acts as a reasoning corrector and beats both the prior model and the unguided LLM. A Wasserstein-distance similarity analysis finds that data quality matters more than quantity: **using only 5% of the training set, chosen for high similarity, as reference data performs about as well as using all of it**, and the LLMs' self-reported confidence tracks their actual error well.

papers.title: Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention
papers.abstract: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by a fixed pattern or, in recent production LLMs, learned per query. In DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), the attention of DeepSeek-V3.2 and the GLM-5 family, every layer is preceded by a lightning indexer that scores the whole cache and keeps the k=2048 highest-scoring tokens for the layer to attend. At long context this indexer scan, not the sparse attention it feeds, is where the decode time goes. But adjacent layers select nearly the same tokens, so a layer can attend the selection of the previous indexer layer instead of its own. This removes the dependency: each indexer then runs concurrently with the attention of its layer. The resulting Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) needs no retraining and no new weights. Its default realization changes no kernel, running inside SGLang's production decode graph; an optional fused decode kernel accelerates it further on DeepSeek-V3.2. MLI composes with IndexCache (the cross-layer reuse GLM-5.2 ships as IndexShare): IndexCache drops the indexer from some layers, and MLI hides the scan on the rest. We serve DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 under IndexCache's protocol at retentions 1/2 to 1/32 (the fraction of layers that keep an indexer) and contexts 10K to 195K. At equal retention the composition decodes faster than IndexCache: up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4, largest where IndexCache keeps the most indexers and growing with context. At retention 1/r it is faster still than IndexCache at 1/(2r) while keeping twice the fresh selections: at 128K it reaches 1.32x the unmodified model's decode throughput at 1/4, above IndexCache's 1.28x at 1/8. Its LongBench, RULER and LongBench v2 accuracy stays within a few percentage points of IndexCache's.
papers.summary: In `DeepSeek Sparse Attention` (`DSA`), used by `DeepSeek-V3.2` and `GLM-5`, a lightning indexer scores the whole cache before every layer to pick the 2,048 tokens that layer attends to, and at long context this scan takes most of the decode time. Because adjacent layers select nearly the same tokens, `Multi-layer Indexer` (`MLI`) lets each layer attend to the previous indexer's selection, so each indexer can run at the same time as its layer's attention. It needs no retraining or new weights and runs inside `SGLang`'s production decode graph. Combined with the cross-layer reuse method `IndexCache`, it decodes up to **14.5% faster than IndexCache alone on DeepSeek-V3.2** and reaches 1.32x the unmodified model's throughput at 128K context, with `LongBench`, `RULER` and `LongBench v2` accuracy within a few points of IndexCache.

papers.title: Metadata-Conditioned Audio Transformers for Adaptive Respiratory Sound Classification
papers.abstract:
Respiratory sound classification from auscultation recordings is confounded by heterogeneous acquisition conditions, including recording device, auscultation site, and patient characteristics, that introduce systematic variability unrelated to the underlying pathology. Although such metadata is often available, existing approaches either ignore it or rely on na\"ive fusion strategies that do not model how distinct metadata sources influence different components of the acoustic representation.
  We propose a family of metadata-conditioning mechanisms for the Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST), progressing from gated residual fusion to Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) adapted to the Transformer architecture. We further introduce two novel variants: Token-Aware FiLM (TAFiLM), which applies distinct modulation to classification and patch tokens, and Soft-Factorized FiLM (SoftFiLM), which learns soft masks to align metadata factors with disentangled feature subspaces.
  Experiments on the ICBHI benchmark demonstrate consistent gains across all conditioning strategies. SoftFiLM achieves 64.11% on the official 4-class task (+3.94% over the baseline) and 72.40% on the 2-class task, establishing a new state-of-the-art on the 2-class task and competitive performance on the 4-class benchmark.
papers.summary: Respiratory sounds recorded with a stethoscope vary with the recording device, the body site and patient characteristics, and this variation has nothing to do with disease. The authors add metadata conditioning to the `Audio Spectrogram Transformer` (`AST`), starting from gated residual fusion and Feature-wise Linear Modulation (`FiLM`), and introduce two new variants: `Token-Aware FiLM` (`TAFiLM`), which modulates classification and patch tokens differently, and `Soft-Factorized FiLM` (`SoftFiLM`), which learns soft masks that map each metadata factor to its own feature subspace. On the `ICBHI` benchmark, `SoftFiLM` reaches 64.11% on the 4-class task (+3.94% over the baseline) and **a state-of-the-art 72.40% on the 2-class task**.

papers.title: RuntimeTickets: Source-Grounded Security Obligations for Agent Skills
papers.abstract: Third-party Agent Skills extend what an autonomous agent can do, but a malicious Skill can hide data exposure or output manipulation inside a legitimate workflow. Neither reading a Skill's description nor granting it tool permissions tells whether its execution meets the user's security requirements. We introduce RuntimeTickets, a protocol that enforces and audits these requirements while a Skill runs. From released malicious-Skill datasets we derive a risk model and build adversarial-benign Skill pairs. From the task's delivery contract, a language model proposes security obligations for that task. Each obligation cites the Skill lines it answers, and the ticket tightens the host's approvals into fine-grained allowed actions but never loosens them. A runtime gate checks the recipient, object and amount of every outbound send before forwarding it, and trusted monitors record the effects within their observation scope. The ticket links these checks and observations to the approved obligations of each Skill run, and a deterministic decoder turns the ticket's status into governable data flows and verifies each obligation. Neither enforcement nor decoding involves a language model, so text injected by a Skill can change the proposal but never the rule that decides a send. We evaluate RuntimeTickets at the network egress boundary of three unmodified agent frameworks against production Skill scanners and runtime baselines, among them an AgentBound-derived allow-list and SkillGuard. RuntimeTickets eliminated both failure modes of current Skill defenses, overlook (malicious Skills let through) and overkill (benign Skills blocked): its overlook rate was 0.0% and its overkill rate 0.0%, while the scanners erred on both sides. RuntimeTickets ties approved requirements to verifiable execution evidence and offers a common foundation for the safe and auditable deployment of third-party Skills.
papers.summary: A malicious third-party Agent Skill can hide data leaks or output tampering inside an otherwise legitimate workflow, and neither reading its description nor granting it tool permissions shows whether a run meets the user's security requirements. `RuntimeTickets` has a language model propose security obligations from the task's delivery contract, each citing the Skill lines it addresses. These obligations can only narrow the host's approvals into fine-grained allowed actions, never widen them. A runtime gate then checks the recipient, object and amount of every outbound send, and a deterministic decoder verifies each obligation; no language model takes part in enforcement, so text injected by a Skill cannot change the rule that decides a send. Tested at the network egress of three unmodified agent frameworks against production Skill scanners and runtime baselines such as `SkillGuard`, it reached **a 0.0% rate of letting malicious Skills through and a 0.0% rate of blocking benign ones**, while the scanners made both kinds of error.

papers.title: What Malware Actually Does: An Empirical Analysis of Post-Infection Behavior Across Malware Families
papers.abstract: Most malware detection research focuses on identifying whether a file is malicious before it executes. Far less attention goes to what happens after infection. This paper presents an empirical analysis of post-infection malware behavior across 37 families, grounded in dynamic sandbox execution using CAPEv2. Behavioral traces are modeled as heterogeneous graphs with five node types and seven typed edge relationships, preserving relational structure that flat feature vectors discard. A voting ensemble trained on graph-derived structural features achieves 94.44% accuracy and MCC of 0.863, outperforming a flat behavioral baseline by 7.4 percentage points in MCC. A multiclass classifier distinguishes 24 malware families, and a per-family behavioral fingerprint analysis characterizes post-infection activity across registry, network, process, and API dimensions. An LLM explanation layer generates analyst-readable reports with MITRE ATT&CK mappings grounded in observed behavioral evidence. The full pipeline is deployed as HeteroScan at https://ama-andam.github.io/heteroscan.
papers.summary: Most malware research asks whether a file is malicious before it runs; this study looks at what 37 malware families actually do after infection, using dynamic execution in the `CAPEv2` sandbox. Behavioral traces are modeled as heterogeneous graphs with five node types and seven edge types, and a voting ensemble on graph-derived structural features reaches **94.44% accuracy and a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.863**, 7.4 points of MCC above a flat-feature baseline. A multiclass classifier separates 24 families, per-family behavioral fingerprints describe registry, network, process and API activity, and an LLM layer writes analyst-readable reports mapped to `MITRE ATT&CK` techniques. The pipeline is deployed as `HeteroScan`.

papers.title: 3D dark matter map of the JWST COSMOS-Web field using diffusion-based generative priors
papers.abstract: Mapping the three-dimensional distribution of dark matter is key to tracing the growth of cosmic structure. Two-dimensional weak lensing mass maps recover its projected distribution, but they blend structures at different distances along the line of sight.
