We reconstruct the three-dimensional matter distribution in the 0.54 deg$^2$ COSMOS-Web field using deep James Webb Space Telescope imaging, with an effective source density of 121 galaxies arcmin$^{-2}$ We combine a physical weak lensing forward model with a diffusion-based Bayesian generative prior learned from cosmological simulations, yielding a posterior distribution of the matter field across 20 lens planes to $z \simeq 2$, doubling the redshift reach of previous Hubble Space Telescope-based 3D reconstructions and approaching cosmic noon, an epoch of rapid galaxy growth. The reconstruction separates structures that overlap in projection and recovers non-Gaussian matter structure across a range of spatial scales, including over-densities associated with independently identified galaxy clusters that were not detected in earlier weak lensing maps. Posterior sampling quantifies the range of three-dimensional matter distributions allowed by the data, enabling a probabilistic visualization of the cosmic web while propagating uncertainties in its inferred structure. Null and simulation-based tests show that the recovered structures are supported by the lensing signal and are consistent with expectations from the fiducial $\Lambda$CDM cosmology. These results extend three-dimensional weak lensing mapping into the high-redshift, non-Gaussian regime and establish a route towards probabilistic mapping of the evolving cosmic web with current wide-field lensing surveys.
papers.summary: Two-dimensional weak-lensing mass maps mix together structures at different distances along the line of sight. Using deep James Webb Space Telescope imaging of the 0.54 square-degree `COSMOS-Web` field, the authors combine a physical weak-lensing forward model with a diffusion-based Bayesian prior learned from cosmological simulations, producing a posterior over the matter field across 20 lens planes. The reconstruction reaches **redshift about 2, double the reach of earlier Hubble-based 3D maps**, separates structures that overlap in projection, and recovers over-densities tied to galaxy clusters missed by earlier lensing maps. Posterior sampling quantifies uncertainty, and null and simulation tests find the structures are supported by the lensing signal and consistent with standard ΛCDM cosmology.

papers.title: BEND 2.0: Benchmarking the Capabilities Needed to Design DNA
papers.abstract: Genomic foundation models are increasingly used to propose DNA sequences and edits. But successful design requires capabilities that current benchmarks do not measure. Here we introduce BEND 2.0 (BENchmark for DNA language models), which tests how well models predict the effects of DNA changes and whether these predictions can guide sequence design. Across eight tasks built on five experimental datasets, we find that model choice and how representations are accessed both affect performance. Linear readouts fitted to frozen representations can match or exceed models' native outputs, and functional post-training substantially improves the models' capabilities. Linear readouts transfer well across experimental assays and genes, suggesting that models capture functional patterns beyond the data used to fit individual predictors. At the same time, strong prediction of average effects can conceal weaker prediction of context-specific effects, and accurate prediction of combined mutation effects does not imply accurate prediction of their interactions. In design tasks, model predictions can reduce the number of candidates needed to find a desired response, but still leave substantial room for better design choices, particularly for context-specific and multi-cell objectives. Our benchmark reveals that genomic models now display signs of general utility but have yet to saturate on performance in even simple tasks.
papers.summary: `BEND 2.0` is a benchmark that tests whether genomic foundation models can predict the effects of DNA changes and use those predictions to guide sequence design, with eight tasks built on five experimental datasets. Linear readouts fitted on frozen model representations can match or beat the models' native outputs and transfer well across assays and genes, and functional post-training substantially improves performance. However, strong prediction of average effects can hide weak prediction of context-specific effects, and getting combined mutation effects right does not mean getting their interactions right. Model guidance reduces the number of candidates needed in design tasks, but **performance is far from saturated even on simple tasks**.

papers.title: AIRoA-0: Long-Horizon, Precise, Cross-Embodiment Manipulation from Handheld Data
papers.abstract: AIRoA-0 (A-0) is a bimanual manipulation system learned from 16,151 hours of handheld demonstrations, with no robot data collected at any stage. The demonstrations are recorded with YUBI, our open-source handheld gripper, which lets people record manipulation data anywhere with no robot present. From a single instruction, A-0 sorts more than a dozen small parts into their numbered cells and changes the mop pads and brush of a robot vacuum; among other tasks, it unzips a pencil case and folds a towel. It performs these tasks using only a camera on each wrist, with no head or scene camera, at a site where none of its training data was recorded. Across the ten tasks of our evaluation, it averages a success rate of 78%, against 27% for the strongest of four other vision-language-action models post-trained on the same task demonstrations. We collect no teleoperation data and use no reinforcement learning or on-robot corrections, and the robot appears only at test time. The system learns which regions of each wrist view matter for the task, predicts the stage the task has reached, and decodes actions as a continuous stream. A-0 is embodiment-agnostic: it runs on robots that mount the YUBI gripper, such as a bimanual Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm and UR. We are releasing the dataset, to our knowledge the largest open dataset of handheld-gripper demonstrations with task and subtask instructions, together with the pre-trained weights and the post-training recipe. Videos of A-0 on every task are on the project page, https://a-0.airoa.io. Anyone can build the gripper, record a task of their own and post-train the model on it in under four hours on a single node of eight H200 GPUs.
papers.summary: `AIRoA-0` is a two-armed manipulation system trained entirely on 16,151 hours of demonstrations recorded with `YUBI`, an open-source handheld gripper, with no robot data, teleoperation, reinforcement learning or on-robot corrections. Using only one camera on each wrist, it does long, precise tasks such as sorting small parts into numbered cells and replacing a robot vacuum's mop pads and brush, at a site where none of its training data was recorded. It learns which regions of each wrist view matter, predicts the current task stage, and decodes actions as a continuous stream. Across ten tasks it averages **78% success versus 27% for the strongest of four other vision-language-action models** post-trained on the same demonstrations, and it runs on several robot arms that mount the gripper; the dataset, weights and post-training recipe are released.

papers.title: Rethinking Next-Visit Diagnosis Prediction Beyond Aggregate Metrics: Retrieval--Memory Multi-Agent Adjudication
papers.abstract: Next-visit diagnosis prediction forecasts the diagnoses documented at a patient's next encounter, turning retrospective electronic health records into prospective clinical prediction. However, conventional aggregate evaluation obscures its multifaceted nature: distributionally, models must handle variable-size diagnosis sets and long-tailed labels; temporally, they must distinguish persistent, newly recorded, and recurrent diagnoses; and both vary with observed history depth. We introduce an evaluation framework along these dimensions and apply it to rule-based heuristics, LLM-based prompting, retrieval, memory, and multi-agent approaches. This reveals that repeating the last visit outperforms most LLM-based approaches overall despite predicting no new or recurrent diagnoses, and that retrieval and memory exhibit distinct profiles whose relative strengths vary across temporal transitions and backbones. Motivated by this, we propose LONGINUS, a retrieval-memory multi-agent adjudication framework combining evidence retrieved from patient records with structured memory of the patient trajectory. Using cross-view agreement as a reliability heuristic, it preserves shared predictions and adjudicates disagreements without revealing their source. Across MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV with four LLM backbones, LONGINUS achieves the best transition-specific performance among LLM-based methods in nearly all settings while remaining competitive with them on aggregate metrics.
papers.summary: Next-visit diagnosis prediction forecasts which diagnoses will appear at a patient's next encounter in electronic health records. The authors argue that aggregate metrics hide important differences, and propose evaluating by diagnosis-set size, label rarity, whether a diagnosis persists, is new, or recurs, and how much history is available. Under this framework, **simply repeating the last visit beats most LLM-based approaches overall** despite never predicting new or recurrent diagnoses, and retrieval and memory methods show distinct strengths. Their `LONGINUS` framework combines record retrieval with structured memory of the patient's trajectory, keeps predictions the two views agree on and has agents adjudicate disagreements, and achieves the best transition-specific results among LLM methods on `MIMIC-III` and `MIMIC-IV` across four backbones.

papers.title: El Agente F\'armaco: A Scalable AI Scientist for Drug Discovery
papers.abstract: Computational drug discovery offers a growing range of tools for proposing and evaluating molecules, but combining them and deciding what to do next still requires substantial expert effort. Here, we introduce El Agente F\'armaco, an AI scientist that uses modern large language model (LLM) technology to turn discovery goals expressed in everyday language into complex, scalable computational screening workflows. The agentic harness selects scientific tools, reviews their results, and adjusts subsequent steps to the target and the user's objectives. Our approach centers on a shared scientific memory: F\'armaco Atlas, which stores molecules, structures, and results together with their provenance -- a record of how they were obtained. The agent uses targeted database queries to retrieve the evidence needed for each decision. A single request can launch calculations for an entire collection of molecules, without requiring a separate LLM decision for every compound. This design limits the information the model must process as screening collections grow, while keeping the underlying results available for inspection and further analysis. The integrated tools support molecule generation, prediction of binding and molecular properties, and searches for compounds available for purchase. In a retrospective comparison with an expert-led campaign, the agent proposed chemically distinct candidates with competitive docking scores and higher calculated drug-likeness under explicitly imposed selection criteria. In a 22-task benchmark against plain tool calls and Codex, the agent achieved the highest observed mean model-judged score, with lower median cumulative token use and peak context. F\'armaco provides a foundation for flexible, scalable drug discovery workflows that connect scientific reasoning with an enduring, traceable record of computational work.
papers.summary: `El Agente Fármaco` is an LLM-based AI scientist that turns drug-discovery goals written in everyday language into large computational screening workflows, choosing tools, reviewing results and adjusting next steps. It is built around a shared database, `Fármaco Atlas`, that stores molecules, structures and results with a record of how each was obtained. The agent retrieves evidence through targeted queries, and a single request can launch calculations over a whole collection of molecules without an LLM decision per compound, which keeps the model's context small as screens grow. In a 22-task benchmark against plain tool calling and `Codex`, it achieved **the highest mean model-judged score with lower median token use and peak context**, and in a retrospective comparison with an expert-led campaign it proposed distinct candidates with competitive docking scores.

papers.title: Low-Rank Hierarchical Merging for Efficient Long-to-Short Reasoning
papers.abstract: Long-to-Short (L2S) model merging seeks to combine the strong reasoning capability of long chain-of-thought models with the concise style of base models, but existing methods that rely on linear interpolation and first-order activation statistics fail to capture how the loss landscape responds to parameter displacement, leading to degraded accuracy on hard tasks. We propose Low-Rank Hierarchical Merging (LHM), a training-free framework that replaces heuristic statistics with lightweight second-order curvature information. LHM consists of three components: (1) a low-rank Hessian approximation that efficiently estimates per-layer Hessian traces via Hutchinson's estimator on random inputs, eliminating the need for task-specific data; (2) a Layer Second-Order Sensitivity (LSOS) index that combines Hessian trace with task-vector norm to quantify per-layer fusion difficulty; and (3) a Dual-Constraint Coefficient Mapping (DCCM) that converts LSOS scores into layer-adaptive merge coefficients while jointly satisfying a fusion-error bound and a global length-reduction target. Experiments across six mathematical benchmarks on 1.5B and 7B models show that LHM outperforms state-of-the-art methods such as ACM-TIES and ORCA, achieving over 4\% accuracy gain and up to 93.1\% reduction in output length relative to the long-CoT model.
papers.summary: Long-to-Short (L2S) model merging tries to combine a long chain-of-thought model's reasoning ability with a base model's concise style, but existing methods rely on linear interpolation and simple activation statistics and lose accuracy on hard problems. `Low-Rank Hierarchical Merging` (`LHM`) is a training-free method that estimates each layer's Hessian trace with Hutchinson's estimator on random inputs, so no task data is needed. It combines this with the task-vector norm into a per-layer sensitivity score, then maps the scores to layer-specific merge coefficients that respect both a fusion-error bound and a target length reduction. On six math benchmarks with 1.5B and 7B models it beats methods such as `ACM-TIES` and `ORCA`, with **over 4% higher accuracy and up to 93.1% shorter outputs** than the long-CoT model.

papers.title: A Conditional Mutual Information Analysis of Response Variety in Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models provide a variety of responses at inference (generation) that conventionally depend on a temperature parameter. Using a conditional mutual information approach, a quantitative, entropy based analysis of response variety is given. Three limiting behaviors are defined: arbiter, independent (conditionally) and neutral (deterministic) that span no to maximal mutual information. We give examples of each behavior and suggest their application to: temperature analysis, language analysis, prompt compression, and knowledge graphs.
papers.summary: The variety of responses a large language model gives, usually controlled by the sampling temperature, is analyzed with an entropy-based conditional mutual information framework. The analysis defines **three limiting behaviors, called arbiter, conditionally independent and neutral (deterministic)**, which range from zero to maximal mutual information. The author gives examples of each and suggests applications to temperature analysis, language analysis, prompt compression and knowledge graphs.

papers.title: PianoBench: Evaluating Musical Perception and Reasoning in Language Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal language models continue to improve on broad music understanding benchmarks, but which musical features can they perceive and reason about? We investigate this question by introducing PianoBench, a benchmark that tasks language models with reasoning about musical performances across congruent acoustic and symbolic input representations. PianoBench is derived from our new multimodal, training-scale dataset comprising more than 20,000 hours of interleaved transcripts of music and spoken musical commentary from instructional piano videos. Open-weight audio-language models achieve at most 52.8% accuracy on PianoBench, and at best only modestly outperform their accuracy on a no-audio control. In contrast, frontier models using chain of thought achieve up to 93.2% accuracy when provided transcripts of music as text, exposing a gap between perceiving musical features from audio and reasoning about musical events when they are given explicitly. We then test whether mid-training on interleaved musical instruction can improve question answering without chain of thought, raising Qwen 3.5 9B Base's zero-shot accuracy on PianoBench with music transcripts from 42.8% to 56.0% after instruction tuning. These experiments suggest that instructional videos may represent an overlooked source of multimodal supervision for music. Available: https://gclef-cmu.org/pianobench.
papers.summary: `PianoBench` tests which musical features language models can perceive and reason about, presenting piano performances both as audio and as symbolic transcripts. It comes from a new dataset of more than 20,000 hours of instructional piano videos, with music transcripts interleaved with spoken commentary. Open-weight audio-language models reach at most 52.8% and barely beat a control with no audio, while **frontier models using chain of thought reach 93.2% when given the music as text**, showing that the bottleneck is perceiving music from audio rather than reasoning about it. Mid-training on the interleaved instructional data raises `Qwen 3.5 9B Base`'s zero-shot accuracy with transcripts from 42.8% to 56.0%.

papers.title: Probabilistic Steering of Generative Priors for Lab-in-the-Loop Antibody Optimization
papers.abstract: Therapeutic antibody development is often framed as comprising two discrete stages: initial discovery of novel binders followed by iterative optimization to refine these hits into therapeutic-grade molecules. Models and methods often reflect these stages, with generative structure models applied to discovery and probabilistic black-box optimization methods applied to refinement. Here we propose to unify these stages by smoothly transitioning a generative discovery model into iterative optimization, allowing the handoff between the structure-based prior and supervision from wet lab data to be guided by the posterior uncertainty of a probabilistic surrogate. We show that this yields improvements in optimization efficiency in the low-N regime, as well as improved diversity amongst the optimized molecules.
papers.summary: Therapeutic antibody development is usually split into discovering binders with generative structure models and then refining them with probabilistic black-box optimization. This work merges the two stages by gradually turning a generative discovery model into an iterative optimizer. The posterior uncertainty of a probabilistic surrogate model decides how much to trust the structure-based prior versus wet-lab data. The authors report **better optimization efficiency when few lab measurements are available**, along with more diverse optimized molecules.

papers.title: LaplaceDiag: Fault Diagnosis through Changes in Learned Actuator Effects
papers.abstract: Identifying faulty components from sensor anomalies is difficult because fault effects can propagate through a plant and different faults can produce similar observations. Detailed component models and labeled fault examples may also be unavailable. We introduce LaplaceDiag, a data-driven method that uses changes in actuator effects to narrow the search for faulty equipment. Actuators act on specific devices and mechanisms, so their changed effects can provide clues to root causes. LaplaceDiag learns a healthy plant model with LaplaceNet, a neural network that operates in Laplace space. It separates nonlinear prediction based on measured history from an explicit matrix that describes how actuator values affect sensor values. Keeping the history predictor fixed allows current actuator effects to be estimated by linear regression without retraining the neural network. Comparison with a healthy reference accounts for estimation uncertainty and normal variation to detect changes and generate actuator-related diagnostic hypotheses. The method supports online and offline diagnosis, providing an intermediate step between anomaly detection and identifying faulty components. We successfully evaluate LaplaceDiag on two datasets.
papers.summary: Finding which component is faulty from sensor anomalies is hard because faults spread through a plant and different faults can look alike, often with no detailed component models or labeled fault examples to work from. `LaplaceDiag` learns a model of the healthy plant with `LaplaceNet`, a neural network that works in Laplace space and separates a nonlinear predictor based on measurement history from an explicit matrix describing how actuators affect sensors. Holding the history predictor fixed, **current actuator effects can be re-estimated by linear regression without retraining**. Comparing them against a healthy reference, with estimation uncertainty and normal variation taken into account, produces actuator-related hypotheses about the root cause. The method supports online and offline diagnosis and was evaluated successfully on two datasets.

papers.title: RoboScope Kit: Unified Interfaces for Fast and Scalable Embodied-AI Evaluation
papers.abstract: Simulation benchmarks are the standard way to compare robot policies, but each benchmark brings its own evaluator, observation layout, and action convention, and evaluation is slow: 500 RoboTwin Easy episodes with one simulator and one model on one GPU take 359.7 minutes. Profiling the official StarVLA evaluator shows that simulation occupies CPU cores while the GPU averages 14.3% utilization. RoboScope Kit wraps each model once in a Python class called a Policy, and each benchmark once in an adapter around the benchmark's own evaluator, so the benchmark's rules and scoring stay unchanged. Scheduling runs simulator workers and Policy replicas as separate pools, sizes both from measured probes, and shards work deterministically across GPU instances; runtime optimization renders only the observations an action-chunk Policy reads. Adapters cover six benchmark families. On LIBERO-Long with a StarVLA checkpoint on one 48 GiB RTX 4090, the concurrency search selects twelve simulator workers sharing three Policy replicas, which evaluate 500 episodes 4.45$\times$ faster than the official StarVLA evaluation with equivalent success rates, 2.78$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 1.52$\times$ faster than vla-eval at its tuned configuration. With CUDA MPS, which lets the replicas run their kernels concurrently, the search selects sixteen workers sharing four replicas, 6.16$\times$ faster than StarVLA, 3.85$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 2.10$\times$ faster than vla-eval. On RoboTwin Easy, four GPUs with chunk-boundary observation complete the 500 episodes in 14.4 minutes, 25.04$\times$ faster than the single-GPU baseline, with identical success outcomes and terminal steps.
papers.summary: Robot simulation benchmarks each come with their own evaluator, observation layout and action conventions, and evaluation is slow: profiling the official `StarVLA` evaluator shows simulation keeping CPU cores busy while the GPU averages 14.3% utilization. `RoboScope Kit` wraps each model once as a Policy class and each benchmark once in an adapter around its own evaluator, leaving scoring unchanged, and covers six benchmark families. It runs simulator workers and Policy replicas as separate pools sized from measured probes, shards work deterministically across GPUs, and renders only the observations a policy reads. On `LIBERO-Long` with one RTX 4090 it evaluates 500 episodes 4.45x faster than the official `StarVLA` evaluator (6.16x with CUDA MPS), and on `RoboTwin Easy` **four GPUs finish 500 episodes in 14.4 minutes, 25x faster than the single-GPU baseline**, with identical outcomes.

papers.title: Why Pay for Long Reasoning When Rewrite Do Trick? Causal Effects of Reasoning History Compaction on Future Generation and Agent Cost
papers.abstract: Reasoning substantially improves language models' ability to solve difficult problems, but long reasoning traces make these gains expensive. Efficient reasoning should express useful analysis in fewer tokens by reducing repetition and text that adds little value to solving the problem. Progress in proprietary models motivates this goal, yet their hidden scratchpads limit direct study of how it is achieved. We investigate whether open-weight models can generate less verbose reasoning by changing the form of their own earlier thoughts, without retraining. Our intervention rewrites prior reasoning into compact state records before pending tool results are revealed, then compares continuations from original and compact histories. Across the tested models, accepted compact histories usually shorten future reasoning; a coding case study also shows less repeated verification after a shared candidate solution. In software-agent deployments, compaction can reduce total spending, although task quality and rewrite-inclusive time depend on the target and compressor. These findings identify reasoning history as one way to reduce future reasoning-token use and motivate model-specific compaction policies evaluated for both efficiency and retained capability.
papers.summary: Long reasoning traces make reasoning models expensive, and proprietary models' hidden scratchpads make it hard to study how they keep reasoning short. The authors test whether open-weight models reason less verbosely when their own earlier thoughts are rewritten, with no retraining: before pending tool results are revealed, prior reasoning is rewritten into compact state records, and continuations from the original and compacted histories are compared. **Accepted compact histories usually shorten future reasoning**, and a coding case study shows less repeated verification after a candidate solution. In software-agent deployments compaction can lower total cost, though task quality and time including the rewrite depend on the target model and the compressor.

papers.title: Performance, Scalability and Maintenance: An Experimental Study of RPA vs. Autonomous Agents in the Healthcare Domain
papers.abstract: Healthcare information systems are fragmented, and retrieving data from legacy web portals is a recurrent need. Robotic Process Automation (RPA) is deterministic but sensitive to interface changes, whereas autonomous agents based on large language models (Agent Process Automation, APA) promise adaptability at a higher computational cost. Following Design Science Research, we developed and compared an RPA solution (Playwright) and an APA solution (browser-use, LangGraph and Gemini 2.5 Flash-lite) to retrieve mammography and breast ultrasound reports from a laboratory portal, treating reports solely as informational artifacts. Across two rounds (T and T+7), RPA reached 98.90% accuracy and 98.27% F1-score versus 96.49% and 94.48% for APA, was about 13 times faster (16.07 s vs. 207.21 s per patient) and cost about six times less per report (USD 0.030 vs. 0.187). Both reached 100% step success rates; APA varied more over time. For a stable interface, RPA was superior.
authors: Ana Paula Wernz da Cunha M\"uller
papers.summary: Healthcare data often has to be pulled from fragmented legacy web portals. The authors compare deterministic Robotic Process Automation (RPA), built with `Playwright`, against an LLM-based agent approach (Agent Process Automation, APA) built with `browser-use`, `LangGraph` and `Gemini 2.5 Flash-lite`, on retrieving mammography and breast ultrasound reports from a lab portal. Over two rounds a week apart, RPA reached 98.90% accuracy versus 96.49% for the agent, was **about 13 times faster (16.07 s vs. 207.21 s per patient)** and about six times cheaper per report, and the agent's results varied more over time. For a stable interface, RPA came out ahead.

papers.title: Predictive gains, causal losses: why interventional competence cannot be learned from data alone
papers.abstract: Retaining predictive gains can require persistent errors in a model's response to interventions. For deterministic predictors with finite second moments under squared-error loss, any observational advantage over the best predictor using only an outcome's direct causes requires dependence on other inputs, regardless of the learning rule. When admissible interventions vary inputs while preserving the worldly outcome, this dependence yields a positive lower bound on root-mean-square intervention-response error. We identify conditions under which population gradient updates introduce this dependence from a parent-only baseline or damage a previously correct mechanism through shared parameters while improving other predictions. These dependencies can also make model behavior vary with how the same intervention is realized. We characterize interventional alignment through a common output mapping across internal states and physical processes realizing the same intervention target and relevant context. Correction is limited by the causal hypotheses currently admitted within inquiry. The relevant hypothesis class comprises these causal alternatives, rather than the function class the computational system could in principle represent. For predictions restricted to these alternatives, interventional mean error cannot fall below the best approximation they permit, whether evidence is observational or interventional. Reducing error below a positive limit requires admitting better hypotheses, which may entail revising the causal variables, mechanism structure, or intervention interpretation. Interventional criticism constrains replacements without determining them. We conjecture that reliably acquiring and maintaining interventional competence when causal commitments fail requires autonomous participation in proposing alternatives, testing their consequences, and revising them in response to error.
papers.summary: This theoretical paper argues that a model's gains in predictive accuracy can require lasting errors in how it responds to interventions. For deterministic predictors under squared-error loss, **any observational advantage over the best predictor using only an outcome's direct causes requires dependence on other inputs**, whatever the learning rule, and when interventions change those inputs without changing the outcome, this gives a positive lower bound on intervention-response error. The authors identify conditions under which gradient updates introduce such dependence or damage a previously correct mechanism through shared parameters. They argue that correction is limited by the causal hypotheses currently under consideration, and conjecture that reliably maintaining interventional competence requires the system to take part in proposing, testing and revising causal alternatives itself.

papers.title: Dr. No: Feature Steering for Abstention in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract:
Large foundation models often answer even when the available visual or textual evidence is insufficient to support a reliable conclusion. This failure to abstain makes them hard to trust in high-stakes or information-seeking settings, where a confident but unsupported answer can be worse than no answer at all. It also raises a natural question: can the internal mechanisms behind this behaviour be identified and controlled at inference time? We present Dr. No, a feature-steering approach that mines sparse autoencoder (SAE) features associated with abstention and commitment, then modulates a small set of them during the prefill pass, without retraining the base model.
  Dr. No is evaluated on LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B across multimodal abstention benchmarks, including UNK-VQA and MM-UPD, and additionally benchmarked on language reasoning tasks using Qwen3.5-2B on AbstentionBench subsets. Against multiple uncertainty-based abstention baselines, feature steering achieves a more favourable balance between correct answering and appropriate abstention than post-hoc rejection methods. The gains are strongest on UNK-VQA and on MM-UPD cases involving image--question or question--answer incompatibility, and transfer most clearly to mathematical reasoning subsets of AbstentionBench. However, performance is more limited on absent-answer detection and retrieval-heavy multi-hop QA, such as MuSiQue. These results suggest that sparse internal features provide lightweight control handles for shaping uncertainty-aware behaviour in foundation models, while also showing that abstention control is source-dependent rather than governed by a single universal signal.
papers.summary: Foundation models often answer even when the image or text does not support a reliable conclusion. `Dr. No` finds sparse autoencoder (SAE) features associated with abstaining or committing to an answer, and adjusts a small set of them during the prefill pass without retraining. Evaluated on `LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B` with the `UNK-VQA` and `MM-UPD` benchmarks, and on `Qwen3.5-2B` with `AbstentionBench` subsets, **feature steering balances correct answers against appropriate abstention better than post-hoc rejection baselines**, especially on `UNK-VQA`, on mismatched image-question or question-answer pairs, and on math reasoning. Gains are smaller for detecting absent answers and for retrieval-heavy multi-hop QA such as `MuSiQue`, suggesting that different sources of uncertainty call for different abstention controls.

papers.title: ExaTune: Exhaustive Hyperparameter Landscape Exploration at Scale
papers.abstract: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) returns a single optimal configuration, systematically discarding the explored performance landscape that encodes how results depend on configuration choices. Fitness landscape analysis comprises a robust collection of methods from evolutionary computation offering ruggedness indices, autocorrelation functions, and fitness-distance correlation that have never been applied to machine learning hyperparameter spaces at scale, given that fine-grained ground-truth enumeration data has not existed. We present ExaTune, an open-source HPC system to produce a new artifact class: the hyperparameter landscape map. ExaTune exhaustively evaluates every point on a discretized hyperparameter grid via $K$-fold cross-validation, aggregates results into reproducible parquet benchmarks, and applies a suite of five formalized landscape metrics: spatial autocorrelation (Moran's $I$), ruggedness, local optima density, fitness-distance correlation (FDC), and variance-based parameter importance. We release a benchmark collection of 8 complete landscape maps (totalling 285,080 exhaustively evaluated configurations) spanning five model families (SVMs, random forests, XGBoost, ridge regression, and $k$-nearest neighbors) across six classification and two regression benchmarks, hosted on HuggingFace. Empirical analysis demonstrates that Bayesian optimization, Optuna, Hyperband, and Random Search at standard trial budgets systematically miss instability regions, secondary optima, and parameter interaction effects that are visible in complete landscapes; information that is structurally unavailable to any optimizer by design.
papers.summary: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) usually reports only the best configuration and throws away the landscape it explored. `ExaTune`, an open-source high-performance computing system, evaluates every point on a discretized hyperparameter grid with K-fold cross-validation and characterizes the results with five fitness-landscape metrics borrowed from evolutionary computation, including Moran's I, ruggedness and fitness-distance correlation. The authors release 8 complete landscape maps covering **285,080 exhaustively evaluated configurations** for SVMs, random forests, `XGBoost`, ridge regression and k-nearest neighbors. Their analysis shows that `Bayesian optimization`, `Optuna`, `Hyperband` and `Random Search` at standard trial budgets consistently miss instability regions, secondary optima and parameter interactions.

papers.title: EvoGroup: A Self-Evolving Harness for Group Agents in Shared Contexts
papers.abstract: With the rise of Group Agent such as Claude Tag, agents increasingly serve as digital workers for long-term team collaboration. These agents operate over shared contexts that continuously accumulate through multi-user interactions. However, existing agent memory systems are mainly designed for individual users and struggle to capture group-level knowledge in shared contexts, including group relationships and collaboratively formed knowledge. Manual memory strategies further limit adaptation to diverse and evolving shared contexts. To this end, we propose \textbf{EvoGroup (EvoG)}, a self-evolving harness for group agents that starts from a minimal six-tool cold start and adapts through interaction with shared context. EvoG uses confidence and task outcomes to select informative trajectories, while also eliciting self-reflections on uncertainty in low-confidence cases. The analysis agent then examines selected trajectories through adaptive progressive disclosure, followed by bucketed analysis to synthesize high-level findings that guide the evolve agent in revising the Harness. Empirically, pass@1 on held-out split of EverMemBench improves from 71.07\% to 89.58\%, surpassing both self-evolving memory and human-designed harnesses, including Claude Code (85.83\%). To evaluate generalization, we freeze the evolved harness and evaluate it on the unseen GroupMemBench, where, with GPT-5.5, it demonstrates effective generalization and outperforms both memory baselines and human-designed harnesses.
papers.summary: Agents deployed as long-term team workers operate over shared contexts that build up across many users, but existing memory systems are designed for a single user and miss group relationships and collectively formed knowledge. `EvoGroup` (`EvoG`) starts from a minimal six-tool harness and evolves it automatically: it selects informative trajectories using confidence and task outcomes, prompts self-reflection on low-confidence cases, and passes the selected trajectories to an analysis agent whose findings guide an evolve agent in revising the harness. On a held-out split of `EverMemBench`, pass@1 rises **from 71.07% to 89.58%**, beating self-evolving memory baselines and human-designed harnesses including `Claude Code` (85.83%). Frozen and tested on the unseen `GroupMemBench` with `GPT-5.5`, the evolved harness still outperforms both kinds of baseline.

papers.title: Learning Almost Complex and Complex Structures
papers.abstract: We study the numerical constructions of almost complex and complex structures on spheres and products of spheres up to real dimension six. Our general set-up parametrises almost complex structures via a global matrix field in an ambient Euclidean space, compressed by the tangent projector. The projector's algebraic residual measures the almost complex condition, while its Nijenhuis tensor is evaluated in the intrinsic norm of the round product metric. Polynomial features and neural networks are trained without prescribed targets to perform general searches for these structures. The almost complex search passes numerical admissibility checks on all nine examples that admit such structures and rejects $S^4$, where a topological obstruction is known. A matrix correction then enforces the almost complex identity, subject to a novel uniform admissibility condition. For integrability, a free polynomial representation with Levenberg-Marquardt optimisation learns the complex structures on $S^2\times S^2$, $S^3\times S^1$, $S^3\times S^3$ and $S^5\times S^1$, with the largest Nijenhuis norms found by adversarial search all below $10^{-9}$. These general searches were unsuccessful on $S^6$, $S^4\times S^2$ and $S^4\times T^2$. Therefore, for these three cases direct numerical reconstructions were built in torus-fibred coordinates. They are integrable by construction, satisfy their compatibility conditions to better than $10^{-11}$, and corroborate the recent constructions on $S^6$ and $S^4\times S^2$.
papers.summary: The authors use polynomial features and neural networks, trained without target structures, to construct almost complex and complex structures numerically on spheres and products of spheres up to real dimension six. Almost complex structures are parametrized by a global matrix field projected onto the tangent space, and integrability is measured by the Nijenhuis tensor. The search correctly finds almost complex structures on all nine admissible examples and rejects S^4, where a topological obstruction is known. Using `Levenberg-Marquardt` optimization, it learns integrable complex structures on four product manifolds with **Nijenhuis norms below 10^-9**; for S^6, S^4×S^2 and S^4×T^2, direct reconstructions in torus-fibred coordinates corroborate recent constructions.

papers.title: INSIGHT-HPC: An Interpretable System Intelligence for Global HPC Telemetry
papers.abstract: Modern high-performance computing (HPC) clusters integrate multi-generation CPUs and GPUs, which generate rich, high-dimensional telemetry streams from out-of-band baseboard management controllers (BMC), job schedulers, and facility power distribution units. Detecting anomalies within this telemetry is critical to prevent energy waste and costly node failures. Existing approaches often rely primarily on statistical deviations and require stronger labels than actual production environments can provide. In addition, these detectors have a limited operational context for interpreting alerts. We present INSIGHT-HPC, a multi-plane anomaly-detection architecture that combines statistical, workload-aware, and physics-guided evidence into operator-interpretable episodes. INSIGHT-HPC integrates heterogeneous, large-scale telemetry streams and transforms noisy minute-resolution observations into de-duplicated fault episodes with operator-facing explanations. This design allows the system to distinguish workload-explained behavior from genuine infrastructure anomalies while producing interpretable alert summaries for operators. On production HPC telemetry with weak operational labels and controlled HPC-relevant fault injections, INSIGHT-HPC achieves a stronger precision-recall balance than all evaluated baselines. The system achieves a precision of 0.913, a recall of 0.817, an F1 score of 0.862, and an AUROC of 0.896. These results demonstrate the value of combining workload context, physical consistency, and explainable episode-level fusion.
papers.summary: High-performance computing (HPC) clusters produce high-dimensional telemetry from baseboard management controllers (BMC), job schedulers and power distribution units, yet existing anomaly detectors rely on statistical deviations, need strong labels, and give operators little context. `INSIGHT-HPC` combines statistical, workload-aware and physics-guided evidence to turn noisy minute-resolution telemetry into de-duplicated fault episodes with operator-facing explanations, separating behavior explained by the workload from genuine infrastructure faults. On production telemetry with weak labels and controlled fault injections, it reaches **an F1 score of 0.862** (precision 0.913, recall 0.817, AUROC 0.896), the best precision-recall balance among the evaluated baselines.

papers.title: Embedding Semantic Entropy: NLI-Free Semantic Uncertainty Estimation with Geometry-Aware Clustering
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often generate fluent yet incorrect responses, making un- certainty estimation important for reliable deployment. Semantic Entropy (SE) estimates uncertainty by clustering responses based on semantic equivalence, but it relies on hard entailment-based clustering. We propose Embedding Semantic Entropy, which replaces entailment-based clustering with K-Medoids in semantic embedding space and uses dynamic cluster selection to account for intra-cluster compactness and inter-cluster separation. We evaluate the method on TriviaQA, SQuAD, NQ-Open, SVAMP, and BioASQ using Falcon- 7B-Instruct, LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-2-7B-Chat, and Gemma-7B. Results show competitive AUROC and AUARC performance, suggesting that NLI-based entailment clustering can be replaced with embedding-space clustering with limited degradation while improving the inspectability of semantic grouping. This matters because semantic uncertainty scores depend on underlying semantic groups; by making these groups explicit, compact, and separable in embedding space, Emb-SE turns uncertainty estimation from a black-box en- tailment decision into an inspectable clustering problem.
papers.summary: `Semantic Entropy` estimates large language model (LLM) uncertainty by clustering sampled responses by meaning, but it depends on hard natural language inference (NLI) entailment checks. `Embedding Semantic Entropy` (`Emb-SE`) replaces those checks with `K-Medoids` clustering in a semantic embedding space, choosing the number of clusters dynamically based on how compact and well separated they are. Across `TriviaQA`, `SQuAD`, `NQ-Open`, `SVAMP` and `BioASQ` with `Falcon-7B-Instruct`, `LLaMA-2-7B`, `LLaMA-2-7B-Chat` and `Gemma-7B`, the method reaches **AUROC and AUARC competitive with NLI-based clustering**, with limited degradation and semantic groups that are easier to inspect.

papers.title: ProofPaths: An AI Agent Framework for Assessing Student Reasoning
papers.abstract: Students can use large language models to complete assignments, but a correct solution does not establish whether they understand the reasoning behind it. Individualized interviews can probe that understanding but require recurring staff effort. We introduce ProofPaths, an AI agentic framework that combines rubric-based grading with individualized and interactive interviews. Multiple grading agents assess a submission against instructor guidance, exchange critiques, and revise their judgments. Their scores determine which review supplies the grade and feedback. An interview agent asks students to justify steps in their submission and uses their answers to guide follow-up questions. Each question is linked to a retrieved submission excerpt, so instructors can compare the student's explanation with the cited passage. The system tracks assessment progress and stores grading reviews and interview transcripts for each submission. Several deterministic tests of the assessment controllers check source handling, score aggregation, and limits on correction attempts. Instructors can inspect all reviews and transcripts and override grades within the assignment workflow.
papers.summary: Students can use LLMs to produce correct solutions without understanding them, and one-on-one interviews that probe understanding take a lot of staff time. `ProofPaths` combines multi-agent rubric grading, in which several grading agents assess a submission, critique each other and revise their judgments, with an interview agent that asks students to justify specific steps and adapts its follow-up questions to their answers. **Every interview question is linked to a retrieved excerpt of the submission**, so instructors can compare the student's explanation with the cited passage, review all transcripts and override grades. The system is validated with deterministic tests of source handling, score aggregation and limits on correction attempts.

papers.title: The Information Limits of Neural Controlled Differential Equations Under Sparse Observations
papers.abstract: Neural controlled differential equations (Neural CDEs) evolve hidden states along continuous paths constructed by interpolating discrete observations. Sparse measurements leave the input between observation times undetermined, and admissible continuous paths consistent with the same data can produce different terminal states. We characterize this ambiguity for planar drivers with bounded speed. The set of compatible terminal states admits a leading-order zonotopic approximation determined by feasible signed areas and transported Lie brackets. Its projection onto a scalar prediction yields a computable, target-specific ambiguity certificate. We also study the number of measurements needed to reduce the remaining uncertainty. For nondegenerate planar CDEs, the optimal worst-case radius over deterministic adaptive sampling policies scales as $N^{-1}$ when speed is bounded and $N^{-2}$ when both speed and acceleration are bounded, where $N$ is the number of observation intervals. Synthetic experiments assess the certificate using admissible continuous completions and examine the role of path regularity.
papers.summary: Neural controlled differential equations (`Neural CDEs`) interpolate sparse observations into continuous paths, but many different paths fit the same data and can lead to different terminal states. For planar drivers with bounded speed, the authors show that the set of compatible terminal states has a leading-order zonotope approximation determined by feasible signed areas and transported Lie brackets, which yields a computable ambiguity certificate for any scalar prediction. They also prove that the best worst-case uncertainty radius under adaptive sampling **scales as N^-1 with bounded speed and N^-2 when acceleration is also bounded**, where N is the number of observation intervals. Synthetic experiments test the certificate and the role of path regularity.

papers.title: Hardware-Aware Design and Layout Selection in Quantum Reservoir Computing for Insurance Claims Forecasting
papers.abstract: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) processes temporal information through quantum dynamics, but it remains unclear whether small QRC models can forecast real data competitively with classical models and whether their predictions survive the transfer from ideal simulation to noisy hardware. We address both questions for a six-qubit gate-based reservoir that forecasts next-day motor-insurance claim counts. Five reservoir candidates were selected and frozen using hardware-native interaction graphs, Trotterized Ising dynamics, memory and measurement-robustness criteria, circuit cost, and calibrated-noise screening. On 232 held-out test days, the ideal candidates reached root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 5.66-6.12 claims/day, compared with 5.36 for ridge regression. For four of the five, the difference from ridge was not significant under a 95% block bootstrap, and their accuracy was comparable with classical recurrent and reservoir baselines. On the 156-qubit IBM Kingston processor, we ran 63 evaluations in 21 paired rounds, comparing hardware-aware, random-native, and Qiskit optimization level 1 layouts. Hardware-aware placement gave lower RMSE than Qiskit in every round, with a maximum transfer distortion of 7.59 claims/day (11.84 for Qiskit), and avoided the severe transfer failures seen for some random layouts. Most of the hardware distortion appeared as a systematic forecast shift, which a short hardware probe on training inputs detected before the test runs. Longer replay windows raised circuit cost without a consistent gain in forecasting accuracy or hardware transfer. Small QRC models can thus reach competitive accuracy on this task, and hardware-aware layout selection makes their transfer to IBM Kingston more consistent.
papers.summary: The study asks whether a small quantum reservoir computing (QRC) model can forecast real data competitively and still hold up when moved from ideal simulation to noisy hardware, using a six-qubit gate-based reservoir that predicts next-day motor-insurance claim counts. In simulation, the five frozen candidates reached RMSEs of 5.66 to 6.12 claims per day against 5.36 for ridge regression, a difference that was not significant for four of them. On IBM's 156-qubit `Kingston` processor, **hardware-aware qubit placement beat `Qiskit` level-1 layouts in every one of 21 paired rounds** and avoided the severe transfer failures seen with some random layouts. Most of the distortion introduced by hardware was a systematic forecast shift that a short probe on training inputs could detect before testing.

papers.title: EpiLoRA: Fusing Many LoRA Adapters into Low-Precision GEMMs for Serving and RL
papers.abstract: Low-rank adapters (LoRA) let one base model serve many fine-tuned variants: multi-tenant engines keep a single copy of the base and batch the requests of many tenants, each with its own adapter. As base models move to 8-bit (FP8) and 4-bit formats, their general matrix multiplications (GEMMs) become cheaper, but the adapters do not: engines run them as separate small GPU kernels beside the GEMM, whose latency takes a growing share of every decoding step. An adapter projects its input down to a low rank and back up, and our key observation is that the GEMM needs the down-projection only in its epilogue, the final stage in which it writes its output. EpiLoRA, a plugin for the vLLM engine, therefore launches the down-projection first and the low-precision GEMM as a dependent kernel that streams its weights meanwhile and adds every tenant's up-projection in its epilogue. On NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, EpiLoRA decodes for a single adapter with up to 24% lower time per token than vLLM's fastest configuration, and faster than SGLang and TensorRT-LLM; with many tenants, its adapter kernels deliver more throughput than vLLM's on most GPU-model pairs we tested. The same low-precision base also trains: a LoRA reinforcement-learning trainer that computes on the engine's FP8 weights needs no 16-bit copy, so a 27B model trains on one 48 GB GPU, and an engine that then keeps activations in 16 bits removes most of the remaining mismatch between the model generating training data and the one trained.
papers.summary: As base models move to FP8 and 4-bit formats, their matrix multiplications (GEMMs) get cheaper, but low-rank adapters (LoRA) still run as separate small GPU kernels that take up a growing share of each decoding step. `EpiLoRA`, a `vLLM` plugin, launches the adapter down-projection first and runs the low-precision GEMM as a dependent kernel that adds every tenant's up-projection in its final output stage (the epilogue). On NVIDIA Hopper GPUs it decodes a single adapter with **up to 24% lower time per token than vLLM's fastest configuration**, beats `SGLang` and `TensorRT-LLM`, and delivers higher multi-tenant adapter throughput on most configurations tested. The same FP8 base supports LoRA reinforcement-learning training without a 16-bit weight copy, so a 27B model trains on a single 48 GB GPU.

papers.title: When Latent Dynamics Meet Data Assimilation: A Benchmark of Koopman-Type Representations
papers.abstract: Koopman representations describe nonlinear dynamics through linear evolution in a transformed space, offering an attractive framework for their linear simplicity and generality. Yet these advantages do not necessarily translate into improved performance in deep latent data assimilation (LDA). We systematically compare seven representative methods and structural baselines across five systems spanning approximately periodic to strongly chaotic dynamics and a broad range of state dimensions. We evaluate forecast and assimilation accuracy, physical state recovery, latent-trajectory behavior, and dynamical consistency, and assess Gaussian error assumptions, objective convexity, and uniqueness of analysis solutions. Our results reveal a trade-off between representational flexibility and optimization tractability. Linear evolution of the latent state can stabilize short-term forecasts but restrict expressiveness in strongly chaotic and high-dimensional systems, without consistently improving assimilation accuracy. Parameterized linear operators offer greater flexibility, yet their joint optimization with the encoder--decoder remains nonconvex. Methods with closed-form analysis updates generally perform better and exhibit greater robustness in our experiments, although matrix inversion remains a computational bottleneck. These findings show that the practical benefits of Koopman structure depend on both sufficient observational information and the choice of assimilation procedure.
papers.summary: Koopman representations model nonlinear dynamics as linear evolution in a learned space, and this benchmark tests whether that structure actually helps deep latent data assimilation (LDA). Seven methods and structural baselines are compared on five systems ranging from roughly periodic to strongly chaotic, measuring forecast and assimilation accuracy, state recovery, and dynamical consistency, and checking assumptions such as Gaussian errors and the convexity of the objective. Linear latent evolution stabilizes short-term forecasts but limits expressiveness in chaotic, high-dimensional systems without consistently improving assimilation, while **methods with closed-form analysis updates generally perform best and are most robust**, at the cost of matrix inversion.

papers.title: Sequential auditing of connected forecast errors under partial observations
papers.abstract: Graph forecasting systems often rely on prediction intervals to quantify uncertainty across connected locations, but the true outcomes needed for evaluation may be only partially observed. We study how an auditor can selectively retrieve missing outcomes to determine whether there exists a connected group whose outcomes violate the same side of their respective forecast intervals. The audit stops when the observed labels determine the event or the query budget is exhausted. On three public graph time series, MOMS reduces mean queries by 19.6% to 38.5% relative to screened random acquisition when 30% of labels are hidden. Under localized masking on METR-LA, shortest witness finds more positive cases within ten queries, although the difference depends on node ordering. Direct component traversal reproduces all 9,696 screened random traces without enumerating connected subsets. The experiments show that reducing queries to a decision does not necessarily improve early event discovery or reduce local computation.
papers.summary: Graph forecasting systems issue prediction intervals for connected locations, but the true outcomes needed to check them may be only partly observed. The authors study how an auditor can choose which missing outcomes to retrieve in order to decide whether some connected group of locations violates the same side of its forecast intervals, stopping once the answer is settled or the query budget runs out. On three public graph time series with 30% of labels hidden, the `MOMS` strategy **reduces mean queries by 19.6% to 38.5%** compared with screened random acquisition. However, fewer queries to reach a decision does not necessarily mean earlier discovery of violations or less local computation.

papers.title: What Is This Memory Useful For? Measuring Task-Conditioned Utility in Long-Term Agent Memory
papers.abstract:
A stored experience may answer one future question and offer little help with another. We measure this task-conditioned utility rather than assigning each memory a single importance score. A task-blind writer stores a memory without seeing the later task; a frozen reader then answers that task with and without the memory, using identical filler. A cost ledger records the resources used to form, store and expose the memory.
  On single-call factual-recall tasks built from LongMemEval-V2 web-agent memories, the same memory helps more when it contains information needed for the answer. Its mean paired reward gain on these answer-bearing task pairs exceeds that on matched-control pairs by $+0.33$ (95% interval $+0.21$ to $+0.46$). The tested task-blind summaries and structured records yield smaller gains than Raw, including at fixed total context; a budget sweep is consistent with retention of answer-bearing content contributing to the difference. The bearing--control contrast remains positive in a new session with randomized memory position and under a second reader, although individual memory--task labels change. Generic retrieval performs above chance but misses most screen-defined answer-bearing memories. The factual-recall gains do not extend to the tested software-engineering and scientific-coding benchmarks, where even raw memories have no measurable effect. We provide a public, versioned Conditional Memory Utility Dataset of paired measurements and costs. The practical takeaway is to evaluate memory compression by the task utility it preserves alongside its costs. Task-conditioned measurements make this comparison possible; their stability must also be checked.
papers.summary: Instead of giving each stored agent memory a single importance score, the authors measure how much it helps with a specific later task: a writer stores the memory without seeing the task, a frozen reader answers with and without it, and a ledger records the costs of forming, storing and exposing it. On factual-recall tasks built from `LongMemEval-V2` web-agent memories, memories containing the needed information give **a +0.33 higher paired reward gain than matched controls**, and raw memories beat task-blind summaries and structured records even at a fixed total context size. Generic retrieval misses most of the memories that contain the answer, and none of the memories, raw ones included, measurably help on the software-engineering and scientific-coding benchmarks tested. The authors release a versioned `Conditional Memory Utility Dataset` of paired measurements and costs.

papers.title: Accelerating FastDEC Clustering Algorithm with GPUs
papers.abstract: Fast Dominance Estimation Clustering (FastDEC) is an efficient variant of Density Peak Clustering (DPC) that achieves high clustering quality through dominance-based density estimation, but remains constrained by the computational cost of exact k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) construction and dominance component (DC) processing. We present SymWarp-FastDEC, a GPU-accelerated implementation of FastDEC. At its core is SymTrikNN, an exact self-k-NN kernel that exploits search symmetry using upper-triangular traversal and warp-cooperative top-k selection. We also introduce WP-DC, a warp-parallel DC reduction algorithm designed for modern GPUs. Combined with memory-adaptive execution planning and stream scheduling, WP-DC eliminates DC reduction as a runtime bottleneck. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that SymWarp-FastDEC produces clustering outputs identical to the original FastDEC on all evaluated equivalence benchmarks. Compared with a FastDEC variant using FAISS GpuIndexFlatL2 for exact k-NN search, our approach achieves approximately 1.7x to 4.9x higher end-to-end performance, with the advantage generally increasing with dimensionality. Compared with the original single-threaded Python FastDEC implementation, speedups reach approximately 2.5 x 10^4 in a very high-dimensional case where its k-d-tree-based search degrades; this extreme result is not representative of typical acceleration.
papers.summary: Fast Dominance Estimation Clustering (`FastDEC`), a variant of Density Peak Clustering, is limited by the cost of exact k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) search and dominance component (DC) processing. `SymWarp-FastDEC` moves it to the GPU with `SymTrikNN`, an exact self-k-NN kernel that exploits search symmetry through upper-triangular traversal and warp-cooperative top-k selection, and `WP-DC`, a warp-parallel DC reduction. The outputs are identical to the original `FastDEC`, and the system runs **1.7x to 4.9x faster end to end than a FAISS-based GPU variant**, with the advantage generally growing with dimensionality.

papers.title: Camera Radar LiDAR Fusion via Point-Cloud Projection for Multi-Task Learning
papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles require robust perception systems to operate safely under diverse environmental conditions. While cameras provide high-resolution visual data, their performance significantly degrades in low-light and adverse weather. High Definition (HD) radar offers superior reliability and angular resolution under such conditions but lacks rich visual feature recognition. LiDAR, though expensive, delivers highly precise distance measurements and dense point clouds. Each sensor exhibits unique trade-offs, necessitating the development of advanced sensor fusion algorithms to harness complementary strengths while minimizing computational complexity and maintaining accuracy. In this study, the proposed fusion architecture performs early fusion by combining camera images with perspective-view point cloud data from HD radar and LiDAR sensors. The proposed model is trained to detect vehicles and segment free drivable space simultaneously. Experiments are performed on the RADIal dataset where we demonstrate that fusing point cloud data with camera images in front-view surpasses the performances of the most recent standalone and fusion models.
papers.summary: Cameras degrade in low light and bad weather, high-definition (HD) radar is robust but poor at recognizing visual features, and LiDAR is precise but expensive, so autonomous driving perception benefits from fusing all three. The proposed architecture performs early fusion by projecting radar and LiDAR point clouds into the camera's front view and trains a single model to detect vehicles and segment drivable free space at the same time. On the `RADIal` dataset, **front-view fusion of point clouds with camera images outperforms recent standalone and fusion models**.

papers.title: We Ran a Research Sprint With AI. The AI Worked. The Research Didn't
papers.abstract: Generative AI tools for research are widely deployed, yet individual productivity gains do not guarantee better team research. We argue that how AI use is structured matters alongside access. Personal AI tools may amplify two failures under deadline pressure: a consumption bottleneck, in which generation outpaces team-visible evaluation, and AI-induced research silos, in which private human-AI loops displace shared decision-making. We motivate this position with a mechanism-generating pilot: a 100-minute research sprint with twelve researchers in three independently operating teams, within a seventeen-person session. Both patterns recurred across teams and evidence sources. Of 33 logged AI interactions, one was accepted outright and 27 lacked a recorded disposition; missing records alone do not establish absent evaluation. A parallel autonomous pipeline produced a complete draft without in-session human evaluation, illustrating production capacity rather than comparative quality. We propose Human-AI-Human collaboration: an interaction topology in which AI connects researchers' contexts and supports inspectable collective evaluation and decision-making. The pilot does not isolate AI-specific effects from time pressure or workflow practices. We close with seven modular, falsifiable design hypotheses, prioritizing shared context and team-visible evaluation checkpoints for controlled follow-up.
papers.summary: The authors argue that the way AI use is organized in a research team matters as much as access to AI tools. A pilot 100-minute research sprint with twelve researchers in three teams surfaced two recurring failures: generation outpacing the team's ability to evaluate it, and private human-AI loops replacing shared decision-making. **Of 33 logged AI interactions, only one was accepted outright and 27 had no recorded disposition**, and a parallel autonomous pipeline produced a full draft that no human evaluated during the session. The authors propose a "Human-AI-Human" collaboration structure built around shared context and team-visible evaluation checkpoints, and offer seven falsifiable design hypotheses, while acknowledging that the pilot cannot separate AI effects from time pressure.

papers.title: Balancing Chain-of-Thought and Answer Supervision for Small Language Models on Medical Question Answering
papers.abstract: Small language models (<=9B parameters) can support local medical question answering (QA) while reducing privacy and latency concerns, but effective fine-tuning remains challenging. This paper compares two chain-of-thought (CoT) supervised fine-tuning methods: Uniform-across-Sequence (UaS), which applies equal loss weighting to the full CoT-and-answer sequence, and Segment-weighted (SwS), which separately weights CoT and answer losses. We evaluate six general- and medical-domain models on multiple-choice QA (MedQA and EMS-MCQA) and free-text QA (Med-O1). Results show that neither method is universally best: on multiple-choice QA (MedQA and EMS-MCQA), SwS generally performs better, with general-purpose models benefiting most; notably, Qwen3.5-4B improves by up to 44.8% over its zero-shot baseline on MedQA. In contrast, medical-domain models show smaller or even negative gains on MCQs. On free-text QA (Med-O1), UaS performs best for nearly all models and provides consistent improvements across both model types, with the 3B Llama-3.2 model approaching the performance of much larger 7B medical-domain models. We also find that excessively long CoT generation is associated with lower performance in some models on either multiple-choice or free-text QA tasks, suggesting that limiting the CoT length during training may benefit selected models. Overall, the results show that CoT loss weighting should be matched to the task format and the knowledge already encoded in the base model, rather than using a single fine-tuning strategy for all clinical QA tasks.
papers.summary: Small language models (9B parameters or fewer) can answer medical questions locally, which reduces privacy and latency concerns, but the best way to fine-tune them with chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision is unclear. The study compares Uniform-across-Sequence (`UaS`) loss weighting, which weights reasoning and answer tokens equally, with Segment-weighted (`SwS`) weighting, which weights them separately, across six models on `MedQA`, `EMS-MCQA` and `Med-O1`. `SwS` generally wins on multiple-choice questions, with **`Qwen3.5-4B` improving up to 44.8% over zero-shot on `MedQA`**, while `UaS` is best on free-text QA, bringing the 3B `Llama-3.2` close to 7B medical models. Overly long CoT outputs are associated with lower accuracy in some models.

papers.title: Do We Still Need Rotation-Invariant Architectures? A Statistical Robustness Benchmark for Point Cloud Classification
papers.abstract: A substantial line of work builds rotation invariance directly into point cloud architectures. We benchmark 10 architectures (PointNet, PointNet++, DGCNN, RIConv, RIConv++, RISurConv, PointMLP, PointTransformer, and the equivariant VN-PointNet and VN-DGCNN) across 5 domains under pose, noise, and occlusion, and analyze the results with confirmatory hypothesis tests rather than point estimates. The three rotation-invariant (RI) architectures achieve the best pose robustness but rank among the lowest on noise robustness in 4 of 5 domains. We ask whether this cost is intrinsic to invariance or specific to how invariance is obtained. We retrain all 10 architectures unchanged, with a simple invariance loss on the embedding and three training seeds each, and evaluate all models on the independently designed ModelNet40-C. Invariance training transfers narrowly but reliably. It improves exactly the corruption families its perturbations target wherever the baseline has headroom (mean occlusion +10.5, lidar +13.4 percentage points of accuracy). At matched training budget the best standard backbone and the best RI architecture end on par on unseen corruptions (within 2.5 percentage points in every seed), and invariance-trained RIConv++ is the most seed-stable top model. Once rotation augmentation is widened, standard backbones concede only a flat, angle-independent accuracy offset under full-sphere rotation. We release the benchmark along with a package for analyzing point cloud robustness and reproducing our results.
papers.summary: The benchmark tests whether point cloud architectures with built-in rotation invariance are still needed, comparing 10 models including `PointNet++`, `DGCNN`, `RIConv++`, `PointTransformer` and the equivariant `VN-DGCNN` under pose, noise and occlusion across 5 domains, with confirmatory hypothesis tests rather than single point estimates. The rotation-invariant (RI) architectures are the most robust to pose changes but among the least robust to noise in 4 of 5 domains. After retraining every model with a simple embedding invariance loss and evaluating on `ModelNet40-C`, **the best standard backbone and the best RI architecture finish within 2.5 percentage points of each other on unseen corruptions**, and with wider rotation augmentation, standard backbones lose only a flat accuracy offset under full-sphere rotation.

papers.title: P$^2$-MOPD: Accelerating Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation via Parameter Priors
papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation consolidates expert capabilities by supervising student-generated trajectories, whereas task arithmetic offers a training-free alternative through linear parameter combinations. We view the linear combination of student and expert parameters as a single differentiable model and propose P$^2$-MOPD, which jointly optimizes the mixing coefficients and the student weights under the same on-policy distillation objective. Unlike task arithmetic, which stays within the span of the frozen student and expert parameters for any choice of merging coefficients, P$^2$-MOPD keeps the student trainable, so the experts act as parameter priors without confining it to this span. Across four domains at 1.7B and 4B scales, P$^2$-MOPD achieves faster and more balanced recovery than MOPD from the same initialization, surpassing its final average recovery in half the training steps. At the end of training, our 1.7B model reaches 94.7% average recovery, versus 80.9% for MOPD.
papers.summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (`MOPD`) merges the skills of several expert models by supervising trajectories the student generates, while task arithmetic merges models without training by combining their parameters linearly. `P^2-MOPD` treats the linear mix of student and expert parameters as one differentiable model and trains both the mixing coefficients and the student weights under the distillation objective, so the experts act as parameter priors without restricting the student to their span. Across four domains at 1.7B and 4B scale, it surpasses MOPD's final recovery in half the training steps, and **the 1.7B model reaches 94.7% average recovery versus 80.9% for MOPD**.

papers.title: Forget What Comes Next: LLM Unlearning via Statistical Independence
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can memorize and reproduce fragments of their training data, raising privacy and legal concerns that motivate machine unlearning. Yet poisoned training examples can remain statistically detectable after unlearning, which raises the question of whether current unlearning objectives remove what the model has memorized at all. In this work, we introduce PINT, a novel algorithm for machine unlearning that uses the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) to reduce the statistical dependence between tokens to be forgotten and the internal representations used to predict them. We formally relate our HSIC-based objective to Exact Memorization through a computable upper bound, connecting the training objective directly to the model's ability to reproduce the forgotten tokens. In extensive experiments, we compare forgetting-utility trade-offs across eight settings with models up to 7B parameters and demonstrate scalability to 70B parameter models. Our evaluations cover unlearning Gaussian poisons, personal information, hazardous knowledge in biology and cybersecurity, and copyrighted books and news articles. PINT achieves the strongest forgetting-utility trade-off on average and is the only method to make Gaussian poisons undetectable while maintaining near-original model utility. Code is available at: https://github.com/shkabrii/PINT
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can memorize training data, and poisoned examples often remain statistically detectable after unlearning, which suggests current methods do not fully remove what was memorized. `PINT` uses the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) to reduce the statistical dependence between the tokens to forget and the internal representations that predict them, and the authors connect this objective to exact memorization through a computable upper bound. Evaluated on Gaussian poisons, personal information, hazardous biology and cybersecurity knowledge, and copyrighted text with models up to 7B parameters, and scaled to 70B, PINT achieves the best average forgetting-utility trade-off and is **the only method that makes Gaussian poisons undetectable while preserving near-original utility**.

papers.title: Sampling Interventional Distributions with Orthogonal MMD Flow
papers.abstract: Many causal inference problems require sampling from interventional outcome distributions rather than estimating low-dimensional summaries. Existing approaches often rely on fitting generative models of the target distribution together with additional nuisance components, which can be computationally demanding for high-dimensional outcomes. We propose Interventional Maximum Mean Discrepancy Flow (IMMD-Flow), a particle-based method that instead represents the target interventional distribution through its kernel mean embedding. This kernel embedding admits a doubly robust, Neyman-orthogonal estimator with finite-sample guarantees and can be efficiently reused to sample from the interventional distribution via MMD gradient flow. IMMD-Flow accommodates both hard and soft interventions, admits theoretical guarantees for estimation and particle approximation, and extends to high-dimensional image outcomes through frozen encoders. Across image-based benchmarks, IMMD-Flow matches or improves upon state-of-the-art generative approaches while showing significant speed advantages.
papers.summary: Many causal inference problems require sampling from the full distribution of outcomes under an intervention, not just estimating averages, and existing generative approaches can be expensive for high-dimensional outcomes. Interventional Maximum Mean Discrepancy Flow (`IMMD-Flow`) represents the target distribution by its kernel mean embedding, which has a doubly robust estimator with finite-sample guarantees, and draws samples by moving particles along an MMD gradient flow. It handles both hard and soft interventions and extends to image outcomes through frozen encoders, and on image benchmarks it **matches or beats state-of-the-art generative approaches while running significantly faster**.
