papers.title: ProteoCraft: Protein Design as Proposal-Verification Search
papers.abstract: Protein-protein interactions underpin nearly all biological processes. Yet, designing proteins with desired interactions remains challenging due to the structural complexity governing molecular recognition. This study views protein design as a search optimization problem over a combinatorial sequence space under expensive structural evaluation. Toward this goal, we introduce a novel tree-based search framework, ProteoCraft, that employs approximate structural gradients from diffusion-based structure predictors as effective proposal policies to specify where the search should explore. Complete no-gradient inference of folding models separately assigns values to the resulting sequences, determining what is good. ProteoCraft allocates this verification budget through a coarse-to-fine paradigm: multi-site edits first explore distinct sequence basins, then verified promising states undergo strict single-site refinement. Across fourteen de novo binder-design settings spanning eight target proteins, five immune-relevant TCR-facing targets, and four localized CDR redesign tasks, ProteoCraft improves design quality and high-confidence yield. These improvements persist under independent AF2-IG and Rosetta-based interface evaluation. Prospective experimental validation further yielded an 82.9% binding hit rate for PD-L1 miniproteins, with a best measured KD of 0.879 nM, and confirmed binding of designed IFNAR2 VHH. Our code is available at https://github.com/smiles724/ProteoCraft_v1.
papers.summary: Designing proteins that bind a chosen target is treated here as a combinatorial search over sequences where every candidate evaluation is expensive, and `ProteoCraft` organizes that search as a tree in which approximate structural gradients from diffusion-based structure predictors propose where to edit while gradient-free folding-model inference scores the resulting sequences. The search budget is spent coarse-to-fine: multi-site edits first spread candidates across distinct sequence basins, then verified promising states get strict single-site refinement. Across fourteen de novo binder-design settings covering eight targets, five T-cell-receptor-facing immune targets, and four CDR redesign tasks, design quality and high-confidence yield improved, and the gains held under independent `AF2-IG` and `Rosetta` interface scoring. Wet-lab testing gave an **82.9% binding hit rate for PD-L1 miniproteins** with a best measured dissociation constant of 0.879 nM, plus confirmed binding for a designed IFNAR2 VHH.

papers.title: Ermakov--Based embeddings as a parameter-free layer for physics-informed neural networks
papers.abstract: Evolution equations with time-dependent coefficients force a neural solver to spend capacity on a scale that the equation already determines. We show that a single classical object, the Ermakov-Pinney scale function $\rho$, can be written into the input layer of a physics-informed neural network as a parameter-free embedding. One construction covers three problem families through the two signs of the Pinney constant $c$: linear diffusion ($c=-1$, $\omega\equiv0$), diffusion in a time-dependent confining trap ($c=-1$, $\omega\neq0$), and the quantum oscillator with time-dependent frequency ($c=+1$). An exact moment identity gives $\rho$ in closed form from the initial data alone, so no auxiliary network or knowledge of the solution is needed. Our central finding is comparative: each family requires a different component of the construction and has a different honest control. In family I, the diffusive-time reparametrisation alone reproduces most of the gain, so that family is a poor test of the idea and shows why an ablation is mandatory. In family II no time reparametrisation exists, the control degrades accuracy, and the amplitude prefactor becomes essential (40.8x). In family III the adiabatic approximation also fails, and the quadratic phase factor is what matters (5.7x). The method does not help when the reduced solution does not converge to a fixed point: its extrapolation advantage then disappears. The reduction itself is the classical scaling-variable change of the self-similar-asymptotics literature; what is new is the moment identity that makes it architectural for time-dependent coefficients, and the comparative anatomy above.
papers.summary: Evolution equations whose coefficients change over time make a physics-informed neural network (PINN) waste capacity learning a scale the equation already fixes, so the proposed fix writes the classical Ermakov-Pinney scale function into the input layer as a parameter-free embedding, obtained in closed form from the initial data via an exact moment identity. One construction covers linear diffusion, diffusion in a time-dependent confining trap, and the quantum oscillator with time-dependent frequency, depending on the sign of the Pinney constant. The headline is comparative rather than a single score: **each family needs a different component of the construction, with the amplitude prefactor worth 40.8x in the trapped-diffusion case and the quadratic phase factor 5.7x for the oscillator**, while plain time reparametrisation already captures most of the gain for simple diffusion — which the authors use to argue ablations are mandatory. The advantage disappears when the reduced solution does not converge to a fixed point.

papers.title: Stacking-Based Weighting for Large Language Bayes in M-Open Settings
papers.abstract: Large Language Bayes (LLB) transforms a natural language problem description into a collection of candidate probabilistic programs and performs inference within each model, combining their predictions using Bayesian model averaging. While this provides a flexible framework for probabilistic inference without manual model specification, the resulting candidate model set is often misspecified in practice, and likelihood-based aggregation can concentrate on a single model, under-representing uncertainty across the sampled models. We propose a stacking-based aggregation method for LLB that selects model weights by optimizing predictive performance rather than marginal likelihood, while preserving the original language-model-driven model generation and within-model inference pipeline. Because leave-one-out predictive quantities are intractable in latent-variable models, we derive a variational lower bound that yields a tractable ELBO-based stacking objective. Across real-world probabilistic inference tasks, our method achieves comparable predictive performance to Bayesian model averaging while yielding more dispersed model weights, reducing concentration on a single candidate model under misspecification.
papers.summary: `Large Language Bayes` turns a natural-language problem description into several candidate probabilistic programs, runs inference in each, and averages their predictions, but in practice the candidate set is misspecified and likelihood-based averaging tends to pile nearly all weight onto one program, understating uncertainty. The proposed alternative keeps the language-model program generation and within-model inference untouched and instead chooses weights by stacking, optimizing predictive performance rather than marginal likelihood. Because leave-one-out predictive quantities are intractable in latent-variable models, the authors derive a variational lower bound giving a tractable evidence-lower-bound stacking objective. On real inference tasks it matches Bayesian model averaging's predictive accuracy while producing **more dispersed model weights**, reducing concentration on a single candidate.

papers.title: One Mistake, Three Layers: Persistence Rules Under Depth Correlation
papers.abstract:
Probing frozen representations layer by layer is now standard practice, but reporting when a signal first becomes decodable requires a rule for reading a depth curve, and the obvious rule is wrong. On synthetic curves with known ground truth, requiring a probe score to exceed a null-calibrated threshold for three consecutive stages reports an onset nineteen stages early under transformer-like depth correlation, with every resample returning an onset. The failure follows from correlation between neighboring layers, a hazard known in neuroimaging but not, to our knowledge, checked for depth curves.
  We give an estimator whose error rate is calibrated rather than assumed. Null trajectories are built by permuting labels within each evaluation unit and holding each permutation fixed across depth, preserving the correlation structure the rule must survive; thresholds are per-layer order statistics; and the persistence requirement is calibrated rather than chosen.
  Applied to pocket information in a frozen co-folding trunk, stratifying 1,820 post-cutoff targets by protein-family and pocket familiarity, the five-stage rule fires on 4 to 7 per cent of null trajectories against a nominal 5 per cent and the three-stage rule on 12 to 17: the synthetic failure reproduces on real data. Pocket membership is decodable above threshold at all 48 blocks in all four regimes, so the onset cannot discriminate them; the pre-declared accumulation depth does, and is latest for familiar families with structurally novel pockets in every feature set. That regime is also the weakest, by a margin surviving controls for length, pocket measure and alignment depth.
  Separately, a widely used public co-folding checkpoint loads against its own code with 128 trunk parameters missing; those would be randomly initialized, and every representation extracted would be partly noise while appearing normal.
papers.summary: Layer-by-layer probing of frozen representations usually reports the depth at which a signal first becomes decodable, and the common rule — a probe score beating a null-calibrated threshold for three consecutive layers — turns out to be badly miscalibrated because neighbouring layers are correlated, a hazard long known in neuroimaging. On synthetic curves with known ground truth that rule **fires nineteen stages early and never fails to report an onset**; a corrected estimator builds null trajectories by permuting labels within each evaluation unit and holding the permutation fixed across depth, uses per-layer order statistics as thresholds, and calibrates the persistence requirement rather than picking it. Applied to pocket information in a frozen co-folding trunk over 1,820 post-cutoff targets, the three-stage rule fires on 12-17% of null trajectories against a nominal 5%, onset fails to distinguish any of four familiarity regimes, and a pre-declared accumulation-depth measure does. Separately, the authors report that a widely used public co-folding checkpoint loads against its own code with 128 trunk parameters missing and silently randomly initialized.

papers.title: Must AI Spell It Out? Pragmatic Comprehension of Alerts in a Time-Critical Task
papers.abstract: Assistive systems typically tell users everything, often spending time and attention on what a user already knows, leaving less for what happens next. People, on the other hand, leave out what they expect the listener can supply. Can people use their prior knowledge to understand an incomplete message when the speaker is a machine though? We studied this pragmatic comprehension in a monitoring task controlling users' prior knowledge and the available time to detect critical situations. In a preregistered study (N=114), we compared a pragmatic planner that reasons over a model of the listener's knowledge to decide what to say, when, and how explicitly, with a baseline specifying problems fully in onset order. Participants resolved underspecified alerts almost as reliably as fully specified ones and sooner, detected more problems, and rated the pragmatic assistant helpful more often, with no increase in reported mental demand. Our findings show that people can recover what the system left implicit and that pragmatic communication can support effective assistance under the constraints of a changing world.
papers.summary: Assistive systems tend to state problems in full, spending the user's limited time and attention on things they already know, whereas human speakers omit what the listener can infer — and whether people extend that cooperative inference to a machine speaker was untested. A preregistered study with 114 participants in a time-critical monitoring task compared a pragmatic planner that reasons over a model of the listener's knowledge to decide what to say, when, and how explicitly against a baseline that fully specified every problem in onset order. Participants **resolved underspecified alerts almost as reliably as fully specified ones and did so sooner, detected more problems, and rated the pragmatic assistant helpful more often, with no rise in reported mental demand**.

papers.title: Measuring Model-Specific Alignment Drift in LLM-Based Opinion Dynamics
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used as synthetic participants in opinion-dynamics experiments, often assuming that an agent's behaviour is fully determined by its prompt. We test this assumption with a framework in which LLM agents discuss a contested policy issue over repeated rounds while their stance is quantified by a fixed psychometric instrument independent of any dynamics model. Across six LLMs, committed personas are intrinsically stable: in each of the five models tested without peer input, every agent keeps its assigned side for 20 rounds. The observed loss of alignment under discussion is therefore interaction-induced, we call it alignment drift, and model-specific: gpt-4.1 keeps opinion clusters apart, claude-sonnet-5 holds them partially, and gpt-5.6-sol and claude-opus-5 abandon them. Under selective attention, one LLM maintains separated opinion clusters under stance-homophilous attention. Qualitative profiles persist at doubled population and horizon and on a second issue. Such heterogeneity makes the LLM choice a first-class validity variable for social simulation.
papers.summary: Studies that use large language model agents as synthetic participants in opinion-dynamics experiments generally assume the prompt fully determines behaviour, and this work tests that by having agents debate a contested policy issue over repeated rounds while a fixed psychometric instrument, independent of any dynamics model, measures their stance. Without peer input, committed personas are intrinsically stable: across five models every agent held its assigned side for 20 rounds, so **any loss of alignment comes from interaction and is strongly model-specific** — `gpt-4.1` keeps opinion clusters separated, `claude-sonnet-5` partially, while `gpt-5.6-sol` and `claude-opus-5` abandon them. One model maintained separated clusters under stance-homophilous selective attention, and the qualitative profiles persisted at doubled population and horizon and on a second issue, which the authors read as making the choice of model a first-class validity variable for social simulation.

papers.title: Rapid Mean-Field Formation Transport with a Shared-Representation Neural Fokker-Planck Controller
papers.abstract: This paper develops a mean-field formation transport method with low online computational cost for large-scale multi-agent systems. Classical mean-field planners often require repeated solutions of coupled forward and backward partial differential equations, making online replanning computationally demanding. Density and control are therefore approximated by a common parameterized nonlinear map with separate scalar density and vector control outputs. Parameters are optimized using Fokker--Planck and initial-condition residuals, formation-matching costs on numerically simulated closed-loop particle trajectories, and control effort. Numerical computations are restricted to a bounded region of the state space, with an additional penalty on probability flux across its boundary. For the periodic-domain model, we establish well-posedness of the induced density evolution and bound the density-approximation error in terms of the dynamics and initial-condition residuals. Parameter optimization precedes online operation, during which controller coefficients remain fixed. Experiments quantify the accuracy--runtime trade-off relative to a mean-field planner, show lower transport error than classical feedback baselines, and demonstrate the benefits of the common parameterization.
papers.summary: Mean-field planners that steer large swarms into formations normally require repeatedly solving coupled forward and backward partial differential equations, which is too slow for online replanning. The approach here approximates density and control with a single parameterized nonlinear map that has separate scalar density and vector control outputs, fitted offline against Fokker-Planck and initial-condition residuals, formation-matching costs on simulated closed-loop particle trajectories, control effort, and a penalty on probability flux leaving a bounded region of state space; at run time the coefficients are frozen. For the periodic-domain model the authors prove well-posedness of the induced density evolution and bound the density-approximation error by the dynamics and initial-condition residuals. Experiments quantify the accuracy-runtime trade-off against a full mean-field planner and show **lower transport error than classical feedback baselines**, with ablations supporting the shared parameterization.

papers.title: SLATE: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Long-Horizon API Selection in E-commerce Tool Use
papers.abstract: Enterprises increasingly want LLM agents to automate standard operating procedures over their software stacks -- mapping each step of a procedure to the right call among thousands of internal APIs, without hand-authored step-to-API mappings. The core difficulty is API selection at scale: choosing and composing the correct tools over a long horizon, judged only by whether the overall task succeeds. Current tool-use benchmarks do not test this regime -- they expose only a handful of tools, evaluate single-step invocation, or grade multi-step behavior with subjective LLM-as-a-judge scores that penalize valid alternative trajectories. We introduce SLATE (Synthetic Large-scale API Toolkit for E-commerce), a large-scale benchmark that tests large-toolset, long-horizon API selection in a realistic enterprise domain. SLATE couples (i) queries decomposed into hierarchical, tool-grounded procedures over a ~1,000-tool e-commerce library, (ii) a deterministic, context-aware simulator that returns recorded outputs for matching calls and default responses otherwise, and (iii) an end-to-end task-success metric -- a task succeeds when it reaches every reference outcome -- that credits diverse-but-valid trajectories while remaining fully automatic and reproducible. Experiments with six open decision models and the language models they are built on, from 3B to 12B parameters, show that even the best model completes only 5.0% of the tasks, establishing SLATE as a challenging testbed for reliable enterprise tool use. We release SLATE, its simulator, and the evaluation harness at https://geshijoker.github.io/slate/
papers.summary: Enterprises want agents to execute standard operating procedures across internal software, which means picking and composing the right calls from thousands of APIs over a long horizon without hand-written step-to-API mappings — a regime existing tool-use benchmarks miss by exposing only a few tools, grading single invocations, or scoring multi-step behaviour with subjective LLM-as-a-judge rubrics that punish valid alternative routes. `SLATE` (Synthetic Large-scale API Toolkit for E-commerce) pairs queries decomposed into hierarchical tool-grounded procedures over a roughly 1,000-tool e-commerce library with a deterministic context-aware simulator and an end-to-end success metric that counts a task solved only when every reference outcome is reached, which credits diverse-but-valid trajectories while staying automatic and reproducible. Across six open decision models and their underlying language models from 3B to 12B parameters, **the best model finishes only 5.0% of tasks**. The benchmark, simulator, and evaluation harness are released.

papers.title: A Guideline-Grounded Multi-Agent Framework for Personalized Exercise Prescription from Clinical and Wearable Data
papers.abstract: Translating population-level exercise guidance into individualized prescriptions requires integrating clinical and wearable data, including diagnoses, medications, functional limitations, and baseline activity, with condition-specific recommendations, a process difficult to scale beyond specialist rehabilitation settings. We developed FITTER, a multi-agent framework that integrates these data with condition-specific guidance to generate personalized FITT-VP prescriptions and applies deterministic safety audit and repair to correct rule-checkable violations. We evaluated FITTER using data from 400 All of Us participants (300 cancer, 100 stroke) against five LLM comparators through computational evaluation, ablation, and structured clinician review. FITTER achieved 98.5% safety-constraint compliance versus 75.8-85.8% for comparators and showed greater quantitative dosing precision and guideline alignment. Cancer-cohort ablation identified safety audit and repair as the largest contributor to safety-constraint compliance. Clinicians reviewed 80 prescriptions across safety, personalization, instruction concreteness, anticipated effectiveness, and clinical acceptability. FITTER provides a clinician-facing approach integrating clinical and wearable data, guidance, and explicit safety constraints.

papers.summary: Turning population-level exercise guidelines into an individual prescription means reconciling diagnoses, medications, functional limitations, and baseline activity from clinical and wearable records with condition-specific recommendations, which rarely scales past specialist rehabilitation clinics. `FITTER` is a multi-agent framework that combines those inputs into personalized FITT-VP prescriptions (frequency, intensity, time, type, volume, progression) and then runs a deterministic safety audit that repairs rule-checkable violations. Evaluated on 400 `All of Us` participants (300 with cancer, 100 post-stroke) against five language-model comparators, it reached **98.5% safety-constraint compliance versus 75.8-85.8%**, with better dosing precision and guideline alignment; ablation on the cancer cohort attributed most of the safety gain to the audit-and-repair step, and clinicians reviewed 80 prescriptions across safety, personalization, concreteness, expected effectiveness, and acceptability.

papers.title: Thinking Fast, Trading Late: System One Decision Models vs the Market
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) read company news at scale, and backtests suggest that their readings predict stock returns. We ask how much of that predictability survives a test that rules out look-ahead, memorization and selection. We propose OLIVIA, a protocol for such tests: point-in-time inputs with company identities masked, selection on validation data only, an analysis plan frozen by cryptographic hash, and a test period unblinded once through a logged lock. We apply it to AI decision models, non-generative language models that return probabilities for typed questions, reading news about S&P 500 stocks: an open-weights model we fine-tuned on 2024-2025 data, three commercial models and standard baselines. The fine-tuned model's signal replicated on two validation quarters (daily information coefficients 0.055 and 0.065) but fell to 0.020 (t = 1.7) on the blinded January-July 2026 test. The commercial models' readings line up with the overnight move to the open (information coefficient 0.074 to 0.077) but not with the move after it, so the news is priced by the time a trader can act on it at the open. No model can tell over- from under-reaction, and no pre-registered strategy survives costs and a deflated Sharpe ratio. Commercial models identify masked companies in 62% to 74% of cases against a 28% baseline: masking hides names, not companies. The market reads the news first.
papers.summary: Backtests suggest language models reading company news can predict stock returns, and the question asked here is how much of that survives controls for look-ahead bias, memorization, and selection. `OLIVIA` is a protocol for that test: point-in-time inputs with company identities masked, model selection done only on validation data, an analysis plan frozen by cryptographic hash, and a test period unblinded exactly once through a logged lock. Applied to non-generative decision models reading S&P 500 news, a fine-tuned open-weights model replicated on two validation quarters (daily information coefficients 0.055 and 0.065) but **fell to 0.020 with a t-statistic of 1.7 on the blinded January-July 2026 test**, while commercial models' readings correlate with the overnight move to the open and not with anything after it, so the news is already priced by the time a trader can act. No model separates over- from under-reaction, no pre-registered strategy survives costs and a deflated Sharpe ratio, and the commercial models re-identify masked companies 62-74% of the time against a 28% baseline.

papers.title: FlagRot: Selective Rotation for Low-Bit KV Caches
papers.abstract: Long-context inference is bound by the KV cache, which 2-bit codes could shrink about sixfold if their error stays in check. The usual remedy rotates keys before quantizing, assuming rotation always helps. However, we observe that it does not: rotation flattens a spiky piece of a key but can give a flat one a new peak, and both coexist within one key. We therefore propose FlagRot, which stores each 32-channel piece rotated or as is, whichever has the smaller calibrated attention error, and rotates the query instead when reading. We further show that how often to decide follows the quantization axis: per-channel caches such as KIVI need one decision per head, at no write cost, while per-token caches decide per key, with the choice stored in existing sign bits. At 2.5 bits per value, FlagRot lowers the twelve-model KL divergence of KIVI from 18.7 to 12.4 x 10^-3, below RotateKV on 9 of 12 models. Served as a vLLM plugin, it raises RULER at 128k tokens by +2.9 points and the LongBench v1 mean by +0.4 to +1.9 points on the three of four models where 2-bit KIVI loses accuracy. It also lowers the error of 4-bit integer and FP4 caches.
papers.summary: Long-context inference is limited by the key-value cache, and 2-bit codes would shrink it roughly sixfold if quantization error stayed bounded; the standard trick is to rotate keys first, on the assumption rotation always reduces error. The observation driving `FlagRot` is that it does not — rotation flattens spiky channel groups but can introduce a new peak in flat ones, and both kinds coexist inside a single key — so each 32-channel piece is stored rotated or unrotated depending on which gives smaller calibrated attention error, with the query rotated instead at read time. How often to decide follows the quantization axis: per-channel caches like `KIVI` need one decision per head at no write cost, while per-token caches decide per key and hide the choice in existing sign bits. At 2.5 bits per value it **cuts twelve-model KL divergence for `KIVI` from 18.7 to 12.4 x 10^-3**, beats `RotateKV` on 9 of 12 models, and as a `vLLM` plugin raises `RULER` at 128k tokens by 2.9 points and `LongBench v1` means by 0.4-1.9 points where 2-bit `KIVI` loses accuracy.

papers.title: Whose startup does the AI back? An algorithm audit of reputation and demographic signals in LLM-assisted crowdfunding
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) assistants increasingly advise backers on which crowdfunding campaigns to support. LLMs have known race and gender problems, and it is unsettled whether they reproduce, erase, or reverse the discrimination documented in entrepreneurial finance. We ask when, and through which decision process, LLM assistants use founders' gender and ethnicity. In a pre-specified choice-based conjoint experiment, seven LLMs chose among five synthetic campaigns with independently randomized quality signals and founder names, under three backer personas and a persona-free control (40,248 responses). By default, founder names barely matter: under budget-conscious and delivery-focused personas, gender and Black-name effects are statistically equivalent to zero. When the backer wants to support underrepresented creators, the models favor Black-signaled (+8.1 percentage points; positive in all seven models) and female-signaled (+5.1) founders. They do so most strongly among near-tied campaigns and for the founder who alone carries the signal, and they almost never name gender or ethnicity in their reasons. The results fit an agency account of algorithmic discrimination: an aligned assistant takes its demographic preferences from its user rather than from its training data.
papers.summary: As language model assistants start advising people on which crowdfunding campaigns to back, it is unclear whether they reproduce, erase, or invert the race and gender discrimination documented in entrepreneurial finance. A pre-specified choice-based conjoint experiment had seven models pick among five synthetic campaigns with independently randomized quality signals and founder names, under three backer personas plus a persona-free control, yielding 40,248 responses. By default founder names barely register — under budget-conscious and delivery-focused personas, gender and Black-name effects are statistically equivalent to zero — but **when the backer says they want to support underrepresented creators, the models favor Black-signaled founders by 8.1 percentage points (positive in all seven models) and female-signaled founders by 5.1**, most strongly among near-tied campaigns, and almost never cite gender or ethnicity in their stated reasons. The authors read this as an agency account of algorithmic discrimination: the assistant takes demographic preferences from its user rather than its training data.

papers.title: When Music Needs Meaning: Semantic Communication as a Transformative Enabler for the Musical Metaverse
papers.abstract: The Musical Metaverse (MM) enables geographically distributed musicians, audiences, sound engineers, and AI agents to interact through synchronized audio, visual, kinematic, and haptic streams, imposing latency, synchronization, bandwidth, and scalability requirements that are difficult to satisfy with conventional bit-level communication. This paper argues that semantic communication, understood here as the transmission of musically meaningful information rather than raw audio-visual-haptic samples, provides a principled communication paradigm for the MM. We define the MM from a communication perspective and derive modality-specific require ments; propose a three-pillar framework for musical semantic communication comprising semantics extraction, semantic-aware orchestration, and cross-modal semantic synchronization; survey representative work across semantic communication, music AI and edge orchestration, identifying the gaps that prevent their integration; and propose a semantic-first reference architecture based on device-side semantic encoders, edge semantic routers, and cross-modal semantic synchronization. The resulting framework positions the MM as a concrete and demanding use case for 6G semantic communication.
papers.summary: Shared virtual music venues, where distributed musicians, audiences, sound engineers, and AI agents interact over synchronized audio, visual, kinematic, and haptic streams, impose latency, synchronization, bandwidth, and scalability demands that bit-level transmission struggles to meet. The position taken is that **semantic communication — sending musically meaningful information rather than raw samples — is the right paradigm**, developed through a communication-oriented definition of the setting, modality-specific requirements, a three-pillar framework of semantics extraction, semantic-aware orchestration, and cross-modal semantic synchronization, and a survey of semantic communication, music AI, and edge orchestration that names the gaps blocking their integration. The paper closes with a semantic-first reference architecture built from device-side semantic encoders, edge semantic routers, and cross-modal synchronization, framed as a demanding use case for 6G.

papers.title: Measure Before You Repair: An Explainable Agent for Blind Restoration of Multi-Artifact 3-D MRI
papers.abstract: A brain MRI scan can carry an unknown mix of artifacts, so restoration has to be blind, yet most deep-learning methods are built to correct one known artifact. We present Dx-Rx, an agent in which a multimodal large language model (MLLM) measures suspected artifacts before it repairs them. To our knowledge, it is the first agent to restore whole 3-D MRI volumes, whereas earlier MRI agents restore 2-D slices. In a loop, it looks at slices of the 3-D volume, calls five diagnostic tools (noise, spike, ghosting, bias field, motion) and four restoration tools in any order it chooses, checks each repair, can return to any earlier version to change the order, and ends with a radiology-style report of its diagnostic reasons, the repairs it applied and their results. We simulated up to five artifacts on 148 whole 3-D T1-weighted volumes, at levels calibrated to radiologists' grades of real scans. An MLLM that only looked at the image, as earlier MRI agents do, removed at most 19.7 % of the artifact error. With the best of five MLLMs, Dx-Rx removed a mean 64.5 %, nearly matching the 64.6 % of the same tools given the ground-truth artifacts, which are never known for a clinical scan. With all five models, it made no volume worse and was on par with or better than an expert rule-based pipeline built from the same tools (62.3 %). Code and demo are public at https://itu-biai.github.io/measure-before-you-repair.
papers.summary: A brain MRI can contain an unknown mixture of artifacts, so restoration has to work blind, while most deep-learning correctors assume one known artifact type. `Dx-Rx` is an agent in which a multimodal large language model (MLLM) measures suspected artifacts before repairing them: it inspects slices of the full 3-D volume, calls five diagnostic tools (noise, spike, ghosting, bias field, motion) and four restoration tools in any order, checks each repair, can roll back to an earlier version to change the order, and ends with a radiology-style report of its reasoning and results. On 148 whole T1-weighted volumes with up to five simulated artifacts calibrated to radiologist grades, an MLLM looking only at the image removed at most 19.7% of artifact error, whereas **`Dx-Rx` with its best backbone removed 64.5%, essentially matching the 64.6% achieved by the same tools given ground-truth artifact labels**; across all five backbones it never made a volume worse and matched or beat an expert rule-based pipeline at 62.3%.

papers.title: Dory1.0-4B: A Looped Normalized-GPT
papers.abstract: We introduce Dory1.0-4B, a 4-billion-parameter looped (latent-recurrent) language model with elastic depth: a single checkpoint serves different inference compute budgets. Dory1.0-4B is built on a normalized Transformer (nGPT) backbone with interleaved sliding-window and full-attention layers, organized into an input block, a shared recurrent block, and an output block. At inference, the recurrent block can be applied a variable number of times. We pre-trained Dory1.0-4B on 6 trillion tokens. The first 4.5 trillion tokens were trained in NVFP4, and additional pre-training then extended the context length to 256K tokens. Next, we post-trained the model using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), with a difficulty-aware loop curriculum that routes harder prompts to deeper loops. Increasing the loop count improves accuracy, with the largest gains on coding, agentic, and long-context benchmarks. With two or more loops, Dory1.0-4B outperforms larger models such as Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma 4 12B, and Gemma 4 26B-A4B on average across 12 benchmarks. Looping also makes Dory1.0-4B more token-efficient on agentic benchmarks: with four loops, it generates 1.3-2.5x fewer tokens than with one loop, as the extra computation is spent in latent space rather than on longer outputs. To reduce memory during looping, Dory1.0-4B caches keys and values only from the last loop, keeping its KV-cache footprint equal to that of a non-looped model at any loop count while retaining most of the accuracy gains. We open-source the BF16, MXFP8, NVFP4, and GGUF quantized checkpoints.
papers.summary: `Dory1.0-4B` is a 4-billion-parameter latent-recurrent language model with elastic depth, meaning one checkpoint serves several inference compute budgets: a normalized-Transformer (`nGPT`) backbone with interleaved sliding-window and full attention is split into an input block, a shared recurrent block applied a variable number of times, and an output block. Pre-training ran over 6 trillion tokens (the first 4.5 trillion in NVFP4, then a context extension to 256K), followed by supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards using a difficulty-aware curriculum that routes harder prompts to deeper loops. More loops means more accuracy, with the largest gains on coding, agentic, and long-context work: **at two or more loops it beats the larger `Qwen3.5-9B`, `Gemma 4 12B`, and `Gemma 4 26B-A4B` on a 12-benchmark average**, and at four loops it emits 1.3-2.5x fewer tokens than at one because the extra computation happens in latent space. Caching keys and values only from the final loop holds the KV-cache footprint at non-looped size while keeping most of the gain, and BF16, MXFP8, NVFP4, and GGUF checkpoints are open-sourced.

papers.title: WASP-Mem: Let Agent Organize Procedural Memory. Human Spend Effort on Diagnosis
papers.abstract: LLM agents struggle to automate complex enterprise procedures because static, pre-built harness cannot capture proprietary policies, undocumented behaviors, or state-dependent recovery paths that surface only during execution. Procedural memory accrued from agent experience offers a training-free path to closing this gap -- yet unlike episodic records or semantic facts, it must consolidate repeated successes and diagnosed failures into reusable actions and recovery strategies. We introduce WASP-Mem (Wiki-based Agent-Synthesized Procedural Memory), a nimble but effective method that distills execution traces and feedback into persistent, interlinked wiki pages, enabling continual agent learning. On TheAgentCompany benchmark, WASP-Mem raises the checkpoint pass rate by 4.6-6.1% over the strongest baseline we compared across three models while requiring 57-61% less storage. We further present a systematic controlled study spanning consolidation method, feedback type, trace ingestion scope, and refinement rounds. Our results reveal that prescriptive knowledge organization such as human defined schemas and explicit deduplication rules hurts performance rather than closing the procedural-knowledge gap. In contrast, human diagnosis converts failed traces into corrective knowledge and drives sustained improvement: a single round of human diagnosis outperforms four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0-10.9%. These findings point to a simple division of labor: let agents organize procedural memory, and invest human effort where it matters most -- diagnosis.
papers.summary: Agents fail at enterprise procedures because a pre-built static harness cannot encode proprietary policies, undocumented system behaviour, or state-dependent recovery paths that only appear during execution, and procedural memory accumulated from experience offers a training-free way to close that gap — but it must consolidate repeated successes and diagnosed failures into reusable actions, not just store episodes or facts. `WASP-Mem` (Wiki-based Agent-Synthesized Procedural Memory) distils execution traces and feedback into persistent interlinked wiki pages that the agent keeps extending. On `TheAgentCompany` it raises checkpoint pass rate by 4.6-6.1% over the strongest baseline across three models while using 57-61% less storage. A controlled study over consolidation method, feedback type, trace ingestion scope, and refinement rounds finds that imposing human-defined schemas and explicit deduplication rules hurts rather than helps, while **one round of human diagnosis of failed traces beats four rounds of agent self-judgment by 7.0-10.9%**, suggesting agents should organize the memory and humans should spend their effort diagnosing.

papers.title: Characterizing Adversarial GEO via Implicit Brand Injection
papers.abstract: Generative search engines increasingly shape how users discover products, services, and commercial entities by generating answers from retrieved web content. This creates an opportunity to influence which brands appear in these answers by modifying the content available to the retrieval system. In this work, we study an adversarial generative engine optimization (GEO) setting in which a predefined brand is added to an article through a single contextually integrated mention. The challenge is to make the mention fit the surrounding article without making the content overtly promotional, while keeping it relevant enough to be retrieved and to influence the generated answer. To study this, we introduce Implicit Brand Injection (IBI), a multi-agent framework that identifies insertion locations, rewrites the selected sentence, verifies the edit, and selects the final candidate. To evaluate IBI at scale, we construct IBIBench, which contains 1,000 web articles and 60 synthetic brands across 12 diverse domains, with both endemic and non-endemic brand placements. We compare IBI with Direct Prompting and Best-of-N with ranking under an equivalent budget, evaluating insertion quality, target-chunk retrieval, and downstream brand propagation. Compared with the baselines, IBI produces insertions that better preserve semantics and disrupt perplexity less, while improving Hit@k across all evaluated cutoffs, query regimes, and placement settings. IBI achieves up to 82.2% Hit@10 and 0.74 MRR@10, while Brand Mention Rate (BMR) and Conditional Propagation (CP) reach up to 62.7% and 75.9%, respectively. These results show that a single brand mention can increase both retrieval exposure and brand visibility in generated responses, highlighting the need for defenses against implicit content manipulation in generative search.
papers.summary: Generative search engines answer from retrieved web pages, which means whoever controls that content can influence which brands surface in the answers; this work characterizes that exposure by studying what happens when a single contextually integrated brand mention is added to an article, so the text stays non-promotional yet relevant enough to be retrieved. `Implicit Brand Injection` is a multi-agent pipeline that picks an insertion point, rewrites the sentence, verifies the edit, and selects a final candidate, evaluated on `IBIBench` — 1,000 web articles and 60 synthetic brands over 12 domains, covering both brands native to a domain and unrelated ones — against direct prompting and best-of-N ranking at equal budget. The edits preserve semantics better and disturb perplexity less while improving retrieval Hit@k at every cutoff, query regime, and placement setting, reaching **82.2% Hit@10 and 0.74 MRR@10, with brand mention rates up to 62.7% in generated answers**. The authors frame the result as evidence that one sentence can move both retrieval exposure and answer-level brand visibility, arguing for defenses against this kind of content manipulation.

papers.title: Controlling Action-Head Co-Adaptation to VLM Representation Anisotropy
papers.abstract: Modern learning systems increasingly combine pretrained models with downstream heads. Despite the growing importance of such modular designs, how the downstream model co-adapts to the geometry of pretrained representations remains relatively underexplored. We study this problem through vision-language-action models (VLAs), where a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) conditions an action model for control. We find that the action model progressively concentrates its sensitivity on high-variance dimensions of the VLM outputs. Through controlled experiments across different backbone-head models, we further show that counteracting this sensitivity concentration can be beneficial under representation--task mismatch settings. Motivated by these observations, we introduce \emph{Adaptive Interface Equalizer} (AdaIE), a parameter-free mechanism that reweights pretrained representations according to the evolving downstream sensitivity during training. AdaIE improves VLA success rates on simulation benchmarks, with gains of up to $+5.28$ percentage points (pp) on RoboCasa-GR1 and $+1.68$ pp on RoboTwin 2.0, and achieves an average gain of $+19$ pp across five real-world manipulation tasks. It further generalizes to diffusion policies and world models, improving downstream performance in both settings. Our results highlight interface co-adaptation as an important optimization problem when coupling pretrained representations with downstream models.
papers.summary: Modular systems that bolt a trained head onto a frozen pretrained encoder are everywhere, but how the head adapts to the geometry of those pretrained features is little studied; the setting examined here is vision-language-action models (VLAs), where a pretrained vision-language model conditions an action model for robot control. The action model turns out to progressively concentrate its sensitivity on the highest-variance dimensions of the vision-language model's output, and controlled experiments across backbone-head pairs show that counteracting this concentration helps when representation and task are mismatched. `Adaptive Interface Equalizer` (`AdaIE`) is the resulting parameter-free mechanism, reweighting pretrained representations according to the head's evolving sensitivity during training; it adds up to 5.28 percentage points on `RoboCasa-GR1` and 1.68 on `RoboTwin 2.0`, with an **average 19-point gain across five real-world manipulation tasks**, and also transfers to diffusion policies and world models.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Identification of Tensegrity Prestress across Taut-Slack Transitions
papers.abstract: Prestress governs the stability, stiffness, and dynamic behavior of tensegrity structures, but it is not directly observable from sparse structural measurements, and it may decrease during service life. Under strong excitation, the cables may slacken and the dynamics become nonsmooth. Existing identification methods are limited to the taut regime, and physics-informed networks for tensegrities solve only the forward problem of predicting the response from known member parameters. This study formulates the inverse problem. Neural networks are trained on the equation-of-motion residual in constrained Cartesian coordinates, where the mass matrix is constant and the force densities enter linearly. The force densities, damping, and axial stiffness are trainable parameters, and the tension-only cable law is kept. A Fisher-information analysis shows, before inversion, which member parameters a record can determine. The method is tested on simulated planar tensegrity frames with up to five modules and a three-dimensional prism, and on measured records of a biomimetic leg and a full-scale tensegrity simplex. On the one-module frame, the identifiable force densities are recovered within 1.5% from noisy accelerations at half the free coordinates, on records with and without taut-slack transitions. Records with transitions determine members that taut records leave undetermined. On the five-module frame, a 16-cable two-span bridge, the median force-density error rises moderately, to 4.2%. On measured records, an identified spring stiffness is within 0.1% of its independently measured value on average, and the identified simplex prestress at 13 levels agrees with its cable force transducers to 2.9% root-mean-square.
papers.summary: Prestress sets the stability, stiffness, and dynamics of tensegrity structures but cannot be read directly from sparse sensors and decays in service, and under strong excitation slackening cables make the dynamics nonsmooth — existing identification methods only handle the taut regime, while physics-informed networks for tensegrities have only solved the forward problem. This work sets up the inverse problem by training networks on the equation-of-motion residual in constrained Cartesian coordinates, where the mass matrix is constant and force densities enter linearly, treating force densities, damping, and axial stiffness as trainable parameters while keeping the tension-only cable law; a Fisher-information analysis says in advance which parameters a given record can determine. On a one-module frame, identifiable force densities are recovered **within 1.5% from noisy accelerations at half the free coordinates**, and records that include taut-slack transitions pin down members that purely taut records leave undetermined; error rises to 4.2% median on a five-module 16-cable bridge, and on measured data an identified spring stiffness lands within 0.1% of its independent measurement while simplex prestress agrees with cable force transducers to 2.9% root-mean-square.

papers.title: Decision Transformer with Task-Aware Representations for Offline Meta-Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: To enable effective generalization in offline meta-RL, it is essential to accurately infer the underlying task through latent task representations, which provide a compact and transferable summary of task-specific characteristics for guiding policy generation. In this paper, we propose Contrastive Task-Aware Decision Transformer (CoTA-DT), a DT-based offline meta-RL framework that learns task representations by jointly integrating four complementary components: (i) contrastive learning from offline trajectories, (ii) alignment with natural-language task descriptions, (iii) one-step supervision via a task-conditioned world model, and (iv) long-term supervision via a task-conditioned Q function. The learned task representations are used as conditioning signals for a DT-based policy, enabling task-aware meta-policy learning. To further support generalization in both zero-shot and few-shot settings, we design a language-grounded, self-adaptive strategy that enables effective and reliable adaptation to unseen tasks. Notably, in CoTA-DT, the pretrained LLM serves as a shared backbone for language encoding, world modeling, Q-function estimation, and policy learning. This unified design facilitates parameter sharing, improving both efficiency and generalization. Extensive experiments across diverse offline meta-RL benchmarks demonstrate that CoTA-DT consistently outperforms prior methods, particularly in challenging zero-shot generalization scenarios.
papers.summary: Offline meta-reinforcement learning depends on inferring the task from logged data into a compact latent representation that a policy can condition on. `CoTA-DT` (Contrastive Task-Aware Decision Transformer) learns those representations from four complementary signals at once: contrastive learning over offline trajectories, alignment with natural-language task descriptions, one-step supervision from a task-conditioned world model, and long-horizon supervision from a task-conditioned Q function, then feeds the result to a Decision Transformer policy. A language-grounded self-adaptive strategy handles both zero-shot and few-shot adaptation to unseen tasks, and notably **a single pretrained language model serves as the shared backbone for language encoding, world modeling, Q-function estimation, and policy learning**, so parameters are reused across all four roles. Across several offline meta-RL benchmarks it reports consistent gains over prior methods, most clearly in zero-shot generalization.

papers.title: A Practical Causal Framework for Autonomous Mobile Robots: From Simulation to Real-World Human Environments
papers.abstract: Causal inference has emerged as a powerful paradigm enabling robots to make safe, efficient decisions by reasoning about the ``why'' behind events. However, its real-world application is hindered by the difficulty of collecting causal data, especially in human-populated environments where training takes time, while users expect immediate operation. To this end, we tackle the challenge of transferring simulation-learnt causal relations to the real world with minimal effort. While retaining the invariant high-level causal structure, we empirically demonstrate the system adapts efficiently to real-world situations by updating only the causal model parameters with a limited set of new observations. Our results show that the parameter update enables rapid sim-to-real transfer. The framework runs efficiently onboard of a mobile robot and significantly outperforms a non-causal baselines navigating successfully and safely in complex human-shared scenarios.
papers.summary: Causal reasoning can help robots make safe decisions, but collecting causal data in places full of people is slow, and users expect a robot to work right away. The authors learn causal relations in simulation and keep the high-level causal structure fixed when moving to the real world. They then update only the causal model's parameters, using a small set of new real-world observations. This parameter-only update gives **rapid sim-to-real transfer**, and the framework runs onboard a mobile robot, navigating complex spaces shared with humans more successfully and safely than non-causal baselines.

papers.title: Language Model Augmented Decision Transformer for Multi-Task Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Offline multi-task reinforcement learning (MTRL) aims to learn a unified policy from heterogeneous offline datasets that generalizes across tasks. However, existing offline MTRL methods often struggle with two fundamental issues: severe per-task data scarcity and limited cross-task generalization. In this paper, we propose Language-Model Augmented Decision Transformer (LaMA-DT), a unified sequence-modeling framework that leverages a single large language model (LLM) for both trajectory augmentation and multi-task policy learning. LaMA-DT uses natural-language task descriptions to guide task-aligned trajectory augmentation through a set of supervised generation and alignment objectives, and incorporates a scoring-and-filtering mechanism to retain high-quality augmented trajectories. The same LLM is then repurposed as a language-conditioned Decision Transformer and fine-tuned on a mixture of real and augmented data. Experiments on Meta-World and MuJoCo multi-task benchmarks demonstrate that LaMA-DT consistently outperforms competitive baselines, particularly in low-data regimes, showing that language-guided data augmentation substantially improves cross-task generalization.
papers.summary: Offline multi-task reinforcement learning (MTRL) learns one policy from mixed offline datasets, but it struggles when each task has little data and when skills must carry over between tasks. `LaMA-DT` (Language-Model Augmented Decision Transformer) uses a single large language model for two jobs. First, it generates extra trajectories guided by natural-language task descriptions, keeping only high-quality ones through a scoring-and-filtering step. Then the same model is fine-tuned as a language-conditioned `Decision Transformer` on a mix of real and generated data. On `Meta-World` and `MuJoCo` multi-task benchmarks it consistently beats competitive baselines, **especially when data is scarce**.

papers.title: ROCm InferaSim: Cut LLM Serving Trial Costs and Deploy the Best Configuration
papers.abstract: Serving an LLM efficiently depends on the engine, how the model is split across GPUs, precision, scheduler settings, speculative decoding, KV-cache management, and prefill-decode disaggregation. The best configuration depends on the model, hardware, workload, and objective. Operators usually find it by trial and error. Exhaustively measuring the candidates in our study would take about 25,000 GPU-hours. ROCm InferaSim predicts serving performance from a few short measurements. Choices such as batch size, prompt length, and GPU count change the amount of work per GPU without changing the kernels. ROCm InferaSim benchmarks each distinct set of kernels once, on at most one node. We call this measurement an anchor. Analytical laws carry that anchor to other deployments that run the same kernels. For multi-node deployments, ROCm InferaSim reduces the configuration to a single-node equivalent, measures it, and scales the result analytically. A simulator replays multi-turn traffic, and a tuning agent searches configurations using the predictions. On AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs with vLLM, SGLang, and ATOM, 11 anchors took 9.1 GPU-hours, against 204 GPU-hours to measure the 226 fixed-length configurations they cover. On 172 configurations, time per output token has 8.1% median error. On a multi-turn coding workload, throughput is within 8%. For 159 disaggregated deployments, none used as an anchor, throughput is within 5.5%. A five-candidate short list contains a deployment within 12% of the best feasible pairing of model and latency target.
papers.summary: Finding the best way to serve an LLM means choosing an engine, how to split the model across GPUs, numeric precision, scheduler settings, speculative decoding, KV-cache handling, and whether to separate the prefill and decode stages; operators usually find it by trial and error, which in this study would have cost about 25,000 GPU-hours. `ROCm InferaSim` benchmarks each distinct set of GPU kernels once, on at most one node, then uses analytical scaling laws to predict performance for other deployments that run the same kernels. A traffic simulator and a tuning agent use these predictions to search configurations. On AMD `MI355X` GPUs running `vLLM`, `SGLang`, and `ATOM`, 11 such measurements took **9.1 GPU-hours instead of 204** and predicted time per output token with 8.1% median error, and throughput for disaggregated deployments was within 5.5%.

papers.title: Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems
papers.abstract: Foundation models in changing environments can encounter unfamiliar domain knowledge that their original training did not cover. However, new domains rarely provide large amounts of expert-created training data or reliable supervisory signals for further training. We introduce Recursa, a foundation model system that adapts to new domains by learning from its own experience without human experts or a stronger teacher model. Recursa uses a knowledge repository to store what it learns: domain-specific skills and instructions on when to apply them, along with memories of past task experiences and reflections on what to improve. Recursa bootstraps the repository from domain materials and then refines it through recursive self-improvement. It uses parallel learners to execute tasks and synthesize local improvements, then validates and merges the improvements into the knowledge repository. On Harvey LAB's Firm Knowledge benchmark, Recursa raises the all-pass rate on held-out test tasks from 30.0% to 55.0% with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and from 35.0% to 46.0% with Qwen3.8-Flash.
papers.summary: Foundation models deployed in new domains often meet knowledge their training did not cover, and those domains rarely offer much expert-written training data or reliable supervision. `Recursa` adapts by learning from its own experience, with no human experts or stronger teacher model. It keeps a knowledge repository of domain skills, notes on when to apply them, memories of past tasks, and reflections on what to improve. The repository is first built from domain materials, then refined recursively: parallel learners carry out tasks and propose improvements, which are validated and merged back in. On Harvey LAB's `Firm Knowledge` benchmark, Recursa raises the all-pass rate on held-out tasks **from 30.0% to 55.0%** with `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` and from 35.0% to 46.0% with `Qwen3.8-Flash`.
papers.highlight_summary:
Foundation models deployed in new, knowledge-heavy domains often lack both the domain facts and the judgment to apply them, and such domains rarely offer expert training data or a stronger teacher model. `Recursa` adapts without either: the system's own model builds a text knowledge repository of instructions, skills and memory, then keeps refining it from its own task experience while the model weights and the agent harness stay fixed.

- The harness has the model act by writing Python in a persistent REPL, keeps the full interaction history in an append-only event log it can query with code, and lets agents hand work to parallel subagents; on its own, with `Qwen3.8-27B`, it reaches **37.2% all-pass** on Harvey LAB's `Firm Knowledge` benchmark versus 31.0% for the best published "study" configuration.
- Bootstrapping maps the 9,288-file, roughly 108M-token legal corpus into 14 skills and practices on self-generated tasks, which cuts turns and input tokens by **about a fifth to a quarter** but barely changes accuracy.
- During recursive self-improvement, a top-level learner splits the 150 training tasks by topic among parallel child learners, which solve, diagnose, edit and validate the repository; the parent then merges the edits and records reflections in memory, raising held-out all-pass from **30.0% to 55.0%** with `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` and **35.0% to 46.0%** with `Qwen3.8-Flash`.
- Splitting the work across learners matters: a single learner given the same tasks and starting point reaches only 43.0% and 37.0% test all-pass, and with `Qwen3.8-Flash` it falls below the bootstrap baseline on training tasks (**30.0% vs 37.3%**).
- The results are fragile: performance moves a lot from round to round (`DeepSeek` drops from 55.0% to 43.0% one round later), the reported round matches the best or near-best test score, all grading uses a single `Qwen3.8-Max` judge on rubrics the authors revised (46 criteria across 30 tasks), and testing covers only one synthetic legal benchmark.

papers.title: When Model Complexity Matters in Cross-Subject Naturalistic fMRI Prediction
papers.abstract: Increasingly complex neural models predict blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) responses to naturalistic stimuli, but the predictive value of this added complexity remains unclear. We ask when pretrained stimulus representations help and how much downstream complexity is needed, with and without recent measured BOLD history. We compare linear diagnostic references and nonlinear predictors across HCP movie fMRI (154 subjects), BOLD Moments (10 subjects), and Algonauts 2025 (4 subjects). Under a shared offline protocol, models are fitted on training subjects and evaluated on held-out subjects viewing largely familiar stimuli, without refitting. Pretrained visual features generally improve prediction over raw pixels; for linear autoregression, this advantage becomes more pronounced over longer rollouts (recursive predictions without additional measured BOLD). Measured BOLD history provides substantial gains that generally diminish {as rollouts lengthen}. Nonlinear stimulus-only predictors can improve on linear readouts, whereas linear autoregression provides a strong history-conditioned baseline. Controls examine context length, regularization, fitting procedures, and model capacity. Regional response consistency across subjects is associated with held-out prediction accuracy, while less consistent regions tend to gain more from measured history. In paired simulations with fixed linear neural dynamics, slower hemodynamic responses generally sustain high temporal prediction correlations over longer rollouts, illustrating how the observation process can contribute to predictive persistence. Together, these findings support evaluating stimulus representations and downstream complexity separately, using history-conditioned linear prediction as a diagnostic reference under matched inputs and measurement availability.
papers.summary: Increasingly complex neural models are used to predict blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) brain responses to natural stimuli such as movies, but it is unclear how much the added complexity actually helps. The authors compare linear reference models with nonlinear predictors on `HCP` movie fMRI, `BOLD Moments`, and `Algonauts 2025`, fitting on some subjects and testing on others without refitting. Pretrained visual features generally beat raw pixels, and recent measured BOLD history gives substantial gains that shrink over longer recursive predictions. **Linear autoregression is a strong baseline when history is available**, so the authors recommend evaluating stimulus representations and downstream model complexity separately.

papers.title: Testing Processor Contracts in Speculative Decoding Engines
papers.abstract: Speculative sampling can accelerate decoding without changing the target distribution. Its standard guarantee assumes that logits processors, which enforce constraints or modify token scores, receive the appropriate token prefix and state at each verification position. We formalize this processor-prefix contract and present BADC (branch-aware differential conformance testing). BADC combines enumerated references on tiny random models, checks of processor inputs and state, and simultaneous confidence bounds on output-event probabilities. Preregistered, source-informed experiments on selected Transformers and llama-cpp-python releases confirm two causes: processors read unverified drafts or advance state without rollback. For one pilot-selected prompt on a trained checkpoint, fresh samples give a 60.26-percentage-point lower bound on the difference in the probability of a predefined first-token event between ordinary and prompt-lookup decoding, with nominal simultaneous 95% coverage under within-arm i.i.d. sampling. Controlled comparisons establish no cause-recovery advantage of directed selection over random selection, while permutation testing detects each tested family at least as often as BADC. These findings connect processor-interface failures to observable decoding differences without establishing diagnostic superiority or workload prevalence.
papers.summary: Speculative sampling is supposed to speed up decoding without changing the output distribution, but that guarantee assumes logits processors (components that enforce constraints or modify token scores) see the correct token prefix and state at each verification position. The authors formalize this contract and introduce `BADC` (branch-aware differential conformance testing), which compares against exactly enumerated tiny random models, checks processor inputs and state, and puts simultaneous confidence bounds on output probabilities. Experiments on releases of `Transformers` and `llama-cpp-python` confirm two bug causes: **processors reading unverified draft tokens, or advancing state without rolling it back**. In one case, ordinary and prompt-lookup decoding differed by at least 60 percentage points in the probability of a predefined first-token event, although plain permutation testing detected each bug family at least as often as BADC.

papers.title: Denoising Is Stein: Moment Access and a Resource Hierarchy for Learning Hidden Structure in Diffusion Models
papers.abstract:
We study score learning from denoising pairs when the data contain a hidden non-Gaussian component. If covariance reveals the component, its subspace can be recovered directly. If covariance is isotropic, the first distinguishing moment has order $k^\ast$, and the learner must extract that moment from clean points and their noisy views.
  Correlations in the denoising loss are Stein discrepancies against a baseline; for polynomial fields they determine exactly the corresponding moment differences. Averaging fresh noisy views conditional on a clean point gives an exact moment query on the clean distribution. In the covariance-matched regime, orientation-independent dictionaries satisfying an $L^4/L^2$ condition need order $d^{k^\ast-1}$ features, and the stated dot-product kernel ridge models need the same power in samples. Small-step online SGD on one unit has this exponent up to logarithms. A two-stage learner uses the curvature of a smoothed denoising loss to recover the hidden direction, then sharpens it and fits a scalar readout. For every even $k^\ast$, it obtains a fixed score gain over the Gaussian baseline from $O(d^{k^\ast/2}\log d)$ clean points. In the covariance-visible regime, the frozen-feature threshold occurs at $d^J/J!$, while projection onto principal components makes the fitted-model, score-risk and generated-law distributions independent of ambient dimension.
  In the covariance-matched experiments, the measured partial-trace overlaps are consistent with the proposed spectral transition. A width-8 network trained with clean-point reuse shows a $d^2$-like training-set threshold over $d=64$--$192$, with fixed validation and calibration overhead.
papers.summary: The paper studies how many samples and features a diffusion model needs to learn the score function from denoising pairs when the data hides a non-Gaussian component. The authors show that correlations in the denoising loss are Stein discrepancies, and that averaging fresh noisy views of a clean point gives exact moment queries on the clean data. When the covariance gives no hint of the hidden direction, fixed-feature models and small-step online `SGD` need on the order of d^(k*−1) resources, where d is the dimension and k* is the order of the first moment that differs from a Gaussian. A two-stage learner that uses the curvature of a smoothed denoising loss **does better, needing only O(d^(k*/2) log d) clean points**, and experiments with small networks show matching sample thresholds.

papers.title: Exploit or conform? How norm utility prompting changes the way LLMs use community beliefs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) serve both as tools for aiding human decision-making in everyday life and as models of human agents in experimental simulation studies. Alignment on prototypical social decisions -- such as whether to cooperate on a collective action -- therefore has immediate practical consequences for researchers and for society at large. Here we systematically explore the impact of ``norm utility'' -- the non-material components of utility that account for an individual's desire to conform to social norms and to be internally consistent -- on the strategic decision-making of three open-weight LLMs in one-shot, two-player social dilemmas. We find that when a social dilemma is presented together with information about community beliefs -- but without any indication of how those beliefs should matter -- models tend to treat community belief as strategic information, so that in the Snowdrift game cooperation falls as community belief in cooperation increases. When we explicitly prompt the components of norm utility this relationship inverts, and cooperation increases with community belief, in broad agreement with the predictions of a simple norm utility model. We then show that prompting norm utility reduces the volatility of strategic decisions with respect to changes in the underlying social context, and generates more consistent reasoning habits across models. Taken together, our results suggest that prompting norm utility can help generate more human-like and consistent behavior across models and lower volatility within models.
papers.summary: LLMs are used both to help people decide and to stand in for human participants in simulations, so how they behave in social dilemmas matters. The authors test three open-weight LLMs in one-shot, two-player games, varying information about what the community believes and whether "norm utility" (the wish to conform to social norms and stay internally consistent) is spelled out in the prompt. Without explicit guidance, models treat community beliefs as strategic information, so in the Snowdrift game they cooperate less as belief in cooperation rises. **Prompting norm utility reverses this**, making cooperation rise with community belief as a simple norm model predicts, while also making decisions less volatile and reasoning more consistent across models.

papers.title: Forgetting to Improve: Principled Data Removal in Active Learning
papers.abstract: The uncertainty of a statistical model is most commonly factorized into an aleatoric and an epistemic part. This factorization changes how predictions are interpreted in downstream decision tasks. Importantly, except for the idealistic scenario with no model mismatch, the quantification is a characteristic of the model and not the data generating process. In this paper, we propose Forgetting to Improve a method that reduces this discrepancy by incorporating the task into the modeling framework. Our key insight is to acknowledge that in scenarios of model mismatch, data can have a detrimental effect on the modeling for a specific task. Based on this insight, we propose an influence function for Gaussian process models that allows for principled removal of detrimental data samples. We showcase the flexibility of this approach by demonstrating significant improvements across a range of tasks, including Bayesian optimization, model-based reinforcement learning, and transductive learning.
papers.summary: Splitting a model's uncertainty into aleatoric (noise) and epistemic (knowledge) parts describes the model rather than the true data process whenever the model is misspecified. `Forgetting to Improve` builds the downstream task into the modeling, based on the idea that under model mismatch **some data actively hurts performance on a given task**. The authors derive an influence function for Gaussian process models that identifies and removes such harmful samples in a principled way. They report significant improvements in Bayesian optimization, model-based reinforcement learning, and transductive learning.

papers.title: HybridSpec: Throughput-Aware Speculative Decoding for Hybrid GDN-MoE Models
papers.abstract: In speculative decoding, parallel drafters such as DFlash make drafting cheap, so target verification dominates each round. A central choice is the verification length, the number of tokens that the target processes in each round. Verifying more draft tokens can accept more of them, but work after the first rejection is wasted. For hybrid target models that combine Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers, verification time grows much faster with this length than for dense models. In a single-request profile of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B with DFlash, it grew by 71% from length 4 to 16, almost entirely in GDN and MoE layers, compared with 4%-6% for a dense Qwen3-4B target. Each GDN layer must update a recurrent state at every token and recover it at the end of the accepted prefix. The MoE cost depends on the experts that the tokens activate, which are known only once verification runs. We present HybridSpec, which selects the verification length on the GPU from draft-side acceptance estimates and measured target latency. Verification then runs this length plus one extra token up to the first MoE router, before any expert runs. There, a lightweight routing correction uses the observed expert assignments to decide whether to keep that token. The rest of verification runs only on the selected tokens. Block-parallel GDN kernels avoid storing a state after every token and reconstruct the accepted state of every GDN layer in one launch. In isolated benchmarks at verification lengths 4 to 16 with every draft token accepted, these kernels, including accepted-state reconstruction, are $1.54\times$-$4.04\times$ faster than the default kernels. With three GDN-MoE target models in single-request greedy decoding, HybridSpec is $1.75\times$-$1.88\times$ faster than autoregressive decoding and $1.30\times$-$1.33\times$ faster than DFlash.
papers.summary: In speculative decoding with cheap parallel drafters like `DFlash`, most time goes to the target model checking the draft, and for hybrid targets that mix Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers, that verification time grows much faster with the number of tokens checked than it does for dense models. `HybridSpec` chooses the verification length on the GPU from draft acceptance estimates and measured latency. It then decides whether to keep one extra token based on the expert assignments seen at the first MoE router. Custom block-parallel GDN kernels rebuild the accepted recurrent state in one launch. With three GDN-MoE targets in single-request greedy decoding, HybridSpec is **1.75×–1.88× faster than autoregressive decoding** and 1.30×–1.33× faster than DFlash.

papers.title: Structured Priors: Towards an algebra of component priors for prior-data fitted networks
papers.abstract: Prior-data fitted networks are typically trained using synthetic data generated by a single, manually constructed generator. In cases where such a generator combines multiple components, e.g., in TabPFN, Mitra, or TabICLv2, this is achieved through a mixture using manually specified weights, the impact of which on the network only becomes apparent after pre-training. Instead of such a hand-built generator, this work proposes a structured prior: a small set of named component priors, linked by operators whose algebraic properties are formally proven and whose influence on the trained network has been validated. Within a measure-theoretic framework, the operators of mixture, convolution, amplitude scaling, local transform, and projection are defined. Their governing laws are proven. These operators are implemented in the macl2l software package. Experiments demonstrate that the implemented generators reproduce the identities within the resolution of a permutation test. Furthermore, it is shown that trained networks obey the distributive law; that a mixed prior composed of small components performs as well as or better than any individual component in seven out of eight open regression benchmarks; and that on two of these tables a structured prior reaches, with a ninth of the data budget, an error that a generic random-function prior does not reach even with the full budget. A theorem on model averaging demonstrates that networks trained on individual components constitute the Bayes predictor for the mixture, provided that the component networks are themselves the Bayes predictors for their respective priors. However, the pre-registered test of this averaged predictor with trained component networks failed, because the networks identify the generating component too rarely. The paper proposes a research program focused on the algebra of structured priors for prior-data fitted networks.
papers.summary: Prior-data fitted networks such as `TabPFN` are trained on synthetic data from hand-built generators that mix several components using weights chosen by hand, and the effect of those weights only shows up after pre-training.
