The authors instead propose a structured prior: a small set of named component priors combined with operators (mixture, convolution, amplitude scaling, local transform, projection) whose algebraic laws are formally proven and implemented in the `macl2l` package. Trained networks follow the distributive law, a mixture of small components matches or beats any single component on seven of eight regression benchmarks, and on two tables **a structured prior reaches, with a ninth of the data budget, an error that a generic prior cannot reach with the full budget**. A preregistered test of averaging component networks failed, because the networks too rarely identify which component generated the data.

papers.title: Look Before You Launch: Learned Throughput Prediction for Hardware Selection in a Production Training Fleet
papers.abstract: In mixed-vendor accelerator fleets, many training jobs can run on several hardware types, and the best choice depends on each job's throughput on each type. Routing a job needs a throughput estimate for every candidate type before the job runs. We present LEAP, a machine learning performance prediction service that predicts each training job's throughput on every candidate hardware type at submission time and ranks the candidates by predicted throughput per unit cost. It routes tens of thousands of training job attempts a day across hundreds of different model types and more than 20 hardware types in a production fleet. LEAP predicts throughput from submission-time training configuration, including each job's prior throughput. LEAP reaches an accuracy of 77% over 30 nightly retrains, higher than the lookup table it replaced and at least as high as every alternative model we tested, including fine-tuned language models. Over six months, the share of eligible training GPU-hours that received a ranking by LEAP grew from 58% to 95%, and we estimate that it saves about 3% of training computational cost. In this paper, we identify the drivers that actually move accuracy and those that do not. We offer these as lessons for teams building performance predictors at fleet scale.
papers.summary: In accelerator fleets that mix vendors, many training jobs can run on several hardware types, and routing them well requires predicting throughput on each type before the job starts. `LEAP` is a production machine-learning service that predicts each job's throughput on every candidate hardware type at submission time and ranks the options by throughput per unit cost. It routes tens of thousands of job attempts a day across hundreds of model types and more than 20 hardware types, reaching 77% accuracy, beating the lookup table it replaced and matching or beating every alternative tested, including fine-tuned language models. Over six months its coverage of eligible GPU-hours grew from 58% to 95%, with **estimated savings of about 3% of training compute**, and the authors share which factors actually changed accuracy and which did not.

papers.title: Query-based Submodular Data Selection for Efficient Instruction Tuning
papers.abstract: As large language models are fine-tuned for increasingly specialized tasks, their performance depends more on which training examples are selected than on how many. Given a large heterogeneous training pool and a small target set specifying the desired capability, targeted data selection aims to find a compact subset that maximizes downstream performance. Existing methods score each candidate independently against the target and select the top-ranked examples, yet this point-wise strategy ignores inter-example interactions: at tight budgets the selected subset is dominated by near-redundant points that waste capacity on overlapping information. We propose Query-based Submodular functions with Gradient-guided Synthesis (QSGS), which formulates targeted selection as a submodular graph cut over a gradient similarity graph. A modular relevance term pulls selected examples toward the target task, while a pairwise dispersion penalty suppresses intra-subset redundancy. The resulting objective balances target relevance and intra-subset redundancy using the same formulation across different selection budgets. Empirically, the benefit of diversity-aware selection becomes increasingly pronounced as the data budget decreases. To further close coverage gaps that no selection from existing data can bridge, we introduce a gradient-guided synthesis step that identifies under-covered target directions via residual subspace analysis and generates synthetic examples to fill them. Experiments on MMLU, BBH, and TydiQA across Llama-2, Llama-3, and Mistral, show that QSGS at a 0.5% budget matches or exceeds full-data performance on Mistral-7B, outperforms the strongest baseline across all benchmarks, and yields increasing gains as the budget shrinks.
papers.summary: Targeted data selection for instruction tuning usually scores each candidate example against a target set on its own, so at small budgets the chosen subset fills up with near-duplicates. `QSGS` (Query-based Submodular functions with Gradient-guided Synthesis) frames selection as a submodular graph cut over a graph of gradient similarity, balancing relevance to the target against redundancy within the subset. A synthesis step then finds target directions the selected data does not cover and generates synthetic examples to fill them. Across `MMLU`, `BBH`, and `TydiQA` with `Llama-2`, `Llama-3`, and `Mistral`, **a 0.5% data budget matches or exceeds full-data performance on `Mistral-7B`**, and the gains grow as the budget shrinks.

papers.title: On the Primacy Bias in RLVR Training
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) has emerged as a promising approach for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models. However, it still remains unclear whether RLVR can extend reasoning capabilities beyond what is already encoded in the base model. In this paper, we study this question through the lens of primacy bias: the tendency of models to over-rely on already-learned representations, disproportionately improving performance on problems they already handle well while underexploring harder ones that require departing from those representations. Through our controlled experiments and large-scale analysis, we show that RLVR training on mixed data tends to further sharpen performance on easier problems while yielding only marginal gains on harder ones. We find that although hard problems lead to modest gains overall, they are actually the ones that help most in expanding the model's reasoning capabilities and pushing the representations. However, prolonged training on these hard problems may also hurt and lead to forgetting on easy problems. These findings help to better understand some of the prior conflicting observations about RLVR, specifically, why on (OOD) domains where the base model performs poorly, improvements on hard problems can expand reasoning; while on well-trained domains, forgetting can reduce performance and mask genuine gains obtained from hard problems.
papers.summary: It is unclear whether Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) teaches language models new reasoning or only sharpens what the base model already knows. The authors study this through primacy bias, the tendency to keep relying on already-learned representations. Controlled experiments and large-scale analysis show that RLVR on mixed data **mostly sharpens performance on easy problems while giving only marginal gains on hard ones**. Hard problems turn out to be what actually expands reasoning ability, but training on them for too long causes forgetting on easy problems, which helps explain earlier conflicting reports about RLVR on new versus well-trained domains.

papers.title: StreamLTT: Risk Certification for Policy Selection under Stream Dependence
papers.abstract: Learn-then-Test (LTT) provides a general framework for certifying deployment policies against a prescribed risk target, but its standard formulation targets a fixed population risk estimated from calibration losses. In sequential deployment, losses may instead be dependent and nonstationary, so the risk of a fixed policy can evolve with the observed history. We introduce StreamLTT, which replaces this fixed population risk with average predictable risk, defined by conditioning each decision's loss on the information available before its outcome is revealed. Conditional centering turns empirical deviations from this target into a martingale sum, enabling both a test that adapts to predictable variance and a finite-sample Hoeffding alternative. Combined with family-wise error rate control, StreamLTT yields a simultaneously certified policy region that supports subsequent deployment selection. Across seven forecasting datasets and seven deployment risks, StreamLTT places the certified frontier substantially closer to the prescribed risk target than IID, robust-variance, block-bootstrap, and concentration-based alternatives, while empirical family-wise error closely follows the prescribed level. A finite-sample ablation further shows that the predictable-risk formulation drives the tighter risk frontier, while adaptation to predictable variance makes more effective use of the available family-wise error budget. StreamLTT therefore extends risk-certified policy selection to dependent deployment streams by addressing both what risk should be certified and how it should be tested.
papers.summary: Learn-then-Test (LTT) certifies that a deployment policy meets a risk target, but it assumes a fixed population risk, which breaks down when losses arrive in dependent, shifting streams. `StreamLTT` instead certifies average predictable risk, conditioning each loss on what was known before its outcome was revealed. This turns deviations into a martingale, which supports a test that adapts to variance and a finite-sample Hoeffding alternative, both combined with family-wise error control. Across seven forecasting datasets and seven deployment risks, it **places the certified frontier much closer to the risk target** than IID, robust-variance, block-bootstrap, and concentration-based alternatives, while keeping family-wise error near the set level.

papers.title: TB-Transolver: Parallelized and Coherent Long-Horizon Rollouts via Temporal Bundling for Time-Dependent PDEs
papers.abstract: Transolver has recently gained widespread adoption for solving diverse physical problems on unstructured geometric meshes by leveraging its Physics-Attention mechanism, which seamlessly extends standard softmax attention to handle physical domains at scale. For time-dependent problems, existing literature relies on time-conditioned or autoregressive rollouts to preserve temporal causality while retaining Physics-Attention as the spatial backbone. However, a fundamental limitation of this formulation is its sequential execution model, wherein computational costs scale linearly with the temporal horizon, rendering standard Transolver inefficient for transient problems despite its exceptional spatial efficacy. This bottleneck has historically hindered its broader application in time-dependent physical modeling. To address this limitation, we introduce TB-Transolver (also referred to as Temporally Bundled Transolver), an efficient framework built on temporal bundling that scales Transolver for time-dependent PDEs. Furthermore, we propose \emph{spatiotemporal coherence} (${\rm C(K)}$) as a general metric to systematically quantify snapshot correlation within a temporal bundle, enabling the \emph{a priori} selection of optimal bundle widths using training data alone, thereby avoiding expensive grid searches. We demonstrate the computational efficacy of TB-Transolver across four physically distinct domains, namely, plasticity, fluid dynamics, reaction-diffusion, and global weather forecasting; achieving training speedups of up to $29\times$ over conventional autoregressive and time-conditioned baselines. Finally, these computational gains are further amplified through distributed multi-node and multi-GPU parallelism, yielding aggregated speedups of up to $45.6\times$ at optimal bundle widths for systems exhibiting high spatiotemporal coherence compared to single-GPU implementations.
papers.summary: `Transolver` handles physics problems on irregular meshes well, but for time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) it runs step by step, so cost grows linearly with the time horizon. `TB-Transolver` uses temporal bundling to predict several time steps at once. It also introduces a spatiotemporal coherence metric, C(K), that picks the best bundle width from training data alone, avoiding grid searches. Across plasticity, fluid dynamics, reaction-diffusion, and global weather forecasting, it achieves **training speedups of up to 29×** over autoregressive and time-conditioned baselines, and up to 45.6× with multi-node, multi-GPU parallelism.

papers.title: Graph-Localized Coverage for Conformal Prediction on Inductive Graphs
papers.abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) provides marginal coverage guarantees, but marginal coverage does not determine where prediction errors occur on a graph. Queries from different graph neighborhoods can exhibit substantially different levels of uncertainty even when aggregate coverage remains near its target. We introduce GLocalCP, an online CP framework for inductive node classification and edge prediction that combines marginal and graph-local calibration with uncertainty-adaptive prediction sets. Specifically, GLocalCP puts forth a novel uncertainty-adaptive nonconformality score that relies on the mutual information obtained from Monte-Carlo (MC) dropout based prediction. Then, it augments a global online threshold with a kernel-based local correction that propagates coverage feedback among similar graph queries. On the theoretical horizon, we establish pathwise $O(N^{-1/2})$ marginal calibration error without exchangeability or stationarity and, for the exact-kernel formulation, an explicit $O(N^{-1/2})$ graph-localized calibration guarantee. Experiments on seven node-classification and seven edge-prediction benchmarks show that similar marginal coverage can conceal substantially different local reliability. Our proposed GLocalCP maintains coverage near the target while consistently reducing graph-local calibration error. Uncertainty scaling in GLocalCP further reduces prediction-set size across all evaluated node and edge datasets while leaving marginal coverage essentially unchanged.
papers.summary: Conformal prediction (CP) guarantees coverage on average, but on graphs that average can hide large differences in reliability between neighborhoods. `GLocalCP` is an online CP framework for inductive node classification and edge prediction. It uses a nonconformity score that adapts to uncertainty, based on mutual information from Monte-Carlo dropout, and adds a kernel-based local correction that shares coverage feedback among similar graph queries. The authors prove O(N^-1/2) calibration error without assuming exchangeability or stationarity, and on 14 benchmarks GLocalCP keeps coverage near the target while **consistently reducing graph-local calibration error** and shrinking prediction sets.

papers.title: Finite-Sample Convergence in Networked Average Reward MARL: Decentralization Pitfalls and Entropy Remedies
papers.abstract: We study the problem of average reward Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) where agents interact within a network. Each agent in the network conducts local updates with information within its $k$-hop neighborhood and collaboratively maximizes the overall reward of the entire network. We first provide impossibility results in achieving convergence to the global optimal joint policies in our setting. These impossibility results highlight the challenges of decentralized learning with local information in multi-agent systems, namely the issues of multiagency, where each agent independently optimizes its policy, and partial observability, where agents have limited visibility into the global state. Given these challenges which indicate that decentralized policy optimization can generally be certified only up to stationarity, we provide finite-sample convergence guarantees for a decentralized actor-critic algorithm with linear function approximation that converges to an approximate stationary point with small gradient norm. To overcome such impossibility results, we further show that adding fixed-state entropy regularization reshapes the objective landscape which leads to even stronger global convergence guarantees for our proposed actor-critic algorithm.
papers.summary: The paper studies average-reward Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) on a network, where each agent updates using only information from its k-hop neighborhood while the group maximizes the network's total reward. The authors first prove impossibility results: because agents optimize independently and see only part of the global state, decentralized learning cannot in general be guaranteed to reach the globally optimal joint policy. They give finite-sample guarantees that a decentralized actor-critic with linear function approximation reaches an approximate stationary point. They then show that **adding fixed-state entropy regularization yields stronger global convergence guarantees**.

papers.title: Computer-Use Agents Gain Little Benefit from a World Model When Conditioned on Tutorials
papers.abstract: Recent work has improved computer-use agents (CUAs) by combining retrieved task-relevant tutorials and look-ahead planning using world models with MLLM judges. However, the contribution of each component -- tutorials, the judge, and the world model -- to overall improvement has not been evaluated in isolation. To fill this gap, we first construct OSWorld-Tutorial and ScienceBoard-Tutorial: two datasets for CUAs with curated multimodal tutorials, covering everyday and scientific domains. We then propose RAG-PolicyJudge (RAG-PJ), a policy-judge framework for CUAs conditioned on task-specific tutorials: the policy proposes candidate actions, and the judge selects among them. To isolate the effect of world models given tutorials, we compare RAG-PJ with and without common world models: using either zero-shot text-based descriptions of next states or an oracle that returns ground-truth visual observations. We find that RAG-PJ gains little benefit from these rollouts when tutorials are present, even with perfect visual futures. This suggests prior world-model gains in tutorial-conditioned methods come mainly from tutorial understanding and the judge's ability to select the proposed actions, rather than from predicted rollouts. Error analysis reveals that the bottleneck is not rollout fidelity, but the judge's ability to reason over future states and recognize task completion. This highlights the need to improve not just next-state prediction in world models, but also reasoning over their predicted rollouts. Datasets and code are available at https://github.com/realjoenguyen/RAGPJ-official.
papers.summary: Recent computer-use agents (CUAs) combine retrieved tutorials, world-model look-ahead, and multimodal LLM judges, but no one had measured each component's contribution on its own. The authors build `OSWorld-Tutorial` and `ScienceBoard-Tutorial`, two datasets of curated multimodal tutorials, and propose `RAG-PJ` (RAG-PolicyJudge), where a policy proposes candidate actions and a judge picks among them. When tutorials are present, **world-model rollouts add little benefit, even from an oracle that returns the true future screens**. Error analysis points to the judge's ability to reason over future states and recognize task completion as the real bottleneck, not how accurate the rollouts are.

papers.title: The Complexity of ReLU Network Synthesis from a Parameter Multiset
papers.abstract: We ask how hard it is to build a neural network when its parameter values are given in advance. An instance supplies a multiset of rational numbers, a target behavior, and a bound on the number of neurons, output included. The question is whether one can choose the graph of a ReLU network within the bound, and place the numbers on its edges and biases so that it meets the target. This separates the numbers from the architecture; permutation training instead fixes the hidden units and only rearranges the output weights. Matching two labeled examples exactly is already $\mathsf{NP}$-complete; we ask what changes when the target must hold on every input or on average. Agreeing with a Boolean circuit on every Boolean input is $\Sigma_2^{\mathsf P}$-complete, already for four neurons. Agreeing with a given ReLU network on every real input lies in $\mathsf{DP}$ for every fixed neuron bound and is $\mathsf{DP}$-complete for three neurons. Approximating a ReLU network on the unit cube within absolute error one everywhere is $\Sigma_2^{\mathsf P}$-complete, even with no hidden neurons and all numbers equal and positive. Deciding whether some network has expected squared loss at most a threshold is $\mathsf{NP}^{\mathsf{PP}}$-complete for uniform Boolean inputs. For uniform inputs on the unit cube and for standard Gaussian inputs with a positive threshold, the same holds for two neurons when a positive risk gap, given in binary and possibly exponentially small, separates yes from no instances. Without a gap, the cube version is complete for guessing a polynomial-length string, then comparing a sum of exponentially many rationals with a threshold, all computable in polynomial time from the input and the guess. Since the graph is chosen too, the reductions must rule out every other network built from the same numbers.
papers.summary: The paper asks how hard it is to build a ReLU network when the parameter values are given in advance as a multiset, and one must choose the network graph within a neuron limit and place the numbers on its edges and biases to meet a target behavior. Matching two labeled examples exactly was already known to be NP-complete. Requiring agreement with a Boolean circuit on every Boolean input is **Σ2^P-complete even with four neurons**, and matching a given ReLU network on every real input is DP-complete with three neurons. Bounding the expected squared loss is NP^PP-complete for uniform Boolean inputs, with related results for inputs on the unit cube and for Gaussian inputs.

papers.title: AlgoPilot: Cross-Paradigm Reasoning in Language Models via Strategy Selection and Guidance
papers.abstract: Real-world problems span diverse domains, including program synthesis, symbolic reasoning, planning, and optimization, and often require fundamentally different solution paradigms. A central challenge for LLM-based reasoning is twofold: identifying an appropriate problem-solving approach and formulating it correctly. In this paper, we propose AlgoPilot, a cross-paradigm reasoning framework that enables adaptive selection of the solving approaches and structured problem formulation prior to execution. The AlgoPilot framework contains three components: 1) a SteerLM, trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), that adaptively selects the solving strategy (paradigm and modes) based on input problems, 2) the corresponding expert GuideLM, trained via SFT, that generates structured formulation guidance tailored to the selected strategy, and 3) an ExecutionLM that generates solutions conditioned on both the selected strategy and its formulation. Unlike prompting-based methods that rely on fixed reasoning templates, our approach learns to adaptively choose and structure problem-solving strategies based on the input. We build AlgoPilot on Qwen3-8B and evaluate across 5 problem categories and 13 benchmarks with 66 unique domains, comparing against both the latest similarly scaled small models and large LLMs. AlgoPilot significantly improves average accuracy for the same model from 38.4% to 72.9%, outperforming the best large LLM prompting baseline GLM-5 by 11.7%. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component. Notably, we show that the learned steering and formulation modules can transfer across execution models, suggesting their potential to improve other LLMs. Project page: https://sites.google.com/view/algopilot.
papers.summary: Problems in program synthesis, symbolic reasoning, planning, and optimization often call for very different ways of solving them, and language models struggle both to pick the right approach and to formulate it correctly. `AlgoPilot` splits the work across three models. A `SteerLM`, trained with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), chooses a solving strategy for each input. An expert `GuideLM` then writes structured formulation guidance for that strategy, and an `ExecutionLM` produces the final solution. Built on `Qwen3-8B` and tested on 13 benchmarks spanning 66 domains, it raises average accuracy **from 38.4% to 72.9%** and beats the strongest large-model prompting baseline, `GLM-5`, by 11.7%. The steering and formulation modules also transfer to other execution models.

papers.title: RAPID: Increasing Efficiency of Internal Distillation via Randomized Methods
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a technique used to transfer the expertise of large teacher models into small, efficient student models. Recent advances have integrated the distillation of internal activations, more directly training students to learn similar representations as the teacher. One of the core challenges of internal distillation is the dimensional incompatibility between the student and teacher internal representations. Existing methods add learnable matrices to project the larger teacher activations into the smaller representation space of the student. This is a notable point of inefficiency, as learning additional parameters for the projectors increases training costs, only for them to be discarded immediately after training. We introduce RAPID (RAndomized Projection for Internal Distillation) a novel distillation methodology which eliminates the wasteful projection learning by leveraging randomized methods. RAPID utilizes an efficient transform construction based on the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma to compress the teacher representations into the student embedding space with strong theoretical guarantees of structural preservation. RAPID also employs a combination of exponential moving average (EMA) and homoscedastic uncertainty weighting in a novel multi-objective function designed for internal distillation. Our experiments in post-training for reasoning demonstrate that RAPID increases training efficiency by as much as 21.1% while maintaining performance comparable to existing methods.
papers.summary: Internal distillation trains a small student model to match a larger teacher's internal activations. Because the two models' representations have different sizes, existing methods learn projection matrices that are thrown away after training. `RAPID` (RAndomized Projection for Internal Distillation) replaces these learned projectors with a random transform based on the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma, which comes with theoretical guarantees that the structure of the teacher's representations is preserved. It also combines an exponential moving average (EMA) with homoscedastic uncertainty weighting in a multi-objective loss. In post-training for reasoning, it improves training efficiency by **up to 21.1%** while matching the performance of existing methods.

papers.title: Follow the Features: SAE Feature-Guided Data-Efficient Instruction-Tuning of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Selecting small, effective instruction-tuning datasets requires identifying which aspects of the original data to retain. We introduce Follow the Features (FtF), a data-selection method that uses sparse autoencoder (SAE) features to characterize training data and guide subset construction. FtF ranks features using dataset-level activation statistics, scores samples by their expression of highly ranked features, and incorporates feature resampling to encourage diversity. The LLM-SAE pair used for selection is independent of the model being fine-tuned, enabling reuse across target models. We evaluate FtF on two model-dataset settings at a training budget of 100 samples with a fixed sequence length of 256 tokens. FtF achieves performance competitive with GRAPE and S2L, with relative rankings varying across settings. On Qwen 3 8B trained on Alpaca, FtF exceeds full-dataset training by 1.59 percentage points in the harmonic mean of an AlpacaEval-based win rate and Open LLM Leaderboard performance, although full-dataset training retains a higher Leaderboard score. These results support SAE feature statistics as a useful signal for data-efficient instruction tuning.
papers.summary: `Follow the Features` (`FtF`) picks small instruction-tuning subsets using sparse autoencoder (SAE) features. It ranks features by dataset-level activation statistics, scores each sample by how strongly it expresses the top-ranked features, and resamples features to keep the subset diverse. Because the language-model and SAE pair used for selection is separate from the model being fine-tuned, one selection can be reused across target models. With a budget of 100 training samples, `FtF` is competitive with `GRAPE` and `S2L`. On `Qwen 3 8B` trained on `Alpaca`, it **exceeds full-dataset training by 1.59 percentage points** on a combined `AlpacaEval` and `Open LLM Leaderboard` metric, though full-dataset training still scores higher on the Leaderboard alone.

papers.title: ScienceVision: Can AI Observe and Reason Like a Scientist?
papers.abstract: Scientific discovery builds on accurate observations interpreted through domain knowledge and reasoning. For scientific 3D data, this requires understanding structures and spatial relationships, from protein contacts to anatomical organization. Existing multimodal benchmarks largely evaluate text and 2D images, while scientific 3D evaluations vary in representations and protocols across disciplines, limiting cross-disciplinary comparison. To assess these foundational capabilities, we introduce ScienceVision, a cross-domain benchmark for scientific 3D understanding and reasoning through expert-level visual question answering (VQA). We construct 250 questions, with 50 each from Biology, Chemistry, Medical Imaging, Mechanical CAD, and Architecture, through a pipeline combining synthetic question generation with domain-expert review and annotation. Each task pairs a native 3D artifact with a scientific question, a specified response format, and a task-specific reference answer, requiring domain knowledge to be applied to geometric or topological evidence. We evaluate 12 models on the same questions in three settings: visual question answering with native 3D artifacts accessed through an agent harness's file and code-execution tools; the same workflow augmented with expert-inspired viewer inspection and measurement tools exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP); and visual question answering from prescribed rendered 2D images using an agent harness. All settings use the same task-specific deterministic final-answer scoring. The inspection environment supports view changes, target isolation, and slice inspection. In this main comparison, the best mean answer score is 0.53 out of 1. Mean scores in the native-artifact workflow without additional MCP tools exceed those in the rendered-image workflow for every model, by 17.2 percentage points on average.
papers.summary: Most multimodal benchmarks test text and 2D images, and existing scientific 3D evaluations use different formats and protocols in each discipline, which makes them hard to compare. `ScienceVision` is a visual question answering (VQA) benchmark of 250 expert-reviewed questions on native 3D artifacts, with 50 each from biology, chemistry, medical imaging, mechanical CAD, and architecture. Twelve models were tested in three settings: an agent harness with file and code-execution tools, the same harness plus viewer and measurement tools exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and rendered 2D images. The **best mean score is only 0.53 out of 1**. Working directly with the native 3D artifacts beat working from rendered images for every model, by 17.2 percentage points on average.

papers.title: Swapping the Judge Changes the Ranking: A Preregistered Study of Cross-Provider Replication in LLM-Judged System Comparisons
papers.abstract: Practitioners who compare systems with an LLM judge and have no human labels often check a conclusion by repeating it with a judge from another provider. We test how far that check can be trusted. In a preregistered study (with a disclosed post-registration reduction of the judge set), five judge models from three providers re-judged 4,000 Chatbot Arena battles (nine systems, 33 system pairs) that carry human votes, each in both response orders. Agreement with the human vote was low at the verdict level (median Cohen's kappa = 0.22), and system rankings did not survive a change of judge: Kendall's tau with the human ranking ranged from 0.17 to 0.89 (median 0.67), so the preregistered hypothesis that rankings remain stable was not supported. Conclusions replicated by two low-cost judges from different providers matched the human conclusion more often than single-judge conclusions (+0.10 precision), but the gain came from filtering out one poorly aligned judge, and replication involving that judge left a conclusion for only 35% of comparisons. Judges that agreed with humans reached a stable conclusion with no more verdicts than human votes required; the others failed to converge on 26-70% of system pairs at the sample sizes tested (up to 100 verdicts per pair). Disagreements with the human vote co-occurred across judges far more often than independence predicts, although a single human vote per battle cannot separate shared judge bias from voter noise.
papers.summary: When practitioners have no human labels, they often check an LLM-judged system comparison by repeating it with a judge from a different provider. This preregistered study tests how far that check can be trusted. Five judge models from three providers re-judged 4,000 `Chatbot Arena` battles that already carry human votes. Verdict-level agreement with humans was low (median Cohen's kappa of 0.22), and **system rankings did not survive a change of judge**: Kendall's tau with the human ranking ranged from 0.17 to 0.89. Replicating a conclusion across two providers raised precision mainly by filtering out one poorly aligned judge, and judges tended to disagree with humans on the same battles far more often than independence would predict.

papers.title: Same Rule, Different Verdicts: Rubric Language and Clause Structure in LLM Judges for Korean Support Dialogues
papers.abstract: Services that operate in Korean often write their evaluation rubrics in Korean and hand them to an LLM judge. We test whether a judge's verdict depends on the language of the rubric and on how a rubric item is phrased. We write 12 criteria for support dialogues in four clause structures (affirmative, negated, conditional, exception) such that two pairs of structures have the same meaning, and we give each item in Korean and in English. Six low-cost models from three providers, plus one reference model, judge 60 translated ESConv dialogues and 144 constructed boundary cases under every combination (51,744 requests across the seven models). The analysis plan was fixed and committed before data collection. Cross-provider agreement is lower with Korean rubrics than with English rubrics (Cohen's kappa 0.687 vs. 0.745; difference -0.058, 95% CI [-0.072,-0.045]). Disagreement concentrates in negated, conditional, and exception items (odds ratio 5.6 relative to affirmative items). A single model changes its verdict between two items with the same meaning in 11-15% of cases. Two hypotheses are not supported: models from the same provider do not agree more than models from different providers, and adding paired examples does not reduce the language gap. We measure consistency only; no human labels are used, and all materials were drafted by an LLM.
papers.summary: Korean-language services often write their LLM-judge rubrics in Korean. This preregistered study asks whether verdicts depend on the rubric's language and on how each item is phrased. Twelve criteria for support dialogues were each written in four clause structures (affirmative, negated, conditional, exception) and in both Korean and English, then applied by seven models to translated `ESConv` dialogues and constructed boundary cases, for 51,744 requests in total. Agreement across providers was lower with Korean rubrics (kappa 0.687 vs. 0.745), disagreement was concentrated in non-affirmative items (**odds ratio 5.6**), and a single model changed its verdict between two items with the same meaning in 11-15% of cases. Models from the same provider did not agree more with each other, and adding paired examples did not close the language gap.

papers.title: ScaleTraj: Scale-Decomposed Human Trajectory Generation
papers.abstract: Individual-level trajectories are essential for applications that rely on user-level mobility behavior. Existing mobility-generation approaches face a fundamental tension between individual-level and population-level statistical fidelity: top-down models reproduce aggregate mobility statistics but struggle to guarantee realistic individual trajectories, while bottom-up generators synthesize individual trajectories yet often fail to preserve key population-level mobility regularities after aggregation. In particular, many bottom-up generated populations fail to reproduce the displacement distribution, whose heavy tail is well summarized by a truncated power law. We formalize this phenomenon as the \textbf{Population-Level Displacement Gap}. To investigate its prevalence, we conduct a systematic evaluation of representative model-driven and data-driven trajectory generators. Our results provide evidence that the Population-Level Displacement Gap is prevalent across diverse generation paradigms. To diagnose this gap, we introduce the \textbf{Scale Fidelity Profile (SFP)}, a scale-decomposed metric that quantifies discrepancies in trip allocations across spatial scales. SFP indicates that population-level displacement mismatches co-occur with systematic errors in how trips are allocated across spatial scales. Motivated by this observation, we develop \textbf{ScaleTraj}, an autoregressive Transformer that decomposes location prediction into a Scale Selection Head that decides the movement scale and a Scale-Aware Cell Selection Head that predicts the destination conditioned on the selected scale. Experiments on two datasets show that ScaleTraj reduces the Population-Level Displacement Gap versus model-driven and data-driven baselines, while preserving fidelity. Our code is available at https://github.com/SCU-TrustworthyAI/ScaleTraj.
papers.summary: Generators of synthetic human mobility traces that work bottom-up, one individual at a time, often fail to reproduce the population's heavy-tailed displacement distribution, which a truncated power law describes well. The authors call this the Population-Level Displacement Gap and show that it appears across many generation paradigms. They introduce a scale-decomposed metric, the `Scale Fidelity Profile`, which links the gap to errors in how trips are allocated across spatial scales. Their `ScaleTraj` model is an autoregressive Transformer that first chooses a movement scale and then predicts a destination conditioned on it. On two datasets it **reduces the displacement gap** compared with baselines while keeping individual-level fidelity.

papers.title: When Strong Reasoners Join the Pool: Small Union Premiums and Costly Runaway Generations in LLM Routing
papers.abstract: Routing benchmarks often judge a router against a hindsight oracle that counts a query as solved whenever any model's recorded answer is correct, but under stochastic decoding that oracle mixes two different objects: the clairvoyant ceiling of committing to one model per query and the premium of calling several models and keeping any correct answer. A companion study measured this premium at 3.5 percentage points (pp) for 11 small open models on MATH-500; how large it is once current reasoning models enter the pool was unknown. We measure it with a fixed-protocol, pre-committed generation on a single NVIDIA B300: all 500 MATH-500 problems, 30 seeded samples per problem, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and NVIDIA's Nemotron Nano 9B v2 and Nemotron Super 49B v1.5 (a NAS derivative of the same 70B) under vendor sampling, a 65,536-token cap, a pinned Math-Verify scorer, and an append-only attempt ledger, for 45,000 scored responses. The two reasoning models both reach 96.1% accuracy against 76.2% for the 70B baseline. The empirical product-coupling premium is 0.215-0.588 pp across all two- and three-model pools; the empirical plug-in selection headroom over always calling Nano is 1.27 pp; and resampling Nano three times gives practically the same empirical any-correct rate as calling all three models once. Only 31 responses reached the cap, 25 of them with exactly periodic tails, yet the capped responses account for up to 60.2% of a model's output-length-squared proxy, and long generations made a fourth planned model, Llama-3.1-8B, too slow to finish. The premium is far below the companion's 3.5 pp, but models, pool size and protocol changed together; an oracle gap should therefore be reported with the pool, the protocol, the samples per cell and the decoding budget that produced it.
papers.summary: Routing benchmarks usually compare a router against a hindsight oracle that counts a query as solved if any model's answer was correct. Under stochastic decoding, that oracle blends two different things: the best possible single-model choice per query, and the bonus from calling several models and keeping any correct answer. The authors measure that bonus with a pre-committed protocol: 45,000 `MATH-500` responses from `Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct`, `Nemotron Nano 9B v2`, and `Nemotron Super 49B v1.5` on a single B300 GPU. Both reasoning models reach 96.1% accuracy, and the multi-model premium is **only 0.215-0.588 percentage points**, far below an earlier 3.5-point estimate for small models. Sampling `Nano` three times matches calling all three models once, and a few runaway generations that hit the token cap dominated compute cost.

papers.title: Evaluation Contracts and Evaluation Leverage: Sliced-Gap Readings in Structured Prediction Can Move Without Model Change
papers.abstract: NLP evaluation reports routinely cite sliced performance differences, most prominently the intra-inter gap in document-level relation extraction, as capability evidence. We show that such gap readings are joint properties of models and evaluation contracts: scoring function, gold version, threshold, output format, and prompt language. With predictions frozen, a method ordering reverses under a gold-standard exchange (+0.0363, CI excluding zero; tie-level after), movement localizing where gold re-partitions: renames are gauge transformations (Delta=0; re-annotation +0.862). We formalize this as an evaluation leverage account centered on the rank-flip condition. Constructively, the audited evaluation reading (AER) is a contract-marginalized, tie-declared, seed-prescribed, gate-filtered procedure whose tie declarations cover every contract-induced flip on the declared WMT19 grids (14/14; held-out 73% vs. union-of-ties 89%), matching the best single metric contract at epsilon=0.10 equivalence. Evidence spans DocRE, HacRED, a UD probe, and released gold revisions; an alternative-reference-set replication extends it beyond our testbeds. Failed predictions retained as boundaries; a 5% violation gate flags unverifiable settings and bounds survivor-selection bias. We release EvalLever, a preregistered workflow with an amendment trail; on LLM-as-judge grids, the audited ensemble stabilizes every unstable pair (13-15 to zero; generic ensemble shrinkage: the preregistered correlation criterion failed, the companion stabilization criterion passed).
papers.summary: NLP papers often cite performance gaps on data slices as evidence of capability, most prominently the intra-document versus inter-document gap in document-level relation extraction. The authors argue that such gaps depend jointly on the model and on the "evaluation contract": the scoring function, gold-label version, threshold, output format, and prompt language. With predictions held fixed, simply **swapping the gold standard reverses a method ordering**. They formalize this as an evaluation-leverage account and propose an audited evaluation reading (`AER`) that averages over contracts and explicitly declares ties. They release `EvalLever`, a preregistered workflow, tested on `DocRE`, `HacRED`, `WMT19`, and LLM-as-judge grids.

papers.title: The Agent Board: Kanban for Machines; Durable Coordination for Agents That Outlive the Conversation
papers.abstract: Harnesses for large language models have converged on a single-threaded shape: one agent, one history, one machine, one sitting. That shape fails work that spans many agents, outlives any one model call, or waits on systems that are not agents. We describe the Agent Board, the coordination substrate in the Corvic harness. The board is a durable, shared table of semi-semantic tasks: a few exact fields the system routes on, and a free-form body that only language models read. Agents post tasks, watch tasks, and block on them, ending their turn and holding no process until a matching post wakes them. A system agent, the Board Keeper, acts as the interrupt handler for the board: it carries events from non-agent parts of the harness onto the board, matches them to waiting tasks by reading their prose, and allocates new agents for tasks that name a kind of agent rather than an instance. Loadable coordination policy kernels give statuses and roles meaning for a given pattern of work, without the board enforcing them. The design mirrors the kanban board a human team puts on a wall. We argue it is what persistent agent products such as Meta Muse, OpenAI dots and SpaceXAI Grok Bot need once an agent must wait, hand off work, or work with agents from another vendor. We view the board as an operating-system scheduler for agents and state where the analogy breaks. We separate what the mechanism guarantees from what it leaves to convention, and report a trace from a live board and three small simulated pilots. In the pilots, the wait cost of the board was flat in wait length while naive polling grew about 165-fold, but a plain external watcher was cheaper than the board. The Board Keeper matched prose waiters with no false wakes but missed 3.6 percent of real wakes.
papers.summary: Most LLM harnesses assume one agent, one conversation history, and one session, which breaks down for work that spans many agents, outlives a single model call, or waits on outside systems. The `Agent Board` in the `Corvic` harness is a durable shared task table, modeled on a kanban board. Each task has a few exact fields the system routes on plus a free-form body that only models read, and agents can post tasks, watch them, or block on them without holding a running process. A system agent called the `Board Keeper` carries events from non-agent parts of the harness onto the board, matches them to waiting tasks by reading their prose, and starts new agents when needed. In small simulated pilots, waiting on the board cost the same regardless of wait length while naive polling cost grew about 165-fold, but a plain external watcher was cheaper still, and the Keeper **missed 3.6% of real wakes** while producing no false ones.

papers.title: Structured Clinical Memory as Context for Probabilistic Decision Models: A Synthetic Evaluation with Jev
papers.abstract: Longitudinal clinical context is often distributed across noisy, repetitive forms and narrative records. We study whether a compact structured memory can improve a probabilistic decision model's answers when the underlying patient vignette is already available. We created 30 fully synthetic cases spanning twelve clinical domains, paired each with synthetically generated structured memory, and evaluated 120 typed questions with Jev. The raw-vignette arm achieved 90.0% accuracy (95% normal-approximation confidence interval: 84.6%-95.4%); adding memory achieved 93.3% (88.9%-97.8%). Five questions changed from incorrect to correct and one changed in the opposite direction (exact McNemar $p=0.219$). Choice log loss decreased from 0.258 to 0.175 and binary Brier score from 0.054 to 0.022. Memory added 310 input tokens per call on average, while observed mean latency was unchanged at approximately 0.5 seconds. These results are directionally positive rather than clinically validating: the cases are synthetic, the labels are single-author judgments, and the memory is an oracle upper bound rather than extracted production output. The pilot supports evaluating structured clinical memory as a reusable state interface for decision models.
papers.summary: A patient's longitudinal clinical context is often scattered across noisy, repetitive forms and narrative notes. This pilot tests whether a compact structured memory improves a probabilistic decision model, `Jev`, even when the raw patient vignette is already provided. On 30 fully synthetic cases with 120 typed questions, accuracy rose from 90.0% to **93.3%** with memory, which was not statistically significant (McNemar p=0.219). Log loss and Brier score both improved, at a cost of about 310 extra input tokens per call and no change in latency. The authors note that the cases are synthetic, the labels come from a single author, and the memory is an idealized upper bound rather than output from a real extraction system.

papers.title: ModelBlaster: Closing the Performance Gap through Learning-Augmented Agents Across Models, Kernels and Hardware Backends
papers.abstract:
Optimizing accelerator code across hardware architectures is difficult. ML compilers search predefined spaces of schedules and micro-kernels, while LLM-guided optimization can explore alternative algorithms, operator decompositions, and hardware-specific techniques. However, existing LLM agents typically target a single programming interface, toolchain, or accelerator family, focus on kernel-level optimization without model-level transforms, and offer limited reuse of experience across hardware targets.
  We present ModelBlaster, a Memory-Augmented In-Context Reinforcement Learning (MAIC-RL) framework for optimizing data-parallel kernels and whole models across heterogeneous SIMD and SIMT accelerators. Its mutable policy is a persistent knowledge base updated at inference time by Actor-Critic Textual Gradient Descent (AC-TGD). The knowledge base maps performance states to actions, outcomes, and constraints, enabling experience reuse across kernels, models, and hardware targets. A model-level optimizer uses kernel-level knowledge to inform whole-model decisions. The same optimization loop and knowledge schema support CUDA on NVIDIA GPUs, OpenCL on Qualcomm GPUs, and RVV intrinsics on RISC-V vector cores, with only lowering and measurement layers specific to each target.
  Compared with PyTorch, ModelBlaster achieves geometric-mean speedups of 1.85x, 5.58x, and 5.18x on KernelBench Levels 1, 2, and 3, and 1.69x on SOL-ExecBench Levels 1 and 2 on a B200 GPU. On Qualcomm Adreno GPUs, it achieves 5.8x over the vendor SDK and 1.7x over Apache TVM; on RISC-V vector cores, it achieves 2.7x over ExecuTorch with XNNPACK across 70 KernelBench problems.
papers.summary: Existing LLM agents for accelerator code tend to target a single programming interface or hardware family, work only at the kernel level, and reuse little experience across targets. `ModelBlaster` is a memory-augmented in-context reinforcement learning framework (`MAIC-RL`) whose policy is a persistent knowledge base. That knowledge base is updated at inference time by actor-critic textual gradient descent (`AC-TGD`) and records performance states, actions, outcomes, and constraints, so lessons carry over across kernels, models, and hardware. The same loop drives CUDA, OpenCL on Qualcomm GPUs, and RISC-V vector intrinsics, with only the lowering and measurement layers specific to each target. It reaches geometric-mean speedups over PyTorch of 1.85x, **5.58x**, and 5.18x on `KernelBench` Levels 1-3 on a B200 GPU, 5.8x over the vendor SDK on Adreno GPUs, and 2.7x over `ExecuTorch` on RISC-V.

papers.title: Structure, Dimensionality, and Distribution Shape - What Makes Pretraining Data Transferable, and Why the Input Pipeline Decides Which
papers.abstract: What makes a pretraining corpus transferable? We describe a corpus by three properties: its structure, its dimensionality, and the distribution shape of each unit's values. We propose the Transfer-Invariance Principle: the same property can be irrelevant to transfer under one input transform and decisive under another, so the model's input transform, not the data modality, decides which properties can matter. To test it we build TransferForge, a generator that places a synthetic population at any prescribed structure, dimensionality, and distribution shape. KernelSynth, the synthetic prior of Chronos, cannot, because it draws independent series. When the model standardizes each input window (PatchTST on UCR), the distribution shape is inert and the structural setting governs. Synthetic pretraining then matches a real corpus of the same size and exceeds it once scaled. When the model encodes calcium fluorescence signals without normalization (POYO Plus), the shape becomes a governing constraint, and a shape-matched synthetic corpus replaces real pretraining with zero real neural activity. Flipping only the input normalization, with the model and data fixed, changes the effect of a shape manipulation by a factor of 5.3, so the pipeline, not the modality, sets the switch. The principle yields a recipe that chooses what to synthesize before any training. Pretraining data then becomes something to manufacture for the model, most valuably where real data is scarce, expensive, or private.
papers.summary: The authors describe a pretraining corpus by three properties (structure, dimensionality, and the distribution shape of its values) and propose a Transfer-Invariance Principle. The principle says the model's input transform, not the data's modality, determines which of these properties matter for transfer. They test it with `TransferForge`, a synthetic data generator that can set each property independently. When inputs are standardized, as with `PatchTST` on `UCR`, distribution shape has no effect and synthetic pretraining matches or beats real data. When raw calcium-imaging signals are fed in unnormalized, as with `POYO Plus`, shape becomes decisive, and a shape-matched synthetic corpus replaces real neural data entirely. With model and data held fixed, toggling only the input normalization **changes the effect of a shape manipulation 5.3-fold**.

papers.title: Say Less, Mean Better: Training-Free Verbosity Control for Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate responses longer than necessary, increasing inference latency and computational cost. While prompting can encourage conciseness, controlling output length without compromising response completeness remains challenging. Aggressive early stopping can reduce generation costs but risks terminating responses prematurely. We introduce MinimalLM, a training-free framework for reliable verbosity control that combines uncertainty-aware, length-dependent stop-token adjustment with structural completeness guardrails. MinimalLM separates the decision of when to stop from whether stopping is structurally appropriate, coordinating response-level instructions, decoding-time intervention, and completion checks without modifying model parameters or requiring auxiliary models. We evaluate MinimalLM across three open-source LLMs and 330 questions, producing 5,940 responses across baseline and ablation configurations. MinimalLM reduces generated tokens by 47.6%, accelerates individual responses by 19-68%, and eliminates structurally truncated outputs in the primary evaluation. Despite substantial token savings, it achieves an average quality score of 8.04/10, compared with 8.42/10 for unmodified models and 6.46/10 for length-matched truncation. Evaluations across diverse subject domains (such as healthcare, programming, law, and science) demonstrate robust efficiency gains, while ablations establish the complementary roles of decoding control and completeness constraints. Our findings highlight that efficient generation requires more than producing fewer tokens: it requires controlling when generation ends while preserving response integrity. MinimalLM offers a lightweight, training-free approach toward this goal.
papers.summary: LLMs often write longer answers than needed, and cutting generation short risks truncating them mid-thought. `MinimalLM` is a training-free method that adjusts the probability of the stop token based on uncertainty and response length. It pairs this with structural completeness checks, so the decision of when to stop is separate from whether stopping is structurally safe. Across three open-source models and 330 questions, it **cuts generated tokens by 47.6%** and speeds up responses by 19-68% with no structurally truncated outputs. Its average quality score is 8.04/10, compared with 8.42 for the unmodified models and 6.46 for truncating to the same length.

papers.title: Separating Common and Unique Directions for Data-Free Model Merging
papers.abstract: Model merging combines multiple fine-tuned models without additional training, and arithmetic methods have emerged as a simple yet effective way to merge models without data. However, existing arithmetic methods treat task vectors in parameter space and apply a single element-wise rule to directions that can differ in mergeability. In a shared directional basis, we find a consistent two-regime structure: a low-dispersion common bulk shared across tasks and a high-dispersion task-dominated tail that carries disproportionate energy. These findings motivate Common--Unique Subspace Decomposition (CUSD), a data-free pre-merging method that separates task vectors into common and unique directional components, merges the common components with downstream arithmetic operator, and retains unique residuals separately. Experiments across $11$ base models, four model families, and four arithmetic-based merging operators show that CUSD improves 42 of 44 model--operator combinations and achieves up to 22.5% improvement over the corresponding baselines. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/stwang666/CUSD
papers.summary: Data-free arithmetic model merging combines fine-tuned models by applying a single element-wise rule to their task vectors, even though some directions in parameter space may merge better than others. In a shared directional basis, the authors find two regimes: a low-dispersion common bulk shared across tasks and a high-dispersion, task-specific tail that carries a disproportionate share of the energy. `Common-Unique Subspace Decomposition` (`CUSD`) separates each task vector into these two parts, merges the common parts with an existing arithmetic operator, and keeps the unique residuals separately. Across 11 base models and four merging operators, it **improves 42 of 44 model-operator combinations**, with gains of up to 22.5%.

papers.title: Generalizable AI-Generated Image Detection with Embedding-Space Explanations
papers.abstract: AI-generated images have reached unprecedented realism, while instruction-driven AI editors re-synthesize images for local changes, leaving no splice boundary to localize. Most detectors are black boxes with unverifiable verdicts and generalize poorly because adapting a backbone on the detection distribution memorizes generator-specific fingerprints that quickly become obsolete. Specialist detectors built on pure-vision representations, particularly DINOv3, generalize well across generators, but explainable methods forgo this advantage: jointly training one multimodal model for classification and language generation subjects its visual representation to the language objective. We therefore require that explanation training cannot alter the verdict. We introduce FOX, which first builds and locks a specialist DINOv3 detector, then uses its representation to guide a lightweight VLM toward forensic explanation. A joint-embedding predictor maps locked visual evidence into a frozen text encoder's semantic space, producing guidance that the VLM verbalizes on demand. FOX achieves 97.4 mean AUC across 14 unseen generators, 69.8 BERTScore on XPlainVerse, and 56.1 on LOKI.
papers.summary: Detectors for AI-generated images tend to be black boxes that generalize poorly to new generators. Explainable detectors that train one multimodal model for both classification and explanation also lose the cross-generator robustness of pure-vision backbones such as `DINOv3`. `FOX` first trains a `DINOv3` detector and locks it, so that later explanation training cannot change its verdicts. A joint-embedding predictor then maps the locked visual evidence into a frozen text encoder's semantic space, and a lightweight vision-language model (VLM) turns that guidance into forensic explanations on demand. It reaches **97.4 mean AUC across 14 unseen generators**, along with 69.8 BERTScore on `XPlainVerse` and 56.1 on `LOKI`.

papers.title: Co-Occurrence Priors Override Visual Spatial Evidence: Understanding False Alarms in Vision-Language Models for Construction Struck-By Hazard Detection
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly support construction hazard monitoring, yet their frequent false alarms remain poorly understood. This study investigates whether false struck-by hazard warnings arise from failures in object recognition, spatial relation encoding, or hazard decisions dominated by learned co-occurrence priors. We evaluated Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B using 355 counterfactual worker-excavator scene pairs with controlled spatial proximity and worker-removal variants, combining behavioral analysis, internal representation probing, causal interventions, and decision correction. Both models recognized the entities and encoded their spatial relations (out-of-fold AUROC: 0.82 and 0.91), assigning higher hazard scores to near than far scenes in 79% and 73% of pairs. Nevertheless, 74% and 100% of far scenes were falsely classified as hazardous. Removing the worker reduced Qwen's hazard rate to 11%, while worker presence exerted 2.4- and 3.2-times greater influence on hazard scores than spatial proximity in the respective models. Attention-head interventions, neuron-level interventions, and activation steering failed to eliminate this co-occurrence bias. However, conditioning hazard decisions on the model's own spatial-relation representation improved Qwen's specificity from 0.36 to 0.58 at matched sensitivity, outperforming threshold recalibration. These findings reveal that VLM struck-by false alarms stem primarily from decision-making failures rather than deficiencies in object recognition or spatial encoding, suggesting that future efforts should prioritize conditioning hazard decisions on encoded spatial evidence rather than further improving visual recognition alone.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) used for construction-site safety frequently raise false struck-by hazard warnings. Using 355 counterfactual worker-excavator scene pairs, the authors probe `Qwen2.5-VL-7B` and `InternVL3.5-8B` to locate where these false alarms come from. Both models recognize the objects and internally encode how close they are (AUROC 0.82 and 0.91), yet they **label 74% and 100% of far-apart scenes as hazardous**, because the mere presence of a worker outweighs spatial proximity by 2.4-3.2 times. Attention-head interventions, neuron-level interventions, and activation steering did not remove this co-occurrence bias. Conditioning the hazard decision on the model's own spatial representation raised `Qwen`'s specificity from 0.36 to 0.58 at the same sensitivity.

papers.title: The Evolution Strategies Paradox: Better Models from Worse Perturbations
papers.abstract: How is it possible for perturbation-based methods like Evolution Strategies (ES) to optimize billion-parameter large language models (LLMs)? Classical search methods are highly dependent on finding good candidates within generated populations. However, when using ES to fine-tune LLMs, a phenomenon can occur where all offspring models consistently perform worse than the parent model, yet during training, the parent model consistently improves. This paradox occurs across models, tasks, and even modalities. This paper characterizes the paradox, then examines how the local reward landscape and properties of the ES estimator contribute to it: in high-dimensional spaces, exploration leads to worse performance, yet still highlights good directions; aggregating those directions then allows for making local improvements. The result can be seen as a new optimization paradigm where a principled interaction of noise and curvature produces the paradox as a byproduct of effective optimization. These findings provide guidance for taking advantage of perturbation-based methods in LLM fine-tuning and in high-dimensional optimization in general.
papers.summary: When Evolution Strategies (ES) are used to fine-tune billion-parameter LLMs, every perturbed offspring model can score worse than its parent while the parent still improves steadily during training. The authors document this paradox across models, tasks, and modalities. They explain it through the local reward landscape and properties of the ES gradient estimator: in very high-dimensional spaces, individual perturbations hurt performance but still point toward good directions, and **averaging those directions yields real improvement**. They present this as an optimization regime in which noise interacting with curvature produces the paradox, and they draw practical guidance for perturbation-based LLM fine-tuning.

papers.title: Decomposing Rank Reversals under Temporal Nonstationarity: Alignment, Aggressiveness, and Instability
papers.abstract: Under temporal nonstationarity, model performance rankings reverse across training horizons due to heterogeneous sensitivities to memory. While existing literature addresses adaptive lookbacks, effective model complexity, and empirical forecast evaluation in isolation, no unified framework explains the structural mechanics driving these rank reversals. We bridge this gap by deriving a model-agnostic decomposition of out-of-sample $R^2$ into target alignment, miscalibrated aggressiveness, and predictive instability. Within this framework, we mathematically characterize complexity phase boundaries, establish closed-form optimal-memory equations for ridge regression under local drift, and extend these guarantees to complex model architectures via surrogate bounds. We validate these theoretical dynamics by benchmarking 14 linear, tree-based, and neural architectures across large-scale financial panels. In doing so, our framework demonstrates that empirical model rank reversals are driven by predictable surges in miscalibrated aggressiveness, providing a rigorous mechanistic diagnosis of generalization under temporal shift.
papers.summary: When data drift over time, the ranking of forecasting models can flip depending on how much history each one is trained on. The authors derive a model-agnostic decomposition of out-of-sample R-squared into three terms: target alignment, miscalibrated aggressiveness, and predictive instability. They also derive closed-form optimal-memory equations for ridge regression under local drift and extend the guarantees to more complex models through surrogate bounds. Benchmarks of 14 linear, tree-based, and neural models on large financial panels show that rank reversals are **driven by predictable surges in miscalibrated aggressiveness**.

papers.title: ScrambleMark: Zero-Query Watermark-Agnostic Black-Box Evasion of Modern Speech Watermarking
papers.abstract:
Speech watermarking is becoming a key defense for digital copyright and content authentication. Existing attacks treat evasion as a removal problem: they erase the watermark, relying on detector access or on speech data that is hard to collect, such as paired clean-watermarked or clean target speaker speech. Commercial platforms are moving to close off these assumptions. TrustedAudio, for instance, restricts detection to authenticated users and denies meaningful detection feedback to unauthorized parties. Adversaries thus cannot tell whether a sample is watermarked or which watermark it carries, nor reliably remove it without degrading speech quality.
  In this work, we show that evading a speech watermark does not require erasing it: detection relies on the structural consistency of the embedded pattern, and disrupting this consistency is enough to defeat it. Building on this observation, we identify harmonic structure as an effective attack surface, as perturbing it breaks watermark consistency while preserving perceptual quality. We therefore propose ScrambleMark, a zero-query, watermark-agnostic, black-box attack that evades detection through harmonic scrambling. ScrambleMark combines a deterministic engine for discovering transferable harmonic perturbations with a generative model that learns randomized scrambling patterns, avoiding reliance on fixed attack rules. Across three commercial platforms (Google SynthID, Resemble AI, and TrustedAudio), ScrambleMark is the only attack to both evade detection and keep speech natural, achieving nearly 97% evasion and a 4.2/5 human rating, far above the 1.1 to 1.7 of prior attacks. Beyond evasion, ScrambleMark withstands adaptive recovery designed to reverse it, evidence that structural evasion is hard to mitigate in practice.
papers.summary: Existing attacks on speech watermarks try to remove the watermark, which typically requires access to the detector or hard-to-collect paired audio. Commercial platforms are increasingly closing off both. The authors show that removal is unnecessary: detection depends on the watermark pattern staying structurally consistent, and perturbing the harmonic structure of speech breaks that consistency while keeping the audio natural. `ScrambleMark` is a zero-query, watermark-agnostic, black-box attack that pairs a deterministic engine for finding transferable harmonic perturbations with a generative model that learns randomized scrambling patterns. Against `Google SynthID`, `Resemble AI`, and `TrustedAudio`, it achieves **nearly 97% evasion with a 4.2/5 human naturalness rating**, compared with 1.1-1.7 for prior attacks, and it holds up against adaptive attempts to recover the watermark.

papers.title: GlucoAgent: Personalized Glucose Forecasting from Multimodal Personal Context
papers.abstract: Continuous glucose monitors, smartwatches, meal logs, and health profiles form a rich multimodal personal context that can significantly enhance glucose forecasting. However, existing methods struggle to effectively utilize these signals to improve glucose prediction because the relevance of different modalities varies drastically across individuals and time. We present GlucoAgent, an LLM-based agentic system that addresses this challenge through dynamic, case-by-case analysis at inference time. For each forecast, GlucoAgent writes and runs code over an individual's multimodal context and returns predictions with a reason and supporting evidence. The generated programs are highly diverse, ranging from retrieving similar past meals to fitting and back-testing physiological and statistical models. On CGMacros, a multimodal glucose dataset, GlucoAgent outperforms time series foundation models on every forecasting horizon, achieving an average RMSE of 22.5 mg/dL compared to 23.5 mg/dL of Chronos-2, the leading multimodal time series foundation model. Furthermore, GlucoAgent is highly effective at leveraging multimodal data. The addition of multimodal data reduces its average RMSE by 1.4 mg/dL (24.0 mg/dL to 22.5 mg/dL), compared to a marginal 0.3 mg/dL (23.8 mg/dL to 23.5 mg/dL) improvement for Chronos-2. This advantage is most pronounced in challenging post-meal windows, where GlucoAgent uses multimodal context to reduce 60-minute forecast RMSE by 4.6 mg/dL (31.0 mg/dL to 26.5 mg/dL), far exceeding the 0.8 mg/dL (31.9 mg/dL to 31.1 mg/dL) reduction achieved by Chronos-2.
papers.summary: Glucose forecasting could draw on continuous glucose monitors, smartwatches, meal logs, and health profiles, but how useful each of these signals is varies a lot between people and over time. `GlucoAgent` is an LLM-based agent that, for each forecast, writes and runs code over the individual's multimodal data. The programs range from retrieving similar past meals to fitting and back-testing physiological models, and each prediction comes with a reason and supporting evidence. On the `CGMacros` dataset it beats time series foundation models at every forecasting horizon, with an average RMSE of 22.5 mg/dL against 23.5 mg/dL for `Chronos-2`. Adding multimodal context helps it far more than it helps `Chronos-2`: in post-meal windows, the extra context cuts its 60-minute error by **4.6 mg/dL**, compared with 0.8 mg/dL for `Chronos-2`.

papers.title: LoopKV: Loop-Aware KV Cache Compression for Serving Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: Looped transformers apply a shared block several times per token to improve accuracy without adding parameters. For models such as Ouro that keep a separate key-value (KV) cache per loop, cache memory limits the batch size that amortizes repeated weight reads. Uniform-bit quantization and fixed rules per loop do not allocate precision according to each layer's sensitivity in each loop. Measurements on Ouro show that quantization sensitivity varies across (loop, layer) cells, and the sum of individual cell damages approximates the overall output damage. Sharing damage also varies by cell, with later loops generally tolerating sharing better. Skipping low-attention values to save reads produces errors that compound across loops. LoopKV uses a one-time offline profile to choose 4-bit storage, 2-bit storage or reuse of the final loop's KV for each cell. The planner minimizes reads under budgets for predicted damage and storage. During decoding, each loop reads the high 2 bits of each 4-bit value and fetches the low bits only where its own attention weights require 4-bit precision. A single fused kernel in vLLM executes the plan. Serving Ouro-1.4B on one RTX PRO 6000, the memory-optimized LoopKV-M plan stores 35% less KV than uniform 4-bit quantization (KIVI-4) on the same fused kernel and CUDA graph. It sustains 1.7-2.2x KIVI-4's goodput under a latency service-level objective with a 16K-token maximum length. None of its averages on six public benchmarks falls significantly below BF16's.
papers.summary: Looped transformers such as `Ouro` run a shared block several times per token and keep a separate key-value (KV) cache for each loop, so cache memory limits the batch size during serving. Measurements show that sensitivity to quantization and to sharing caches varies across (loop, layer) cells, and that per-cell damage roughly adds up to the total output damage. `LoopKV` uses a one-time offline profile to assign each cell 4-bit storage, 2-bit storage, or reuse of the final loop's KV. During decoding it reads the low bits of a 4-bit value only where attention needs that precision, and a single fused kernel in `vLLM` executes the plan. Serving `Ouro-1.4B` on one RTX PRO 6000, the memory-optimized plan stores 35% less KV than uniform 4-bit `KIVI-4` and sustains **1.7-2.2x its goodput** under a latency target, with no significant accuracy loss against BF16 on six benchmarks.

papers.title: Where Do Distilled Students Store Thinking?
papers.abstract: Small students degrade on large reasoning models' (LRMs') long solutions, so recent work shortens them by interpolating an LRM with a short-answer model at ratio $\lambda$. We ask what student weights retain when this teacher stops thinking, comparing LoRA adapters of three students from three teacher pairs at each $\lambda$. In each pair, the adapters' update subspace shifts most where the teacher stops thinking and solutions shorten most, locating the change without attributing it. We identify a shared adapter subspace tied to thinking-like behavior (reflective markers, monologue format and long solutions). Shared by adapters before that point, it keeps about half (post hoc) while one pair's teacher halves its solutions but keeps its think tag, and largely empties after thinking stops. Removing it largely turns this behavior off for every pair, student and benchmark. Only in that pair and one other student does it leave clearly fewer markers than removing the update's top components; elsewhere, same-energy random directions often nearly match it. Grafted into a short-answer student at twice its weight, it turns early markers (a post hoc count) on, like the whole update, but the student rarely finishes. Our work identifies a weight subspace tied to distilled thinking-like behavior.
papers.summary: One recent way to shorten large reasoning model (LRM) outputs for distillation into small students is to interpolate the LRM with a short-answer model; this work asks what the students' weights keep as the interpolated teacher stops thinking. Comparing `LoRA` adapters of three students across three teacher pairs, the authors find that the adapters' update subspace shifts most at the point where the teacher stops thinking. They identify a shared adapter subspace tied to thinking-like behavior: reflective markers, monologue format, and long solutions. **Removing this subspace largely switches that behavior off** for every pair, student, and benchmark, although random directions of the same energy often come close to matching it. Grafting the subspace into a short-answer student brings the markers back, but that student rarely finishes its solutions.

papers.title: Interpretable Early Termination of Web Navigation Agents via Closed Sequential Pattern Mining
papers.abstract: Web navigation agents built on open-weight language models fail often and fail late, with most of the tokens spent after the trajectory has become unrecoverable. Recent work has shown that early termination is a viable cost-reduction strategy, but existing approaches produce opaque termination decisions that do not support diagnosis or human oversight. In this work we apply closed sequential pattern mining (BIDE+) to K-step prefixes of agent execution traces to produce a small, human-reviewable failure-signature library that organizes into a four-category failure taxonomy with associated repair recommendations. We use a multi-variant evaluation protocol that explicitly removes contamination artifacts (zero-step crashes and trivially separable single-step successes) so that reported detection accuracy reflects behavioral discrimination rather than trace-length distributions.
