It identifies optimization-based, policy-based, and knowledge-based approaches as the main routes from representation to action. It also names three roles for ML: building surrogate models, turning raw physical feedback into decision-relevant information, and speeding up or directly generating decisions. The authors argue for **a shift from a model-centric to a system-centric view**, in which performance depends on how sensing, state estimation, computation, decision-making, and continual adaptation interact.

papers.title: Deep Learning Compilers: Architecture, Optimization, and Empirical Characterization
papers.abstract: As deep learning (DL) models become increasingly complex and hardware architectures grow more heterogeneous, DL compilers play a critical role in optimizing computational efficiency and enabling scalable deployment. This paper presents a systematic analysis of DL compilers, covering their architectural evolution, compilation workflows, optimization techniques, and emerging research directions. We organize DL compiler architectures into frontend, middle-end, and backend stages, emphasizing the role of the middle-end in connecting high-level model representations with hardware-specific optimizations. We further examine representative DL compilers and recent optimization techniques across different compilation stages. Beyond architectural and technical analysis, we conduct an empirical evaluation of compiler behaviors to investigate the effectiveness of graph optimization, compilation overhead, and dynamic-shape handling. Experiments using PyTorch/TorchInductor on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 demonstrate that compiler benefits depend strongly on workload characteristics, with speedups of up to 8.21\times for fusion-friendly computation graphs, while other workloads exhibit limited improvements. Our results further reveal that compilation overhead can require thousands of executions to amortize, and dynamic-shape compilation reduces cumulative shape-transition costs by approximately 70\% at the expense of modest steady-state performance degradation. By combining systematic architectural analysis with quantitative experimental evidence, this work provides insights into the design, optimization, and practical deployment of modern DL compilers.
papers.summary: The survey describes deep learning compilers as three stages: a frontend, a middle-end, and a backend, with the middle-end bridging high-level model graphs and hardware-specific optimizations. It reviews representative compilers and optimization techniques at each stage. Experiments with `PyTorch`/`TorchInductor` on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 show that **speedups reach 8.21× for fusion-friendly graphs but are small for other workloads**. Compilation overhead can take thousands of runs to pay back, and dynamic-shape compilation cuts cumulative shape-transition cost by about 70% at the price of slightly slower steady-state performance.

papers.title: Harness-S: Learning from Sibling Harnesses for Generalizable Agent Training
papers.abstract: Harness evolution from a common base exhibits Locality, Complementarity, and Nonstationarity: variants repair different failures, and their utility changes as the policy learns. Rather than seeking a universally superior harness, we introduce Harness-S to selectively rescue failures of a base execution system through sibling harnesses and transfer the resulting capabilities into a single policy that remains effective under the original harness. Directional Harness Evolution develops specialized sibling harnesses along distinct repair directions, forming a reusable Sibling Harness Pool that remains fixed during policy training. Complementary Harness Rescue Training invokes this pool only when all initial attempts under the base harness fail. The same policy generates fresh rollouts under selected auxiliary harnesses, and these trajectories replace the failed group for reinforcement learning. An Adaptive Harness Router selects the Top-k variants using Harness Behavior Profiles and voting across multiple LLMs. Policy-aware profile re-anchoring refreshes this evidence as the policy learns. Across AppWorld, SWE-Gym, and DBBench, the trained policy substantially outperforms policy-only training when returned to the original base harness. Behavioral analyses and held-out cases support the transfer of harness-elicited behaviors into the policy itself. Reusing the router for Rank-1 inference provides additional gains at the same executor rollout count.
papers.summary: Agent harnesses that evolve from a common base each fix different failures, and their usefulness shifts as the policy learns. `Harness-S` uses this to train one policy that works well under the original harness. It builds a fixed pool of sibling harnesses, each specialized along a different repair direction. When every rollout under the base harness fails, it collects fresh rollouts from selected siblings and uses those trajectories in reinforcement learning instead of the failed group. An adaptive router picks the siblings using behavior profiles and voting across several LLMs. Across `AppWorld`, `SWE-Gym`, and `DBBench`, **the trained policy substantially outperforms policy-only training when returned to the base harness**, and reusing the router at inference gives further gains at the same rollout count.

papers.title: Bidirectional Centered Score Matching for Discrete Diffusion Distillation
papers.abstract: Discrete diffusion models with parallel decoding are often distilled using token-wise KL objectives. Although token-wise KL exactly matches the corresponding product-form block distributions, its probability-space optimization geometry and teacher-only candidate truncation may provide insufficient supervision under aggressive few-step distillation. Concrete Score Matching (CSM) provides an alternative within-position objective by aligning relative logit geometry, but its complete pairwise form incurs $\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{V}|^2)$ complexity. We propose Bidirectional Centered Score Matching (BCSM), an efficient within-position distillation objective that constructs an $\mathcal{O}(K)$ bidirectional active set, reduces pairwise comparisons to $\mathcal{O}(K^2)$, and factorizes them into an $\mathcal{O}(K)$ objective. We further introduce cross-timestep transition alignment. Experiments demonstrate strong quality--efficiency trade-offs, including up to $6\times$ NFE reduction with a 16.9\% relative HumanEval gain and a 15.1\% relative MMMU gain at single-step inference.
papers.summary: Discrete diffusion models that decode tokens in parallel are usually distilled with token-wise KL objectives, which can give too little supervision when distilling aggressively down to a few steps. Concrete Score Matching (`CSM`) aligns relative logit geometry instead, but its full pairwise form scales quadratically with vocabulary size. Bidirectional Centered Score Matching (`BCSM`) builds a small bidirectional active set of candidate tokens and factorizes the pairwise comparisons into a linear-cost objective. It also adds an alignment term across timesteps. The authors report **up to 6× fewer function evaluations along with relative gains of 16.9% on `HumanEval` and 15.1% on `MMMU` at single-step inference**.

papers.title: Predicting protein structures at any folding stage from sequence
papers.abstract: Protein structure predictors reliably identify native conformations, but do not describe the continuum connecting unfolded ensembles to folded states. Here we present FoldScape, a sequence-conditioned deep learning framework that generates C$\alpha$ conformational ensembles at a specified folding fraction $Q$. FoldScape reconstructs three-dimensional chains through hierarchical, sliding-window regressions of one-dimensional inter-residue distances, followed by chain assembly and sampling with a rectified-flow decoder. It is trained on multi-scale coarse-grained folding trajectories and all-atom mechanical-unfolding trajectories. Across 20 human proteins (36-857 residues), at matched sample size, FoldScape covers about an order of magnitude more of the folding coordinate than seed-varied AlphaFold 3 ensembles, robustly across proteins, order parameters and binning choices. AlphaFold 3 better anchors the immediate native vicinity, which FoldScape does not reach, making the approaches complementary. FoldScape reconstruction accuracy remains approximately constant along $Q$, from collapsed coil to near-native globule, rather than deteriorating away from the native state. A stride-one crop-and-superpose scheme extends inference to chains several times longer than a single chain-level forward pass. We also show that training trajectories resolve mechanical unfolding at residue resolution, that elongation-conditioned ensembles exhibit reproducible continuous observables across pulling velocities, and that partially unfolded chains form geometrically coherent segments. FoldScape thus combines broad coverage of folding stages with stable reconstruction accuracy, without per-protein simulation.
papers.summary: Structure predictors find native protein conformations but say nothing about the path from unfolded to folded states. `FoldScape` generates Cα conformational ensembles from sequence at a specified folding fraction Q. It regresses inter-residue distances over sliding windows, assembles the chain, and samples with a rectified-flow decoder, trained on coarse-grained folding and all-atom mechanical-unfolding trajectories. Across 20 human proteins, **`FoldScape` covers about an order of magnitude more of the folding coordinate than seed-varied `AlphaFold 3` ensembles**, with reconstruction accuracy roughly constant along Q. `AlphaFold 3` remains better close to the native state, so the authors present the two as complementary.

papers.title: When Debate Amplifies Risk: Social-Bias Vulnerabilities in Multi-Agent Safety Deliberation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented Web applications increasingly employ multi-agent debate (MAD) to aggregate conflicting, noisy, and heterogeneous information, yet deliberation is fundamentally a social process susceptible to interpersonal dynamics. When retrieved Web sources contain latent hazards alongside safe factual content, social biases such as conformity pressure and authority deference can override evidence-grounded safety boundaries. In this work, we investigate whether the social structure of deliberation can paradoxically amplify latent Web safety risks. We introduce SafeConflict-Bias, a controlled counterfactual diagnostic protocol spanning six core Web risk categories, which holds queries and retrieved evidence strictly invariant while isolating conversational majority sway, authority cues, and confidence asymmetry. Empirical evaluation across diverse proprietary and open-source backbones reveals that while isolated models reliably reject unsafe guidance, standard MAD catastrophically capitulates to social pressure---surging unsafe adoption from 0.0\% up to 100.0\% and systematically silencing safe minority evidence. To resolve this systemic fragility without retraining or debate regeneration, we propose RiskTrace-Debias, an inference-time auditing framework uniting evidence-first precommitment, social-metadata masking, and consistency-gated arbitration. RiskTrace-Debias suppresses worst-case unsafe adoption to $\le 2.0\%$ across all architectures without inducing over-refusal, while generating verifiable provenance traces to audit interpersonal manipulation in Web deliberation.
papers.summary: Multi-agent debate (MAD) is increasingly used to reconcile conflicting retrieved web content, but deliberation is a social process that may let pressure override evidence. The `SafeConflict-Bias` protocol holds queries and evidence fixed across six web-risk categories while varying majority sway, authority cues, and confidence asymmetry. Across proprietary and open models, isolated models reliably reject unsafe guidance, but in standard debate **unsafe adoption jumps from 0.0% to as high as 100.0%** and safe minority evidence gets silenced. The proposed inference-time auditor `RiskTrace-Debias` combines evidence-first precommitment, masking of social metadata, and consistency-gated arbitration, and cuts worst-case unsafe adoption to at most 2.0% without causing over-refusal.

papers.title: How Risky Is Your Data-Driven Policy?
papers.abstract:
Data-driven algorithms are ubiquitous across industries, and there is an extensive literature on analyzing their \emph{average} performance. The risk profile of such algorithms, while critical, is much less understood. This paper quantifies the risk of data-driven policies and isolates its sources. We evaluate a policy through the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of its loss over the training sample, any policy randomization, and the future outcome, at a fixed unknown distribution. Regret against an oracle that knows the distribution decomposes into expected post-sample regret (PS), the average outcome-only CVaR gap of the selected action, and a sample-risk premium (SR), the additional tail risk omitted by averaging those evaluations. The analogous premium vanishes under expected loss.
  We characterize when the premium vanishes and how large it is relative to post-sample regret. For losses with a continuous density near the tail cutoff, we identify conditions under which both components decay at the same rate, yet the limiting ratio of the premium to post-sample regret can reach the thousands. When a probability mass at the cutoff moves with the action, the premium can decay more slowly and dominate post-sample regret. We establish conditions under which sample average approximation learns the oracle action at rate $n^{-1/2}$ in both settings, but its combined-risk regret is of order $n^{-1}$ in the first and $n^{-1/2}$ in the second. In finite-sample numerical examples of SAA in both settings, the premium accounts for approximately $74\%$--$97\%$ of regret.
papers.summary: The work measures the tail risk of data-driven policies, not just their average performance, using the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of loss over the training sample, any randomization, and the future outcome. Regret against an oracle splits into expected post-sample regret plus a sample-risk premium, which is the extra tail risk hidden by averaging and which vanishes under expected loss. The authors give conditions under which the premium decays at the same rate as post-sample regret yet is thousands of times larger, and cases where it decays more slowly and dominates. In numerical examples of sample average approximation (`SAA`), **the premium accounts for about 74–97% of regret**.

papers.title: Reciprocity Can Erase Direction:tructural Boundaries and Controlled Utility of Magnetic Graph Networks
papers.abstract: Magnetic graph networks encode direction through phase, but a learned graph can erase the intended directional mechanism before prediction. We characterize this failure for support-based magnetic Laplacians. Exact identities relate imaginary energy and distance from zero phase to amplitude-weighted reciprocity. Top-$k$ selection forces complete collapse when the observed-node count satisfies $m\leq k+1$, and dense support imposes a lower bound on reciprocal-arc fraction. We then construct paired propagation examples with identical node features and symmetric amplitudes but opposite labels, giving a provable chance-level limit for direction-erasing representations. In 72 fixed neural fits, support phase achieved test AUROC 1.0000 on a unilateral ring but 0.5000 on reciprocal ring and complete supports; continuous score phase and a real directed comparator achieved 1.0000 throughout. All models solved the direction-free control. These are oracle-direction mechanism tests, not evidence of learned clinical direction. In the preserved public DeepDRiD development study, continuous phase was active but its robustness difference from zero phase was only $+0.0036$ (descriptive 95\% interval $-0.0014$ to $+0.0095$) on validation patients used for checkpoint selection. The contribution is a structural and experimental framework for distinguishing erased direction from unestablished task utility. It provides a precise circumstance in which magnetic phase preserves useful information, without asserting universal or clinical superiority.
papers.summary: Magnetic graph networks encode edge direction as a complex phase, but a learned graph can make edges reciprocal and erase that directional signal before prediction. For support-based magnetic Laplacians, the authors derive exact identities linking phase energy to reciprocity. They prove that top-k selection forces complete collapse when few nodes are observed, and they build paired examples where direction-erasing representations are provably stuck at chance. In controlled experiments, **support phase hits AUROC 1.0 on a one-directional ring but 0.5 on reciprocal supports**, while continuous score phase stays at 1.0. On the clinical `DeepDRiD` dataset the benefit of phase was negligible.

papers.title: SEAM: Situated Executable Associative Memory for a Co-located Community
papers.abstract: In groups, knowledge is distributed among individuals, and how it is brought together depends on social ties. Taking inspiration from how a single mind recalls and reacts to memories and current stimulus, we build a shared memory that does this for a community, prototyped as a social app, SEAM. Members post arbitrary moments; SEAM works out how fragments relate, distills knowledge about the group, and replies in a situated and associative way. Some of these memories act as instructions that can alter how the system behaves, making it programmable by its members. We deployed SEAM to 46 people in a co-located community for two weeks of open-ended use, and ran a follow-up workshop with 14. Members shared their days, interrogated the memory, and instructed it to track routines and run games; replies introduced them to people and subjects they had never encountered. SEAM points towards communities where knowledge finds people.
papers.summary: `SEAM` is a shared memory for a community, built as a social app inspired by how an individual mind recalls memories and reacts to them. Members post arbitrary moments. The system infers how fragments relate, distills knowledge about the group, and replies in a situated, associative way, and some posted memories act as instructions that change its behavior, so members can program it. In a two-week deployment with 46 people in a co-located community and a follow-up workshop with 14, members used it to share their days, query the memory, track routines, and run games, and **its replies introduced people to members and topics they had not encountered before**.

papers.title: OSGR: Observation-Support Graph Reasoning for Earth Observation Question Answering
papers.abstract: Answering geographic queries over Earth observation (EO) archives requires solving a joint retrieval-and-derivation problem under strict spatiotemporal constraints. Existing LLM agents fail to ground observation items or suffer from search-space explosion. We propose OSGR, a two-stage framework that factorizes this search into offline symbolic concept deduction and online Relation-Conditioned Grounding. OSGR leverages an offline Observation-Support Graph to deduce valid target-to-result support paths at the concept level, and applies spatiotemporal compatibility kernels to instantiate grounded observation-item sets. On Earth-Bench and DisasterM3-Reason, OSGR improves GPT-4o accuracy from 49.3\% to 63.7\% while reducing the execution-step ratio from 2.9 to 2.5.
papers.summary: Answering geographic questions over Earth observation (EO) archives means retrieving the right observations and deriving results under strict spatial and temporal constraints, and LLM agents tend either to misground items or to face an exploding search space. `OSGR` splits the problem in two. Offline, it deduces valid concept-level support paths over an Observation-Support Graph. Online, it grounds those paths into concrete observation sets using spatiotemporal compatibility kernels. On `Earth-Bench` and `DisasterM3-Reason`, **`OSGR` raises `GPT-4o` accuracy from 49.3% to 63.7%** while reducing the execution-step ratio from 2.9 to 2.5.

papers.title: FlowTranslator: Training-Free In-Image Machine Translation with Flow-Based Editing
papers.abstract: In-image machine translation (IIMT) replaces text in an image with its translation while preserving the surrounding visual context. Existing task-specific models achieve convincing performance but require massive paired training images before and after translation. As advanced text-to-image (T2I) models have reached a practically usable level of multilingual text generation, we argue that this capability can be transferred to IIMT and present FlowTranslator. It is a training-free IIMT framework that first employs an OCR model and an LLM to generate the translation prompt, which is injected into the T2I-based diffusion model. To optimize the accurate and natural generation of translated text, we introduce two trajectory controls: Region Coupling Release (RCR) partially decorrelates target-branch noise inside the text region early in the trajectory, while Coupling Expansion (CE) amplifies the emerging edit displacement mid-trajectory. Under the EasyOCR read-back protocol, FlowTranslator achieves average PRIM BLEU and COMET scores of 20.6 and 57.2, respectively, substantially outperforming the strong training-based baseline UniTranslator. On the more challenging and realistic whole-image ScenePair photographs translated into Chinese, it reaches 40.1\% exact-match accuracy and surpasses existing editing systems, some of which only address the text-rendering stage rather than the complete IIMT task. These results establish flow-based editing as a strong, fully training-free baseline for IIMT.
papers.summary: In-image machine translation (IIMT) replaces text in an image with its translation while keeping the surrounding visuals, and existing models need large sets of paired before-and-after images. `FlowTranslator` is training-free. It uses an OCR model and an LLM to build a translation prompt for a flow-based text-to-image diffusion editor, then adds two trajectory controls: `Region Coupling Release`, which decorrelates noise inside the text region early on, and `Coupling Expansion`, which amplifies the emerging edit mid-trajectory. It reaches average BLEU and COMET scores of 20.6 and 57.2 on `PRIM`, outperforming the training-based `UniTranslator`, and **40.1% exact-match accuracy on whole-image `ScenePair` photographs translated into Chinese**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Text in images is usually translated by detecting it with OCR, translating it, and re-rendering it with a trained scene-text editor, and that editor needs scarce paired cross-lingual images. Here every component is frozen, and the trained editor is replaced by region-masked `FlowEdit` on the `Z-Image-Turbo` text-to-image flow model, plus two trajectory controls that fix an "ignition failure" where small text regions never start being edited.

- **How it works:** `PP-OCRv5` finds the text, a commercial LLM writes matched source and target scene captions that differ only in the quoted strings, and an edit confined to a dilated text mask leaves the background latents untouched.
- **Why the edit stalls, and the fix:** both branches share the same noise and differ only in a small region, so their velocity difference stays near zero; `Region Coupling Release` partially decorrelates target-branch noise inside the mask early on, and `Coupling Expansion` amplifies the accumulated displacement mid-trajectory under a sin² gate, with no extra forward passes.
- **Real-world strips (`PRIM`):** it reaches **20.6 average BLEU and 57.2 COMET**, against 12.8 and 50.7 for `UniTranslator`, which was fine-tuned on 7M in-domain pairs; the controls account for 16.9 → 20.6 BLEU, and `Coupling Expansion` alone supplies about 90% of that gain.
- **Synthetic text and scene photos:** on `TTV` it edges out the best training-based system (23.19 vs 21.17 BLEU), though the controls barely matter there and `GPT-Image-1` scores 23.06; on whole-scene `ScenePair` English-to-Chinese it hits **40.1% exact-match accuracy**, ahead of `AnyText` (36.8%) and plain masked `FlowEdit` (33.4%).
- **Limitations:** it can only render scripts the frozen backbone handles well, so Cyrillic largely fails (English-to-Russian scores 4.6 BLEU), similarity to the reference images is lower than tuned systems (SSIM 0.746 vs 0.77–0.80), and scoring relies on reading the output back with `EasyOCR`, which the authors note underestimates rendering quality.

papers.title: Nearly Linear-Time Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader for Weakly Observable Graph Bandits
papers.abstract: We study online learning with directed weakly observable feedback graphs and propose a Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL) policy that achieves best-of-both-worlds guarantee with nearly linear expected time complexity. To preserve the simple structure of FTPL, we develop a novel graph-based loss estimator that combines forced exploration, conditional geometric resampling and adaptive learning rates with surrogate probabilities. Our policy achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\delta_*^{1/3} T^{2/3})$ regret for adversarial regimes as well as $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\delta_* \log T / \Delta_{\min}^2)$ regret for stochastic regimes, where $\delta_*$ and $\Delta$, respectively, denote the fractional weak domination number and the suboptimality gap. These results show that refined guarantees for problems with minimax regret of $\Theta(T^{2/3})$ can be obtained through appropriately designed adaptive learning rates and loss estimators without sacrificing the simplicity of FTPL.
papers.summary: The paper studies online learning in which a directed, weakly observable feedback graph determines which losses the learner sees. It proposes a Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (`FTPL`) policy with nearly linear expected time complexity. The policy relies on a new graph-based loss estimator that combines forced exploration, conditional geometric resampling, and adaptive learning rates with surrogate probabilities. **It achieves a best-of-both-worlds guarantee**: Õ(δ*^{1/3} T^{2/3}) regret in adversarial settings and Õ(δ* log T / Δ_min²) in stochastic ones, where δ* is the fractional weak domination number and Δ_min is the smallest suboptimality gap.

papers.title: What Is the Influence of Task Order in Continual Learning? An Empirical Study and Order-Aware Evaluation for Motion Forecasting
papers.abstract: Aggregate scores for continual learning algorithms rest on a distribution over task orders that is rarely stated. We formulate algorithm comparison as an expectation over a declared order distribution, which separates training variation from order variation, and apply it to motion forecasting with four road-layout tasks from the INTERACTION dataset, all 24 task orders, four algorithms, and three training replicates (288 runs). Task order accounts for 65\% to 91\% of the variation in current-task error and backward transfer, and 90\% to 99\% of this order effect comes from the identity of the starting task: the smallest task cannot be learned from a cold start. Beyond the first stage, the order effect is comparable to training variability. In most orders, the leading algorithm in current-task error and backward transfer is within one replicate standard deviation of the runner-up. Backward transfer depends on the order mainly through its reference term, which weights the first task most heavily, so relative improvement and final error identify different leading algorithms for displacement error. A transition-direction descriptor computed from task statistics tracks the position of the smallest task, and weighting orders by it leaves the algorithm ranking unchanged. These results call for benchmarks that declare their order distribution and report order-resolved, starting-task-resolved, warm-start, and final errors alongside aggregate scores. The code and data are available \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/task-order-cl-4f7b/}{here}.
papers.summary: Aggregate continual-learning scores implicitly average over task orders that are rarely stated. The authors frame algorithm comparison as an expectation over an explicitly declared order distribution and apply it to motion forecasting on four road-layout tasks from the `INTERACTION` dataset, covering all 24 orders, four algorithms, and three replicates (288 runs). **Task order explains 65–91% of the variation in current-task error and backward transfer, and almost all of that comes from which task comes first**, because the smallest task cannot be learned from a cold start. In most orders the leading algorithm is within one replicate standard deviation of the runner-up, so the authors call for benchmarks to report order-resolved, starting-task-resolved, and final errors alongside aggregates.

papers.title: Coarse Semantic Blocks for Efficient Training-Free Sparse Attention
papers.abstract: We introduce a training-free sparse attention method that builds a prompt-specific key index to accelerate both prefill and decoding. The method clusters the keys into large semantic blocks that group tokens from noncontiguous positions. Each query position selects blocks by scoring their centroids and attends to the original keys and values within them. Queries that select the same block are processed together, so prefill stays fast even though each query chooses its own blocks. Large blocks make centroid scoring and this grouped processing cheap, so each query can attend to more tokens in the same time. Larger blocks with a larger token budget can thus be both faster and more accurate on long-context tasks than smaller blocks with a smaller budget. We evaluate two hybrid LLMs, Qwen3.5-4B and 35B-A3B, on one NVIDIA H200. Including the cost of building and using the index, whole-model wall-clock speedups over dense attention are 2.3-2.4x for prefill and 1.7-2.0x for decoding at 512K tokens, and 2.9-3.0x for prefill at 1M. The 35B-A3B model stays close to dense attention on five RULER tasks through 1M, on LongBench-v2 overall, and on MRCR through 256K. The 4B model loses accuracy mainly on multi-key retrieval, yet outperforms dense Qwen3.5-2B, whose latency is similar at 512K, on all three benchmarks.
papers.summary: The training-free sparse attention method clusters keys into large semantic blocks drawn from non-contiguous positions, building a prompt-specific index. Each query scores the block centroids and attends to the original keys and values inside the blocks it selects. Queries that pick the same block are processed together, which keeps prefill fast. Large blocks make this cheap enough to attend to more tokens in the same time, so they can be both faster and more accurate than small blocks. On `Qwen3.5-4B` and `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B` on one H200, **whole-model speedups over dense attention reach 2.3–2.4× for prefill and 1.7–2.0× for decoding at 512K tokens, and 2.9–3.0× for prefill at 1M**. The 35B model stays close to dense accuracy on `RULER`, `LongBench-v2`, and `MRCR`.

papers.title: Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-Agent AI
papers.abstract: Long-horizon multi-agent systems suffer from three tightly coupled failures: task drift, role drift, and state staleness. We test the hypothesis that these share a common representational cause: agent hidden states move away from the directions encoding the active task, assigned role, and current shared state. A pilot study over 14,832 annotated turns supports this: drifted turns collapse near-uniformly across all three anchor subspaces (pairwise r = 0.72-0.78). Existing methods address these failures separately, operating at the surface-text level or treating control directions independently. We introduce ATLAS (Algebraic Task-role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory), a training-free intervention acting on hidden states before a token is generated. ATLAS builds a positive-semidefinite anchor kernel over task, role, and state subspaces and steers hidden states toward their shared high-coherence eigendirections; a low-rank Gram decomposition keeps this tractable. Across long-horizon memory, state maintenance, tool use, least-privilege coordination, and embodied stress tests, ATLAS outperforms prompting, retrieval, memory, and activation-steering baselines. Against A-MEM it improves memory macro-average accuracy by up to 5.7 points and reduces write/read failures by up to 31.7%/24.8%; against MemoryArena-Agent it gains up to 4.8 points. It gains 10.7-12.1 points under perturbation, reaches 93.5% role consistency, and transfers to a 72B backbone (macro-average 61.0 vs. 56.2). Ablating the joint task-role-state span costs 7.2 points against 0.8 for a matched-rank random span, indicating these directions are functionally implicated, not incidental; supplying them by prompt or retrieval recovers 4.3 points less. ATLAS is therefore a representation-level controller for open-weight multi-agent systems, complementary to output-level protocols for black-box agents.
papers.summary: Long-horizon multi-agent systems suffer task drift, role drift, and stale shared state. A pilot study over 14,832 annotated turns suggests a common cause: hidden states drift away from the directions that encode the active task, the assigned role, and the current state. `ATLAS` (Algebraic Task-role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory) is a training-free intervention that builds a positive-semidefinite kernel over these three subspaces. It steers hidden states toward their shared high-coherence eigendirections before each token is generated, using a low-rank decomposition to stay tractable. It beats prompting, retrieval, memory, and activation-steering baselines, improving memory accuracy by up to 5.7 points over `A-MEM`, **reaching 93.5% role consistency**, and transferring to a 72B backbone.

papers.title: Text-to-SQL Models Make Choices Without Saying So
papers.abstract: A text-to-SQL answer can run, return a plausible number and still compute something other than what the analyst meant. This can happen when the request leaves a calculation choice open, such as whether to count rows or distinct entities, and the model settles it without saying so. Standard benchmarks cannot detect this, because they score each question against a single reference interpretation. We introduce SpecBridge, which tests such a choice by varying it alone: it poses three otherwise identical requests, one leaving the choice open and one per interpretation, and scores each answer by running it. The databases are real, and the choices are ones that made models fail on existing benchmarks. On 204 hand-validated tests, four language models usually compute each interpretation when asked for it, yet for the open request return both in only 15-58% of the tests where they can, often without mentioning the choice. The gap lies in reporting, not in computing. Benchmarks even penalize the alternative: on BIRD questions where such a choice changes the answer, over two in five of the answers marked wrong are right under the other interpretation. Because the gap lies in reporting, a system can narrow it without a stronger model: it first decides whether a request leaves a choice open, then answers each interpretation in its own call. On our tests and on AMBROSIA, an existing benchmark of ambiguous questions, this approach raises the share of open requests that get every interpretation by 29-63 points over the single answer that production assistants give, without lowering precision on clear requests. It also needs fewer user turns than asking a clarifying question.
papers.summary: Text-to-SQL models often settle open calculation choices, such as counting rows versus distinct entities, without telling the user, and benchmarks that score against a single reference cannot detect this. `SpecBridge` tests each choice with three otherwise identical requests: one that leaves the choice open and one for each interpretation. It scores every answer by executing it on real databases. Across 204 hand-validated tests, four models usually compute each interpretation when asked, but **for the open request return both in only 15–58% of eligible cases**, and on `BIRD` more than two in five answers marked wrong are correct under the other interpretation. A pipeline that first detects ambiguity and then answers each interpretation in a separate call improves full coverage by 29–63 points on these tests and on `AMBROSIA`, without losing precision on clear requests.

papers.title: Planning-Coding Separation in LLM-Based Code Generation: An Empirical Study
papers.abstract: Planning has been identified as an important factor for improved code generation with Large Language Models (LLMs). However, the interaction between planning capability and coding capability remains largely underexplored, especially when the two capabilities are from different LLMs. In this paper, we conduct the first comprehensive empirical study of planning-coding interaction in LLM-based code generation, where planning and coding are assigned to different LLMs (i.e., planning-coding separation). Specifically, we explore different planner-coder combinations to investigate the effectiveness for coders to utilize planning information from various planners and the impact of further training of coders on planner-coder combinations. Our results demonstrate that almost all planner-coder combinations are as competitive as using the same LLM for planning and coding, and the combination of a stronger planner and a stronger coder typically achieves improved effectiveness. Furthermore, using a large model as the planner paired with a much smaller model as the coder can sometimes be as competitive as using the large model as both the planner and the coder, and further training of the coder can typically boost various planner-coder combinations. These findings provide empirical evidence that planning and coding can be separated to a considerable extent in LLM-based code generation, which may offer a more flexible way to construct code-generation systems.
papers.summary: The empirical study looks at code generation in which one LLM writes the plan and a different LLM writes the code. It tests many planner-coder pairings and the effect of further training the coder. **Almost all combinations are as competitive as using the same model for both roles**, and stronger planners paired with stronger coders generally do better. A large planner paired with a much smaller coder can sometimes match the large model doing both, and additional coder training typically helps across pairings, which suggests planning and coding can be separated to a considerable extent.

papers.title: ATC: Agent Trajectory Control for Role-Contract Enforcement in Black-Box Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems assign different responsibilities to different agents: one plans, another retrieves evidence, another verifies, another executes. This division of labor is only meaningful if each agent stays within the functions it is authorized to perform. Over many turns, however, an agent can produce a locally reasonable message that exercises authority belonging to another role: a verifier that begins planning, a retriever that asserts unsupported conclusions, an executor that changes state no one approved. We formalize this as role drift, a turn-level breach of an agent's role contract. We introduce Agent Trajectory Control (ATC), which makes each role's authority explicit as a contract and enforces it at the point where a message would enter the shared conversation. ATC scores a proposed output for out-of-role deviation, leakage into the functions of other roles, impermissible speech acts, and logical contract breaches, then computes a leakage-regularized target that constrains regeneration; the revised message is re-checked before admission. Enforcement acts on the message rather than the generator, so ATC governs agents whose internal representations are unavailable. Across homogeneous and heterogeneous teams, ATC improves task performance and role consistency while lowering role-drift energy relative to strong baselines spanning prompting, memory, workflow control, and activation editing, with the largest gains under explicit role-confusion stress tests and in larger, more diverse teams.
papers.summary: In multi-agent LLM systems, an agent can drift out of its assigned role over many turns, for example a verifier that starts planning or an executor that changes state nobody approved. The authors call this role drift and propose `Agent Trajectory Control` (`ATC`), which writes each role's authority down as an explicit contract and checks every proposed message before it enters the shared conversation. `ATC` scores each message for out-of-role behavior, leakage into other roles' functions, impermissible speech acts, and logical contract breaches, then constrains regeneration and re-checks the revised message. Because it works on messages rather than model internals, it applies to black-box agents, and it **beats prompting, memory, workflow-control, and activation-editing baselines on both task performance and role consistency**, with the largest gains under role-confusion stress tests and in larger, more diverse teams.

papers.title: FP4Quant: Efficient 4-Bit Communication Compression for Model-Parallel LLM Training
papers.abstract: The rapid scaling of large language models (LLMs) has made communication overhead a critical bottleneck in distributed model-parallel training. Although existing low-precision compression methods can effectively reduce communication costs, further reducing the communication footprint to ultra-low-bit formats such as FP4 introduces new challenges, including limited numerical range, sub-byte storage overhead, and increased computational cost from fine-grained quantization. In this paper, we present \textbf{FP4Quant}, a micro-grouped FP4 compression framework for efficient model-parallel LLM training. FP4Quant integrates a micro-grouped dual-scale FP4 quantization mechanism to preserve local tensor distribution characteristics, a warp-cooperative FP4 packing scheme to enable efficient sub-byte data representation, and a hybrid two-level FWHT pipeline to mitigate quantization errors with GPU-aware execution optimization. Experiments on NVIDIA H100 GPUs with Qwen-7B demonstrate up to 1.56$\times$ end-to-end throughput improvement over BF16, revealing a trade-off between throughput and model quality.
papers.summary: Communication between GPUs is a major bottleneck in model-parallel LLM training, and compressing that traffic to 4-bit floating point (FP4) runs into limited numerical range, sub-byte storage overhead, and the cost of fine-grained quantization. `FP4Quant` addresses these with micro-grouped dual-scale FP4 quantization that preserves local tensor distributions, a warp-cooperative scheme for packing sub-byte data, and a two-level fast Walsh-Hadamard transform (FWHT) pipeline that reduces quantization error. On NVIDIA H100 GPUs training `Qwen-7B`, it reaches **up to 1.56x end-to-end throughput over BF16**, though the authors report a trade-off between throughput and model quality.

papers.title: Anchor: Augmented Cross-Layer Recurrent State for Long-Context Retrieval in Test-Time Training
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient linearization turns a pretrained autoregressive Transformer into an efficient model by hybridizing sliding-window attention (SWA) with a constant-size recurrent memory. But does every layer's recurrent state contribute to long-context retrieval? Investigating an SWA and Test-Time Training (TTT) hybrid, we find that retrieval is sparse across depth, concentrated in a few anchor layers, and that the remaining states hold similar information expressed through layer-specific transformations. We exploit both observations in Anchor: TTT memory placed only at the anchor layers, and a cross-layer recurrent state written once and read by many layers, each through its own learned read map that realizes a layer-specific stretch and rotation, along with demonstrated generalization to other hybrid attentions. On Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, Anchor delivers 2.3-3.1x higher recall and 6.7-8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs with a 10x smaller recurrent state, retains 91-95% of the teacher's MMLU accuracy, and cuts end-to-end latency by up to 4.3x relative to softmax attention.
papers.summary: Linearization turns a pretrained Transformer into a cheaper model by combining sliding-window attention (SWA) with a fixed-size recurrent memory, here Test-Time Training (TTT). Studying such hybrids, the authors find that long-context retrieval is concentrated in a few anchor layers, while the other layers' states hold similar information transformed in layer-specific ways. `Anchor` therefore places TTT memory only at the anchor layers and shares one cross-layer recurrent state that each layer reads through its own learned map. On `Llama-3.1-8B` and `Mistral-7B` it achieves **2.3-3.1x higher recall and 6.7-8.9 points higher `MMLU` accuracy than `LoLCATs` with a 10x smaller recurrent state**, retains 91-95% of the teacher model's `MMLU` accuracy, and cuts end-to-end latency by up to 4.3x compared with softmax attention.

papers.title: CORA: Teacher-Guided Causal O-RAN Adaptation for Jamming Detection
papers.abstract: In mission-critical networks, a missed jamming event is costlier than a false alarm, so detectors should favor recall, operate causally, and work without labeled attack data. Retrospective Key Performance Indicator (KPI) detectors meet the label-free requirement but rely on future context and cannot run in streaming operation. We present CORA, a teacher-guided reinforcement learning (RL) framework that transfers the hindsight of a retrospective detector to a causal one without labels during training or deployment. Offline, a retrospective KPI detector evaluated on unlabeled historical logs defines a recall-weighted reward for a masked controller that adapts the sensitivity, persistence, and grace of a causal KPI detector. At deployment, the teacher is removed and the frozen controller acts causally, with no ground-truth labels and no target-specific calibration. The design maps onto offline training in the Non-Real-Time RIC and causal control in the Near-Real-Time RIC of an Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN). Under leave-one-out transfer across ten 5G O-RAN testbed configurations, CORA reaches recall-oriented operating points on the deployable frontier that none of the evaluated baselines covers. A Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) controller raises mean recall from 0.687 to 0.771 over a fixed default detector on all ten configurations, while a Deep Q-Network (DQN) achieves a comparable F2-score to the best teacher-selected static configuration, with 61% fewer false alarms. Removing the teacher lowers recall on every configuration.
papers.summary: Jamming detectors for mission-critical 5G networks should favor recall, run causally on streaming data, and work without labeled attacks, but label-free detectors built on Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) usually rely on future context. `CORA` is a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that uses a retrospective KPI detector as a teacher on unlabeled historical logs, producing a recall-weighted reward for training a controller that tunes the sensitivity, persistence, and grace of a causal detector; at deployment the teacher is removed. The design maps onto the offline and near-real-time controllers of an Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN). Under leave-one-out transfer across ten 5G testbed configurations, a `PPO` controller **raises mean recall from 0.687 to 0.771** over a fixed default detector, and a `DQN` controller matches the best static configuration's F2-score with 61% fewer false alarms.

papers.title: Patching the Protocol: A Taxonomy of Pre-Registration Repairs in LLM-Proposer Experiments
papers.abstract: Pre-registration is increasingly proposed as a trust mechanism for machine-learning research involving LLM-generated content, but its canonical form assumes a frozen protocol can be executed unchanged. Software-intensive studies violate this assumption: the protocol is partly implemented, and implementations carry defects. We report a three-case study of protocol repairs ("patches") from a program where an LLM proposes executable rules that a programmatic verifier gates, across production scheduling, incentive design, and task assignment. Each protocol required exactly one defect-repair patch: three events in total. None modified a numbered judgment criterion, its threshold, or the scoring rule, and none altered already collected data; two changed pre-registered design parameters before any data were collected, each with a recorded rationale. We propose a two-axis taxonomy of patches (defect class: environmental / feasibility / correctness, x timing: pre-data / post-data), introduce a verifiable non-impact claim for post-data repairs, and distill a nine-item checklist; all nine items were exercised by at least one patch event -- an observation of use, not a validation of sufficiency. The credibility of verifier-bound, LLM-proposer studies depends less on whether patches occur than on whether they are auditable.
papers.summary: Pre-registration assumes a study protocol can be frozen and executed unchanged, but software-heavy studies, where an LLM proposes executable rules and a programmatic verifier gates them, inevitably need bug-fix patches. Across three such studies (production scheduling, incentive design, and task assignment), each protocol needed exactly one repair patch, and **none changed a judgment criterion, a threshold, the scoring rule, or data already collected**. From these cases the authors build a two-axis taxonomy of patches (environmental, feasibility, or correctness defects, applied before or after data collection), define a verifiable non-impact claim for post-data repairs, and distill a nine-item checklist. Their argument is that the credibility of these studies depends on whether patches are auditable, not on whether they occur.

papers.title: Beyond Fine-Tuning: Evaluating Prompt Engineering and Prompt Tuning for Roman Urdu Hate Speech Detection
papers.abstract: Low Resource Languages (LRLs) pose significant challenges for hate speech detection because of a scarcity of readily available annotated data, language variation, non-standard spelling, and context-dependent ambiguity. Beyond the problem of informal conventions of writing in Roman Urdu, there is also the issue of code-mixing. After working on the previous project about zero-shot learning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), this research systematically compares prompt engineering and prompt tuning for Roman Urdu hate speech detection. To study the effect of in-context examples, we will compare the zero-shot and few-shot prompting approaches. To understand the advantage of structured prompting and learnable prompt representations, we will conduct studies of manual vs. mixed prompt-based adaptation strategies. Experimentations are carried out on the PURUT dataset (~72,771 social media comments) with GPT-3.5, LLaMA-3, Mistral-7B, and multilingual BERT in several settings. Experimental results show that few-shot prompting always outperforms zero-shot prompting, with the Mistral-7B model scoring 0.67 F1 compared to 0.56 of the zero-shot models. Based on this observation, prompt-based adaptation is proposed to introduce additional improvements, with the proposed mixed prompt configuration able to yield a F1-score up to 0.87 which further surpasses the performance of regular manual prompts. Despite the larger size of the model, its performance trade-off between inference-based prompting, prompt optimization, and parameter-efficient model adaptation is compared to the previously reported PEFT-based F1-score, which is ~0.93.
papers.summary: Detecting hate speech in Roman Urdu is hard because annotated data is scarce, spelling is non-standard, and text is often code-mixed. The study compares zero-shot and few-shot prompting, and manual versus mixed learnable prompt configurations, using `GPT-3.5`, `LLaMA-3`, `Mistral-7B`, and multilingual `BERT` on the `PURUT` dataset of about 72,771 social media comments. Few-shot prompting consistently beats zero-shot (0.67 versus 0.56 F1 for `Mistral-7B`), and the **mixed prompt configuration reaches an F1 of 0.87**, still below the roughly 0.93 the authors previously reported with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT).

papers.title: Proper Agnostic Learning of Affine Halfspaces under Log-Concave Marginals
papers.abstract: We give a proper constant-factor agnostic learner for affine halfspaces under full-dimensional log-concave marginals. For arbitrary binary labels, the algorithm uses independent labeled samples and returns a single affine halfspace with error at most $C\mathrm{OPT}+\varepsilon$. Its sample and real-arithmetic complexity are polynomial in dimension, inverse accuracy, and the logarithm of the reciprocal failure probability. The mean and covariance of the marginal need not be known, and the sample complexity can be made linear in this logarithmic confidence factor. The main geometric result compares global disagreement with disagreement on a balanced restriction: for a minority halfspace of mass $p$, global disagreement is within universal constant factors of $p$ times conditional disagreement, provided the latter is sufficiently small. To construct the restriction from noisy labels, we estimate the minority cap's mean and covariance robustly, approximately minimize the classical zonoid-depth dual objective, and expand a superlevel set to a marginal quantile. The disagreement comparison cancels the noise amplification caused by conditioning and allows the learned halfspace to be used on the entire space. The analysis combines degree-four sum-of-squares moment bounds for log-concave laws with a translation-based reduction from balanced affine learning to homogeneous halfspace learning.
papers.summary: The authors give a proper agnostic learner for affine halfspaces under full-dimensional log-concave distributions: for arbitrary binary labels, it returns a single affine halfspace with **error at most a constant times the optimum plus epsilon**, using polynomially many samples and arithmetic operations, and it does not need to know the distribution's mean or covariance. The key geometric result relates global disagreement between halfspaces to disagreement on a balanced restriction of the space, which cancels the noise amplification that conditioning would otherwise cause. To build that restriction from noisy labels, the algorithm robustly estimates the minority cap's mean and covariance and approximately minimizes a zonoid-depth dual objective, with an analysis based on degree-four sum-of-squares moment bounds.

papers.title: Sparse Internal Control of Language Models
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly used in text generation, decision support, and automated interaction, creating a need for localized, reversible, and selective control of their behavior. Activation steering demonstrates that internal interventions can alter the behavior of frozen models, but how to select and evaluate compact, multi-site control interfaces remains an open question. I introduce sparse internal control, a framework for steering target behavior by applying inference-time interventions to a small set of internal model nodes. A local target-controllability formulation characterizes candidate site--direction pairs by their behavioral effects and specifies constraints on target recovery, off-target preservation, and intervention energy. Two complementary selectors instantiate this formulation: Driver-OMP selects nodes for sparse reconstruction of a desired behavioral displacement, while Coverage-Driver favors stable coverage across prompts. I propose a six-axis control-evaluation protocol measuring reachability, signed reversal, dose response, feedback controllability, off-target preservation, and held-out reuse. Exploratory experiments on indirect object identification, MMLU multiple-choice question answering, sentiment steering, and refusal steering provide evidence for the feasibility of steering task-defined behavior through sparse internal interventions. The six-axis evaluation characterizes these interventions beyond target movement, revealing distinct control properties that depend on the task and available direction information. Together, the formulation, reference algorithms, and evaluation protocol provide a foundation for the systematic study and development of internal control methods for language models.
papers.summary: The paper introduces sparse internal control, a framework for steering a frozen language model by applying inference-time interventions at a small set of internal nodes. Candidate site-direction pairs are chosen under constraints on reaching the target behavior, preserving off-target behavior, and limiting intervention energy, using two selectors: `Driver-OMP`, which sparsely reconstructs a desired behavioral shift, and `Coverage-Driver`, which favors stable coverage across prompts. The author also proposes a **six-axis evaluation protocol covering reachability, signed reversal, dose response, feedback controllability, off-target preservation, and held-out reuse**. Exploratory experiments on indirect object identification, `MMLU`, sentiment steering, and refusal steering suggest sparse interventions are feasible, with control properties that vary by task.

papers.title: Large Language Models for Forecasting of Electricity Price Spikes
papers.abstract: Can market notices read by a large language model (LLM) improve short-horizon electricity price spike forecasts? We study five regions of Australia's National Electricity Market. A local LLM extracted features once per notice, only notices visible at the forecast origin were used, and a gradient-boosting model produced onset probabilities. In an out-of-sample development back-test (July 2022 to July 2024), notice features did not lower the 60-minute Brier score of a numeric model including the market operator's next-hour forecasts. At 24 hours they did, but rule-based features did so almost equally and attribution to notice content was not established. A locally frozen protocol, not publicly deposited, governed a retrospective single-use holdout from 15 August to 17 October 2026. At 60 minutes, the hypothesis that LLM features lower the numeric model's Brier score was not established (H1; relative Brier skill -0.09%), so the planned comparison with rule-based features was not tested (H2). At 24 hours, the hypothesis that LLM features lower the score against a text-free control was not established (H3; +0.37%, 95% CI [-9.74, 1.39], inconclusive). By the frozen wording rule the non-significant 24-hour improvement comes mainly from recalibration and cannot be attributed to notice content, although post hoc the decomposition could not separate recalibration from resolution. The 24-hour base rate was 1.56% on the holdout against 14.0% in development. With 5 onsets on 3 days and 24-hour positives in 2 of 22 three-day blocks, the holdout neither established nor excluded a 24-hour effect.
papers.summary: The study asks whether market notices read by a local LLM improve short-horizon forecasts of electricity price spikes in five regions of Australia's National Electricity Market. LLM-extracted notice features were fed into a gradient-boosting model, and the authors tested them under a frozen protocol on a single-use holdout period. **None of the pre-registered hypotheses was established**: at 60 minutes the LLM features did not improve on a numeric model that already included the market operator's forecasts, and the small 24-hour improvement was inconclusive and could not be attributed to notice content rather than recalibration. With only 5 spike onsets in the holdout, the test could neither establish nor rule out a 24-hour effect.

papers.title: CloakFEM: Agentic FEM Code Generation for Red-Teaming Computational Resource Exhaustion
papers.abstract: Finite element method (FEM) solvers are foundational to scientific and engineering simulation, yet their susceptibility to \emph{efficiency attacks} remains largely unexplored. An adversary can craft syntactically valid and runnable FEM programs that complete successfully while forcing excessive computational work, enabling computational denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. Finding such inputs is challenging because FEM programs occupy a vast, structured space constrained by numerical, geometric, and constitutive requirements. We introduce CloakFEM, a domain-guided LLM-agent framework for automatically generating runnable adversarial FEM programs that amplify solver computation. CloakFEM combines LLM-guided search with an FEM-specific intermediate representation and a deterministic validity gate that enforces runnable constraints. Across three FEM stacks, 17 problem classes, and 1,068 seeds, CloakFEM discovers adversarial inputs that substantially amplify solver work while remaining valid and solvable. In the most extreme case, solver iterations increase from 43 to 247,367, a \(5{,}752.72\times\) amplification. CloakFEM outperforms five generic black-box baselines and retains an advantage over evolutionary search under a controlled bounded action space. Cross-solver analysis further reveals both problem-intrinsic and solver-specific sources of vulnerability. Our results uncover an underexplored efficiency-attack surface in FEM solvers and show that runnable FEM programs can serve as adversarial inputs.
papers.summary: Finite element method (FEM) solvers can be targeted by efficiency attacks: valid, runnable programs that finish successfully but force excessive computation, enabling computational denial-of-service. `CloakFEM` is an LLM-agent framework that searches for such programs, combining LLM-guided search with an FEM-specific intermediate representation and a deterministic validity gate that keeps every candidate runnable. Across three FEM stacks, 17 problem classes, and 1,068 seeds, it finds inputs that greatly amplify solver work, in the most extreme case **raising solver iterations from 43 to 247,367 (a 5,752.72x amplification)**. It outperforms five generic black-box baselines and keeps an edge over evolutionary search, and cross-solver analysis shows that some vulnerabilities are intrinsic to the problem while others are specific to a solver.

papers.title: Benchmarking Unsupervised Jamming Detection in 5G Open RAN
papers.abstract: Radio Frequency (RF) jamming threatens fifth-generation (5G) networks. Open Radio Access Network (Open RAN) telemetry enables jamming detection without dedicated spectrum monitoring equipment, but labeled attack data are rarely available across deployments, motivating unsupervised detectors. Comparing such detectors across algorithmic families, however, remains difficult without ground-truth labels. This paper benchmarks statistical and reconstruction-based unsupervised jamming detectors using a symmetric evaluation interface that combines detection confidence and temporal interval coherence into a detector-independent composite score. We compare a Statistical Ensemble Method (SEM) detector against Vanilla, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and Variational Autoencoder (VAE) baselines on Key Performance Indicator (KPI) telemetry from ten heterogeneous 5G environments with fixed and variable jamming bursts and dynamic jammer gains. Under leave-one-out (LOO) evaluation, SEM achieves a mean composite score of 0.906, compared with 0.688 for the best autoencoder (AE) per fold. Ground-truth validation yields a mean F1-score of 0.918 for SEM, compared with 0.521 for the best AE variant. The composite ranks SEM first in all environments, consistent with F1 rankings. However, in both within-trace and cross-trace evaluation, it fails for detectors that flag far fewer samples than the jamming prevalence, indicating that rankings are reliable only when detection rate matches the expected prevalence.
papers.summary: Open Radio Access Network (Open RAN) telemetry makes it possible to detect radio-frequency jamming in 5G networks without spectrum monitors, but comparing unsupervised detectors is difficult when ground-truth labels are missing. The authors propose a detector-independent composite score that combines detection confidence with temporal coherence, and use it to benchmark a Statistical Ensemble Method (`SEM`) against vanilla, Long Short-Term Memory (`LSTM`), and Variational Autoencoder (`VAE`) autoencoders on Key Performance Indicator (KPI) data from ten 5G environments. `SEM` **scores 0.906 on the composite and 0.918 F1 against ground truth**, versus 0.688 and 0.521 for the best autoencoder. The composite ranks detectors consistently with F1 but breaks down for detectors that flag far fewer samples than the true jamming prevalence.

papers.title: Embodied AI for Scientific Discovery: From Physical Action to Scientific Evidence
papers.abstract: Scientific experiments are increasingly selected, executed and interpreted by learned systems that act through physical interfaces. Robot learning builds physical competence, whereas AI for science chooses which experiment to run, each reporting different endpoints. This review treats their interface as one problem, embodied AI for science, where the experiment itself is partially observed: specimen state, apparatus state and measurement processes are latent, actions are costly and irreversible, and missingness depends on execution and outcome. We organize the literature by three closures operating at distinct levels: operational closure (the experiment realized is the one intended), epistemic closure (the result updates beliefs or selects subsequent experiments) and evidential closure (the record supports a claim). We analyze workflows through a record-linked evidence cycle - Record, Diagnose, Calibrate, Confirm - as analytic functions with feedback. A taxonomy crosses these closures with six delegated decisions and five embodiment classes. Our formulation separates commanded, realized and observed conditions and models diagnosis with explicit resource, risk and sample-change costs. We compare experiment-selection methods by terminal decision, review perception, protocol compilation, visuomotor policies, world models, recovery and transfer by evidence emission requirements, and compare chemistry, materials, biology, microscopy and field workflows by what their records establish. An appendix provides an evidence map of 28 workflows (26 physical, two software-boundary), characterizing validation pathways and claim confirmation requirements. We propose evaluation that separates actions, valid experiments, campaigns and confirmed claims, framing open challenges as controlled comparisons with measurable failure conditions.
papers.summary: This review brings robot learning and AI-driven experiment selection together under one problem, embodied AI for science, in which the state of the specimen, the apparatus, and the measurement process is only partially observed and actions are costly and irreversible. It organizes the literature by three kinds of closure: operational (the experiment run is the one intended), epistemic (the result updates beliefs or picks the next experiment), and evidential (the record supports a claim). Methods and workflows in chemistry, materials, biology, microscopy, and field science are compared through a Record-Diagnose-Calibrate-Confirm evidence cycle, and an appendix maps 28 workflows. The authors propose **evaluations that separate individual actions, valid experiments, campaigns, and confirmed claims**.

papers.title: Aligning Training and Rollout Policies for End-to-End FP4 RL on Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
papers.abstract: In this work, we study end-to-end FP4 reinforcement learning (RL) post-training for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models. Recent work on FP4 RL has introduced effective recovery recipes that restore accuracy under aggressive low-precision quantization for dense models, but we find that the same approach yields no improvement over the naive FP4 baseline in the MoE setting. We conduct an in-depth study to understand why. Our analysis identifies the root cause in the routing mechanism unique to MoE: because the router makes discrete expert-selection decisions, training-inference policy alignment becomes acutely sensitive to whether the same recovery technique is applied symmetrically on the training and inference sides. When an asymmetric recipe is used-including the dense-model approach, which corrects only the rollout-training-inference alignment deteriorates sharply, as measured by the Pearson correlation coefficient between training and inference probabilities, and router selection matching rates. Building on this finding, we propose MoeResQ, a quantization-recovery recipe for MoE RL post-training that enforces symmetry between the training- and inference-side corrections. MoeResQ restores training-inference alignment and substantially closes the accuracy gap to full precision, establishing symmetric recovery as the key principle in FP4 RL for MoE models.
papers.summary: Recovery recipes that keep accuracy intact during end-to-end FP4 reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of dense models give no improvement over naive FP4 when applied to Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs. The authors trace this to the router: because expert selection is discrete, the probabilities computed during training and during rollout inference stay aligned only if the same correction is applied on both sides, and asymmetric recipes sharply degrade that alignment and the rate at which the router picks the same experts. Their recipe, `MoeResQ`, **applies corrections symmetrically on the training and inference sides**, restoring alignment and substantially closing the accuracy gap to full precision.

papers.title: Understanding Backdoor Attacks in Scene Graph Generation via Global Context Pathway
papers.abstract: Scene Graph Generation (SGG) produces structured scene representations, yet its training-time backdoor risk remains unexplored. Unlike classification, SGG exposes a pair-level attack surface that enables selective corruption of relations involving a designated object category. However, because SGG largely relies on localized evidence, globally placed triggers may face difficulty in manipulating such predictions. Recent SGG architectures increasingly incorporate global context to improve scene modeling, which may in turn facilitate such attacks. In this paper, we systematically study this backdoor risk and investigate the role of the global context pathway in backdoor behavior. Concretely, we first instantiate this attack with an effective method, and propose a three-axis evaluation protocol to characterize backdoor behavior. Experiments on Visual Genome with representative open-vocabulary and closed-set SGG models demonstrate the effectiveness of the attack. Mechanistic analyses reveal that the explicit global context pathway serves as a major carrier of the backdoor effect across the evaluated SGG models. In particular, replacing the poisoned global context representation with its clean counterpart during inference sharply suppresses the attack, yielding 100% and 97% reductions in attack success for the OvSGTR family and RelationFormer, respectively. Moreover, training-time interventions in the OvSGTR family show that suppressing trigger signals in this pathway either reduces attack success or substantially degrades utility. Together, these findings suggest that explicit global context designs may pose a backdoor risk in SGG architectures.
papers.summary: Scene Graph Generation (SGG) models, which predict relations between objects in an image, expose a pair-level attack surface where a training-time backdoor can selectively corrupt relations involving a chosen object category. The authors build such an attack, propose a three-axis evaluation protocol, and show it works on open-vocabulary and closed-set models on `Visual Genome`. Mechanistic analysis shows that the explicit global context pathway in modern SGG architectures carries most of the backdoor: **swapping in the clean global context at inference cuts attack success by 100% for the `OvSGTR` family and 97% for `RelationFormer`**. Suppressing the trigger in this pathway during training either reduces the attack or substantially hurts utility.

papers.title: Twice as Fast, Until It Isn't: Quantized Serving of Mid-Size Open LLMs
papers.abstract: A team serving a 9B-20B open-weight language model on vLLM or SGLang must choose a quantization recipe, and needs two numbers: the speedup over BF16 and the accuracy given up. We assemble every public measurement of these numbers that we could verify and find that the record supplies them only in pieces. Only two checkpoints, both INT4 builds of Gemma 3 12B, have both a vLLM timing and an accuracy score, and that score covers a single MMLU subject, one that the AWQ build was calibrated on. The batch-1 timings predate current engine releases, AMD and Intel Gaudi have no timing in this band at all, and FP4 has none against BF16. The timings that do exist follow one rule. Decoding a small batch is limited by memory bandwidth, so 4-bit weights roughly double speed (2.12x for Qwen2.5-14B on an A100), but the gain vanishes once a large batch makes the GPU compute-bound (1.02x for Gemma 3 12B at batch size 256), where FP8 is the recipe that can still help. Many published accuracy deltas, including every HumanEval delta, lie within benchmark sampling noise. We close with a seven-item reporting checklist for future measurements.
papers.summary: Teams serving a 9B-20B open-weight model on `vLLM` or `SGLang` need to know both the speedup a quantization recipe gives over BF16 and the accuracy it costs, so the authors compiled every public measurement of these numbers they could verify. The record is thin: only two `Gemma 3 12B` INT4 checkpoints have both a `vLLM` timing and an accuracy score, AMD and Intel Gaudi have no timings in this size range, and FP4 has none against BF16. The timings that exist follow one rule: **4-bit weights roughly double speed when small-batch decoding is limited by memory bandwidth (2.12x for `Qwen2.5-14B` on an A100) but give almost nothing at large batch sizes (1.02x at batch 256)**, where FP8 can still help. Many published accuracy deltas, including every `HumanEval` delta, fall within sampling noise, and the paper closes with a seven-item reporting checklist.

papers.title: Spin Spherical Fourier Neural Operators: Efficient Equivariant Learning for Vector and Spin Fields on the Sphere
papers.abstract: Many fields of physical interest on the sphere, such as wind, the polarisation of the cosmic microwave background and the shear of weak gravitational lensing, are spin fields, whose values change phase when the local frame rotates. We extend spherical Fourier neural operators (SFNOs) to fields of any spin, through lifted spherical convolutions that are exactly rotationally equivariant. Lifting spin fields to Mackey functions on the rotation group provides the conceptual framework, while computation is performed exactly and efficiently through their harmonic representation and by appealing to sampling theorems on the sphere and rotation group. We construct spin SFNOs (S$^2$FNOs) from these building blocks. We demonstrate empirically that rotational equivariance holds to machine precision for these layers. We achieve state-of-the-art performance on existing benchmarks, and introduce new benchmarks on which spin-aware models outperform their scalar counterparts.
papers.summary: Many physical fields on the sphere, such as wind, cosmic microwave background polarization, and weak-lensing shear, are spin fields whose values change phase when the local frame rotates. The authors extend spherical Fourier neural operators (SFNOs) to fields of any spin, building spin SFNOs (`S2FNOs`) from lifted spherical convolutions that are computed exactly and efficiently in harmonic space. The layers are **rotationally equivariant to machine precision**, the models reach state-of-the-art results on existing benchmarks, and on new benchmarks introduced here spin-aware models outperform their scalar counterparts.

papers.title: Do Multi-Turn Conversational Capabilities Carry Over from Text to Speech? A Parallel Multilingual Benchmark
papers.abstract: Successful multi-turn voice interaction requires models to retain information from earlier turns, follow persistent instructions, and track revisions to conversational state. These abilities are usually evaluated from transcripts, leaving open whether successes demonstrated from text carry over when the same turns are spoken, and whether this transfer is consistent across languages. We introduce Omnilingua-AudioMC, a strictly parallel multilingual extension of Audio MultiChallenge, to study this question. The benchmark contains 354 conversations and 1,404 rubric items across ten languages, with content, turn structure, cross-turn dependencies, and evaluation criteria aligned across transcript and speech conditions. Across six speech-language models, the shift from reference transcripts to direct speech input is strongly model- and language-dependent: models with similar transcript performance can diverge substantially under speech, and their relative strengths across languages can change. Paired rubric-level analysis shows that aggregate transcript-speech gaps can obscure which conversational requirements are preserved, because losses of transcript-demonstrated successes can be offset by gains on other items. Replacing preceding user turns, the current turn, or both with model-generated transcripts localizes recoverable degradation: for the two models with the largest gaps, history substitution yields a larger macro-level improvement than current-turn substitution in all ten languages, while the strongest direct-speech model gains little from either. These results show that transcript performance is an unreliable proxy for multilingual spoken conversational ability and identify the representation of preceding spoken context as an important source of recoverable degradation. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/QwenLM/Omnilingua-Bench/tree/main/Omnilingua-AudioMC.
papers.summary: Multi-turn voice assistants are usually evaluated on transcripts, which leaves open whether skills such as remembering earlier turns and following persistent instructions survive when the input is actually spoken, and whether that holds across languages. `Omnilingua-AudioMC` is a strictly parallel multilingual benchmark of 354 conversations and 1,404 rubric items in ten languages, aligned across transcript and speech conditions. Across six speech-language models, **the gap between transcript and speech performance depends strongly on the model and language**, and models with similar transcript scores can diverge sharply on speech. Replacing earlier spoken user turns with transcripts helps the two weakest models more than replacing the current turn, which points to the representation of prior spoken context as a major recoverable source of degradation.

papers.title: Human-to-Robot Transfer via Bridging Representation and Action Space in VLAs
