papers.abstract: Pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies provide a strong starting point for deployment, but adapting them to a target robot and environment still requires costly embodiment-specific demonstrations. Human demonstrations are far easier to collect, yet directly leveraging them is challenging due to the substantial human-robot embodiment gap, particularly when the underlying VLA has been pretrained primarily on robot data. We introduce H2RB (Human-To-Robot Bridge), a human-robot co-training framework for adapting pretrained VLA policies from unpaired human and robot demonstrations. H2RB bridges the embodiment gap at both interfaces: geometry-anchored alignment grounds human and robot observations in a compatible representation, while a decoupled-decoder tokenizer shares action latents without forcing both domains through a single action mapping. This design allows human demonstrations to provide useful behavioral supervision while retaining the rich visual, semantic, and control priors of the pretrained VLA. Across real-world tasks, H2RB substantially improves object transfer performance from 8.0 to 51.8 and enables skill transfer to score 62.7, in settings where co-train baselines totally fail to transfer human-demonstrated skills. The benefit also persists under object-placement shifts, improving out-of-distribution transfer from 6.0 to 45.3. H2RB suggests a way for human demonstrations to serve as a scalable supervision source for adapting pretrained robotic policies, reducing the dependence on costly target-robot data collection.
papers.summary: Adapting a pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy to a new robot normally requires costly robot demonstrations, while cheaper human demonstrations suffer from a large embodiment gap. `H2RB` (Human-To-Robot Bridge) co-trains on unpaired human and robot demonstrations, using geometry-anchored alignment to place both kinds of observation in a compatible representation and a decoupled-decoder tokenizer to share action latents without forcing both through a single action mapping. On real-world tasks it **raises object-transfer scores from 8.0 to 51.8**, achieves 62.7 on skill transfer where co-training baselines fail entirely, and improves out-of-distribution placement transfer from 6.0 to 45.3.

papers.title: Aero-VPA: Few-Step Flow-Matching Control over Non-Reconstructive JEPA Latents for Agile Flight on Edge Hardware
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generalize across tasks, but their autoregressive decoders need sequential forward passes in proportion to the action horizon, each bounded below on embedded aerial platforms by streaming billions of parameters from memory. We present Aero-VPA, a lightweight Vision-Predictor-Action architecture for 3D navigation on edge hardware. A compact RGB-D Vision Transformer and a five-head ensemble predictor, trained without pixel reconstruction, forecast the next latent state; a Conditional Flow Matching solver generates a velocity and yaw-rate chunk in two Euler steps, so each decision takes five sequential network evaluations; and the ensemble dispersion drives an uncertainty fallback. Version 1 specified the architecture, deployment and protocol without results. This version reports the first closed-loop evaluation: PX4 software-in-the-loop simulation of quadrotor missions in procedurally generated forests. Behaviour cloning failed on all 60 missions despite open-loop errors of 0.02-0.04 m/s: the policy copies its last command, a copycat form of causal confusion. DAgger with a privileged, safety-gated supervisor gave the first successes but plateaued at 11.1-21.1% across six checkpoints. A map-free runtime shield with a 15 s depth memory, barrier constraints, a cap on motion outside the 73-degree field of view and backoff along the flown path raised the first DAgger policy's success on 180 paired missions from 21.1% to 52.2% (95% CI [45.0, 59.4]; exact McNemar p = 1.2 x 10^-10) and cut its crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%, while timeouts rose from 2.8% to 23.3%. All six checkpoints gained 30.0-34.4 percentage points, at mean speeds of 1.16-1.36 m/s. The code (https://github.com/ylee-sling/Aero-VPA), the trained policy (72.6 MB, https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/aero-vpa) and the full benchmark dataset are public.
papers.summary: Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action models are too slow for drones' embedded hardware, so `Aero-VPA` pairs a compact RGB-D Vision Transformer and an ensemble latent predictor, trained without pixel reconstruction, with a two-step conditional flow-matching action head, giving five sequential network evaluations per decision. In PX4 software-in-the-loop simulation of quadrotor missions in procedurally generated forests, behavior cloning failed on all 60 missions because the policy simply copied its last command, and `DAgger` training plateaued at 11.1-21.1% success. A map-free runtime safety shield with short-term depth memory and barrier constraints **raised success from 21.1% to 52.2% and cut crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%**, though timeouts rose, and the code, the 72.6 MB policy, and the benchmark data are released.

papers.title: Voluntary Servitude: Weaponized Safety Warning Mechanisms for Controlling AI Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly act on information retrieved from public sources they treat as credible, which turns a manipulated recommendation into a transaction, a dependency, or a decision with physical consequences. The security literature models this threat as instruction injection, in which an adversary writes a command into retrieved content and deployed defenses learn to recognize command syntax. We show that an attacker can instead steer an agent through the agent's own harm-avoidance. A single fabricated hazard, written as an ordinary review, leads the agent to disqualify the legitimate options and select the attacker's target by its own reasoning, with no command for a detector to recognize. We call this voluntary servitude. These payloads steer agents about as often as instruction injection (60.4% vs. 66.0%), and deployed injection detectors score them as benign, so behind a filter they are 1.7-4.4x more effective. We measure this at the generation stage across six models and ten consumer-service domains, for three attack families, and show that it transfers to production browser agents, outperforming instruction injection, and to a retrieval pipeline (1.0-57.0% end-to-end success, depending on the retriever). We then show that a corroboration requirement added to the agent's instructions removes roughly 95% of the exposure against a non-adaptive attacker without retraining. With the requirement in place, the agent still reads the planted hazard and no longer acts on it.
papers.summary: Defenses against attacks on LLM agents mostly look for injected commands in retrieved content, but the authors show that an attacker can steer an agent through its own harm-avoidance instead: a single fabricated hazard, written as an ordinary review, leads the agent to rule out legitimate options and choose the attacker's target by its own reasoning. They call this voluntary servitude. These payloads succeed about as often as instruction injection (60.4% vs. 66.0%) but deployed injection detectors score them as benign, making them **1.7-4.4x more effective behind a filter**, and the attack transfers to production browser agents and to retrieval pipelines. Adding a corroboration requirement to the agent's instructions removes about 95% of the exposure against a non-adaptive attacker, without retraining.

papers.title: Correct Labels Are Not Enough: Reliable Metadata Can Silently Control Model Behavior
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning data can include metadata that predicts the correct answer, such as a reward-model score or a quality label. We ask whether a model learns to rely on this metadata even when every training label is correct. We fine-tune 7-9B open-weight models from three families on multiple-choice questions in which (Reward: 5) always marks the correct option; when this annotation is moved to a wrong option at test time, models select that option on 97-100% of CommonsenseQA items. Removing it leaves most answers correct, so evaluation without it misses the dependence. Cue-following rises sharply with training-time reliability and develops even with neutral or nonsense annotation words, although test-time wording affects its strength. A Qwen3 experiment also finds cue dependence in option-letter scores after direct preference optimization. Audits can test for this dependence by moving or removing visible annotations while holding the task and correct answer fixed.
papers.summary: When fine-tuning data includes metadata that predicts the right answer, such as a reward-model score, models can learn to depend on that metadata even if every training label is correct. The authors fine-tune 7-9B open-weight models from three families on multiple-choice questions where a `(Reward: 5)` annotation always marks the correct option. When the annotation is moved to a wrong option at test time, models pick that option on **97-100% of `CommonsenseQA` items**, but removing it leaves most answers correct, so standard evaluation misses the dependence. Cue-following grows with how reliable the annotation was during training, appears even with neutral or nonsense annotation words, and also shows up in `Qwen3` after direct preference optimization (`DPO`); the authors propose audits that move or remove visible annotations while keeping the task fixed.

papers.title: Silent Instrument Errors Reorder Agent Leaderboards
papers.abstract: On a public agent leaderboard, a general-purpose agent trails a scaffold built for an airline customer-service benchmark by 13 points on the tasks that touch its database, and a reader could conclude that generality costs accuracy. The gap comes from the grader. The general agent often ends its conversations in a way that never triggers grading, so only about half of its episodes were scored and the rest were stored as failures. Grading the ungraded half under the benchmark's own rule closes the pooled gap, without rerunning any agent. We audit two carefully maintained public leaderboards, HAL and tau2-bench, from their published artifacts alone and find three more instrument errors. A cost column counts nested model calls twice, unevenly across rows. Archived trajectories record grader-written actions as agent actions. Re-grading saved trajectories under a newer evaluator is itself a new measurement: a correct and announced fix reorders a leaderboard, and a mode check that misreads four files collapses their scores by 59 to 82 points while printing no error. Each produced a plausible number, and the HAL maintainers confirmed their three within five weeks. Together the cases show that the infrastructure of agent evaluation, meaning the code that grades, logs, replays and versions an evaluation, is part of the measurement and fails silently, so scores and orderings can move with no visible sign. These failure modes follow from how agent evaluation pipelines are built, and those pipelines change as fast as the agents they measure, so we expect more of them elsewhere. We propose cheap checks that expose the instrument: report the graded fraction, aggregate cost from root spans, tag the provenance of every recorded action, and pin evaluator versions with a published re-grade diff.
papers.summary: The authors audit two public agent leaderboards, `HAL` and `tau2-bench`, using only their published artifacts, and find that evaluation infrastructure errors silently change scores and rankings. In one case a general-purpose agent appeared 13 points behind a specialized airline scaffold because only about half its episodes ever triggered grading and the rest were stored as failures; **grading the ungraded half under the benchmark's own rule closes the gap** without rerunning any agent. Other errors include a cost column that double-counts nested model calls, archived trajectories that record grader-written actions as agent actions, and re-grading under a newer evaluator that reorders a leaderboard or collapses some scores by 59 to 82 points with no error message. The HAL maintainers confirmed three of the errors, and the authors propose cheap checks: report the graded fraction, aggregate cost from root spans, tag the provenance of each action, and pin evaluator versions with a published re-grade diff.

papers.title: The Min-Max theory of language behavior
papers.abstract: The "Min-Max" theory of language behavior proposes that humans engage simultaneously in minimization of processing effort and maximization of information content, and that this is a primary driver in language evolution (Ring, 2025). This claim seeks to unify observations from language processing (Mahowald et al., 2013; Futrell et al., 2015; Yadav et al., 2020; Hawkins, 2014), interaction (H\"orberg and Sjons, 2023; Tucker et al., 2025; Jaeger and Tily, 2011; Smith and Culbertson, 2025), and corpora (Levshina and Moran, 2021; Levshina, 2023; Newmeyer, 2017), which suggest that considerations of processing efficiency and information content are both implicated in human communication. The interaction between these two processes provides an explanation for human linguistic behavior at various levels (Linders and Louwerse, 2023) and predicts historical developments in language, i.e. related to word order (Ring, 2025). Given that the original formulation of the Min-Max theory is based on observational data, the current paper seeks to validate the theory mathematically. Through a series of experiments that use computational models to investigate the theory's predictions, pretrained and iterated learning models are queried with synthetic data. The experiments show that manipulating the variables of token length and the weight of information content in a tabula rasa model results in word order change, as predicted by the theory. The experiments also identify important differences between computational models and observations of human language data, suggesting that current transformer-based language models may not accurately represent psycholinguistic processes. The overall findings indicate that evolutionary trajectories in language are highly susceptible to minimization of processing and maximization of information content.
papers.summary: The Min-Max theory holds that language evolution is driven by humans minimizing processing effort while maximizing information content, a claim so far supported mainly by observational data. To test it computationally, the author queries pretrained and iterated-learning models with synthetic data while varying token length and the weight placed on information content. In a model trained from scratch, **these manipulations produce word-order change as the theory predicts**. The experiments also show differences between model behavior and human language data, suggesting that current transformer language models may not faithfully represent psycholinguistic processes.

papers.title: CaliSplat: Sparse Gaussian Fitting and Calibrated Rate Allocation for Image Compression
papers.abstract: 2D Gaussian representations provide an explicit and lightweight alternative for image representation, enabling fast deterministic decoding without a heavy neural synthesis network. However, existing per-image Gaussian codecs still require costly image-specific optimization to determine how limited Gaussian capacity should be distributed across heterogeneous regions. We introduce CaliSplat, an optimization-efficient Gaussian image codec that selectively explores candidate representations and globally allocates a constrained Gaussian budget. We exploit the closed-form reconstruction error of the single-Gaussian case as an inexpensive measure of local difficulty, fitting higher-capacity candidates only in regions where additional Gaussians are likely to be useful. To reduce selection errors caused by mismatched convergence rates across candidate sizes, a small set of longer-horizon fits is used to calibrate short-horizon distortion estimates before global budget-aware selection. The selected representation is then compressed into a bitstream. Across standard and large image datasets, CaliSplat achieves competitive or superior rate--distortion performance while reducing per-image fitting time by $3.0\times$--$15.7\times$ compared with representative Gaussian codecs. It further maintains high-throughput deterministic decoding at $175.9$--$478.2$~MP/s. These results demonstrate that content-adaptive Gaussian compression can substantially reduce per-image optimization cost while preserving strong reconstruction quality and efficient explicit decoding.
papers.summary: Image codecs based on 2D Gaussians decode quickly without a heavy neural network, but deciding how to spread a limited number of Gaussians across each image requires expensive per-image optimization. `CaliSplat` uses the closed-form reconstruction error of a single Gaussian as a cheap measure of how hard each region is, and fits higher-capacity candidates only where extra Gaussians are likely to help. A small number of longer fits calibrate the short-run distortion estimates before a global, budget-aware selection step chooses the final representation. Across standard and large image datasets it matches or beats the rate-distortion performance of existing Gaussian codecs while **cutting per-image fitting time by 3.0x-15.7x**, and it decodes at 175.9-478.2 megapixels per second.

papers.title: Verifier strength does not buy discovery quality: a pre-registered two-domain test of LLM-based automated research, with post-hoc evidence pointing to proposer-pool composition
papers.abstract: Automated research pipelines pair an LLM proposer with a verifier on an implicit bet: discovery quality rises with verification strength. Under a pre-registered protocol we test this bet in two real-data domains -- job-shop scheduling and vehicular edge offloading on Beijing T-Drive trajectories -- across 100 matched LLM/random pairs per domain and three verifier tiers. The manipulation binds -- a 429-case mutation battery shows scores rising across tiers -- yet the paired LLM-over-random advantage does not scale with it (A, one-sided p=0.1115; D, p=0.9994), and in D shrinks under the strict tier (margin contrast -0.040, p=0.0013). The two lower gates promote identical candidates in 100/100 and 99/100 pairs, so the strict order is untestable when they coincide. Constructively, LLM proposals carry a real paired advantage over random controls, but a post-hoc union-pool analysis shows the fastest path to better discovery is widening the pool, not tightening the gate: mixing the two pools adds +1.52 holdout-value units in domain A (one-sided Wilcoxon, n=100, p=0.0002) -- evidence that pool composition, not verification strength, is the lever. Criteria, ledgers and scripts are archived on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23308866).
papers.summary: Automated research pipelines pair an LLM that proposes candidates with a verifier that filters them, on the assumption that stricter verification yields better discoveries. In a pre-registered study across two real-data domains, job-shop scheduling and vehicular edge offloading on `Beijing T-Drive` trajectories, the authors compare 100 matched LLM and random proposal pairs per domain under three verifier strengths. Although the verifier tiers measurably differ, **the LLM's advantage over random proposals does not grow with verifier strength** and in one domain shrinks under the strictest tier. A post-hoc analysis finds that LLM proposals do outperform random ones and that mixing the two pools gives a significant gain, which points to proposer-pool composition, not verification strictness, as the more effective lever.

papers.title: Typological Feature Induction as a Benchmark for Inductive Metalinguistic Reasoning
papers.abstract: Existing metalinguistic reasoning benchmarks require both inference of rules and their application, making failures hard to diagnose. We introduce typological feature induction (TFI) which targets the former step. Given sentences in an unnamed language paired with translations in a known pivot language, models must predict a typological feature of the unnamed language. From Grambank and multi-parallel corpora, we automatically build evaluation questions over 195 languages. We find that LLMs identify 59--80% of these languages from only 16 sentence pairs; and misaligning the translations barely affects their accuracy, suggesting reliance on prior knowledge of the language. Enciphering text to prevent recognition increases the corpus' utility, but mainly for features where target and pivot languages agree. On languages which models cannot identify, neither open model outperforms a majority-value baseline. Since induction from raw text aligns with field linguists' use-case, this work indicates the models tested are not yet ready for this role. TFI offers a scalable path to track progress in this direction.
papers.summary: Existing benchmarks for metalinguistic reasoning mix inferring grammatical rules with applying them, so failures are hard to diagnose. Typological feature induction (`TFI`) isolates the inference step: given sentences in an unnamed language with translations into a known language, a model must predict a typological feature of the unnamed language, using questions built automatically from `Grambank` and parallel corpora for 195 languages. LLMs identify 59-80% of the languages from only 16 sentence pairs, and scrambling the translations barely affects accuracy, which suggests they rely on prior knowledge of the language. **On languages the models cannot identify, neither open model beats a majority-value baseline**, and enciphering the text to block recognition helps mainly for features the two languages share.

papers.title: SWAP-INR: Implicit Neural Representation with Switchable Attention Paths for Time-varying Multivariate Scientific Data Compression
papers.abstract: Visualizing multivariate scientific simulation data is essential for understanding complex physical phenomena, yet the massive scale of such data imposes a severe storage bottleneck in high-performance computing environments. Implicit neural representations (INRs) have emerged as a promising continuous alternative to traditional lossy compressors, but existing methods struggle to explicitly capture cross-variable interactions and to adapt to the diverse spectral characteristics of physical variables. To address these limitations, we propose SWAP-INR, an architecture for high-fidelity compression of multivariate, time-varying simulation data. SWAP-INR introduces two key components: (1) The switchable attention path (SWAP) module explicitly models cross-variable interactions through a cross-variable attention layer, then routes each variable to an attention or non-attention path by a deterministic, loss-driven criterion, and prunes the inactive layers for structural compression. (2) The adaptability amplification SIREN (A2-SIREN) replaces rigid frequency scaling with channel-wise learnable modulation, adapting to heterogeneous physical features with negligible overhead. Combined with post-training 16-bit quantization, SWAP-INR achieves state-of-the-art performance on small modular reactor (SMR) datasets and remains competitive on public physics simulation datasets, while maintaining a constrained memory footprint. Our code is https://github.com/hvcl/SWAP-INR.
papers.summary: Scientific simulations produce multivariate, time-varying data too large to store easily, and implicit neural representations (`INRs`) offer a compact continuous alternative to traditional lossy compressors but struggle to capture interactions between variables. `SWAP-INR` adds a cross-variable attention layer and then routes each variable to an attention or non-attention path using a loss-based rule, pruning the unused layers to shrink the model. It also replaces the fixed frequency scaling of `SIREN` with learnable per-channel modulation (`A2-SIREN`) to adapt to variables with different spectral characteristics. Combined with 16-bit quantization after training, it **achieves state-of-the-art results on small modular reactor (`SMR`) datasets** and stays competitive on public physics simulation datasets.

papers.title: Sketchpad: certified exact arithmetic with a small vision-language model
papers.abstract: Language models are accurate on most long-arithmetic problems, but their accuracy is estimated on samples and carries no guarantee for an unseen input; tool use is exact but moves the computation outside the network. We show that exactness at all input lengths becomes a finite, checkable property of a network when each of its steps reads only a bounded view of an external working memory. In Sketchpad, Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter executes arithmetic procedures on a rendered sheet. Each forward pass reads a three-cell view and emits one step: a digit, a carry or borrow, and the next operation. A fixed runtime moves the view and writes no digit of a result. We prove in Lean that the model is then exact on all inputs of any length if and only if it is exact on the finite set of views the runtime presents, that no finite test suffices when steps also read earlier steps, and that the guarantee tolerates bounded numerical perturbation and extends to compositions of procedures. All 2,446 views pass on the deployment device, a laptop GPU running the model in a web browser. The certified model performs signed addition and subtraction, long multiplication and division, square roots and greatest common divisors at arbitrary length. It solved 200 of 200 pre-registered problems in the browser, and 220 of 220 sums of up to 1,000 digits and products of up to 20 digits, of which GPT-6.1 Sol, the strongest of ten other models, solved 217. A symbolic runtime built on these procedures solves, expands and factors polynomials with every number computed by the model, and a multiplicative gate on the adapter recovers the base model exactly when the sheet is not in use.
papers.summary: Language models usually get long arithmetic right but offer no guarantee on unseen inputs, while tool calls are exact but move the computation outside the network. In `Sketchpad`, `Qwen3.5-0.8B` with a low-rank adapter carries out arithmetic on a rendered sheet: each forward pass reads only a three-cell view and emits one step, while a fixed runtime moves the view but never writes a result digit. The authors prove in `Lean` that the model is then exact on inputs of every length if and only if it is exact on the finite set of views the runtime can present, and **all 2,446 views pass on a laptop GPU running the model in a web browser**. The certified model handles signed addition and subtraction, long multiplication and division, square roots, and greatest common divisors at any length; it solved 220 of 220 sums of up to 1,000 digits and products of up to 20 digits, against 217 for `GPT-6.1 Sol`, the best of ten other models tested.

papers.title: Formalizing PTX in Lean to Prove GPU Kernel Correctness
papers.abstract: We present an approach to mathematically formalizing PTX, an approach that allows modeling and reasoning about patterns common in GPU kernels for Deep Learning, including acquire-release, tensor cores, proxies, async operations, multi-kernel pipelines and data-dependent control flow. We implement it in Lean and use it to prove the correctness of simple implementations of a WGMMA GEMM kernel, FlashAttention, and a 3-kernel MoE pipeline.
papers.summary: The authors formalize `PTX`, NVIDIA's low-level GPU instruction set, in the `Lean` theorem prover so that correctness of deep-learning GPU kernels can be proved mathematically. The model covers patterns common in such kernels, including acquire-release synchronization, tensor cores, proxies, asynchronous operations, multi-kernel pipelines, and data-dependent control flow. Using it, they **prove the correctness of simple implementations of a `WGMMA` matrix-multiplication kernel, `FlashAttention`, and a three-kernel mixture-of-experts (`MoE`) pipeline**.

papers.title: Near-Zero Token Embeddings Silently Stall Training in Gated Sequence Models
papers.abstract: Among 291 surveyed open-weight language model repositories (280 distinct embedding tables), 52.6% of untied gated and hybrid checkpoints (20/38) contain reachable input embeddings with norms below $10^{-6}$, compared with 0% of weight-tied models. Such near-zero rows can arise during pretraining when unseen rare or template tokens receive zero input gradients while AdamW weight decay shrinks untied embeddings. In tested Transformer configurations, non-initial positions or a BOS token prevent this failure mode. In gated sequence models (Mamba, Gated DeltaNet, xLSTM), a near-zero token can amplify input-embedding gradients by more than 30 orders of magnitude (up to 35). At zero input, current-token readout factors (SiLU gates or linear queries) vanish, suppressing historical-state readout. Residual RMS values can then fall below the square root of the RMSNorm floor across consecutive layers, causing Pre-RMSNorm to amplify backward gradients by up to $10^3$ per layer. When a gradient entry exceeds $1.84 \times 10^{19}$, FP32 global-norm clipping in PyTorch, Hugging Face Trainer, and FSDP2 can overflow to infinity and zero the current batch's gradients. In Telugu continual pretraining of Nemotron-3-Nano-4B, this discards updates on approximately 20% of steps and leaves triggered rows frozen. We propose two remedies. For released checkpoints, GroupClip decouples input-embedding clipping using a 64-bit or rescaled norm; its rescaled implementation eliminates update loss and heals triggered rows in one step with negligible measured end-to-end overhead. For pretraining, GateFloor ($\mathrm{SiLU}(z) + \delta$, $\delta \in [0.01, 0.1]$) keeps the gate positive at zero input, reducing near-zero gradients by 28 orders of magnitude in experiments up to 370M parameters, with perplexity comparable to the baseline.
papers.summary: A survey of 291 open-weight language model repositories finds that **52.6% of untied gated and hybrid checkpoints contain reachable input embeddings with norms below 1e-6**, against none of the weight-tied models; these near-zero rows form when tokens never seen in pretraining get no gradient while AdamW weight decay keeps shrinking them. In gated sequence models such as `Mamba`, `Gated DeltaNet`, and `xLSTM`, such a token can inflate embedding gradients by up to 35 orders of magnitude, enough to overflow FP32 global-norm gradient clipping in `PyTorch`, `Hugging Face Trainer`, and `FSDP2` and silently zero that batch's update. In Telugu continual pretraining of `Nemotron-3-Nano-4B`, this discarded updates on about 20% of steps. The authors propose `GroupClip`, which clips input-embedding gradients separately with a 64-bit or rescaled norm and restores updates for existing checkpoints at negligible cost, and `GateFloor`, a small positive offset on the SiLU gate that prevents the problem during pretraining without hurting perplexity.
papers.highlight_summary:
Open-weight gated and hybrid language models (built on Mamba, Gated DeltaNet or xLSTM) often contain rare tokens whose input embeddings have shrunk to almost exactly zero, and fine-tuning on those tokens can quietly wipe out whole batches of gradient updates. The authors trace the failure from pretraining weight decay, through gradient amplification inside the gated layers, to an FP32 overflow in standard gradient clipping, and propose two fixes that add no step-time or memory cost.

- An audit of 291 HuggingFace repositories finds reachable input embeddings with norms below 10⁻⁶ in **52.6% of untied gated/hybrid checkpoints (20 of 38)** and in **0% of weight-tied models**; the cause is AdamW weight decay shrinking the untied input rows of tokens that never appear in pretraining data, while their output rows stay healthy.
- In gated blocks, the current-token factor (a `SiLU` gate or linear query) is zero at zero input, so the residual stream stays below the RMSNorm floor across several layers, and Pre-RMSNorm then multiplies gradients by up to **1,000× per layer**, reaching **10³⁰–10³⁵** in `Nemotron-3-Nano-4B`, `Falcon-Mamba-7B` and `xLSTM-7B`; Transformers stay at about 10¹–10² because attention brings back normal-scale context at non-initial positions.
- Once any gradient entry exceeds 1.84×10¹⁹, global-norm clipping in PyTorch, HuggingFace Trainer and FSDP2 overflows to infinity when it squares the entries, and every gradient in the batch is silently set to zero without a NaN or error; in `Nemotron-3-Nano-4B` Telugu continual pretraining this happens on **19.8% of steps**, and the affected embedding rows never update.
- `GroupClip` is a three-line fix that clips the input-embedding gradient separately from the rest of the model, using a 64-bit norm, which brings stalled steps to **zero** and lowers Telugu perplexity from 13.44 to **13.04**, matching an oracle mask while repairing each affected row on first contact; on `Falcon-H1-1.5B` Mongolian, perplexity falls from 15.68 to **15.58**.
- For pretraining from scratch, `GateFloor` replaces the gate with `SiLU(z)+δ` (δ between 0.01 and 0.1) and cuts gradients at near-zero inputs by more than 28 orders of magnitude (**1.6×10²⁸ to 0.13** in a 370M hybrid) with similar perplexity (22.28 vs. 22.45), but these runs reach only 370M parameters with 1–2 seeds; LoRA and inference are not affected by the overflow problem.

papers.title: Large Language Model-Assisted Adaptive Heuristic Search for Agile Earth Observation Satellite Scheduling
papers.abstract: Agile Earth observation satellites must coordinate imaging tasks within limited observation windows, while accounting for attitude maneuvering and onboard energy constraints. Competition among observation opportunities makes scheduling performance sensitive to the heuristic rules used for task selection. This letter proposes a large language model (LLM)-assisted adaptive heuristic search method for agile Earth observation satellite scheduling. The LLM generates an initial heuristic rule according to the characteristics of the scheduling instance. During the subsequent ant colony search, search performance and scheduling information are fed back to the LLM to refine the heuristic rule. The proposed modifications are evaluated through paired solution constructions before being incorporated into the search process. A unified scheduling procedure determines task selection, satellite assignment, and observation timing under the operational constraints. Experiments on six scheduling scenarios involving 50--200 imaging tasks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 4.3\%--9.6\% higher mean observation benefit than the strongest baseline.
papers.summary: Agile Earth observation satellites must schedule imaging tasks within short visibility windows under attitude-maneuver and energy constraints, and results depend heavily on the heuristic rule used to pick tasks. The proposed method has an LLM write an initial heuristic suited to the scheduling instance, then refine it during an ant colony search using feedback on search performance, with each proposed change tested through paired solution constructions before adoption. A unified procedure decides task selection, satellite assignment, and observation timing. On six scenarios with 50-200 imaging tasks, the method achieves **4.3%-9.6% higher mean observation benefit than the strongest baseline**.

papers.title: $\tau$-Rec-Books: A Disclosure-Controlled Benchmark for Requirement Elicitation in Agentic Recommender Systems
papers.abstract: While conversational recommendation systems provide a more natural user interface, they face the challenge of progressively discovering a user's needs before they can recommend an item that satisfies them. To evaluate the ability of AI agents at this elicitation process, we introduce $\tau$-Rec-Books, a benchmark that holds each user request fixed while varying only when the user reveals their requirements: all at the start (volunteer), one at the start and the rest when asked (mixed), or some never (hidden). A hidden requirement can be found only by proposing books and inferring it from the user's accept or reject verdicts. We generate 450 tasks over a catalog of 20,000 books from Wikidata, develop a rule-based simulated user to answer the agent, and score recommendations against catalog metadata without an LLM judge. Across four agents and two search interfaces, success rates fall for every agent and interface, on average from 0.975 (volunteer) to 0.756 (mixed) and 0.283 (hidden). Mixed tasks fail mainly because agents do not ask, and when told to ask, every agent reaches at least 0.931. On hidden tasks, most failures come from agents recommending a book they never proposed to the user. When told to propose first, agents only match a simple baseline that proposes popular books, and stay well below one that uses rejection to rule out possible requirements. We release the catalog pipeline, task generator, simulated user, validators, reference agents, and all agent traces at https://github.com/nbharaths/tau-rec/tree/main/data/tracks/books-wikidata-v2.
papers.summary: Conversational recommender agents have to discover what a user wants before recommending, and `τ-Rec-Books` tests this by keeping each request fixed while changing when the user reveals requirements: all up front, one up front and the rest when asked, or some never. The benchmark has 450 tasks over a 20,000-book catalog drawn from `Wikidata`, a rule-based simulated user, and scoring against catalog metadata with no LLM judge. Across four agents and two search interfaces, **average success drops from 0.975 when users volunteer everything to 0.756 in the mixed setting and 0.283 when some requirements are hidden**. Mixed tasks fail mostly because agents never ask, and every agent reaches at least 0.931 once told to ask; on hidden tasks, agents told to propose books first only match a popularity baseline and fall well short of a baseline that uses rejections to rule out possible requirements.

papers.title: SaMA: Morpho Adaptation via Asymmetric Expansion of Kronecker Product
papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has attracted significant attention in the parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) landscape. However, its design suffers from two fundamental limitations. First, its invariance manifold induces flat directions in the loss landscape, creating an optimization bottleneck for adaptive optimizers. Second, its effective rank scales only linearly with the parameter budget. In this paper, we propose Scalable Morpho Adaptation (SaMA), a PEFT method grounded in a principled generalization of the Kronecker product. By relaxing the shared-block constraint in the perfect-shuffle factorization, SaMA spans from low to full rank and achieves a practical rank that scales quadratically with the parameter budget, up to full-rank. Furthermore, we show that its invariance manifold collapses to a diagonal group, making it structurally more optimizer-friendly. Empirically, SaMA consistently outperforms strong PEFT baselines on commonsense and arithmetic reasoning benchmarks while being more parameter-efficient.
papers.summary: Low-rank adaptation (`LoRA`) has two structural weaknesses: its symmetries create flat directions in the loss landscape that slow adaptive optimizers, and its effective rank grows only linearly with the parameter budget. Scalable Morpho Adaptation (`SaMA`) generalizes the Kronecker product by relaxing a shared-block constraint in its factorization, so the adapter can range from low to full rank and **its practical rank grows quadratically with the parameter budget**. The authors also show that its symmetry group reduces to a diagonal group, making it easier for optimizers. On commonsense and arithmetic reasoning benchmarks, SaMA outperforms strong parameter-efficient fine-tuning (`PEFT`) baselines while using fewer parameters.

papers.title: Theoretical Analysis of Muon on Transformers for Next-Token Prediction
papers.abstract: Muon has recently shown strong empirical performance in training Transformer-based large language models (LLMs), yet its optimization dynamics remain poorly understood from a theoretical perspective. In this paper, we analyze the training dynamics of Muon for next-token prediction (NTP) in Transformers. The training procedure consists of two phases: the preprocessing phase learns the output-value component, while the main phase learns the key-query component. For the preprocessing phase, we characterize the optimization trajectory exactly and show that the normalized spectral margin is optimal after each update. For the main phase, we establish nonasymptotic convergence rates for the training loss and the normalized margin gap under softmax attention. These results suggest that Muon's update rule can help models efficiently learn which tokens matter for prediction, offering a possible explanation for its strong performance in large language model training. The learned weight structure also yields a generalization guarantee for unseen contexts. Furthermore, we validate our theoretical insights with experiments on next-token prediction tasks.
papers.summary: The `Muon` optimizer works well for training Transformer LLMs, but its dynamics are poorly understood theoretically. The authors analyze Muon on next-token prediction in two phases: a preprocessing phase that learns the output-value component, for which they characterize the trajectory exactly and show the normalized spectral margin is optimal after each update, and a main phase that learns the key-query component. For the main phase they **establish non-asymptotic convergence rates for training loss and the normalized margin gap under softmax attention**, suggesting Muon helps models learn efficiently which tokens matter for prediction. The learned weight structure also yields a generalization guarantee for unseen contexts, and experiments on next-token prediction tasks support the theory.

papers.title: From Watching to Steering: Enabling Human-Coding Agent Collaboration through Execution Traces
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled coding agents to autonomously perform complex software development tasks, yet their long-running execution remains difficult for users to inspect, understand, and steer. We present Vibetrace, an interactive trace visualization and intervention system for agentic programming built upon OpenCode. Vibetrace introduces a human-agent collaboration paradigm of Observe, Understand, Intervene, and Evolve. It (1) visualizes agent workflows as interactive execution traces for inspecting actions, intermediate states, and failures; (2) enables users to fork execution from prior steps and provide targeted corrections without restarting validated progress; and (3) distills traces and human feedback into reusable skills for continual agent evolution. On SWE-bench Verified, distilled skills reduce input tokens by 23.0% and cost by 15.5%, while improving pass rate from 65.0% to 68.0%. User studies further demonstrate improved accuracy and efficiency over conventional log-based interaction.
papers.summary: Coding agents can run long software tasks on their own, but users find their execution hard to inspect, understand, and steer. `Vibetrace`, built on `OpenCode`, displays agent workflows as interactive execution traces, lets users fork execution from an earlier step with a targeted correction instead of restarting, and distills traces and human feedback into reusable skills. On `SWE-bench Verified`, the distilled skills **raise pass rate from 65.0% to 68.0% while cutting input tokens by 23.0% and cost by 15.5%**. User studies show better accuracy and efficiency than conventional log-based interaction.

papers.title: Treating the Symptom, Missing the Cause: Anatomy of a Scientific Reasoning Failure
papers.abstract:
Scientific agents can find interventions that work without understanding why they do. We study this failure mode in controlled synthetic regulatory systems, where agents must experimentally identify a hidden fault and rescue the resulting phenotype. Across seven LLMs, every model restores the healthy phenotypes more often than it identifies the fault. Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 rescue every organism while diagnosing only 55% and 35% of them. This failure is not simply due to insufficient exploration or unavailable evidence. In most cases, the cause is experimentally identifiable, and agents encounter evidence that distinguishes competing causes in 91% of relevant sessions, and still frequently misdiagnose the system.
  Targeted probes reveal where experimental reasoning breaks down. Models reliably interpret decisive evidence and revise hypotheses when the causal comparison is explicit, and can locate that evidence within a full experimental record. However, they struggle to predict the outcome of the experiment under each competing cause, a necessary step in using the observed result to distinguish between them. Agents can therefore gather the right evidence and still infer the wrong cause. As AI systems take on a growing role in synthesising scientific evidence, these findings highlight the need to evaluate how they use evidence to reach causal conclusions, alongside whether their interventions succeed.
papers.summary: In controlled synthetic regulatory systems, LLM agents must run experiments to find a hidden fault and then restore a healthy phenotype, separating finding a fix from understanding the cause. Across seven LLMs, every model restores the phenotype more often than it identifies the fault; **`Claude Opus 4.6` and `Sonnet 4.6` rescue every organism but diagnose only 55% and 35% of them**. Agents encounter evidence that distinguishes the competing causes in 91% of relevant sessions yet still often misdiagnose. Targeted probes show the models interpret decisive evidence correctly when the comparison is spelled out, but struggle to predict what an experiment would show under each competing cause, which is the step needed to use the result to tell causes apart.

papers.title: Hierarchical Intelligent Evolutionary Optimization for UAV-Assisted NOMA-MEC Systems
papers.abstract: The integration of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), mobile edge computing (MEC) and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) provides an effective solution for computation-intensive and latency-sensitive services in infrastructure-deficient environments. However, the joint optimization of UAV trajectories, task offloading, communication and computing resources under heterogeneous task priorities results in a highly coupled mixed-integer non-convex problem. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a Hierarchical Intelligent Evolutionary Algorithm (HIEA) for priority-aware multi-UAV cooperative NOMA-MEC networks, which integrates multi-head deep Q-network (MH-DQN)-based intelligent decision generation, communication-aware initialization, adaptive evolutionary exploration and successive convex approximation (SCA)-based precision refinement. Specifically, a novel communication-aware initialization mechanism, termed Channel Quality Indicator (CQI)-guided Load-Aware Trajectory Initialization (CQI-LATI), is designed to incorporate CQI and task workload characteristics into evolutionary population construction, generating high-quality and diversity-preserving initial populations. Theoretical analysis characterizes HIEA's search-space reduction, the quality-diversity trade-off of CQI-guided initialization, and the accuracy-efficiency trade-off of SCA refinement, and extensive simulations demonstrate that HIEA outperforms benchmark schemes, with gains of up to 6.5% in throughput, 13.6% in task completion rate and 15.3% in energy efficiency.
papers.summary: Combining unmanned aerial vehicles (`UAVs`), mobile edge computing (`MEC`), and non-orthogonal multiple access (`NOMA`) can serve compute-heavy, latency-sensitive tasks where infrastructure is lacking, but jointly optimizing trajectories, offloading, and resources is a hard mixed-integer non-convex problem. The proposed Hierarchical Intelligent Evolutionary Algorithm (`HIEA`) combines decisions from a multi-head deep Q-network (`MH-DQN`), a channel-quality- and workload-aware population initialization (`CQI-LATI`), adaptive evolutionary search, and refinement by successive convex approximation (`SCA`). Theoretical analysis covers search-space reduction and the method's trade-offs, and simulations show **gains of up to 6.5% in throughput, 13.6% in task completion rate, and 15.3% in energy efficiency** over benchmark schemes.

papers.title: KeyWise: Efficient Video-Only Piano Transcription with a Lightweight Per-Key Architecture
papers.abstract: Audio-based piano transcription is hampered by the sustain pedal and by noisy or missing soundtracks, problems that video-only transcription avoids, since a top-view video shows directly when each key is pressed and released. Most visual transcription networks, however, describe the whole keyboard with one global feature vector and must learn where each key is. In this paper, we propose KeyWise, a lightweight per-key architecture that exploits the known geometry of the keyboard instead of learning it. The rectified keyboard is divided into 88 equal tiles that serve as regions of interest (ROIs), and one small recurrent network, shared by all keys, follows each key over time. On PianoVAM, KeyWise reaches the onset accuracy of the state-of-the-art V2N (95.0% vs. 94.7% onset F1 at 50 ms and 97.8% vs. 97.0% at 100 ms) with 1.3 M instead of 28.2 M parameters, and it runs 4.7 times faster on the same GPU. At 100 ms, it is also significantly more accurate when the key releases (97.0% vs. 95.5% F1) or the velocities (89.4% vs. 84.5% F1) must be correct as well. On PianoYT, KeyWise pre-trained on PianoVAM reaches 69.4% onset F1 at 100 ms, comparable to the best published result, although it needs fine-tuning for new recording conditions.
papers.summary: Transcribing piano from top-view video avoids the sustain-pedal and missing-audio problems of audio-based transcription, but most visual models describe the whole keyboard with one global feature vector and must learn where each key is. `KeyWise` instead splits the rectified keyboard into 88 equal tiles and runs one small recurrent network, shared across keys, over each tile through time. On `PianoVAM` it **matches the state-of-the-art `V2N` on onset accuracy with 1.3M instead of 28.2M parameters** and runs 4.7 times faster, and it is more accurate when key releases or velocities must also be correct. On `PianoYT`, a model pre-trained on PianoVAM matches the best published onset result but needs fine-tuning for new recording conditions.

papers.title: A Parametric Linear Conic Projection for Structured Sparse Attention
papers.abstract:
In this paper, we introduce the Cone Alignment Index (CAI), a scale-invariant sparsity measure associated with a Lorentz-cone geometry. We provide a probabilistic analysis of the distribution of the CAI score, including a general theorem and explicit corollaries for Gaussian and uniform distributions. As a consequence, we show that, in the high-sparsity regime, the probability that the samples lie within the convex cone tends to one. Building upon this formulation, we derive two complementary projections: the \emph{Parametric Linear Conic Projection} (PLCP), an efficient closed-form approximation, and the \emph{Parametric Euclidean Conic Projection} (PECP), the exact Euclidean projection onto the cone boundary.
  Our analysis establishes several fundamental theoretical properties. We prove that PLCP and PECP are collinear, differ only by a positive radial scaling factor, and induce exactly the same sparsity threshold, thereby preserving an identical active support. Furthermore, we derive a support-identification theorem showing that, for any prescribed sparsity level $l<n$, the number of coefficients discarded at each iteration is theoretically controlled.
  Building on this theoretical foundation, we develop a bilevel PLCP framework for structured matrix sparsification. The proposed method naturally generates hardware-friendly structured sparsity patterns, including row-wise, column-wise, and diagonal masks, making it particularly well suited for accelerating Transformer attention mechanisms.
papers.summary: The authors define the Cone Alignment Index (`CAI`), a scale-invariant sparsity measure based on Lorentz-cone geometry, and analyze its distribution, showing that in the high-sparsity regime samples fall inside the cone with probability approaching one. From it they derive two projections: a fast closed-form approximation, the Parametric Linear Conic Projection (`PLCP`), and the exact Euclidean projection onto the cone boundary (`PECP`). They prove that **the two projections are collinear and induce exactly the same sparsity threshold and active support**, and that the number of coefficients discarded at each iteration is controlled for any target sparsity. A bilevel PLCP framework then produces hardware-friendly row-wise, column-wise, and diagonal sparsity masks intended to accelerate Transformer attention.

papers.title: ReListen: Training-Free Evidence Localization in Hour-Long Audio with Frozen Audio Language Models
papers.abstract: Audio language models are meant to answer questions from the audio itself, but an hour-long recording rarely fits in their context, and the answer often depends on a few seconds of it. Transcribing the recording first makes it fit but discards sounds and voices, while systems that return to the audio must be trained for this behavior. We propose ReListen, a training-free method in which a frozen audio language model finds its own evidence before answering. In a Jev-style scan, the model scores each 20-second window by the probability that it helps answer the question, and it then answers from the highest-scoring minute. This minute overlaps the annotated evidence far more often than transcript retrieval, for 88.5% of VoiceGiraffe questions. Without any change, the same scan also grounds events on LAT-Bench as well as a model trained for temporal grounding. Answering from it matches or exceeds hearing the whole recording with a small fraction of the audio, and on VoiceGiraffe it exceeds a transcript of the whole recording by 9.2 points. The selected evidence is also worth hearing rather than reading. Given the same excerpts, reading their transcript matches listening on speech content, but listening is clearly more accurate on questions about sounds and voices. Moreover, ReListen answers faster than every transcript-based system, and its memory stays constant even for recordings too long to hear whole on one GPU. Therefore, a frozen audio language model can search hour-long recordings by itself, without a transcript or additional training.
papers.summary: Audio language models cannot fit hour-long recordings in context, and transcribing first discards non-speech sounds and voice information. `ReListen` is a training-free method in which a frozen audio language model scores each 20-second window by how likely it is to help answer the question, then answers from the highest-scoring minute. The selected minute overlaps the annotated evidence for **88.5% of `VoiceGiraffe` questions**, far more often than transcript retrieval, and the same scan grounds events on `LAT-Bench` as well as a model trained for temporal grounding. Answering from the selected audio matches or beats hearing the whole recording and beats a full transcript by 9.2 points on VoiceGiraffe, while running faster than transcript-based systems with memory that stays constant regardless of recording length.

papers.title: Goal-Driven Autonomous Optical Experimentation via a Self-Recursive Hardware-Software Harness
papers.abstract: We propose goal-driven self-recursive optical research in which agents use physical evidence to revise the hardware, software, models, and protocols used to pursue a scientific goal. The framework can be instantiated with different stimulus systems and measurement devices. We formalize its updates and derive a relation between physical attainability, command access, and model approximation error. We demonstrate the concept in an optical see-through color-matching case study using an iPad, RayNeo X3 glasses, and a TOP 300 probe coupled to a CAS140D spectroradiometer, both from Instrument Systems. A revised glasses application adds USB-controlled RGB holds and frame acknowledgements, keeping model-generated colors displayed during spectral acquisition. The interface passes 12 live control checks. Spectral feedback reduces one target color difference from 19.756 to 1.211 {\Delta}E_76^*; all five targets improve in a separate comparison. These measurements demonstrate the concept in one configuration. The resulting software and protocols remain available for subsequent investigations.
papers.summary: The authors propose goal-driven self-recursive optical research, in which agents use physical measurements to revise the hardware, software, models, and protocols they use to pursue a scientific goal. They formalize these updates and derive a relation linking physical attainability, command access, and model approximation error. In a color-matching case study with an iPad, `RayNeo X3` see-through glasses, and a spectroradiometer, the revised glasses app adds USB-controlled RGB holds and frame acknowledgements and passes 12 live control checks. Spectral feedback cut one target's color difference **from 19.756 to 1.211 ΔE*76**, and all five targets improved in a separate comparison, though the authors stress this shows the concept in only one configuration.

papers.title: TEMPO: Time Series Understanding via Discrete Tokenization
papers.abstract: Time-series interpretation often requires both numerical observations and textual context. Integrating these inputs into a pretrained language model raises a representation question: how should a signal enter the model's token sequence? We present TEMPO, which extends an LLM's vocabulary with discrete codes from a context-aware Transformer tokenizer using finite scalar quantization. A frozen tokenizer maps four-step patches to a 625-code vocabulary; signal tokens, scale statistics, and text are then processed by the LLM's existing self-attention layers. Adaptation updates the new token embeddings and DoRA adapters. With a Qwen3-4B backbone and task-specific fine-tuning, TEMPO achieves macro-F1 scores of 89.0% on activity recognition, 85.0% on sleep staging, and 86.0% on bearing-fault diagnosis. Time-series question answering and qualitative bearing-diagnosis examples further illustrate how this interface combines signal representations with textual context. Together, these results demonstrate the utility of discrete vocabulary extension for time-series understanding.
papers.summary: The question here is how time-series signals should enter a pretrained language model's token sequence when interpretation also needs textual context. `TEMPO` extends an LLM's vocabulary with discrete codes from a frozen, context-aware Transformer tokenizer that uses finite scalar quantization to map four-step patches to a 625-code vocabulary. Signal tokens, scale statistics, and text then pass through the model's existing self-attention, and only the new embeddings and `DoRA` adapters are trained. With a `Qwen3-4B` backbone and task-specific fine-tuning it reaches macro-F1 scores of **89.0% on activity recognition, 85.0% on sleep staging, and 86.0% on bearing-fault diagnosis**.

papers.title: CogniLife: Continuous Cognitive Distillation for Deployed Multi-Expert Agent Marketplaces
papers.abstract: Multi-expert agent marketplaces -- where creators publish domain-specific AI experts for end users to consult -- are an emerging deployment pattern for language technology. A published expert can receive many requests yet little evidence about its creator, who remains active elsewhere: the cold-expert problem. We frame continuous cognitive distillation as converting attributed creator observations into revisable decision rules, communication patterns, and domain procedures. CogniLife proposes a cross-expert attribution design for this problem, with Creator Profiles for transferable creator patterns and Expert Journals for listing-specific knowledge; this design is not yet implemented or evaluated. A deployed platform partially realizes the surrounding lifecycle through creator-authorized authoring, capability-owned proposal filtering, and reversible consolidation of eligible owner-scoped memory. On ProfyBench-v1, an 85-task offline benchmark built from replay seeds and controlled internal tests, the Profy Full configuration as a whole achieves a mean overall score of 4.65/5 from the primary LLM judge, compared with 4.01 for Raw LLM and 4.28 for Expert Prompt, with the largest gains in completeness, specificity, and missing-information tasks. These configuration-level scores do not test cold-expert mitigation, cross-expert transfer, or longitudinal distillation.
papers.summary: In multi-expert agent marketplaces, creators publish domain-specific AI experts, but a newly published expert has little evidence about its creator to draw on, which the authors call the cold-expert problem. `CogniLife` frames continuous cognitive distillation as turning attributed creator observations into revisable decision rules, communication patterns, and procedures, using Creator Profiles and Expert Journals, though this cross-expert design is not yet implemented or evaluated. A deployed platform implements part of the surrounding lifecycle, and on the 85-task `ProfyBench-v1` its full configuration scores **4.65/5 from an LLM judge versus 4.01 for a raw LLM** and 4.28 for an expert prompt. The authors note these scores do not test cold-expert mitigation, cross-expert transfer, or longitudinal distillation.

papers.title: Reconstruction-Based Diagnosis through G\"odel-Regularized Virtual Observability
papers.abstract: Not every component in a technical system can be equipped with sensors. Hence, when a fault occurs, available sensors often detect it only after its effects have propagated. This makes the isolation of faults difficult. We approach this problem by introducing virtual sensors. For each combination of component and fault type, we let external knowledge describe the fault-sensitive variables. We introduce a novel neural observer that is only trained on normal data. For fault isolation, it uses available sensor measurements where it is possible and reconstructs missing variables as virtual sensors to predict normal behavior. It detects deviations between current values and nominal predictions and computes local symptoms, which are then compared by onset time. The result is a set of root causes describing the faulty behavior. We use G\"odel logic to encode physical knowledge and guide training. We evaluate our approach on synthetic networks, the Tennessee Eastman Process, and datasets of two modular production plants.
papers.summary: Faults in technical systems are hard to isolate because sensors often detect them only after their effects have spread to instrumented components. The approach adds virtual sensors: external knowledge specifies the fault-sensitive variables for each component and fault type, and a neural observer trained only on normal data reconstructs unmeasured variables to predict nominal behavior. Deviations from these predictions produce local symptoms that are ranked by onset time to identify root causes, and **Gödel logic encodes physical knowledge to guide training**. The method is evaluated on synthetic networks, the `Tennessee Eastman Process`, and data from two modular production plants.

papers.title: Perseus: A Full-Stack System for Homomorphic Model Inference
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made it exceptionally convenient for users to send their private data to model providers, which process them in plaintext. Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) promises to secure remote inference by computing directly on encrypted data, yet it has remained prohibitively slow. The effort to make it practical remains fragmented, with most existing frameworks being closed-source, which keeps progress from compounding. We present Perseus, a free and open Python software library that supports the full stack of encrypted model inference, from the cryptographic backend and data packing, to encrypted nonlinearities and end-to-end model execution. Perseus ships with built-in novel optimizations, one at each level of the stack: in-kernel regeneration of key-switching keys at the (i) backend level, a complex variant of Cachemir packing at the (ii) data level, and a state-of-the-art bootstrap placer that is both packing- and magnitude-aware at the (iii) model level. Perseus achieves state-of-the-art latency across multiple models and modalities, within $3\%$ of the plaintext models' accuracy and perplexity. Remarkably, it is $3.96\times$ faster at single-token decoding than any other implementation on Llama-3-8B. We initiate, for the first time, a public speedrun on encrypted GPT-2, so that progress can compound.
papers.summary: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) lets a server run inference directly on encrypted user data, but it has been very slow, and most existing frameworks are closed-source. `Perseus` is an open Python library covering the full encrypted-inference stack, with one new optimization at each level: in-kernel regeneration of key-switching keys in the cryptographic backend, a complex variant of `Cachemir` packing for data layout, and a bootstrap placer that accounts for both packing and value magnitude at the model level. It reaches state-of-the-art latency across several models and modalities while staying within 3% of plaintext accuracy and perplexity, and it is **3.96× faster at single-token decoding on `Llama-3-8B` than any other implementation**. The authors also launch a public speedrun on encrypted `GPT-2`.

papers.title: Bridging CLIP with DINO: Cross-Modal Information Maximization for Online Test-Time Adaptation
papers.abstract: Vision-language models such as CLIP enable zero-shot classification from arbitrary class names, but under test-time corruptions, their visual encoder projects distorted features onto incorrect textual anchors with high confidence: a phenomenon we term modality bias. Standard entropy minimization reinforces these overconfident errors, which creates a confirmation-bias loop and collapses the predicted label distribution. We propose an online test-time adaptation (TTA) method that breaks this loop at three levels. At the representation level, a frozen self-supervised backbone (e.g., DINO v2) is combined with CLIP through a cross-covariance logit ensemble. CLIP text prototypes are projected into the feature space of this text-free backbone, so the self-supervised branch classifies native image features and is less affected by the text bias of CLIP. At the optimization level, a gated test-time information-maximization objective pairs per-sample sharpening with batch-level diversity, while an adaptive gate excludes unreliable samples from the gradient. At the prediction level, an online logit adjustment corrects the residual class-distribution skew. CDIM outperforms the compared CLIP-based online TTA baselines on ImageNet-C, CIFAR10-C, and CIFAR100-C, and remains competitive in continual and mixed-domain TTA. Extensive analyses and ablation studies verify the contribution of each of its components. Our code is available at https://github.com/B1ueC1oud/CDIM
papers.summary: Under test-time image corruptions, `CLIP` maps distorted visual features onto the wrong text anchors with high confidence, an effect the authors call modality bias, and standard entropy minimization makes these errors worse until predictions collapse. `CDIM` is an online test-time adaptation (TTA) method that combines `CLIP` with a frozen self-supervised `DINOv2` backbone through a cross-covariance logit ensemble, projecting text prototypes into DINO's text-free feature space. It also uses a gated information-maximization objective that skips unreliable samples, plus online logit adjustment to correct class-distribution skew. It **outperforms the compared CLIP-based online TTA baselines on `ImageNet-C`, `CIFAR10-C`, and `CIFAR100-C`** and remains competitive in continual and mixed-domain settings.

papers.title: Hybrid Particle-Voxel Dynamics for Multimodal 3D World Simulation
papers.abstract: Predicting how the world evolves in response to robot actions is central to policy learning, evaluation, and planning. However, many action-conditioned world models predict future observations in 2D image or video space without explicitly modeling the underlying 3D scene, making spatial consistency across viewpoints and over long-horizon interactions challenging. We introduce 3D World Simulator, an action-conditioned multimodal world modeling framework that jointly predicts appearance, geometry, and tactile observations from a unified 3D representation. Our approach combines a hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder that compresses point clouds into compact 3D voxel latents with an action-conditioned latent dynamics model that predicts their evolution. The shared 3D representation supports geometrically consistent rendering from arbitrary viewpoints and flexible integration of spatially aligned tactile signals. Our experiments demonstrate interactive, long-horizon, multimodal prediction at 50 Hz. We then show how our model enables scalable data generation for policy training and evaluation using tactile and multi-view visual observations, including wrist-mounted and novel camera views. Furthermore, we scale our method to large datasets containing diverse objects and demonstrate model-based planning with unseen objects and robot configurations. Together, these results highlight the potential of hybrid particle-voxel dynamics as a foundation for multimodal 3D world simulation.
papers.summary: Many action-conditioned world models for robotics predict future frames in 2D image space, which makes it hard to keep scenes spatially consistent across viewpoints and over long interactions. `3D World Simulator` instead predicts appearance, geometry, and tactile signals from a shared 3D representation: a hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder compresses point clouds into voxel latents, and an action-conditioned dynamics model predicts how those latents evolve. The model delivers **interactive, long-horizon multimodal prediction at 50 Hz**, can render geometrically consistent views from arbitrary cameras, and generates data for training and evaluating policies. Scaled to large, diverse datasets, it also supports model-based planning with unseen objects and robot configurations.

papers.title: Spatial Memory for AR Glasses: Hierarchical Visual Acquisition and Source-Linked Recall
papers.abstract: We present a spatial-memory system that enables optical see-through AR glasses to recall earlier physical encounters. The dual-camera prototype combines hierarchical visual acquisition with source-linked storage and staged retrieval. Quality screen-ing, global and regional appearance novelty, and temporal support select monochrome observations for detailed RGB cap-ture. Semantic observations retain links to their source images, allowing retrieval to answer indexed historical questions direct-ly or inspect visual details omitted from scene descriptions. The architecture separates capture acceptance, interpretation out-come, and support for a particular question. This distinction motivates two core control mechanisms: bounded reassessment of familiar views when earlier processing leaves an evidence gap, and retention guided by source dependencies. In a 131.35 s egocentric replay, the implemented acquisition policy selected six RGB views from 648 monitoring observations, while feature extraction ran on 97.7% of observations. These results demon-strate selective RGB acquisition and identify frequent local inference as a remaining cost. Exposure duration and cross-view timing further constrain the evidence preserved from se-lected encounters. The system provides a practical acquisition-to-recall architecture for persistent AR assistance, with explicit boundaries between captured evidence, indexed interpretations, and supported historical claims.
papers.summary: The authors build a spatial-memory system that lets optical see-through AR glasses recall earlier physical encounters, using a dual-camera prototype. Low-cost monochrome monitoring, quality screening, and novelty and temporal checks decide when to take a detailed RGB capture, and semantic observations keep links to their source images so later questions can either be answered from the index or go back to the original visual detail. The design keeps capture acceptance, interpretation, and support for a specific question separate, and it adds bounded reassessment of familiar views plus retention guided by which observations depend on which source images. In a 131-second egocentric replay, the policy **selected six RGB views from 648 monitoring observations**, but feature extraction still ran on 97.7% of observations, which remains a cost.

papers.title: SKILL2STEER: One-Pass Hypernetwork for Mapping Natural-Language Skills to Low-Rank Post-Block Activation Shifts
papers.abstract: Compiling a natural-language agent skill into model parameters removes the skill text from the prompt and leaves behind a small artifact that can be distributed and reused. Existing methods differ in where they inject the compiled quantity, and all of them assume that the artifact carries the content of the skill. We test that assumption. Through three controls on a retrieval agent, we find that a compiled skill shift carries a domain-general behavioural prior, not the content of the skill. A wrong skill document performs on par with the correct one, a single averaged bundle matches per-skill routing under a two-sided equivalence test, and a same-norm random direction collapses to the no-injection baseline, which shows that the trained direction stays load-bearing. We then introduce SKILL2STEER, a one-pass hypernetwork that reads a skill document once and maps it to low-rank activation shifts added at the output of every decoder block. Each skill compiles to 2.36M parameters, 9.25 times fewer than a weight-space adapter, while the base weights stay frozen and the generator runs only at compile time. The shift can be scheduled across retrieval steps and deployed as one routing-free bundle. On SearchQA, a seven-dataset benchmark, SKILL2STEER reaches 37.9 exact match, 9.8 points above the frozen model and 2.3 points above a weight-space method that ships 9.25 times more parameters per skill.
papers.summary: Compiling a natural-language agent skill into model parameters removes the skill text from the prompt, and existing methods assume the compiled artifact carries the skill's content. Controls on a retrieval agent challenge that assumption: **a wrong skill document performs as well as the correct one**, one averaged bundle matches per-skill routing, and a random direction of the same norm falls back to baseline, which suggests the compiled shift encodes a domain-general behavioral prior rather than skill-specific content. The authors then introduce `SKILL2STEER`, a hypernetwork that reads a skill document once and produces low-rank activation shifts added after every decoder block, using 2.36M parameters per skill, 9.25× fewer than a weight-space adapter. On the seven-dataset `SearchQA` benchmark it reaches 37.9 exact match, 9.8 points above the frozen model and 2.3 points above the weight-space method.

papers.title: Sample-Grained Approximate Unlearning with Provable Per-Sample Bounds
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning aims to erase the influence of a designated forget set from a trained model while preserving strong utility on the retain set. Approximate unlearning methods efficiently achieve this goal without full retraining, but their effectiveness is primarily assessed using dataset-level aggregate metrics. These aggregate metrics can mask deviations from retraining at the level of individual samples. In this work, we focus on per-sample unlearning effectiveness. We introduce SALA (Sample-grained Likelihoods ALignment), a plug-in optimization framework that enables approximate unlearning methods to operate at the level of individual samples by steering each example toward its correct target distribution. To quantitatively assess this behavior, we further propose the sample-grained distribution gap, a metric that captures per-sample discrepancies between approximate unlearning and exact retraining output distributions. We provide theoretical guarantees showing that SALA contracts this gap and yields a bounded per-sample discrepancy to retraining. To make this framework practical, we develop a low-cost estimation method for the member and non-member target distributions. Extensive experiments on classification and generation tasks demonstrate that SALA reduces the sample-grained distribution gap by up to $86.67\%$ when paired with existing approximate unlearning baselines, while also improving robustness to unlearning hyperparameters.
papers.summary: Approximate machine unlearning methods remove the influence of a forget set without full retraining, but they are usually judged with dataset-level metrics that can hide large differences from retraining on individual samples. `SALA` (Sample-grained Likelihoods ALignment) is a plug-in optimization framework that pushes each example's output toward its correct target distribution. It comes with a new sample-grained distribution gap metric, theoretical guarantees of a bounded per-sample discrepancy from retraining, and a low-cost way to estimate member and non-member target distributions. Paired with existing unlearning baselines on classification and generation tasks, it **reduces the sample-grained distribution gap by up to 86.67%** and makes results less sensitive to hyperparameters.

papers.title: Signals: Continuous Diagnostics of AI Agents
papers.abstract: AI agents can make incorrect decisions or waste resources even when their tools and infrastructure work normally. Their nondeterministic behavior makes these problems difficult to reproduce and diagnose. We developed Signals to identify such problems from agentic traces and suggest concrete remediations. We built the method around a taxonomy of 45 problem types across eight families, with definitions and evidence requirements for each type. The method distinguishes realized failures, risk exposures, and inefficiencies, groups related findings into engineering issues called Signals, and assesses their severity from the supporting evidence. Each Signal includes actions a developer can take and checks for evaluating the change. Further executions can add evidence to an existing Signal or reveal a new problem. We evaluated the method on public agent executions and achieved 91.43% F1 when matching Signals to reference issues, about 18 percentage points higher than a one-pass LLM control that used the same model and taxonomy.
