papers.abstract: Identifying the primary diagnosis alone does not fully characterize a model's diagnosis-generation performance. We introduce CardioVascBench, a retrospective benchmark for prioritized diagnosis generation from real-world Chinese cardiovascular inpatient records. It contains 3,262 de-identified cases, with 2,174 for training and 1,088 for evaluation, linking clinical narratives and textual ECG reports to expert-verified, ordered discharge diagnoses standardized to ICD-10. An English translation of the evaluation set supports aligned cross-lingual comparison. Our evaluation protocol combines terminology normalization and rank-aware scoring to separately assess primary-diagnosis identification, reference-diagnosis coverage, and list precision. Evaluation across 36 systems shows that higher primary-diagnosis accuracy does not necessarily imply higher list precision against discharge references. We also provide CardioKG-Agent, a knowledge-enhanced baseline combining entity normalization, constrained graph retrieval, and guideline evidence. In a staged comparison of three baseline models, supervised fine-tuning plus the agent achieves a 73.5% higher mean composite score than fine-tuning alone, representing a system-level gain. These results measure retrospective agreement with recorded diagnoses; agreement between metric rankings and physician judgments remains to be validated. CardioVascBench supports research on diagnosis prioritization and knowledge-enhanced generation.
papers.summary: `CardioVascBench` evaluates prioritized diagnosis generation, meaning producing an ordered list of diagnoses rather than only the primary one. It uses 3,262 de-identified Chinese cardiovascular inpatient records linked to expert-verified discharge diagnoses coded in ICD-10, plus an English translation of the evaluation set. Its rank-aware protocol scores primary-diagnosis identification, coverage, and list precision separately, and across 36 systems **higher primary-diagnosis accuracy did not necessarily mean higher list precision**. A knowledge-enhanced baseline, `CardioKG-Agent`, combined with supervised fine-tuning scores 73.5% higher on a composite metric than fine-tuning alone.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Prototype Learning for Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation
papers.abstract: Open-set test-time adaptation (TTA) aims to adapt source-trained models to unlabeled test streams where covariate-shifted in-distribution (csID) samples and covariate-shifted out-of-distribution (csOOD) samples may coexist. Existing TTA methods are typically designed under a closed-set assumption and therefore lack explicit mechanisms for reliably distinguishing csID from csOOD samples. Consequently, csOOD samples may be mistakenly included in confidence-enhancing adaptation, producing harmful gradients that degrade known-class performance. To address this, we propose Uncertainty-Aware Prototype Learning for Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation (UAPA), a plug-and-play method for reliable open-set adaptation. Specifically, we first introduce Uncertainty-Driven ID/OOD Separation, which combines a classifier-prototype score with a mini-batch-normalized evidence-derived uncertainty score to distinguish csID from csOOD samples. We then propose a Dynamic Prototype Refinement strategy that periodically refines class-specific target prototypes using buffered csID features to progressively follow the estimated class directions. Lastly, we introduce Contrastive Prototype Entropy Adaptation, which applies entropy minimization to csID samples and entropy maximization to csOOD samples, while prototype-level contrastive learning aligns csID features with their corresponding target prototypes and reduces the maximum similarity between csOOD features and known-class prototypes. Empirically, UAPA outperforms the strongest baselines on the CIFAR benchmarks and Tiny-ImageNet-C, improving average OSCR by 2.08 and 1.28 percentage points, respectively.
papers.summary: Open-set test-time adaptation (TTA) adapts a trained model to an unlabeled test stream that mixes distribution-shifted known-class samples with out-of-distribution ones. Treating the out-of-distribution samples as known classes produces harmful updates. `UAPA` separates the two kinds of sample using a prototype score combined with an uncertainty score derived from evidence. It then periodically refines class prototypes and applies entropy minimization to in-distribution samples and entropy maximization to out-of-distribution ones, alongside prototype-level contrastive learning. It **improves average OSCR by 2.08 points on CIFAR benchmarks and 1.28 points on `Tiny-ImageNet-C`** over the strongest baselines.

papers.title: Surrogate Models for Stochastic Al-Cu Phase-Field Solidification
papers.abstract: Phase-field models resolve microstructural evolution during rapid alloy solidification, but their computational cost limits long trajectories, stochastic ensembles, and studies across process conditions. We present a variance-preserving denoising diffusion bridge model (VP-DDBM) for state-conditioned prediction of two-dimensional Al-Cu solidification. Given the current phase, concentration, and prescribed temperature fields, the model predicts the subsequent state and is applied autoregressively. Across two held-out thermal gradients, VP-DDBM produces lower long-horizon errors than deterministic U-Net and SI-ConvNeXt baselines in domain-mean phase, domain-mean Cu concentration, and leading-tip position. It also retains fine dendritic structure over long rollouts, whereas the deterministic U-Net progressively smooths the morphology. VP-DDBM predicts the phase and concentration evolution approximately $73\times$ faster than the phase-field solver, showing potential for faster process-condition screening and ensemble-based microstructure studies.
papers.summary: Phase-field simulations of rapid aluminum-copper alloy solidification are too expensive for long trajectories or large ensembles. The authors train a variance-preserving denoising diffusion bridge model (`VP-DDBM`) that predicts the next phase and concentration fields from the current state and temperature, and they apply it autoregressively. On held-out thermal gradients it has lower long-horizon error than deterministic `U-Net` and `SI-ConvNeXt` baselines and keeps fine dendritic structure that the `U-Net` blurs away. It runs **about 73 times faster than the phase-field solver**.

papers.title: When Ground Truth Is Not Ground Truth: Automatic Labeling for Hallucination Detection
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) remain a major challenge, as they can produce misleading, factually incorrect, or unverifiable information, thereby undermining their trustworthiness and reliability. However, reliable ground-truth labels remain a key challenge in evaluating hallucination detectors. Recent studies often construct labels automatically by comparing model generations with reference answers using similarity metrics such as BLEURT. This implicitly treats BLEURT similarity as a proxy for hallucination, despite its English-centric supervision, unbounded score range, and design as a similarity metric rather than a factuality measure, making threshold-based ground-truth construction potentially unreliable. Through comprehensive experiments using 15 automatic supervision judges, seven hallucination detection baselines, two generator models, two QA datasets, and five languages, we demonstrate that detector performance varies substantially with the choice of supervision judge. Human validation reveals substantial differences in labeling reliability, with QGen-9B achieving the lowest overall misclassification rate (12.86%), while BLEURT and BLEURT-n exhibit rates of 47.23% and 47.32%, respectively. Our findings highlight the limitations of automatic similarity-based labeling and the need for more reliable judging methods that better capture semantic and factual correctness.
papers.summary: Hallucination detectors for large language models (LLMs) are often evaluated against labels created automatically by thresholding the similarity between a generated answer and a reference, commonly with `BLEURT`. The authors test 15 automatic labeling judges with seven detectors, two generators, two QA datasets, and five languages, and find that detector rankings shift substantially with the choice of judge. Human validation shows **`BLEURT`-based labels are wrong about 47% of the time, compared with 12.86% for the best judge, `QGen-9B`**. The results suggest that hallucination benchmarks built on similarity-based labels may be unreliable.

papers.title: One-shot Distributed Learning via Weighted Averaging with Server-side Information
papers.abstract:
Distributed learning has drawn considerable attention due to its capability of learning from distributed data without aggregating raw observations. However, frequent exchange of model updates can become the main bottleneck of communication. Therefore, one-shot approaches where each worker fits a local model and sends it to the server to aggregate emerge. It is known that averaging can achieve the so-called pooled-data mean squared error (MSE) order of a hypothetical node that has access to data from the server and all the workers, and performs empirical risk minimization (ERM) on it. However, when the number of workers increases too fast compared to the local sample size, nonzero local estimation bias prevents averaging from achieving this order.
  In this paper, we study whether independent server data can overcome this limitation. We consider $m$ workers with $n$ observations each and a server with $p$ observations, all i.i.d., giving $N=mn+p$ observations in total. Under certain regularity conditions, a pooled-data ERM achieves MSE of order $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$. We analyze deterministic nonnegative averaging of convex-loss M-estimators, with equal worker weights and the server's own estimator included. Under our assumptions, including nonzero local bias of order $n^{-\alpha}$, $\alpha\geq1$, sample-size weighted averaging achieves the pooled-data MSE order whenever $m=\mathcal O(n^{2\alpha-1})$. Above this worker scale, it does so if and only if $p=\Omega(nm\cdot m/n^{2\alpha-1})$. Hence, server-only estimation, whose MSE is of order $\mathcal{O}(p^{-1})$, can achieve pooled-data order while sample-size weighting fails. Analytical examples and synthetic experiments illustrate when averaging matches the pooled-data MSE order, complemented by CIFAR-10 experiments comparing aggregation strategies with linear and nonlinear classifiers.
papers.summary: In one-shot distributed learning, each worker fits a local model and the server averages them. This can match the error of training on all the pooled data, except when the number of workers grows too fast relative to local sample size and local estimation bias takes over. The authors analyze weighted averaging of convex-loss estimators that also includes an estimator fit on the server's own independent data. They derive exact worker-scale conditions under which sample-size weighting reaches the pooled-data error rate, and show that **beyond those conditions, sufficient server data can reach that rate where averaging fails**. Synthetic and `CIFAR-10` experiments illustrate the theory.

papers.title: CLARA: A Cognitively-Driven Clarification Framework for Grounding Ambiguous Requests
papers.abstract: Robotics and AI systems are increasingly deploying large vision-language models (LVLMs) to follow high-level instructions, from routine household chores to more complex organizational tasks. Yet, broad directives like "clean the room" or "organize the desk" frequently omit crucial details about user preferences and specific arrangement of objects that influence the desired outcome. Without any further guidance, such models tend to overestimate their grasp of ambiguous instructions and frequently assume they have sufficient understanding despite missing important details. In this paper, we propose CLARA (Conversational cLArification for Robotic Arrangement), a cognitively-driven clarification framework that proactively elicits key information from users, in a similar fashion as humans' clarification seeking behavior. Through targeted questioning, CLARA refines ambiguous requests into structured, detailed instructions describing precisely how objects should be organized or rearranged, according to the user's preferences. These clarifications then guide a diffusion-based image generation pipeline, producing realistic visual renderings of the final, desired scene. This final rendering also serves as a visual confirmation of the system's understanding from the user. Experimental results and user studies demonstrate that CLARA leads to more accurate and consistent outcomes compared to another State-of-the-Art LVLM system, highlighting the importance of interactive clarification for bridging the gap between vague directives and fully grounded task specifications.
papers.summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) given vague instructions such as "organize the desk" tend to assume they understand enough and skip details about user preferences. `CLARA` asks the user targeted clarifying questions, modeled on how humans seek clarification, and turns the vague request into a detailed specification of how objects should be arranged. A diffusion-based image generator then renders the intended final scene so the user can confirm it. In experiments and user studies, **`CLARA` produced more accurate and consistent outcomes** than a state-of-the-art LVLM system.

papers.title: DenseTwins: Dense Modality Decoupling for Multimodal Self-Supervision
papers.abstract: Multimodal perception is central to many computer vision applications, including robotics and autonomous driving, where different sensing modalities provide complementary cues. Self-supervised learning offers a scalable solution for exploiting large amounts of unlabeled multimodal data. However, existing methods either neglect modality-specific information by enforcing feature-space alignment between modalities or learn only global representations without preserving spatial structure. We propose DenseTwins, a multimodal self-supervised framework that learns dense representations by explicitly decoupling the dense feature space into shared and modality-specific components. The proposed approach combines dense cross-modal correspondences with redundancy-reduction objectives, enabling the model to capture both shared semantics and modality-specific cues within a structured dense embedding space. DenseTwins jointly optimizes an intra-modal objective across augmented views and a cross-modal objective that aligns shared features while decorrelating modality-specific information. We evaluate DenseTwins across multiple multimodal benchmarks and sensing setups, achieving state-of-the-art or competitive performance across multimodal self-supervised baselines. Code available at: https://github.com/CarloSgaravatti/DenseTwins.
papers.summary: Multimodal self-supervised learning methods either force features from different sensors into a shared space, losing modality-specific information, or learn only global representations without spatial structure. `DenseTwins` learns dense, spatial representations whose features are explicitly split into shared and modality-specific components. It combines dense cross-modal correspondences with redundancy-reduction objectives that align the shared features and decorrelate the modality-specific ones. Across multiple multimodal benchmarks and sensor setups it achieves **state-of-the-art or competitive performance** against multimodal self-supervised baselines.

papers.title: Cycle WAM: Coupling Action and Video through Cycle Consistency
papers.abstract: Recent advances in video modeling have driven substantial progress in world action models (WAMs). Existing approaches exploit pretrained video priors by decoding actions from latent representations or inferring them from generated videos. The underlying link is causal: robot actions produce changes in the scene, and video observations of these changes provide evidence for inferring the actions that produced them. However, existing training formulations do not by themselves ensure that actions and their predicted visual consequences are consistent, potentially limiting the use of pretrained capabilities. We treat video and action as paired modalities linked by this causal relationship and learn their correspondence through a unified training framework designed to better exploit pretrained video priors. Cycle WAM first augments video-action co-training with bidirectional conversion to reinforce cross-modal correspondence and recover forward and inverse dynamics. It then introduces a differentiable cycle-reconstruction objective to further couple the two mappings. The resulting model supports both forward and inverse dynamics, with the potential to improve performance through more effective use of pretrained video priors. Cycle WAM achieves state-of-the-art performance among comparable methods on LIBERO-Pro and substantially improves DreamZero on DROID. Comparisons with UWM characterize its inverse-dynamics performance and show sharper visual detail in the displayed forward-dynamics predictions.
papers.summary: World action models (WAMs) use pretrained video models for robot control, but their training does not ensure that predicted actions and their predicted visual consequences agree. `Cycle WAM` treats video and action as paired modalities: it co-trains conversion in both directions to learn forward and inverse dynamics, then adds a differentiable cycle-reconstruction objective that ties the two mappings together. It **reaches state-of-the-art results among comparable methods on `LIBERO-Pro`** and substantially improves `DreamZero` on `DROID`.

papers.title: Hybrid acoustic and pretrained embedding feature fusion for unmanned aerial vehicle detection using stacking ensemble learning under a leakage-aware evaluation protocol
papers.abstract: Small multirotor drones produce a characteristic acoustic signature, and microphones offer a low-cost way to detect them. High accuracies have been reported on public drone audio benchmarks, often with random clip-level splits of datasets built from a few long recordings and pieces of existing sound collections, so pieces of one source can appear in both training and test data. We study the binary task of the public DroneAudioDataset (11,704 one-second clips). Its 1,332 drone clips come from 257 five-second chunks of 7 recordings, and 96.4% of its non-drone clips are pieces of the 2,000 clips of the ESC-50 sound dataset. A grouped, source-disjoint protocol (five folds, three repeats) is compared with a random split. Each clip is described by 57 hand-crafted acoustic descriptors, reduced by a hybrid minimum-redundancy maximum-relevance and ReliefF selection or by NSGA-II multi-objective search, and by a 1024-dimensional embedding from the pretrained YAMNet network. Random Forest and XGBoost learners on both views form a stacking ensemble. Under the grouped protocol, the two-view stack reached a mean accuracy of 95.29% (SD 1.62 points over 15 test folds), a specificity of 98.29% and an area under the ROC curve of 0.990, and it correctly classified 98.78% of unseen ESC-50 source clips as non-drone. The random split overstated accuracy by 1.89 to 3.22 points for the four models. Adding YAMNet embeddings to the hand-crafted view raised accuracy by 1.11 points (higher in 12 of 15 folds). Hybrid selection matched the accuracy of all 44 baseline descriptors with 16 to 18 features, and NSGA-II retained 4 to 6 features at lower accuracy. The stack took 51.0 ms per clip on one CPU thread. Source-disjoint evaluation is needed for a fair benchmark on this dataset, and fusing hand-crafted descriptors with pretrained embeddings gives a small but consistent gain at modest computational cost.
papers.summary: Reported accuracies on the public `DroneAudioDataset` for acoustic drone detection come from random clip-level splits, even though its clips are pieces of a few long recordings and of `ESC-50` sounds, so the same source can appear in both training and test data. Under a grouped, source-disjoint protocol, a stacking ensemble of `Random Forest` and `XGBoost` built on hand-crafted acoustic descriptors and `YAMNet` embeddings reaches **95.29% mean accuracy**. Random splits overstate accuracy by 1.89 to 3.22 points. Adding the pretrained embeddings gives a small but consistent gain, and the ensemble takes 51 ms per clip on one CPU thread.

papers.title: TAPES: Task-Aligned Joint Predictive Pretraining for Transaction Event Sequences
papers.abstract: Transaction event sequences support diverse prediction tasks in online commerce and digital financial services. The same transaction records can yield prediction targets with different semantics, including values, changes, and relations to past events. These targets impose different constraints on history representations, but their predictability alone does not establish the downstream utility of a target set. Moreover, target-wise prediction losses do not explicitly model conditional co-occurrence among targets. To address these challenges, we propose TAPES, a task-aligned joint predictive pretraining framework for transaction sequences. TAPES constructs a finite collection of candidate target sets from admissible field-operator combinations. It selects a target set according to the downstream utility of representations learned through short joint pretraining trials under matched budgets. It then reinitializes the encoder and pretrains it on the selected targets through a joint likelihood parameterized by a shared discrete latent variable, before downstream supervised adaptation. Experiments in a real-world transaction-risk setting and on multiple public financial benchmarks spanning diverse downstream tasks demonstrate that TAPES outperforms representative baselines. Ablation studies further validate the contributions of predictive target selection and joint modeling.
papers.summary: Transaction event sequences in commerce and finance support many possible pretraining targets, but how predictable a target is does not show whether it helps downstream tasks. `TAPES` enumerates candidate target sets from combinations of fields and operations, picks one based on the downstream utility of short pretraining trials, and then pretrains on the chosen targets jointly through a shared discrete latent variable. On a real-world transaction-risk task and several public financial benchmarks, **`TAPES` outperforms representative baselines**, and ablations credit both target selection and joint modeling.

papers.title: What Does It Mean to Remove an Edge? Intervention-Aware Fidelity for Graph Neural Network Explanations
papers.abstract: Graph neural network explanations are often evaluated via deletion fidelity, i.e., by deleting their top-ranked edges and measuring the resulting change in model output. Yet, in a message-passing GNN, "deleting an edge" does not specify a unique intervention. Structural deletion removes the edge from the graph and recomputes quantities such as degree normalization and attention, whereas message suppression leaves this structural context intact while blocking the message carried by the edge. The meaning of deletion fidelity therefore depends on what the intervention targets in the model computation. We formalize this distinction and derive sufficient conditions for exact equivalence. The two interventions coincide for additive message passing with edge-set-independent coefficients, but can diverge when aggregation depends on the presence of zero messages or when removing an edge changes the coefficients applied to surviving messages. We then construct intervention-specific edge attributions and evaluate each resulting ranking under both interventions, testing whether their relative fidelity changes with the evaluation intervention. Across nine datasets and a panel of GIN, GCN, and GATv2 models at depths 2--5, all nine GIN controls satisfy the equivalence predicted by the theory. On the target logit, the relative fidelity of the two rankings depends on the evaluation intervention in 10 of 11 reportable GCN and GATv2 cells, and in nine of them each ranking has the larger deletion area under the intervention it was built with. Deletion fidelity is thus not a property of an edge ranking alone. Evaluation protocols should explicitly report the intervention, output functional, target, and perturbation unit, and test alternative intervention semantics when the scientific question does not uniquely determine one.
papers.summary: Graph neural network (GNN) explanations are often scored by deletion fidelity, which deletes the top-ranked edges and measures the change in output. However, "deleting an edge" can mean removing it from the graph structure or only blocking the message it carries. The authors prove the two interventions are equivalent for additive message passing such as `GIN`, and show they can diverge for `GCN` and `GATv2`. Experiments on nine datasets confirm this: **an edge ranking's fidelity depends on which intervention is used to evaluate it**, so evaluation protocols should state the intervention explicitly.

papers.title: Non-Interfering Asymmetric AdamW Updates for Constrained Exploration of Equifinality in Hybrid Models
papers.abstract: Hybrid models let neural networks supply the unresolved parameters of a process-based simulator, and are fitted to observations that constrain aggregate fluxes and storages but not the internal partitioning that produces them. Such a fit is equifinal: configurations indistinguishable in the observed aggregates can disagree substantially about the unobserved internals, and therefore about the mechanism they attribute to the same data. We study evapotranspiration, whose total flux is observed while its split into transpiration and evaporation is not. A model ensemble built from random seeds alone spans only a narrow band of the partitionings the data admit. We produce the spread deliberately, training members under auxiliary repulsion on transpiration, subject to the fit to observations not degrading. Non-interference is usually arranged by making the auxiliary gradient orthogonal to the main one, but under AdamW the applied step is a preconditioned momentum direction, so orthogonality between raw gradients no longer implies it. We introduce Non-interfering Asymmetric Network Optimization (NANO), an update whose first-order effect on the main loss is exactly that of the main objective alone, whose auxiliary step is bounded, and which concentrates repulsion in the coordinates the main gradient leaves idle.
papers.summary: Hybrid models, in which neural networks supply parameters to a process-based simulator, can fit observed totals such as evapotranspiration equally well while disagreeing on how those totals split into unobserved parts such as transpiration and evaporation. Ensembles that differ only by random seed cover a narrow range of these splits. To explore the range deliberately, the authors train ensemble members with an auxiliary repulsion objective. They introduce `NANO`, an `AdamW`-compatible update whose **first-order effect on the main loss exactly matches that of the main objective alone**, which ordinary gradient orthogonalization cannot guarantee under adaptive optimizers.

papers.title: When Should an LLM Steering Edit Depend on the Input?
papers.abstract: An activation steering edit should depend on the input exactly when the destination varies \emph{inside} the class a query requests, and that is measurable before any rule is fitted or applied. Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) adds one fixed direction to every input, the difference of the class means. Conditioning it on the requested class accounts for the between-class variation in the required displacement and leaves the within-class variation untouched, which no rule that reads only the source state can express. We study the impact of increasing input-dependence in the steering edit, moving from a difference of means to a destination retrieved per query --- the mean of the $k$ stored states nearest the query, inside the requested class --- in which the two baselines are endpoints: at $k$ equal to the class size the retrieved rule \emph{is} the class-conditional difference of means. We measure input-dependent steering on six substitution corpora that vary in whether the edit changes a word or a clause, and on an external benchmark, and find that input-dependent steering outperforms fixed-direction steering when the destination varies within the class. Retrieval wins at every layer of every substitution corpus in two models, and the level of input-dependence needed governs how to apply it: word-level edits are best made in the first tenth of the network from a few neighbours, clause-level edits at any depth from the class mean. Where the class already determines the answer the class mean suffices and retrieval only matches it, though a fixed direction still fails there. Four quantities computed from the states alone identify the regime in which the edit should be applied.
papers.summary: Contrastive Activation Addition (`CAA`) steers a large language model by adding one fixed direction, the difference between class means, to every input's activations. The authors study steering edits that depend more on the input, up to retrieving a per-query destination from the mean of the k nearest stored states within the requested class. They find that **input-dependent retrieval beats fixed-direction steering at every layer when the target varies within the class**. Word-level edits work best in the first tenth of the network with a few neighbors, and clause-level edits work at any depth using the class mean. Four quantities computed from the activations alone indicate which regime applies.

papers.title: Koopman Generative Operators for Efficient Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Probabilistic time-series forecasting requires models that simultaneously capture structured temporal dynamics, expressive uncertainty, and efficient inference, yet existing approaches fall short of this goal: latent dynamical models impose structure but rely on restrictive generation mechanisms, while modern generative methods such as diffusion and flow matching achieve flexibility at the cost of iterative and computationally expensive sampling. We introduce the Koopman Generative Operator (KGO), a probabilistic forecasting method that conceptualizes prediction as the evolution of structured uncertainty. KGO integrates three core components: (1) Koopman Patch Embedding (KoPE) for temporally consistent latent trajectory extrapolation; (2) Koopman Flow Matching (KoFM), which enables fast, single-step generation through a closed-form matrix exponential in a Koopman latent space, bypassing iterative sampling; and (3) an Adaptive Uncertainty Gate (AUG), which provides probabilistic forecasts by adapting uncertainty per-variable and per-horizon, corresponding to a learned decomposition of aleatoric uncertainty without manual tuning. By unifying these components, KGO achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on 13/17 ProbTS benchmarks in CRPS and 16/17 in NMAE. Further, by eliminating iterative sampling, KGO delivers at least a 25$\times$ reduction in inference time compared to iterative generative models. These results position KGO as a practical and principled framework that advances the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in probabilistic time-series forecasting, combining leading accuracy on the evaluated benchmarks with fast, single-step generation.
papers.summary: Probabilistic time-series forecasters usually have to choose between structured latent dynamics with limited generative flexibility and flexible diffusion or flow-matching models that need slow, iterative sampling. The proposed `Koopman Generative Operator` (`KGO`) has three parts. `Koopman Patch Embedding` (`KoPE`) extrapolates latent trajectories. `Koopman Flow Matching` (`KoFM`) generates samples in a single step through a closed-form matrix exponential in a Koopman latent space. An `Adaptive Uncertainty Gate` (`AUG`) adjusts uncertainty for each variable and each forecast horizon. `KGO` reaches state-of-the-art accuracy on 13 of 17 `ProbTS` benchmarks by continuous ranked probability score (`CRPS`) and 16 of 17 by normalized mean absolute error (`NMAE`), with **at least a 25x reduction in inference time** compared with iterative generative models.

papers.title: TactiNavi: Serving and Revising an LLM Game Coach with Explicit Strategy Conditions
papers.abstract: A deployed LLM coaching agent answers requests whose correct response depends on player state and game version, so advice that is right for one player can be wrong for the next. We describe TactiNavi, the serving system behind the LLM coach of a commercial open-world game, which makes strategy applicability an explicit artifact shared by offline compilation, online execution, failure diagnosis, and release. An offline compiler turns versioned game evidence and expert guidance into strategy packages with explicit prerequisites, the serving plane evaluates those prerequisites as three-valued conditions over structured player state and records decision traces, and a control plane uses the resulting condition-rule dependencies to validate revisions on held-out traffic before release. In a retrospective evaluation of 1,122 logged coaching turns from three deployment periods, condition-bearing packages raise correctness from 57.9% to 82.0% over atomic facts and reduce strategy misapplication under changed player state from 18.1% to 10.4%, while trace-based claim verification reaches 86.4% precision at a median reply latency of 2.07 s. The deployment also showed that most apparent fixes are generation noise, because an unchanged-system rerun recovers 38.4% of failing turns and only one of 15 shipped revision units passes the release checks retrospectively. We distill these results into lessons on treating applicability as a first-class serving object, sizing traces for later diagnosis, and building the null model into the release path.
papers.summary: A deployed LLM coaching agent for a commercial open-world game has to give advice whose correctness depends on the player's state and the game version. `TactiNavi` handles this by compiling versioned game evidence and expert guidance into strategy packages with explicit prerequisites. At serving time it evaluates these prerequisites as three-valued conditions over structured player state and logs decision traces, and a control plane uses those traces to validate revisions before release. On 1,122 logged coaching turns, condition-bearing packages raised correctness **from 57.9% to 82.0%** over atomic facts and reduced strategy misapplication from 18.1% to 10.4%, at a median reply latency of 2.07 s. The deployment also showed that most apparent fixes were generation noise: rerunning the unchanged system recovered 38.4% of failing turns, and only one of 15 shipped revision units passed the release checks retrospectively.

papers.title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Submodular Trajectory Rewards
papers.abstract: We study cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning with decoupled dynamics and a monotone submodular reward function over joint trajectories. Due to the non-additive reward, an optimal policy may depend on the history of all agents. This dependence makes exact optimization exponential in the horizon and the number of agents. To overcome this challenge while retaining theoretical guarantees, we introduce pre-window curvature $c_m$, which quantifies how states visited more than $m$ steps earlier reduce current marginal gains. Using this curvature to control the error from restricting the policy of each agent to depend only on its last $m+1$ states, we propose a greedy algorithm that exploits the decoupled dynamics to optimize local policies sequentially. For fixed $m$, the algorithm achieves a $\frac{1-c_m}{2-c_m}$ approximation guarantee up to estimation error, and its computation time is polynomial in the number of agents and the horizon. We recover the known $1/2$-factor approximation for time-additive rewards and obtain an approximation factor no smaller than the known total-curvature bound for a single agent. We formulate multi-agent traffic monitoring as an example of this framework and evaluate our algorithm on it.
papers.summary: The setting is cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning in which each agent's dynamics are independent but the team's reward is a monotone submodular function of the joint trajectories, so optimal policies can depend on the full history of every agent. The authors define a pre-window curvature that measures how much states visited more than m steps ago reduce current marginal gains. They use it to bound the error from restricting each agent to its last m+1 states, and then propose a greedy algorithm that optimizes local policies one agent at a time. For fixed m the algorithm achieves a **(1-c_m)/(2-c_m) approximation guarantee** in time polynomial in the number of agents and the horizon. This recovers the known 1/2 factor for time-additive rewards, and the method is evaluated on multi-agent traffic monitoring.

papers.title: Replica-Aware Split Inference for Edge IoT Systems
papers.abstract: Split Inference (SI) addresses the hardware resource limitations of Internet of Things (IoT) devices by distributing tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) model segments across multiple IoT devices. However, a device failure can interrupt the inference pipeline. This paper proposes a replica-aware recovery approach that deploys replicas of TinyML model segments originally hosted on failed devices onto surviving devices. We formulate the joint selection of replica hosts and communication protocols as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem that minimizes post-reconfiguration inference latency, accounting for computation and transmission latencies, under flash memory and runtime memory constraints. Simulations using MobileNetV2 on heterogeneous IoT networks compare the proposed approach with four baselines. We implement the model in a network of 15 IoT devices with a maximum link-rate reduction of 75%, and show that MILP approach achieves an average modeled end-to-end inference latency that is 6.8% lower than that of Computation Greedy and 18.3% lower than that of Random. Index Terms TinyML, split inference, Internet of Things, fault tolerance, replica placement.
papers.summary: Split Inference (SI) spreads segments of a tiny machine learning (`TinyML`) model across several Internet of Things (IoT) devices, so a single device failure can break the inference pipeline. The proposed recovery approach places replicas of the failed device's model segments on surviving devices. It chooses replica hosts and communication protocols jointly with a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) that minimizes post-reconfiguration latency under flash and runtime memory constraints. On a 15-device network running `MobileNetV2` with link rates reduced by up to 75%, the MILP approach gives **6.8% lower modeled end-to-end latency than Computation Greedy** and 18.3% lower than Random placement.

papers.title: LIPS-PC: Learning Illumination Patterns for Single-Pixel Classification
papers.abstract: In single-pixel (ghost) imaging, known illumination patterns probe an object and a detector with no spatial resolution returns one number per pattern. Each measurement costs acquisition time and photons and, for ionizing probes, contributes to delivered dose. Motivated by automated radiographic defect screening, where a class label suffices, we introduce Learning Illumination Patterns for Single-Pixel Classification (LIPS-PC). The patterns are learned end-to-end while the measurement operator remains one fixed linear matrix, identical for every input. We parameterize it as a residual correction to a two-dimensional discrete cosine transform (2D-DCT), $D=D_{\mathrm{base}}+\Delta$, and jointly train the correction and a compact classifier using cross-entropy, without a reconstruction objective. This yields a task-driven linear embedding through optimization. We evaluate LIPS-PC numerically on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST under a controlled protocol, then on RIAWELC, a real industrial X-ray weld-radiograph dataset. Across five budgets, $M\in{8,16,32,64,128}$, corresponding to sampling ratios from below 1% to 12.5%, the learned operator outperforms the best tested fixed transform by 9-15 percentage points at $M=8$ on all three datasets. Its eight-measurement accuracy requires roughly 16-32 measurements with the best fixed transform, indicating a $2\times$ to $4\times$ saving at comparable accuracy. The advantage generally shrinks as $M$ increases, with a small reversal on RIAWELC at higher budgets. These results show that learning what to measure is especially valuable when measurements are scarce.
papers.summary: In single-pixel (ghost) imaging, every illumination pattern costs acquisition time and photons, and with X-rays it also adds radiation dose. For defect screening, a class label is enough and no image reconstruction is needed. `LIPS-PC` learns one fixed linear measurement operator, parameterized as a residual correction to a 2D discrete cosine transform (DCT), and trains it jointly with a compact classifier using only cross-entropy loss. On `MNIST`, `Fashion-MNIST`, and the industrial X-ray weld dataset `RIAWELC`, the learned patterns **beat the best fixed transform by 9-15 percentage points at 8 measurements**, which corresponds to a 2x to 4x saving in measurements at similar accuracy. The advantage generally shrinks as the measurement budget grows and reverses slightly on `RIAWELC` at higher budgets.

papers.title: Reducing Logprob Without Causal Verification: Diagnosing SAE-Based PII Suppression in LLMs
papers.abstract: SAE-based feature-level interventions to suppress PII leakage in LLMs are primarily evaluated by log-probability reduction. We show that this criterion cannot distinguish feature specific suppression from a magnitude artifact: a direction-agnostic effect of sufficiently large activation perturbations. Across 36 (model, layer, PII type) cases, we compare selected SAE feature interventions with coherencematched random direction controls using logprob and rank-aware metrics. While 17 cases (47%) appear successful under logprob-only evaluation, only 1 case (2.8%) passes our multimetric framework. The rest reveal two failure modes: random directions outperform selected features, and feature selection collapse across PII types. These results indicate that existing evaluations cannot verify whether interventions target causal pathways of PII leakage. A 9,000 run causal mediation feasibility study corroborates this: the verifier separates candidates reliably, but correlation-selected candidates rarely pass it. We therefore propose a new research mission for NLP: causally grounded PII suppression through circuit-level localization and causal mediation analysis.
papers.summary: Interventions on sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that aim to stop LLMs from leaking personally identifiable information (PII) are usually judged by how much they reduce log-probability. The authors argue that this criterion cannot tell feature-specific suppression apart from a generic effect of large activation perturbations. Across 36 combinations of model, layer, and PII type, they compare selected SAE features against random directions matched for coherence, using both logprob and rank-aware metrics. Logprob alone makes 17 cases (47%) look successful, but **only 1 case (2.8%) passes the multi-metric test**; in the other cases random directions often do better, or feature selection collapses across PII types. A 9,000-run causal mediation study supports the conclusion, and the authors call for PII suppression grounded in circuit-level causal analysis.

papers.title: Kierston & KierstonBench: Simulation of Allentown, PA and Evaluation of Language Models in Crime Investigation and Surveillance Tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models are candidates for collecting and analyzing records in criminal investigations and mass surveillance. Their capability and accuracy in this work cannot currently be measured. Real deployments lack the ground truth needed to score a model's conclusions, and no benchmark evaluates these capabilities in a simulated environment. We present Kierston, a city-scale simulation engine, and KierstonBench, a benchmark that tests these capabilities against known simulated events. Kierston models approximately 125,000 residents of Allentown, Pennsylvania, generating their daily activities and the telecommunications, financial, administrative and license-plate records that surveillance and investigative systems collect about them. These records derive from a common behavioral timeline and are distributed across sources representing separate providers. Models investigate through a restricted records interface, linking observations across sources without access to the underlying simulation. The benchmark comprises 32 task families covering record linkage, routine reconstruction, incident investigation and assessment of deceptive accounts. In an evaluation of sixteen language models, most could not perform records investigation and submitted identifications the records did not support. A small number of frontier models solved most of the tasks and abstained when evidence was insufficient. In some cases these models still fell for common deceptions and assumptions, and none replaced an investigator.
papers.summary: No existing benchmark can measure how accurately language models perform criminal-investigation and surveillance work, because real deployments lack ground truth. `Kierston` simulates about 125,000 residents of Allentown, Pennsylvania, and generates the telecom, financial, administrative, and license-plate records that would be held by separate providers. `KierstonBench` poses 32 task families, including record linkage, routine reconstruction, incident investigation, and detecting deceptive accounts, which models must solve through a restricted records interface. Among sixteen models evaluated, **most could not carry out records investigation and submitted identifications the records did not support**. A few frontier models solved most tasks and abstained when evidence was insufficient, but they still sometimes fell for deceptions and could not replace an investigator.

papers.title: ReSI-Math: Exploring Recoverable Capability Frontiers for Efficient Reasoning Improvement
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an effective approach for improving mathematical reasoning in large language models. However, a fundamental question remains: when a model fails to solve a problem, does it truly lack the underlying capability? In this work, we reveal that direct failure does not necessarily imply inability. Some reasoning failures can be recovered by exploring the model's own trajectories, exposing a recoverable capability frontier: a policy-dependent region where solutions are not reliably generated through direct decoding but can be elicited through trajectory-level search. Based on this observation, we introduce ReSI-Math, a framework that explores recoverable capability frontiers and converts recovered capabilities into data-efficient RLVR supervision. ReSI-Math uses Self-Judge-guided evolutionary search to identify recoverable failures under a fixed policy and adaptively selects frontier problems for sequential RLVR as the policy evolves. On Qwen3-VL-8B, correct-incorrect trajectory crossover produces 272 verifier-confirmed correct offspring from 621 attempts (43.8%). After three sequential one-shot RLVR stages, the MATH500 and WE-MATH average improves from 78.71 to 80.16. Under matched single-problem RLVR, random selection reaches only 53.31 versus 54.16 for frontier-guided Q1.
papers.summary: When a model fails a math problem under reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), the failure does not always mean it lacks the capability; some failures can be recovered by searching over the model's own reasoning trajectories. `ReSI-Math` uses evolutionary search guided by a self-judge, including crossover between correct and incorrect trajectories, to find these recoverable problems. It then selects such frontier problems as RLVR training data as the policy improves. On `Qwen3-VL-8B`, crossover produced 272 verified correct solutions from 621 attempts (43.8%), and three sequential one-shot RLVR stages raised the average score on `MATH500` and `WE-MATH` **from 78.71 to 80.16**.

papers.title: Density-Aware Reward Scaling: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Reward-Proportional Sampling
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning objectives that maximize expected return can concentrate probability mass on a small subset of high-reward outcomes, limiting diversity when multiple distinct solutions are desirable. We introduce Density-Aware Reward Scaling (DARS), a simple reward-processing mechanism that promotes reward-proportional sampling in continuous outcome spaces while retaining standard policy-gradient training. DARS estimates the local density of outcomes within each on-policy rollout group and inversely scales rewards by this density. The method requires no learned density model, auxiliary objective, critic, or modification to the underlying policy-gradient objective. In a controlled multimodal navigation task, DARS-GRPO avoids the single-mode collapse exhibited by GRPO and closely recovers the target mode allocation. Applied to text-to-image prompt adaptation, DARS-GRPO consistently improves image and prompt diversity across datasets, Policy LMs, and reward settings while maintaining good semantic alignment. These results show that density-aware reward scaling provides a lightweight way to improve coverage of diverse high-reward outcomes within existing reinforcement-learning pipelines.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning that maximizes expected return tends to concentrate probability on a few high-reward outcomes, which hurts diversity when many good solutions exist. `Density-Aware Reward Scaling` (`DARS`) estimates how densely outcomes are packed within each on-policy rollout group and divides rewards by that density, which pushes sampling toward being proportional to reward. It needs no learned density model, critic, or change to the policy-gradient objective. In a multimodal navigation task, `DARS-GRPO` **avoids the single-mode collapse seen with `GRPO`** and closely recovers the target allocation across modes. In text-to-image prompt adaptation it improves image and prompt diversity while keeping semantic alignment good.

papers.title: Accelerating Offloading-Based MoE Inference by Interleaving Concurrent Requests
papers.abstract: Expert offloading enables large mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models to run locally, but conventional batching stalls the GPU while missing experts are fetched. A popular remedy, known as prefetching, is to predict what experts will be needed soon and fetch them using idle link bandwidth. Imprecise prediction, however, wastes bandwidth and GPU memory on fetching unnecessary experts. Our key finding is that prefetching can be harmful when there is an expert cache in GPU memory. This is because as the cache includes more necessary experts, expert prediction becomes less precise. Our key insight is that proper request scheduling beats prefetching. Building on this insight, we present Bevy, an MoE inference system based on runahead inference for concurrent requests. A request whose experts are available can run ahead to later layers while other requests wait for fetches, revealing the experts it needs next. Bevy can then fetch the missing experts so identified while computing ready requests, overlapping computation and fetching without predicting expert selections. Running requests separately, however, repeats reads of shared weights in GPU memory and increases compute time. To limit this cost, Bevy's self-balancing scheduler batches ready requests at each layer and prioritizes lagging requests, adapting their grouping as expert availability changes. Across two local platforms, Bevy delivers up to 3.46$\times$ the decode throughput of llama.cpp and up to 1.55$\times$ that of the fastest prefetching baseline.
papers.summary: Running a large mixture-of-experts (MoE) model locally with expert offloading stalls the GPU while missing experts are fetched. The common fix of predicting and prefetching experts can actually hurt when an expert cache is present, because prediction gets less precise as the cache fills with the experts that are needed. `Bevy` instead uses runahead inference across concurrent requests: requests whose experts are already available proceed to later layers, revealing which experts they need next, while fetches for other requests overlap with computation. A self-balancing scheduler batches ready requests at each layer and prioritizes those that are lagging. On two local platforms, `Bevy` achieves **up to 3.46x the decode throughput of `llama.cpp`** and up to 1.55x that of the fastest prefetching baseline.

papers.title: Training Specialist LLMs on Your Phone: Forward-Only Optimization via Block-Spectral Coordinates
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) on personal devices keep user data local, but limited memory restricts their general capability. Since most user-specific tasks do not require the breadth of frontier models, a practical solution is to adapt a shared on-device model into lightweight specialists. However, backpropagation is prohibitive in memory, and users rarely provide labeled data. We present MobileSpec, a system that trains specialists with forward passes alone and learns from automatically checked task outcomes, as in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Because forward-only updates are built from random perturbations, training is efficient only when these perturbations resemble the weight changes of RLVR, which largely preserve the singular values of pretrained weights and rotate their singular vectors. The core algorithm of MobileSpec, FuRA-S, produces such perturbations while training only the block-spectral coordinates of pretrained weights, namely the singular values of their column blocks. As we show theoretically and empirically, rescaling these blocks independently shifts their relative contributions to each weight matrix and thereby rotates its singular vectors. Since this update can be rewritten as a transformation of the layer input, FuRA-S also adapts INT4 models without modifying their weights. With specialists of only 1-5 MB that update 0.015-0.05% of the parameters, MobileSpec raises the success rate of a phone-use agent from 6-23% up to 89-100% and trains a personalized 8B model on an iPhone 16 Pro overnight. On RLVR benchmarks, FuRA-S is competitive with full-parameter evolution strategies (ES) and outperforms ES over LoRA adapters and quantized ES on INT4 models.
papers.summary: `MobileSpec` adapts an on-device LLM into small task specialists using forward passes only, which avoids the memory cost of backpropagation. It learns from automatically checked task outcomes, in the style of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Its core algorithm, `FuRA-S`, trains only the singular values of column blocks of pretrained weights. This produces random perturbations that rotate singular vectors, mimicking how RLVR updates weights, and it can adapt `INT4` models without modifying their weights. With specialists of 1-5 MB that update 0.015-0.05% of parameters, `MobileSpec` **raises a phone-use agent's success rate from 6-23% to 89-100%** and trains a personalized 8B model on an iPhone 16 Pro overnight. On RLVR benchmarks it is competitive with full-parameter evolution strategies.

papers.title: Where Is the Truth When AI Agents Disagree? Dependence-Aware Belief Propagation for Unsupervised Truth Discovery (Extended Version)
papers.abstract: LLM agents often give conflicting answers to the same question, and many deployed agents are variants of one base model, so their errors are correlated. We study truth discovery among such agents: inferring the true answer and each agent's reliability without labels. Classical truth-discovery and crowdsourcing estimators reward an agreeing bloc and can fall below majority vote. We propose BP-TD, which adds per-agent decorrelation weights to mean-field variational inference on a one-coin Dawid-Skene model, so that agents sharing a base model count together as about one vote. Its first iteration is exactly a weighted vote; later iterations estimate agent reliability. With 13 local agents on MMLU, BP-TD beats majority vote without any labels (0.716 vs. 0.624 on 160 questions; 0.707 vs. 0.674 on 10,000) and ranks agents by their true accuracy, which classical estimators invert. The gain depends on the pool: over 2,852 sub-pools of four benchmarks, decorrelation helps when the largest correlated bloc is weaker than the other agents and hurts when it is the strongest, and we found no label-free statistic that tells the two cases apart. Labels change the picture quickly: with 20 labelled questions, selecting the single best agent is more accurate than every aggregator we tested on MMLU, ARC and TruthfulQA.
papers.summary: LLM agents often disagree, and agents built on the same base model make correlated errors. As a result, classical truth-discovery and crowdsourcing estimators reward agreeing blocs and can do worse than majority vote. `BP-TD` adds per-agent decorrelation weights to mean-field variational inference on a one-coin `Dawid-Skene` model, so that agents sharing a base model count together as roughly one vote. With 13 local agents on `MMLU`, it **beats majority vote without labels (0.716 vs. 0.624 on 160 questions)** and ranks agents in line with their true accuracy. Across 2,852 sub-pools, however, decorrelation helps only when the largest correlated bloc is weaker than the other agents, and with just 20 labeled questions, picking the single best agent beats every aggregator tested.

papers.title: On the Complexity of Finite-Sum Nonconvex-Strongly-Concave Minimax Optimization with Exact Proximal Oracles
papers.abstract: Finite-sum nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax problems arise in adversarial training and distributionally robust learning. Their known lower bounds cover only linear-span algorithms, zero-respecting algorithms, or a restricted proximal protocol. They leave open the power of exact component proximal steps, whose responses are global saddle points of regularized component problems and can expose directions that gradients do not reveal. We show that neither unrestricted adaptivity nor exact proximal access improves the polynomial complexity. We consider $n$ components with joint mean-squared smoothness $L$ and condition number $\kappa$, started from a point with primal gap at most $\Delta$ and joint gradient norm at most $\sqrt{2L\Delta}$. For $\varepsilon^2/(L\Delta)$ below a universal constant, every randomized adaptive algorithm with exact component values, gradients, and proximal responses needs $\Omega(n+\min\{\sqrt n\,\kappa,n^{3/4}\sqrt\kappa\}L\Delta/\varepsilon^2)$ component queries in the worst case to find an $\varepsilon$-stationary point of the value function. A method using only component gradients attains this rate up to a factor $\log^2(2+\kappa)$, including initialization. Zhou (arXiv:2610.04944) concurrently proves the same rate for zero-respecting first-order methods. In our hard instances, every component admits proximal steps with the same step sizes, and a response for a component reveals hidden directions only up to the first one assigned to another component.
papers.summary: Finite-sum nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax problems appear in adversarial training and distributionally robust learning. Existing lower bounds on their complexity cover only restricted classes of algorithms. The authors prove that even randomized adaptive algorithms with exact component proximal oracles need on the order of n + min(sqrt(n)·kappa, n^(3/4)·sqrt(kappa))·L·Delta/epsilon^2 component queries to find an epsilon-stationary point. They also show that **a gradient-only method matches this bound up to a log-squared factor**, so neither unrestricted adaptivity nor exact proximal access improves the polynomial rate.

papers.title: Asymptotic Optimality of $c\mu$-Rule for LLM Inference Scheduling under Memory Constraint
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference, the process by which a pre-trained model receives an input prompt and generates output tokens sequentially, has become increasingly important with the widespread deployment of LLM-based applications. As inference workloads continue to scale, GPU memory has emerged as a critical bottleneck: the long input prompts and generation sequences common in agentic and reasoning workloads lead to substantial key-value (KV) cache usage. In this paper, we study the resulting online scheduling problem from a queueing perspective. Requests arrive stochastically with heterogeneous prompt and output lengths, undergo prefill and autoregressive decode, and compete for a finite KV-cache capacity. Unlike classical queueing models, the duration of a processing step depends on both prefill computation and KV-cache I/O, so service capacity is jointly determined by computation, memory access, and memory occupancy. We develop a fluid model that reduces the system to a multiclass single-server queue with effective service rates capturing computation, memory access, and memory capacity. This fluid analysis yields a $c\mu$ priority rule, where the effective service rate $\mu$ is jointly determined by computational speed, memory bandwidth, and memory capacity. We prove that this rule minimizes cumulative holding cost in the fluid model and, for a finite workload, also minimizes completion time and maximizes full-run output-token throughput. We then construct a feasible scheduling policy for the original finite system and prove that its scaled dynamics converge to the optimal fluid policy. Finally, experiments on a real LLM serving engine using an NVIDIA H800 show that practical implementations of the proposed priority rule substantially reduce average latency while maintaining high throughput relative to existing scheduling policies.
papers.summary: LLM inference scheduling is limited by key-value (KV) cache memory, especially for the long prompts and outputs of agentic and reasoning workloads. The authors model the system as a queue in which step duration depends on prefill computation, KV-cache input/output, and memory occupancy. A fluid approximation reduces it to a multiclass single-server queue, which yields a c-mu priority rule whose effective service rate combines compute speed, memory bandwidth, and memory capacity. The rule is **proven to minimize cumulative holding cost in the fluid model**, and a feasible policy for the finite system is shown to converge to it. Experiments on a real serving engine on an `NVIDIA H800` show substantially lower average latency than existing schedulers while keeping throughput high.

papers.title: RAHC: Rule-Augmented Hyper-Relational Knowledge Graph Completion for Materials Synthesis
papers.abstract: Scientific discovery depends on reusing experimental knowledge, yet records scattered across papers and repositories are often incomplete. In materials synthesis, recovering missing conditions requires reasoning about the target material and the observed context of a specific experiment. Hyper-relational knowledge graphs (HKGs) represent this context through qualifiers, but existing completion methods leave domain knowledge and experimental regularities implicit. We propose RAHC, a rule-augmented HKG framework for single-slot and joint multi-slot synthesis-condition completion. RAHC builds a traceable rule catalog from training records and retrieved literature, retrieves rules for each query-candidate pair, and separately encodes graph structure and rule evidence. Hard rules constrain candidate validity, while soft rules guide ranking. RAHC-G aggregates rules using global reliability; RAHC-Q additionally learns query-specific relevance. Gated fusion combines structural and rule representations, while tuple-conclusion rules provide cross-condition evidence for joint completion. Experiments on five materials-synthesis datasets show improvements in single-slot and joint completion under Semi-inductive and Open-Answer Inductive settings, with Semi-inductive MRR gains of up to 15.6% over MAYPL. RAHC also improves performance on the entity-disjoint ILPC'22 Small benchmark, supporting transfer to fully inductive KG completion. These results support experimental condition selection, synthesis planning, and the reuse of scientific knowledge.
papers.summary: Records of materials-synthesis experiments are often incomplete, and recovering missing conditions requires reasoning about the target material and the context of each experiment. `RAHC` augments hyper-relational knowledge graph (HKG) completion with a traceable rule catalog mined from training records and retrieved literature. Hard rules constrain which candidates are valid, soft rules guide ranking, and gated fusion combines rule evidence with graph structure for single-slot and joint multi-slot completion. Across five materials-synthesis datasets it achieves **up to 15.6% mean reciprocal rank (MRR) gains over `MAYPL`** in the semi-inductive setting, and it also improves results on the `ILPC'22 Small` inductive benchmark.

papers.title: AgenticFinBench: Benchmarking Financial Agents on Diverse Tasks from Real-World Requests
papers.abstract: Financial agents are becoming an important class of real-world AI systems. Financial tasks vary widely in type and difficulty, and many are open-ended with no ground-truth answers. However, existing benchmarks neither capture this breadth and open-endedness nor separate grounding from correctness. To bridge this gap, we introduce $\textbf{AgenticFinBench}$, a benchmark of 230 real-world financial tasks spanning 8 categories, 2 languages, and 4 complexity levels. We also propose a reference-free evaluation framework that combines question-specific rubrics with a two-stage claim audit that detects hallucinations, defined as claims absent from the agent's trace and refuted by external evidence. This framework better matches how financial work is assessed in practice. Experiments across 18 agent configurations reveal three key findings: (1) Ignoring hallucinations can overstate agent performance: hallucination auditing lowers the baseline leader's score by 7.58 points and moves it to fourth place. (2) Harness differences explain more variation in evidence grounding than model differences (28.6% vs 8.8%). (3) Quality scores fall from 89.44 on direct retrieval to 79.18 on the most complex tasks. Case studies show that agents struggle to explain how events affect company profits or stock prices, compare financial data on a consistent basis, and justify their conclusions. By releasing AgenticFinBench, we aim to advance financial reasoning, factual verification, and agent design for more reliable responses to diverse real-world financial requests. Our project page is at $\textbf{https://nashnovaresearch.github.io/AgenticFinBench/}$.
papers.summary: `AgenticFinBench` contains 230 real-world financial requests spanning 8 categories, 2 languages, and 4 complexity levels. Many of the tasks are open-ended with no single correct answer. Evaluation is reference-free: question-specific rubrics are combined with a two-stage claim audit that flags hallucinations, defined as claims absent from the agent's trace and refuted by external evidence. Across 18 agent configurations, hallucination auditing drops the leading baseline by 7.58 points and to fourth place. **Differences in agent harness explain more of the variation in evidence grounding than differences in model (28.6% vs. 8.8%)**, and quality falls from 89.44 on direct retrieval to 79.18 on the most complex tasks.

papers.title: Think Less, Locally: Local Preference Learning for Reasoning Compression
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models achieve strong performance on challenging tasks, but their long chain-of-thought often incurs substantial inference costs by continuing to deliberate after sufficient information has been obtained. Existing reasoning compression methods primarily operate on reasoning trajectories, paying less attention to the local decision of whether further reasoning is necessary given the current state. We propose LoCo, a local preference learning method for reasoning compression. LoCo detects candidate overthinking states from the model's own traces, freezes the corresponding reasoning prefixes, regenerates shorter verified continuations from the same states, and trains on the resulting state-conditioned preference pairs with DPO. This formulation teaches the model when to continue reasoning and when to conclude, rather than simply encouraging shorter trajectories overall. We construct training data entirely from self-generated mathematical traces and evaluate LoCo on five mathematical and three code generation benchmarks. LoCo reduces completion length by 41.7\%--45.4\% on mathematics and 23.4\%--36.3\% on code, while maintaining or improving accuracy and achieving the best AUC across all code benchmarks. LoCo consistently improves the accuracy-efficiency trade-off on mathematics and transfers effectively to code generation despite math-only training, demonstrating the cross-domain generality of local preference learning for reasoning compression. The code and model will be publicly released at https://github.com/MuyaoYuan/LoCo.
papers.summary: Large reasoning models often keep deliberating after they already have enough information, which inflates inference cost. `LoCo` finds likely overthinking points in the model's own traces, freezes the reasoning prefix at each point, and regenerates shorter verified continuations from the same state. It then trains on these state-conditioned preference pairs with direct preference optimization (`DPO`), teaching the model when to stop rather than simply rewarding shorter outputs. Trained only on self-generated math traces, `LoCo` **cuts completion length by 41.7-45.4% on math and 23.4-36.3% on code** across eight benchmarks while maintaining or improving accuracy.

papers.title: The Pen is Mightier than the Pixel: Natural Textual Unlearnable Example for Large Vision Language Models
papers.abstract: The proliferation of Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs), trained on vast and often sensitive datasets, raised concerns regarding data privacy and unauthorized usage. Unlearnable Examples (UEs), which subtly perturb training data to mislead the models, have emerged as a promising defense method. This paper presents the first exploration of UEs specifically on LVLMs, which poses unique challenges due to their inherent multimodal nature. We propose a novel text-based perturbation method, Natural Textual Unlearnable Examples (NTUE), which can effectively mislead LVLMs by subtly manipulating the image label, establishing a shortcut between an identity of interest and a separate target, without introducing factual misinformation or affecting readability. Comprehensive experiments compared with traditional UE methods demonstrate the superior performance of NTUE. Our findings show that NTUE achieves a high success rate with a poison rate as low as 5%, underscoring its potential as a practical and robust solution for protecting multimodal data in the era of LVLMs.
papers.summary: Unlearnable examples perturb training data so that models trained on it learn little from it. The authors present what they describe as the first study of unlearnable examples for large vision language models (LVLMs), aimed at protecting sensitive data from unauthorized training. `Natural Textual Unlearnable Examples` (`NTUE`) perturbs the text label rather than the image, creating a shortcut between an identity of interest and a separate target without adding factual misinformation or hurting readability. Compared with traditional pixel-based methods, `NTUE` performs better and **achieves a high success rate with a poison rate as low as 5%**.

papers.title: Sleep-Disordered Breathing Detection with Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks
papers.abstract: This work investigates the application of Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks to the binary classification of sleep-disordered breathing events in time-series data, aiming to distinguish between apneic and normal breathing episodes. A variational classical--quantum architecture is proposed and evaluated against classical Recurrent Neural Network models. Experiments were conducted on multiple real-world datasets with varying levels of complexity to assess the strengths and limitations of the quantum approach. In the comparative analysis, both classical and quantum models showed comparable performance. The quantum model achieved superior performance on the smallest dataset, while yielding slightly weaker results in the most complex setting. However, the quantum approach exhibited notable strengths, such as competitive performance despite a drastically reduced parameter count and low-qubit regime, as well as good generalization capabilities. These results suggest that, despite current hardware and algorithmic limitations, variational quantum recurrent models represent a promising alternative for time-series classification as Quantum Computing technologies continue to mature.
papers.summary: The authors compare a hybrid classical-quantum variational recurrent neural network with classical recurrent networks for classifying apneic versus normal breathing in sleep time-series data. Across several real-world datasets of varying complexity, the two approaches performed comparably overall. The quantum model **did better on the smallest dataset and slightly worse on the most complex one**, while using far fewer parameters and few qubits.

papers.title: Reconstructing Fraudulent Strategies in Online Payments via Interpretable Inverse Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Payment fraud causes financial losses and undermines users' trust in web payment services. Although fraud detection is a critical defense for payment security, complex and diverse fraudulent behaviors can still evade detection. Generating fraud samples for data augmentation can broaden detectors' coverage of different fraud patterns. However, existing methods matching the distribution of transaction attributes alone do not ensure that generated sequences preserve the sequential relationships among transaction choices, payment feedback, and subsequent behavioral adjustments. To this end, we propose PaySeqGen, an interpretable inverse reinforcement learning framework that reconstructs fraud behavior policies from fraudsters' observed payment trajectories. We design a mechanism for constructing candidate actions to support plausible payment sequence generation while enabling exploration. The framework also learns interpretable behavioral rewards that capture fraudsters' preferences across different transaction contexts. By alternating between reward learning and policy optimization, the framework reconstructs policies that generate new fraud sequences for detector augmentation and learns interpretable rewards supporting sequential fraud-pattern analysis in real trajectories. Experiments in real-world payment scenarios at Ant International, a leading global digital payment provider, show that PaySeqGen outperforms state-of-the-art generative augmentation methods. Reward-based trajectory analysis also identifies fraud patterns of practical value, helping analyst locating suspicious segments and examine multistep fraud tactics. Evaluation in the deployed system of online payment further confirms its effectiveness.
papers.summary: Generating synthetic fraud samples can widen a fraud detector's coverage, but methods that only match the distribution of transaction attributes lose the sequential link between a fraudster's choices, payment feedback, and later adjustments. `PaySeqGen` uses interpretable inverse reinforcement learning to reconstruct fraudsters' behavior policies from observed payment trajectories, alternating between learning rewards and optimizing policies. A candidate-action mechanism keeps generated sequences plausible while still allowing exploration. In real payment scenarios at Ant International, it **outperforms state-of-the-art generative augmentation methods**. Its learned rewards help analysts locate suspicious segments and examine multi-step fraud tactics, and evaluation in the deployed online payment system confirms its effectiveness.

papers.title: UniFlow: Unified Multi-Scale Flow Matching for Time Series Generation
papers.abstract: Real-world time series exhibit complex dynamics across multiple temporal resolutions, yet effectively incorporating multi-scale information into generative modeling remains challenging without increasing generative complexity. We propose UniFlow, a unified framework that integrates multi-scale representation learning with efficient non-autoregressive generation through a shared-semantic discrete interface. Specifically, a multi-scale tokenizer employs shared-index voting to consolidate complementary temporal information into a single public-ID sequence, while scale-specific codebooks preserve the information required for reconstruction. Building on this unified representation, we develop geometry-aware categorical flow matching, which initializes transport from learned low-rank anchors and generates public identities non-autoregressively. This design captures multi-scale temporal structure without requiring multiple generative token streams or sequential token decoding. Experiments across four benchmarks and both short- and long-term settings demonstrate improved generative fidelity, strong cross-scale consistency, and substantial inference speedups over representative autoregressive and diffusion-based baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/William-Liwei/uniflow
papers.summary: Real-world time series carry structure at several temporal resolutions, but adding multi-scale information to generative models usually means more token streams or slower sequential decoding. `UniFlow` uses a multi-scale tokenizer that merges information from all scales into a single sequence of shared IDs through voting, while scale-specific codebooks keep what is needed for reconstruction. A geometry-aware categorical flow-matching model then generates these IDs non-autoregressively, starting from learned low-rank anchors. Across four benchmarks in short- and long-term settings, the method reports better generation fidelity, strong cross-scale consistency, and **substantial inference speedups over autoregressive and diffusion baselines**.

papers.title: Feeling of Knowing in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Post-training updates change what large language models (LLMs) can answer, but may leave their answerability judgments misaligned.
