papers.summary: Saliency maps are often offered as a way to catch mistakes by medical image classifiers, but they are rarely tested on data from other hospitals. The authors trained a convolutional network and a vision transformer on `NIH ChestX-ray14` and evaluated 303,768 decisions per model at the training hospital and two external sites in the USA and Vietnam, scoring how strongly each explanation concentrated on the relevant anatomy. `Grad-CAM` localized findings less often than radiologists (hit rate at most 0.575 versus 0.888), and **adding saliency to a confidence-based error detector raised its AUC by no more than 0.011**. For the convolutional network, the relationship between saliency and correctness even reversed at new hospitals, so the authors recommend monitoring with model confidence rather than saliency.

papers.title: Rethinking GA2Ms: performance and out-of-distribution generalisation
papers.abstract: Generalised Additive Models (GAMs) are a cornerstone of interpretable machine learning, offering transparent predictions through structured additive decompositions. Despite advances from classical GAMs to modern neural and spline-based variants, two notable gaps remain. First, comprehensive benchmarking of spline-based GAMs on large-scale tabular learning tasks, the dominant modality in applied settings, is lacking. Second, their robustness under distribution shift, a setting where structured inductive biases should confer advantages, remains unexplored. We propose a multi-resolution, higher-order Composite Generalised Additive Model (CoGA2M) and evaluate it on the TALENT benchmark suite. CoGA2M ranks in the top third across all baselines (29 for regression, 32 for classification), establishing competitive performance with state-of-the-art tabular methods. We further extend TALENT with out-of-distribution (OOD) splits exhibiting train-test distributional shift and benchmark CoGA2M against LightGBM, a consistently top-performing model on TALENT. Under distribution shift, CoGA2M outperforms LightGBM, demonstrating a clear structural advantage. Our results position spline-based GAMs as strong contenders for tabular prediction and reveal a previously unrecognised benefit of additive structure in the OOD regime.
papers.summary: Generalised Additive Models (GAMs) give interpretable predictions, but spline-based GAMs have not been benchmarked thoroughly on large tabular datasets or under distribution shift. The authors propose `CoGA2M`, a multi-resolution, higher-order composite GAM, and evaluate it on the `TALENT` tabular benchmark, where it ranks in the top third against 29 regression and 32 classification baselines. On new out-of-distribution splits added to `TALENT`, **`CoGA2M` outperforms `LightGBM`**, suggesting that additive structure gives an advantage under distribution shift.

papers.title: Finite Spectral Depth Controls Gaussian Entrance Rank and Avoidance of the First Gradient-Flow Saddle
papers.abstract: Matrix factorization provides a simple model for studying the training dynamics of neural networks. Recent studies of gradient flow under small initialization have analyzed how trajectories escape from a neighborhood of the origin and approach their first nonzero stationary point. In this paper, we study continuous-time dynamics that applies a finite number of Newton-Schulz iterations to the normalized matrix gradient (Muon). We show that the number of Newton-Schulz steps can change the rank selected during the early stages of training and allow the resulting trajectory to bypass the first nonzero stationary point approached by gradient flow. Under an additional residual-inertia condition, we prove that bypass occurs for all sufficiently large finite Newton-Schulz depths and provide an explicit sufficient threshold. We also construct an example in which the bypass threshold is four.
papers.summary: Using matrix factorization as a simple model of neural network training, the authors study a continuous-time version of the `Muon` optimizer, which applies a finite number of Newton-Schulz iterations to the normalized gradient. They show that the number of Newton-Schulz steps can change which rank is selected early in training and can let the trajectory skip the first saddle point that ordinary gradient flow reaches from small initialization. Under an extra residual-inertia condition, they prove that **this bypass happens for all sufficiently large finite depths, with an explicit sufficient threshold**, and give an example where the threshold is four.

papers.title: RGB Photo Enhancement with Deep Learning on Smartphone GPUs: Mobile AI 2026 Challenge Report
papers.abstract: On-device RGB photo enhancement is a popular task that is needed for quality improvement of photos captured with mobile devices as well as for retouching of images acquired through other sources. This creates a need for efficient deep learning models for this problem that are not only performant but can also be deployed on constrained mobile hardware. In this Mobile AI challenge, we address this problem and propose participants to design fast solutions that can perform comprehensive enhancement of RGB photos while running on popular smartphone GPUs from Qualcomm and Arm. For this, the participants were provided with a large-scale DPED dataset consisting of RGB image pairs captured with an old iPhone 3GS smartphone and a professional Canon 70D DSLR camera. The runtime of all models was evaluated on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and Dimensity 9500 chipsets with the Adreno and Mali GPUs, respectively. Top solutions proposed in this challenge are able to enhance Full HD resolution RGB images on both platforms under 300 milliseconds. A comprehensive description of the models developed in the challenge is provided in this paper.
papers.summary: This report covers a Mobile AI 2026 challenge on deep learning models that fully enhance RGB photos while running on smartphone GPUs. Participants trained on the `DPED` dataset, which pairs photos from an iPhone 3GS with photos from a Canon 70D DSLR. Runtime was measured on Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 (Adreno) and Dimensity 9500 (Mali) chipsets. **Top solutions enhance Full HD images in under 300 milliseconds on both platforms**, and the report describes the submitted models.

papers.title: DRAP: Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity for Continual Learning in Physical AI
papers.abstract: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. Each deviation may move the agent outside the training distribution, increase subsequent prediction errors, and ultimately cause closed-loop task failure. This work introduces Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP), a replay-free method that estimates the historical importance of adaptable model tensors from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk. A ridge-regularized local linear model is fitted to expert state-action transitions, and the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix provides a policy-independent, Lyapunov-inspired estimate of one-step perturbation amplification. After each task, risk-weighted squared gradients are accumulated in a tensor-level importance memory. During subsequent tasks, DRAP uses normalized cumulative importance to scale the effective AdamW learning rate of each tensor, immediately reducing the plasticity of components that supported previous behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory points. We instantiate DRAP on a fixed KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA and evaluate replay-free sequential adaptation across the LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites. Compared with standard AdamW fine-tuning and EWC, the results show substantially improved retention of previously learned behaviors while preserving strong new-suite acquisition.
papers.summary: In robot control, small per-step policy errors compound over a trajectory, so forgetting during continual learning is especially damaging. `DRAP` (Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity) fits a local linear model to expert transitions and uses its largest singular value to estimate how much a one-step error will grow. It then weights each sample's action gradients by that risk and accumulates per-tensor importance across tasks. On later tasks, this importance scales down the `AdamW` learning rate of tensors that mattered for earlier behavior, without replaying old data. Applied to a subnetwork of `OpenVLA` across the `LIBERO` Spatial, Object, and Goal suites, **`DRAP` retains previously learned behaviors substantially better than standard fine-tuning and `EWC`** while still learning new tasks well.

papers.title: Comparing model representations and fitting methods for port-Hamiltonian system identification
papers.abstract: Port-Hamiltonian models describe physical systems by separating stored energy, dissipation and external inputs. Learning such models from data requires a choice of representation and fitting method. We compare using neural networks, analytic expressions and combinations of the two for representing the different components of the port-Hamiltonian system, and compare fitting the models with gradient-based optimisation or sparse regression. Testing on simulations of mechanical and electrical systems, with and without added noise, we present prediction accuracy and computational cost of the different approaches.
papers.summary: Port-Hamiltonian models describe physical systems by separating stored energy, dissipation, and external inputs, and learning them from data requires choosing both a model representation and a fitting method. The study compares neural networks, analytic expressions, and hybrids of the two for each model component, fitted with either gradient-based optimization or sparse regression. Tested on simulated mechanical and electrical systems with and without noise, **the comparison reports the prediction accuracy and computational cost of each combination**.

papers.title: Whose Effect Is It? How Objectives Inflate Learned Subspace Interventions
papers.abstract: Interpretability often locates concepts by copying part of a language model's state from one input into another (activation patching). A larger output change counts as stronger evidence that this part carries the concept. Methods that learn which part to copy often change the output more than the whole state does. By that reading, learned parts isolate the concept more cleanly. Yet the whole contains the part. So whose effect is this excess, the network's or the method's? Copying the whole state learns nothing, so it shows what the network produces. We prove that, to first order, the effects of orthogonal parts add up to that of the whole. A part therefore exceeds the whole exactly when the rest moves the output back, which does not require isolating the concept more cleanly. Objectives that reward a larger effect select such parts. Distributed alignment search with cross-entropy, for example, exceeds the whole-state copy just before the output on almost all tasks, and inside the network at most sites. In both, changing only its objective to target what the network produces removes most of the excess. It therefore comes largely from the objective, so a larger learned effect alone is not stronger evidence.
papers.summary: Interpretability researchers often locate concepts in a language model by copying part of its internal state from one input into another (`activation patching`). When the copied part was learned, it frequently changes the output more than copying the whole state does, and that larger effect is usually read as stronger evidence that the part isolates the concept. The authors prove that, to first order, the effects of orthogonal parts add up to the effect of the whole state, so a part can exceed the whole only when the rest of the state pushes the output back. They show that `distributed alignment search` trained with cross-entropy exceeds the whole-state copy on almost all tasks, and that **retargeting the objective to what the network itself produces removes most of the excess**. They conclude that the excess comes largely from the training objective, so a larger learned effect is not by itself stronger evidence.

papers.title: Federated Transfer Learning for Medical Image Classification under Mixed Skew
papers.abstract: Deep learning in medical imaging is constrained by data scarcity and by privacy regulations that make centralizing patient data across institutions impractical. Federated Learning (FL) addresses these constraints by keeping data local, but its distributed nature exposes training to strong statistical heterogeneity. Multicentric medical data is particularly affected, exhibiting a mixed skew that combines feature, label, concept, and quantity shifts across centers. Personalized FL mitigates heterogeneity by tailoring a model to each client, yet most methods assume training from scratch, which is unrealistic given the high dimensionality of medical features relative to the limited data available. We propose the Personalized Aligner Federated Pretrained (PAFP) framework, a personalized FL approach built on a pre-trained backbone. PAFP inserts client-specific Feature Alignment modules before the fine-tuned blocks to realign hidden feature distributions toward a server-aggregated target. On the FedISIC benchmark, PAFP attains the highest unweighted balanced accuracy while reducing inter-client performance variance roughly six-fold relative to the strongest baseline, yielding accuracy and cross-client equity jointly. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Alexandre-Leclercq/PAFP.
papers.summary: Federated Learning (FL) lets hospitals train shared medical imaging models without centralizing patient data. Data across centers is heterogeneous in several ways at once (feature, label, concept and quantity shifts), and most personalized FL methods assume training from scratch. The proposed `PAFP` (Personalized Aligner Federated Pretrained) framework starts from a pre-trained backbone and inserts client-specific Feature Alignment modules that pull each client's hidden feature distributions toward a target aggregated on the server. On the `FedISIC` benchmark it reaches the highest unweighted balanced accuracy while **cutting the variance in performance between clients roughly six-fold** compared with the strongest baseline.

papers.title: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.abstract: Large language models are deployed as long-horizon agents that compose diverse tools across MCP services into executable workflows. Existing MCP environment-scaling methods are data-centric: they first synthesize a database and scenario, then derive tools and tasks from them. As a result, tool interfaces may not match real ones, tool compositions are not grounded in execution, and tasks rarely span more than one environment. We propose ToolSpace, a tool-centric framework that reverses this order. ToolSpace mines data, state, and retry dependencies from adjacent calls in execution traces of real MCP services and open agent corpora, using deterministic rules rather than LLM judgment, and clusters the resulting weighted tool-composition graph into environments. Databases are synthesized only for state-mutating environments, while query and stateless tools replay recorded returns. ToolSpace then performs state-aware random walks with rollback and decompiles each chain into a natural-language task with assertion-based checks, keeping only samples that replay successfully from the initial state. Applied to AutomationBench and tau3-Bench Banking, the pipeline produces harder Pro versions on which 7 frontier models drop by up to 38.2 points. Across seven long-horizon tool-use benchmarks, ToolSpace raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 23.0 to 41.0 average score (43.2 with RL) and GLM-5.2 from 44.6 to 56.6, on par with Claude Opus 5. Ablations show that execution-witnessed edges clearly outperform LLM-judged ones, and performance keeps improving with data and environment scale.
papers.summary: Training LLM agents to chain tools across MCP (Model Context Protocol) services needs realistic environments, but existing synthesis pipelines generate a database first and derive tools and tasks from it, so the results drift from real interfaces. `ToolSpace` works in the other direction: it mines data, state and retry dependencies from execution traces of real MCP services using deterministic rules, clusters the resulting tool-composition graph into environments, and generates tasks through state-aware random walks that are checked by replaying them from the initial state. Harder versions of `AutomationBench` and `tau3-Bench Banking` built this way drop the scores of seven frontier models by up to 38.2 points. Training on the synthesized data **raises `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` from 23.0 to 41.0 average score across seven long-horizon tool-use benchmarks** and lifts `GLM-5.2` to a level on par with `Claude Opus 5`. Ablations show that dependency edges observed in real executions clearly beat edges judged by an LLM.
papers.highlight_summary:
Existing environment-scaling methods for MCP tool-use agents synthesize a database first and then derive tools and tasks from it, so tool interfaces drift from real ones and tasks rarely cross environments. `ToolSpace` reverses that order: it builds the tool-composition graph from real execution traces, then synthesizes environments and verifiable long-horizon tasks on top of that graph.

- Deterministic rules turn adjacent calls in real MCP and open agent traces into data, state, and retry edges, with no LLM judgment involved; the resulting graph has 77,760 nodes from 2,042 tools and is clustered into **804 environments**, and databases are synthesized only for the 22.5% that mutate state, while stateless tools replay cached returns.
- State-aware random walks with rollback sample successors by edge weight and execute each step, then each chain is decompiled into a natural-language task with state, trace, and output assertions, and kept only if it replays from the initial state; the result is **34,376 trajectories** averaging 18.86 tool calls and 2.29 environments each.
- Fine-tuning lifts `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` from **23.0 to 41.0** average across seven long-horizon benchmarks (**43.2** with GRPO RL), and `GLM-5.2` goes from 44.6 to **56.6**, matching `Claude Opus 5` and beating both `GPT 5.6 Sol` (48.9) and the `Kimi K3` teacher.
- Applied to `AutomationBench` and `τ³-Bench Banking`, the pipeline produces Pro splits on which seven frontier models drop by up to **38.2 points**, and ablations show that LLM-judged edges perform almost as badly as removing state edges entirely.
- Gains are uneven: the 8B model still scores 0.0 on `Harvey LAB` and under 4.1 on `SkillsBench`, the claimed **55.3%** synthesis-cost saving is measured only as a count of generated files rather than tokens or compute, and the Pro benchmarks come from the same pipeline that produces the training data.

papers.title: ALBI: LLM-Guided Inductive Logic Programming via Iterative Generate-Test-Constrain Refineme
papers.abstract: We introduce ALBI (Agent for Learning By Induction), a neuro-symbolic ILP framework that replaces the ASP-based hypothesis generator in the Learning from Failures (LFF) paradigm with a Large Language Model (LLM), while retaining SWI-Prolog as a formal verifier. ALBI implements an iterative generate-test-constrain loop: the LLM proposes candidate hypotheses from structured prompts; Prolog tests each candidate; and diagnostic feedback drives refinement. We further introduce semantic anonymization, a metamorphic testing methodology, to distinguish structural symbolic induction from surface-level pattern matching on predicate names. Experiments on 30 standard ILP benchmarks show that ALBI achieves 100% success across three frontier LLMs (Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT 5.4 Pro, Claude Opus 4.6), matching Popper while requiring only 1.4-1.7 iterations on average. Under anonymization, all models maintain 100% success with a moderate iteration increase (1.36-1.67 times), providing evidence of robust symbolic reasoning.
papers.summary: `ALBI` (Agent for Learning By Induction) is a neuro-symbolic Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) system. It keeps the Learning from Failures loop but replaces the Answer Set Programming hypothesis generator with an LLM, and uses `SWI-Prolog` to verify candidates and return diagnostic feedback. To check that the models perform symbolic induction rather than guessing from predicate names, the authors introduce semantic anonymization, a metamorphic test that renames predicates. On 30 standard ILP benchmarks, ALBI reaches **100% success with `Gemini 3.1 Pro`, `GPT 5.4 Pro` and `Claude Opus 4.6`**, matching `Popper` in only 1.4 to 1.7 iterations on average. Success stays at 100% under anonymization, with only a moderate rise in iterations.

papers.title: Positional Encoding is All You Need for Scalable Equivariance Constraint Relaxation
papers.abstract: Equivariant neural networks incorporate known symmetries of the data, such as permutations, rotations, or translations, directly into their architecture, often improving sample efficiency and generalization. However, strict equivariance can make optimization difficult, for example, when the data only approximately satisfy the assumed symmetry, or when the equivariance constraints induce a challenging loss landscape. Recent studies have shown that relaxing equivariance during training by introducing non-equivariant dense linear layers can ease optimization in such cases and improve the performance of the resulting strictly equivariant model, after removing the relaxation layers at test time. While effective, this approach incurs a significant computational overhead, limiting its applicability in scalable architectures. In this work, we propose a more efficient constraint-relaxation method based on positional encoding (PE). Our framework injects a positional encoding with learnable scale that breaks the model's original symmetry. This positional signal is gradually annealed to zero, recovering the original equivariant model by the end of training. Empirically, we demonstrate significant improvements for translational and rotational equivariant models with only marginal compute and memory overhead.
papers.summary: Equivariant networks build data symmetries into their architecture, but strict equivariance can make optimization harder. Earlier fixes relax the constraint during training with extra dense non-equivariant layers, which is computationally expensive. This work instead breaks the symmetry by injecting a positional encoding with a learnable scale and annealing it to zero during training, so the final model is strictly equivariant. The authors report **significant gains for translation- and rotation-equivariant models with only marginal compute and memory overhead**.

papers.title: Effects of Parton Pair Correlations on Direct-Photon Yields and Elliptic Flow in Heavy-Ion Collisions
papers.abstract: Direct photons escape heavy-ion collisions with little rescattering, carrying information from the full emission history. Yet describing the measured direct-photon yield and the sizable elliptic flow $v_2$ together remains a long-standing challenge. Here we explore how correlations between emitting partons may affect both observables. The local $2\to2$ photon rate depends on the joint distribution of incoming partons, so a connected correlation between them can change photon emission without changing the one-particle distribution of medium particles. Once folded over the evolving medium in Au+Au and Pb+Pb collisions, the correlation raises the photon yield toward the fitted PHENIX and ALICE data and increases $v_2$ mainly at intermediate $p_T$. The fitted temperature dependence accounts for most of the net flow increase in this region, suggesting that the correlation changes the relative contributions between hotter and cooler regions.
papers.summary: In heavy-ion collisions, models struggle to reproduce both the measured yield of direct photons and their sizable elliptic flow (`v_2`). The authors note that the local 2-to-2 photon emission rate depends on the joint distribution of the incoming partons, so correlations between parton pairs can change photon emission without changing single-particle distributions. Folding such a correlation over the evolving medium in Au+Au and Pb+Pb collisions **raises the photon yield toward the fitted `PHENIX` and `ALICE` data and increases `v_2` mainly at intermediate transverse momentum**. The fitted temperature dependence of the correlation accounts for most of this flow increase.

papers.title: Ablating Design Choices for Protein Ensemble Generators Across Structural Regimes
papers.abstract: Generative models of protein conformational ensembles inherit much of their design from structure prediction for folded proteins. Ordered and disordered proteins, however, occupy distinct structural regimes, and we investigate how design choices hold up across them. Using a minimal C$\alpha$ flow-matching model, we ablate choices of architecture, sequence conditioning, rigid-body alignment and training source, and evaluate each variant against experimental SAXS and NMR chemical-shift data partitioned into ordered, disordered, multi-domain and transitional proteins. Mixture-of-experts routing, a static pair representation and a disorder probe have no detectable effect, a smaller protein language model performs worse on ordered proteins but not on disordered ones, and alignment in the loss degrades agreement with SAXS. Replacing coarse-grained simulations of disordered proteins with fragment-assembled ensembles improves agreement with chemical shifts at a cost to SAXS, while an equal mixture of the two keeps most of the gain at a smaller cost. This points to the training data, rather than the architecture, as the main constraint.
papers.summary: Generative models of protein conformational ensembles borrow most of their design from structure prediction for folded proteins, even though ordered and disordered proteins behave very differently. Using a minimal C-alpha flow-matching model, the authors ablate architecture, sequence conditioning, rigid-body alignment and training data, scoring each variant against experimental SAXS and NMR chemical-shift data split by structural regime. Mixture-of-experts routing, a static pair representation and a disorder probe have no detectable effect, while alignment in the loss hurts agreement with SAXS. Changing the training ensembles for disordered proteins has the largest effects, which leads the authors to conclude that **training data, not architecture, is the main constraint**.

papers.title: Do Agentic Policies Need to Look at Every Step? Geometric Abstraction for Reasoning and Action
papers.abstract: Recent multimodal language models can reason directly about robot scenes, but it is unclear whether they need to repeatedly reinterpret raw visual observations at every step of an interaction. We propose shifting routine spatial reasoning from images to text and symbols through a 3D geometric abstraction that is refreshed locally from observations and read directly by the language models. Specifically, our interface represents scene geometry via typed, evidence-aware symbolic references to object parts, grounds them from calibrated RGB-D, and returns compact textual checkpoints with metric residuals after each action. Symbolic task structure can thus be reused across decisions while metric values are rebound to the current scene, with direct visual reasoning invoked only on demand. Across offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution, reasoning over grounded text and symbols improves multi-step manipulation completion while substantially reducing repeated multimodal queries, positioning explicit geometric state as an effective substrate for agentic robot policies.
papers.summary: Multimodal language models can control robots, but they typically re-read raw images at every step of a task. The authors move routine spatial reasoning into text through a 3D geometric abstraction: typed symbolic references to object parts, grounded from calibrated RGB-D data, with compact textual checkpoints and metric residuals returned after each action. The symbolic task structure can then be reused across decisions, and direct visual reasoning is invoked only on demand. In both offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution, this approach **improves completion of multi-step manipulation tasks while substantially reducing repeated multimodal queries**.

papers.title: FloMo: 3D Scene Flow as a World Action Model Intermediate for Learning from Human Video
papers.abstract: Pretrained video generation models distill internet-scale motion priors into robot policies, but full video is a redundant signal for action prediction. We argue that dense 3D motion is the medium through which video pretraining best transfers to robot actions, and that predicting motion rather than video affords better sample-efficiency for action prediction. FloMo is a 5B video-generation model fine-tuned to predict 3D scene-flow and action tokens. Rendering scene flow as RGB and encoding it into the same latent space as video enables a pretrained video generation backbone to efficiently adapt to predict 3D scene flow. Co-trained on action-free human video and action-labeled robot teleoperation data, our model benefits from human-video pretraining and generalizes to unseen objects, motion primitives, and tasks. Replacing motion prediction with a video prediction objective degrades out-of-distribution generalization, while adding a video prediction target alongside motion lowers policy success rather than improving it. When motion, video, and action are predicted jointly, action tokens attend far more to motion than to video, suggesting that predicting video wastes model capacity. Together, these results indicate that motion effectively mediates the transfer from video pretraining to action. More information can be found at flomo-wam.github.io.
papers.summary: Pretrained video generation models carry useful motion priors for robot policies, but full video is a redundant signal for predicting actions. `FloMo` fine-tunes a 5B-parameter video generation model to predict 3D scene flow, rendered as RGB into the same latent space as video, together with action tokens. It is co-trained on action-free human video and action-labeled robot teleoperation data, and it generalizes to unseen objects, motion primitives and tasks. Swapping motion prediction for video prediction hurts out-of-distribution generalization, and **adding a video target alongside motion lowers policy success**, with action tokens attending far more to motion than to video.

papers.title: VIGOR: Visual Gain Ordering for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Discrete Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate responses through iterative mask prediction and offer a promising alternative to autoregressive large vision-language models. However, they still suffer from hallucination, producing outputs that are plausible under language priors but insufficiently grounded in the image. We argue that hallucination in multimodal dLLMs is not only a token prediction problem, but also a premature commitment problem: during iterative denoising, some masked positions are unmasked too early because their confidence is driven more by language priors than by visual evidence, and these early commitments can bias later generation. To address this issue, we propose Visual Gain Ordering (VIGOR), a training-free and plug-and-play inference strategy that reorders masked positions according to counterfactual visual evidence. At each denoising step, VIGOR compares the confidence of each candidate token under the original image-conditioned pass and an additional visual-ablation pass, and prioritizes positions whose predictions are more strongly supported by the image. Experiments on LLaDA-V and Lumina-DiMOO show that VIGOR consistently reduces hallucination and improves multimodal reasoning performance across benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/THU-BPM/Vigor.
papers.summary: Multimodal discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate text by iteratively unmasking tokens, and they still hallucinate content not supported by the image. The authors argue that part of the cause is premature commitment: some positions are unmasked early because language priors make them look confident, and these early choices bias the rest of the output. `VIGOR` (Visual Gain Ordering) is a training-free inference strategy that compares each candidate token's confidence with and without the image, and unmasks first the positions most supported by visual evidence. On `LLaDA-V` and `Lumina-DiMOO` it **consistently reduces hallucination** and improves multimodal reasoning across benchmarks.

papers.title: Trajectory Evaluation via Rollout-Free World Model for End-to-end Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Although existing candidate trajectory evaluators have substantially improved end-to-end planning accuracy, their underlying mechanism remains suboptimal. Model-based evaluators typically make scoring future-aware by explicitly predicting candidate-conditioned future states over the planning horizon, which we term rollout. However, rollout incurs high inference cost and accumulates prediction errors. We argue that planning does not require reconstructing a full future scene for each candidate, but only future-relevant information for reliable comparison. We therefore propose RFWorld, a Rollout-Free World model for end-to-end trajectory evaluation. RFWorld constructs a shared scene memory and shapes it into a future-readable representation via lightweight training-time temporal readout with semantic supervision, keeping training overhead low. At inference time, candidate trajectories directly query the shared memory via sparse spatial readout for scoring, reducing computation by roughly the planning horizon times the number of candidate trajectories, while avoiding recursive rollout errors. Experiments on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive show that RFWorld learns a more planning-aligned world representation and achieves state-of-the-art performance.
papers.summary: End-to-end driving planners often score candidate trajectories by explicitly predicting the future scene that each candidate would produce. This rollout step is expensive and accumulates errors. `RFWorld` (Rollout-Free World model) builds one shared scene memory, trained with a lightweight temporal readout and semantic supervision so that future-relevant information can be read from it. Each candidate trajectory then queries the memory through a sparse spatial readout. This **cuts computation by roughly the planning horizon times the number of candidates**, and the method reports state-of-the-art results on `NAVSIM` and `Bench2Drive`.

papers.title: Data informed Ansatz Selection for Variational Quantum Circuits
papers.abstract: Choosing a variational quantum circuit (VQC) usually means searching over ansatze and depths, and training each candidate. We give three rules that fix these choices from the data and the gate set alone, before any training. First, a circuit without entangling gates has a rank-one Fourier coefficient tensor on every subset of qubits. A singular value decomposition of a dataset's Fourier coefficients therefore indicates whether entanglement is needed, which qubits it connects, and a lower bound on the error of omitting it. Second, the rank of the quantum Fisher information matrix grows by $p_0$ per layer, after a first-layer deficit $d_0$, until it reaches a ceiling set by the dynamical Lie algebra. This law fixes the depth. Third, reading out all $2^N - 1$ Pauli-Z products from one batch of shots resolves half of the state's directions, the most any single-basis readout can. A single-qubit readout resolves an exponentially small fraction. For the Madelon dataset, the rules prescribe 7 blocks of 3 qubits at depth 3: a 239-parameter classifier with 78.5% test accuracy, found without a grid search. Ablations confirm three predicted effects: shallower circuits, smaller blocks and dropping reuploading all lower accuracy.
papers.summary: Choosing a variational quantum circuit (VQC) usually means searching over circuit templates (ansätze) and depths and training every candidate. The authors give three rules that fix these choices from the data and gate set before any training. A singular value decomposition of the dataset's Fourier coefficients shows whether entanglement is needed and between which qubits. The growth of the quantum Fisher information rank per layer fixes the depth, and reading out all Pauli-Z products resolves the most state directions any single-basis readout can. On the `Madelon` dataset the rules prescribe **a 239-parameter classifier reaching 78.5% test accuracy without a grid search**, and ablations confirm the predicted effects.

papers.title: CRONOS: Benchmarking Non-Episodic Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for adapting robot policies to unstructured real-world environments. However, standard RL pipelines rely on episodic training with frequent scene resets, which is impractical for real-world deployment due to the need for substantial human intervention. While prior work has studied non-episodic RL in relatively small policies trained from scratch, its behavior when fine-tuning modern large-scale pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) models remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce CRONOS, a simulation benchmark for RL fine-tuning of VLAs under non-episodic scene resets. CRONOS leverages high-fidelity physics simulators and adopts shared-scene multi-task settings. Using CRONOS, we show that naively fine-tuning pre-trained policies fails in non-episodic settings due to shifts in object configurations and end-effector poses; however, these challenges can be mitigated through targeted reset allocation and by addressing biases in pre-trained models. Moreover, we find that non-episodic training enhances long-horizon manipulation and improves generalization to previously unseen object configurations and task sequences. Project page: https://embodiedai-ntu.github.io/cronos/
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning of robot policies usually assumes episodic training with frequent scene resets, which is impractical in the real world because it needs a lot of human intervention. `CRONOS` is a simulation benchmark for RL fine-tuning of pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) models without such resets, using shared-scene multi-task settings in high-fidelity physics simulators. Naive fine-tuning fails as object configurations and end-effector poses drift, but targeted reset allocation and correcting biases in the pre-trained models mitigate the problem. The authors also find that **non-episodic training improves long-horizon manipulation and generalization to unseen object configurations and task sequences**.

papers.title: LatentTriad: Pre-Action Risk Representations for Malicious Agent Skill Detection
papers.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly extended with reusable skills, but untrusted skill content can induce operations outside the user's task. Detecting this contextual risk requires more than suspicious-pattern matching, while dynamic analysis incurs the cost of skill execution. We find that hidden states formed during prefill contain readable information about task-operation consistency, including across held-out expression forms in controlled evaluations. Matched Operation-state interventions also affect later Boundary states and shift fixed risk readouts toward the donor label. Based on these findings, we introduce LatentTriad, which combines contextual Boundary features, group-adjusted Operation directions, and departures from benign state relationships. All branches share one prefill: detection generates no output tokens, invokes no tools, and executes no skill code. Across 5,830 skill packages from five sources and seven backbones, LatentTriad achieves 99.0-99.2% pooled F1 and 93.0-94.6% source-macro F1. A separately measured compact implementation completes prefill and detection in a median of 259-284 ms. These results connect pre-action risk readability and functional influence to execution-free skill screening.
papers.summary: LLM agents increasingly load reusable skills, and untrusted skill content can make an agent perform operations outside the user's task. Static pattern matching misses this kind of contextual risk, while running the skill to observe it is costly. The authors find that hidden states formed during prefill already encode whether the operations match the task. `LatentTriad` builds a detector on these states that generates no tokens, calls no tools and executes no skill code. Across 5,830 skill packages from five sources and seven backbone models, it reaches **99.0 to 99.2% pooled F1**, with a median latency of about 259 to 284 ms for a compact implementation.

papers.title: The Platonic Brain: Representational Convergence in EEG Foundation Models
papers.abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) predicts that artificial neural networks converge on shared representations as scale and performance increase. We test whether these predictions hold for representations of the human brain with EEG foundation models. Using EEG recordings from six participants watching a television series, together with aligned visual and language content, we tested whether EEG foundation-model representations converge within and across modalities as their embeddings become better at decoding an informative set of EEG markers. We found that EEG models with greater decodability showed stronger cross-family alignment in both local neighbourhood similarity and global structure, not consistently increasing with model parameter count. Cross-modal convergence was modality and metric dependent: greater EEG decodability was associated with stronger global alignment to language, but not consistently to vision models, while local alignment showed no consistent association. This dissociation may reflect local sensitivity to low-level sensory features, whereas global geometry may capture weaker shared semantic structure.
papers.summary: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) predicts that neural networks converge on shared representations as their scale and performance grow. The authors test it for EEG foundation models, using recordings from six participants watching a television series together with aligned visual and language content. Models whose embeddings better decode informative EEG markers show **stronger alignment across model families**, and this does not consistently track parameter count. Better decodability is also associated with stronger global alignment to language models, but not consistently to vision models, and local alignment shows no consistent association.

papers.title: Dual-VaDE: Efficient and Robust Prototype Learning via Variational Dual-Domain Mixture Priors
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose Dual-VaDE, an unsupervised generative framework for learning interpretable anatomical prototypes from unlabeled medical images. In contrast to previous variational methods that rely on a single spatial latent code, which often entangles global geometry with local textures and fails to capture their cross-domain dependencies, Dual-VaDE introduces a dual-domain Gaussian mixture prior that explicitly couples spatial anatomy with phase-preserving Fourier spectral representations. We derive an exact, closed-form variational lower bound that fuses this joint prior into the decoder and optimizes the entire network end-to-end via an alternating EM formulation, avoiding heuristic two-stage clustering while ensuring superior training stability and robustness. Evaluated on OASIS-3 brain MRI, Dual-VaDE delivers substantially sharper and more plausible prototypes, achieves superior cluster separation with improvements of up to 94% over spatial-only baselines, exhibits markedly reduced variance across random seeds, and incurs negligible inference overhead (0.28 ms per image).
papers.summary: `Dual-VaDE` is an unsupervised generative model that learns interpretable anatomical prototypes from unlabeled medical images. Earlier variational methods use a single spatial latent code, which mixes global geometry with local texture. Dual-VaDE instead uses a Gaussian mixture prior that couples spatial anatomy with phase-preserving Fourier spectral representations, trained end-to-end through an exact closed-form variational bound and an alternating EM (expectation-maximization) procedure. On `OASIS-3` brain MRI it produces sharper prototypes, **improves cluster separation by up to 94% over spatial-only baselines**, varies less across random seeds, and adds 0.28 ms of inference time per image.

papers.title: Molecular Prior Networks
papers.abstract: Predicting affinity between small molecules and their protein targets remains one of the central problems in drug discovery. Due to the substantial cost of wet-lab experiments, machine learning models of drug-target affinity are usually trained on relatively small datasets, ranging from tens to hundreds of molecules. Given the inherent difficulty of generalization between different targets and chemical series, existing datasets of protein-ligand affinities are typically not used for new projects. At the same time, tabular foundation models, including Prior-data Fitted Networks, have recently shown how transformers can be used to solve machine learning problems in a single forward pass of the network, after being trained over a large corpus of, typically, synthetic datasets. Inspired by that line of work, we propose a novel affinity modelling approach, in which the labels of the query molecules are predicted from the labelled support molecules in a single forward pass of a transformer model. The model is trained on thousands of existing affinity datasets, enabling it to capture the general patterns of molecular activity across different targets, chemical series and dataset sizes. For the smallest support sets, our model matches the state of the art on the regression variant of the FS-Mol benchmark, while being faster than existing methods, thanks to the lack of task-specific training. A comparison against a reduced variant of our architecture, which amounts to kernel regression in a meta-learned feature space, shows that the predictive performance of the transformer model is only partially explained by simple molecular similarity.
papers.summary: Drug-target affinity models are usually trained on small per-project datasets, and existing affinity datasets are rarely reused for new projects. Inspired by tabular foundation models such as `Prior-data Fitted Networks`, the authors train a transformer on thousands of existing affinity datasets so that it predicts the labels of query molecules from a labeled support set in a single forward pass. For the smallest support sets, it **matches the state of the art on the regression variant of `FS-Mol`** and runs faster because it needs no task-specific training. A comparison with a kernel-regression variant shows that the model's accuracy is only partly explained by simple molecular similarity.

papers.title: Workload-Static Optical Circuit Switching For Scalable LLM Inference Decode
papers.abstract: LLM inference decode executes fine-grained collectives whose latency directly limits per-user interactivity, yet scale-up fabrics are still built from electronic packet switches designed for training. We observe that, for a given model deployment and parallelization, the communication structure of decode is fixed, and propose workload-static optical circuit switching (OCS): circuits are configured once per deployment, co-designed with model parallelism and with topology-aware collective schedules that turn spare accelerator ports into fewer communication phases or higher bandwidth. We evaluate this design with GXNET, a graph-based workload emulator coupled to analytical and flit-level network models grounded in hardware measurements. In a 576-accelerator scale-up domain serving 5T-parameter MoE models with up to 5M tokens of context, all-OCS fabrics improve interactivity by up to 65% and energy efficiency by up to 119% over 4:1 oversubscribed packet-switched fabrics.
papers.summary: During LLM inference decode, fine-grained collective communication limits per-user interactivity, yet scale-up networks still use electronic packet switches designed for training. The authors observe that decode communication patterns are fixed for a given deployment and parallelization. They propose optical circuit switching (OCS) configured once per deployment and co-designed with model parallelism and topology-aware collective schedules. Using the `GXNET` emulator on a 576-accelerator domain serving 5T-parameter MoE (mixture-of-experts) models, all-OCS fabrics **improve interactivity by up to 65% and energy efficiency by up to 119%** compared with 4:1 oversubscribed packet-switched fabrics.

papers.title: From AutoResearch to Continual AutoResearch: Do Agents Learn Across Tasks?
papers.abstract: Autoresearch has shown that agents can autonomously write code, run experiments, and iteratively improve machine learning solutions. Yet most evaluations start a new agent session from scratch for each new problem, making them costly and leaving unclear whether agents can retain and apply prior insights when adapting to new tasks. We introduce CONTINUAL AUTORESEARCH, an open-ended environment that compares persistent and reset instances of the same agent under matched task streams, data, and time budget. Continual AutoResearch covers nine task families, spanning synthetic tasks, symbolic regression, time-series forecasting, and tabular AutoML. Across five frontier agents, we measure first-solution quality, research efficiency, and final held-out performance. To distinguish insight transfer from session continuity, we run a memory ablation that vary what information agents retain from prior tasks. We show that persistent state improves research efficiency of all five agents, allowing them to find stronger solutions sooner. However, these gains do not consistently translate into better final solutions. Overall, our findings suggest that retaining experience and utilizing it effectively are distinct capabilities.
papers.summary: Autoresearch agents can write code and run ML experiments, but evaluations usually start each new problem in a fresh session, so it is unclear whether agents carry insights from one task to the next. `Continual AutoResearch` compares persistent and reset instances of the same agent on matched task streams across nine task families, including symbolic regression, time-series forecasting and tabular AutoML, with a memory ablation that separates insight transfer from session continuity. Across five frontier agents, **persistent state improves research efficiency for all of them, but not consistently their final solutions**. The authors conclude that retaining experience and using it effectively are distinct capabilities.

papers.title: Beyond Multi-Index Models: Learning Intersections of Degree-2 PTFs
papers.abstract:
We give an algorithm for PAC learning intersections of $k$ degree-2 polynomial threshold functions over $R^d$ under a Gaussian distribution. Our algorithm achieves classification error $\epsilon$ using $d^{O(k)}2^{O_k(\log^3(1/\epsilon))}$ time and samples, improving over the $d^{O(k^2/\epsilon^2)}$ running time of the polynomial regression approach. To our knowledge, our result is the first to obtain a dimension exponent independent of the accuracy parameter, even for $k=2$. We complement our algorithmic result with an SQ lower bound showing that the complexity dependence of $d^{\Omega(k)}$ is unavoidable.
  Lifting the input to polynomial features turns the target into an intersection of $k$ halfspaces. This suggests using the first two labeled moments for subspace recovery. In the lifted space, however, these moments can reveal nothing. Our starting point is a Gaussian comparison theorem showing that, for sufficiently regular defining quadratics, the labeled moments needed for subspace recovery are approximately preserved. To handle arbitrary defining quadratics, we establish a new structural result showing that every direction with significant resampling influence can be detected through degree-$O(k)$ moments. These results yield an initial $d^{O(k)}2^{\mathrm{poly}_k(1/\epsilon)}$-time learner using adaptive restrictions.
  To improve the exponential dependence on $1/\epsilon$, we develop a two-stage dimension-reduction approach that avoids the costly adaptive partitioning. After identifying a subspace containing all directions with large influence, we use generalized regularity and Gaussian comparison to recover the remaining relevant quadratic features through a new derivative-based moment operator. The recovered features support an intersection close to the target. Combining them with robust hinge-loss minimization gives our quasipolynomial-time learner.
papers.summary: The paper studies PAC learning of intersections of k degree-2 polynomial threshold functions (PTFs) under a Gaussian distribution. The algorithm combines a Gaussian comparison theorem, a new structural result on directions with high resampling influence, and two-stage dimension reduction with a derivative-based moment operator. It runs in time d^O(k) times a quasipolynomial factor in 1/epsilon, improving on the d^O(k^2/epsilon^2) of polynomial regression. It is **the first such result whose dimension exponent does not depend on the accuracy parameter**, and a statistical query (SQ) lower bound shows the d^Omega(k) dependence is unavoidable.

papers.title: Distributed Linear Bandits for Freshness-Aware Preprocessing in MEC-Enabled Digital Twin Networks
papers.abstract: Digital twins (DTs) require timely updates from Internet of Things (IoT) devices to accurately represent the state of the corresponding physical systems, but transmitting large data volumes can compromise freshness. Moreover, different task classes have distinct computational demands and freshness requirements, while stochastic task generation and sizes complicate resource allocation. In this paper, we propose a freshness-aware framework in which multi-access edge computing (MEC) servers preprocess IoT data, reducing transmission volume and DT-server processing load. The framework establishes mutual support between DT and MEC servers. The DTs determine feasible CPU-allocation strategies guaranteeing class-specific age-of-information (AoI) requirements under specified workload, delay, and update-generation bounds. MEC servers collaboratively identify the feasible strategy minimizing expected freshness-normalized preprocessing delay. We formulate CPU-strategy selection as a fixed-confidence distributed best-arm identification problem in linear bandits, with MEC servers as agents and CPU allocations across task classes as arms. We employ DistLinGapE, a distributed collaborative learning method, to coordinate exploration and share observations. Numerical results show that the method identifies the optimal feasible strategy and reduces preprocessing delay when deployed under stationary task-class assignments and workload statistics. Collaboration yields an identification speedup nearly proportional to the number of participating MEC servers in the evaluated settings.
papers.summary: Digital twins need fresh data from Internet of Things (IoT) devices, but sending large raw data volumes delays updates. The authors have multi-access edge computing (MEC) servers preprocess IoT data before it reaches the digital twin servers. The digital twins compute which CPU-allocation strategies meet each task class's age-of-information (AoI) requirement, and the MEC servers then jointly search for the feasible strategy with the lowest freshness-normalized preprocessing delay. This search is posed as distributed best-arm identification in linear bandits and solved with `DistLinGapE`. In simulations with stationary workloads, the method finds the optimal strategy, and collaboration gives an **identification speedup nearly proportional to the number of participating MEC servers**.

papers.title: Towards an Optimal Control Foundation of Early Exits - Turnpikes and ResNets
papers.abstract: The feed-forward propagation through neural networks is crucial for training and inference. To trade off efficiency and accuracy, it has been proposed to consider intermediate outputs of hidden states as data-dependent regularization during training and, ultimately, as early-exits during inference. In this work, we analyze the joint optimization of loss functions computed for the output layer and intermediate layers using optimal control theory. We prove that ResNets trained in this joint fashion exhibit the so-called turnpike phenomenon, this implies that the number of layers required to reach a prescribed loss level is bounded from above independently of the overall network depth. This induces a similarity property across the internal representations of early-exiting networks of varying depths. We connect the turnpike to the overthinking phenomenon, and provide theoretical insights into the success of early-exit criteria derived from softmax probabilities, specifically entropy and max-probability. In a range of experiments, we demonstrate the existence and effect of turnpikes and the resulting similarity in the early-exit performance for ResNets of varying depths.
papers.summary: Early-exit networks train on losses at intermediate layers so inference can stop early, but there has been little theory explaining why this works. Using optimal control theory, the authors analyze `ResNets` trained jointly on output-layer and intermediate-layer losses. They prove these networks exhibit a turnpike phenomenon, so **the number of layers needed to reach a given loss is bounded independently of total depth**. This implies that early-exiting networks of different depths have similar internal representations. The analysis also connects turnpikes to overthinking and explains why entropy and max-probability exit criteria work, and experiments confirm the predicted behavior.

papers.title: The Right Source Is Not Enough: Understanding History Interference in Speech-LLM Memory
papers.abstract: Speech large language models retain audio history to support multi-turn conversations. Yet remembering an event does not ensure that its information is used only when relevant. We investigate why irrelevant historical audio changes answers even when the queried event remains represented. Controlled experiments on MOSS-Audio and MiMo-Audio show that historical values direct errors toward specific competing answers, beyond a generic effect of context length. Causal interventions distinguish two paths. In open-ended question answering, most history-value errors disappear when subsequent computation cannot directly access the irrelevant source. In multiple-choice answering, many errors persist: early historical influence is carried by question-candidate states even after direct source access is blocked. Low-dimensional interventions further separate source-role information from answer-value information. Their effects peak at different depths, and changing the source-role signal does not eliminate the causal influence of competing values. On naturally occurring errors, strengthening the queried role and counteracting the historical value each improve answers; their joint intervention gives the greatest recovery. These findings support a failure of downstream evidence use beyond source identification alone: source-role information can influence a decision without exclusively controlling which historical values affect it. Reliable conversational memory therefore requires not only retention and retrieval, but also control over how retained information enters answer computation.
papers.summary: Speech large language models keep audio history for multi-turn conversations, but irrelevant past audio can change answers even when the queried event is still represented. Controlled experiments on `MOSS-Audio` and `MiMo-Audio` show that historical values steer errors toward specific competing answers, which is more than a generic context-length effect. Causal interventions find that in open-ended question answering, most of these errors disappear when direct access to the irrelevant source is blocked. In multiple-choice answering, many errors persist because historical influence is already carried in the question-candidate states. The authors conclude that **identifying the correct source is not enough**: reliable conversational memory also requires controlling how retained information enters answer computation.

papers.title: Do Ray-Traced Cities Make a Better Channel Prior for an Unseen Site? A Pre-Registered Study in Simulation, and a Test on Measured Channels that Reverses It
papers.abstract: Channel estimators at a newly deployed base station usually start from 3GPP stochastic channel models, which describe no particular street. We ask whether a channel prior pooled from many ray-traced cities serves an unseen site better than the 3GPP CDL models, and whether learned estimators make the difference. With Sionna RT on 14 city scenes, LMMSE estimation from covariance priors, leave-one-city-out evaluation, and pass/fail bars written down before each main experiment, we find in simulation that the pooled prior sits about 0.6 dB from a site-trained estimator with no site measurements, about what CDL reaches after 50 measurements. Learned models added little: at most 0.65 dB in estimation, and in channel prediction a simple classical method beat CNN predictors by 1.8-12 dB from 2 ms ahead. On measured channels from the DICHASUS outdoor dataset (1.272 GHz, three 2x8 arrays on one building) the result reversed: the pooled ray-traced prior was 3.2-4.1 dB worse than CDL. The simulated channels were too clean; with users at the real distances, even a scattering level tuned from 50 site measurements left the prior about 2 dB behind CDL. A pre-registered follow-on on two more measured environments found the generic CDL prior 2.1-4.7 dB from a site-trained one: no further in a factory hall than on the street, furthest in a small lab room. Finally, a hallway model calibrated to measurements by differentiable ray tracing reproduced delay spread, but as a prior in an unmeasured part of the hallway it was 4.5 dB worse than CDL on the full array. All measured results come from one sounder.
papers.summary: The study asks whether a wireless channel prior pooled from many ray-traced cities serves a newly deployed base station better than the standard 3GPP `CDL` stochastic models. Experiments used `Sionna RT` on 14 city scenes, linear minimum mean-square error (LMMSE) estimation, leave-one-city-out evaluation, and pass/fail criteria registered before each main experiment. In simulation, the pooled prior came within about 0.6 dB of a site-trained estimator without any site measurements, and learned models added little. On measured channels from the `DICHASUS` dataset, however, the result reversed: **the ray-traced prior was 3.2–4.1 dB worse than CDL**, because the simulated channels were too clean.

papers.title: Solving the Nonlinear Westervelt Equation in Ultrasound Propagation Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Modeling the nonlinear acoustic wave propagation in biological tissues needs accuracy, especially in ultrasound imaging and therapeutic applications. The 1D Westervelt equation, \( p_{xx} - p_{tt} + \gamma\, p_{ttt} + \eta\,(p^{2})_{tt}=0, \) could be used to describe a finite-amplitude ultrasound propagation in these tissues. This equation accounts for nonlinearity, \(\eta\), and attenuation, \(\gamma\). To solve this equation, we observe that traditional solvers may struggle to do so correctly. This is due to the difficulties arising from the nonlinear nature of the equation. We solve the equation by defining three synthetic cases - linear (\(\eta=0.001\), \(\gamma=10^{-6}\)), shock-dominated (\(\eta=0.02\), \(\gamma=10^{-6}\)), and dissipation-dominated (\(\eta=0.01\), \(\gamma=5\times10^{-4}\)) - and using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to showcase the solution. A sinusoidal activation function is used to capture the oscillatory behavior of the problem. The results of our study, with PDE residual converging to at least \(10^{-6}\), boundary condition loss to \(10^{-5}\), and the PINN loss converging to \(10^{-5}\) for each case at \(30,000\) epochs, show that \(\gamma\) scales the rate of amplitude decay, while \(\eta\) governs frequency-dependent phase speeds.
papers.summary: The 1D Westervelt equation describes finite-amplitude ultrasound propagation in biological tissue, but its nonlinearity makes it hard for traditional solvers. The authors solve it with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) using a sinusoidal activation function to capture oscillatory behavior. They test three synthetic regimes: linear, shock-dominated, and dissipation-dominated. In each case, the PDE residual converges to at least 10⁻⁶ within 30,000 epochs. The solutions show that **the attenuation term sets the rate of amplitude decay, while the nonlinearity term governs frequency-dependent phase speeds**.

papers.title: PAC Learning with Multiple Correct Answers
papers.abstract:
We study PAC learning when each example comes with a set of at most $\ell$ correct labels and a prediction is correct if it belongs to this set. Training may reveal the full set, only whether a proposed label is correct (bandit feedback), or one correct label chosen by a demonstrator (emonstrations).
  Our main finding is that demonstrations can be much harder than full sets, and even than bandit feedback, both in which classes can be learned and in how many examples are needed. For finite label spaces, a generalized Natarajan dimension characterizes learnability from full sets and from bandit feedback, in both the realizable and the agnostic setting. From demonstrations, however, a class is realizably learnable if and only if the intersections of at most $\ell+1$ of its hypotheses are learnable from full sets. Already with three labels, this condition can fail for a class learnable from a single full-set example or even a single bandit answer. When the condition holds, we show that $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-\ell})$ demonstrations suffice, and the exponent $\ell$ cannot be improved in general, even for classes learnable from $\widetilde O(1/\varepsilon)$ full sets or bandit answers.
  For countable label spaces and $\ell \geq 2$, our packed dimension, which asks for many disjoint groups of at most $\ell+1$ hypotheses with no common label, characterizes full-set learnability, and demonstrations still reduce to intersections. Agnostic learning from demonstrations, already for finite label spaces, is not determined by the dimensions of the intersection class that characterize realizable learning.
  Finally, we show that the uniform bound $\ell$ on the number of correct labels is essential. Without this bound, it is impossible to characterize learnability by any dimension determined by finite subclasses.
papers.summary: The paper studies PAC learning when each example has a set of at most ℓ correct labels. Training feedback comes in one of three forms: the full set of correct labels, bandit feedback saying whether a proposed label is correct, or a single correct label chosen by a demonstrator. The main finding is that **learning from demonstrations can be much harder than learning from full sets or even from bandit feedback**. For demonstrations, a class is learnable only if intersections of up to ℓ+1 of its hypotheses are learnable, and the sample complexity scales as Õ(ε^-ℓ), an exponent that cannot be improved in general. For full sets and bandit feedback, a generalized `Natarajan dimension` characterizes learnability, and the authors also show that without the uniform bound ℓ, no dimension based on finite subclasses can characterize learnability.

papers.title: From Opinions to Commitments: Unstable Assignments and Silent Choices in AI-Mediated Proposals
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to turn citizens' opinions into collective proposals. These proposals can make assignments: who should act, what must be done, how much one should spend and by when. However, if the assignments change when the same opinions are processed again, publishing a single proposal can hide alternatives that participants never get to see. We examined this issue in four LLM mediators (three open-weight and one commercial) using opinions from DeliberationBank and Polis. For each task, a mediator drafted a proposal from thirty opinions five times, varying either the random seed or the order of the opinions. In 17% of five-run sets from the open-weight mediators and 20% from the commercial one, some runs contained assignments while others did not. Reordering the opinions changed the assignments almost as often as replacing them with opinions from different citizens. Three human annotators confirmed that the detected differences between runs were real, although the LLM judge overstated how often they occurred. Substantial variation remained under four safeguards: temperature zero, a commercial mediator, draft selection, and draft merging. The mediator's objective also shaped representation: prompts seeking agreement covered minority positions much less often than prompts asking to describe differences. A single proposal can therefore obscure choices in both the assignments it proposes and the views it excludes. We propose audits that make alternative assignments visible and disclose the objective behind each proposal.
papers.summary: LLMs are increasingly used to turn citizens' opinions into collective proposals that assign who should act, what must be done, and with what budget and deadline. The authors ran four LLM mediators five times each on 30 opinions from `DeliberationBank` and `Polis`, varying only the random seed or the order of the opinions. In **17–20% of five-run sets, some runs contained assignments while others did not**, and reordering the opinions changed assignments almost as often as replacing them with different citizens' opinions. This variation persisted at temperature zero, with a commercial model, and with draft selection or merging. Prompts seeking agreement also covered minority positions much less often than prompts asking to describe differences, so the authors propose audits that expose alternative assignments and disclose each proposal's objective.

papers.title: A Random Matrix Analysis of Symmetric Tensor Unfolding
papers.abstract: We study a fundamental problem in machine learning: partial recovery of a planted signal $\boldsymbol{v} \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$ from a spiked tensor $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{X}} = \lambda \, \boldsymbol{v}^{\otimes p} + \boldsymbol{\mathsf{Z}}$, where $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{Z}}$ has symmetric Gaussian entries of variance $\asymp n^{-1}$. While previous works replace $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{Z}}$ by an i.i.d. standard Gaussian tensor to circumvent technical difficulties caused by dependencies, this paper directly analyzes the symmetric model via random matrix theory. We show that the square unfolding algorithm is subject to a sharp phase transition for partial recovery at $\lambda \asymp n^{(p-2) / 4}$, validating an open conjecture from Montanari and Richard (2014). We get precise expressions for the limiting spectral distribution, deterministic equivalent, phase transition threshold and overlap. The main message is that unfolded symmetric tensors spectrally behave like standard Wigner matrices, up to simple transformations accounting for high-order symmetries. We consider extensions to multiple orthogonal spikes, recursive unfolding and non-square unfolding via disproportionate random matrix theory, leading to an interesting conjectured statistical-computational tradeoff regarding the choice of unfolding: square versus long.
papers.summary: The paper studies recovering a planted signal from a spiked tensor with symmetric Gaussian noise. It analyzes the symmetric noise model directly with random matrix theory, rather than substituting i.i.d. noise as earlier work did to avoid technical difficulties. The authors prove that the square unfolding algorithm undergoes **a sharp phase transition for partial recovery at λ ≍ n^((p−2)/4)**, confirming a 2014 conjecture by Montanari and Richard. They also derive exact expressions for the limiting spectrum and the overlap with the signal, finding that unfolded symmetric tensors behave like Wigner matrices. Extensions to multiple spikes, recursive unfolding, and non-square unfolding lead to a conjectured statistical-computational tradeoff between square and long unfoldings.

papers.title: Meta$^2$: Precomputing Reusable Knowledge for Online Harness Evolution in Long-Horizon Agents
papers.abstract: Harness optimization improves long-horizon agents by refining the prompts, tools, memory, and hooks around a frozen model. Offline methods can learn from completed trajectories, but deploy one shared harness that may overfit training tasks and cannot react to evidence revealed during a new run. Online evolution can adapt before, during, or after one run through an evolver, but may have to reason about every intervention from scratch or rely on verifier feedback that is usually unavailable at test time. We introduce Meta$^2$, which moves offline optimization one level up: rather than optimizing a shared harness, it learns reusable knowledge for harness evolution and applies it within each task online. Offline, Meta$^2$ learns a textual Meta-Skill $M$ by contrasting training rollouts of the same task agent under three configurations: without an evolver, with an evolver guided by the current version of $M$, and with an evolver given privileged verifier information available only in training. Contrasts in trajectories and outcomes are aggregated across tasks to refine $M$ into reusable guidance on when and how to evolve, when to leave the harness unchanged, and which interventions to avoid. Online, an evolver combines the frozen $M$ with emerging trajectory evidence to decide whether to KEEP the harness unchanged or EVOLVE it through a task-local edit. Each edit applies to the rest of the same run without resetting its environment or progress. Thus, evolution guidance transfers across tasks while harness edits remain task-local, and held-out verifier feedback is never available to the evolver. On two long-horizon benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1, Meta$^2$ achieves the highest performance among evaluated methods with GPT-5.6-Terra, reaching 81.00% and 44.44%, respectively. Ablations support the value of contrastive evolution guidance and keeping online harness edits task-local.
papers.summary: Harness optimization improves long-horizon agents by refining the prompts, tools, memory, and hooks around a frozen model. Offline methods deploy one shared harness that may overfit, and online methods must reason about every change from scratch. `Meta²` instead learns, offline, a textual Meta-Skill that encodes when and how to modify a harness. It does this by contrasting training rollouts without an evolver, with a Meta-Skill-guided evolver, and with an evolver given privileged verifier information. At test time, an evolver uses the frozen Meta-Skill and evidence from the current run to either keep the harness or make a task-local edit, without verifier feedback. With `GPT-5.6-Terra`, it achieves **the best results among evaluated methods: 81.00% on `Terminal-Bench 2.1` and 44.44% on `DeepSWE 1.1`**.

papers.title: Beyond Foundation Models: PFN Priors Improve Tabular Hyperparameter Optimization
papers.abstract: Synthetic priors have so far served one purpose: pretraining tabular foundation models. We ask whether the same priors can improve conventional tabular models, which are trained from scratch on each dataset. We propose PriorTune, a method that meta-tunes hyperparameter configurations on synthetic tasks alone. Offline, for a given model, we fit a pool of configurations on datasets sampled from a published PFN prior and greedily select the subset with the highest winrate over the random baseline. Online, a new dataset fits only the selected configurations, so the gain comes at no extra cost. Empirically, we observe that scaling both the number of configurations and synthetic datasets has an equal scaling effect on the performance of the final subset of configurations, which we also explain theoretically. On the full BeyondArena benchmark, LightGBM with TabPrep features with our configurations ranks above TabPFN-3 and RealMLP, while being much more efficient at inference. Overall, our results establish existing PFN priors as a scalable source of meta-training data for hyperparameter selection for non-foundational tabular models.
papers.summary: Synthetic data priors have mainly been used to pretrain tabular foundation models. `PriorTune` instead uses them to meta-tune hyperparameters for conventional tabular models trained from scratch on each dataset. Offline, it fits a pool of configurations on datasets sampled from a published PFN prior and greedily selects the subset with the highest win rate, so a new dataset only needs to fit that small subset. The authors find that scaling the number of configurations and the number of synthetic datasets have equal effects, and they explain this theoretically. On `BeyondArena`, **`LightGBM` with `TabPrep` features and PriorTune configurations ranks above `TabPFN-3` and `RealMLP`** while being much cheaper at inference.

papers.title: GM League Arena: An Interactive Long-Horizon Task Benchmark Based on Professional Sports League Management
papers.abstract: Long-horizon decision-making under sustained competition requires large language models (LLMs) to balance immediate investment with future resource needs. However, local success in multi-step interactions can not adequately capture cumulative decision effects or demonstrate long-term goal achievement under resource constraints and sustained competition. To address this gap, we introduce GM Bench, a benchmark for managing professional sports teams across seasons under resource constraints and competition among teams. We build the environment simulators for four sports and add financial constraints, player demands, and market mechanisms to establish a unified task across sports. Diverse rosters of comparable strength are constructed from real-world player data, and each LLM is evaluated as a team general manager to assess its long-term management capabilities. We evaluate competitive performance, cash reserves, and cross-season improvement across four sports. Over five NBA seasons, Claude Opus 5.5 ranks first among 29 LLMs, while GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol combine strong performance with larger cash reserves.
