papers.summary: Benchmarks of multi-step LLM interaction rarely capture how decisions add up over long horizons under resource constraints and sustained competition. `GM Bench` has LLMs act as general managers of professional sports teams over multiple seasons, using simulators for four sports with financial constraints, player demands, and market mechanisms. Rosters of comparable strength are built from real-world player data, and models are scored on competitive performance, cash reserves, and improvement across seasons. Over five NBA seasons, **`Claude Opus 5.5` ranks first among 29 LLMs**, while `GPT-6 Astra` and `GPT-6.1 Sol` combine strong results with larger cash reserves.

papers.title: Creating Power Flexibility in Datacenters via Query Routing
papers.abstract: The growing energy requirements of large language model inference highlight the need for datacenters to support safe grid operation by providing power demand flexibility, while maintaining service for interactive workloads. This work investigates query routing as a mechanism to enable such capability by dynamically allocating queries across different language model instances without deferring requests. We develop a general analytical framework that connects query arrival rates and sequence length distributions to token iteration time, request residence time, serving capacity, and power consumption of model instances. Leveraging this framework, we characterize the feasible query routing allocations and the corresponding power demand flexibilities, enabling the selection of routing strategies to achieve desired power consumption behavior. We validate our framework across four GPU platforms on language models ranging from 1B to 70B parameters, obtaining 2.8% mean absolute percentage error in estimating achievable power flexibility. We evaluate our approach on a real trace-driven simulation of a 10,000 H100 GPUs datacenter, exhibiting flexibility up to 16% of total power consumption, with 90% of the desired power reduction achieved within approximately 10 seconds. These results establish query routing as an effective mechanism for datacenter power demand flexibility and demonstrate the broader applicability of our proposed framework to datacenter level planning and orchestration.
papers.summary: As LLM inference consumes more energy, datacenters need to flex their power demand to support grid operation without degrading interactive service. The authors propose query routing across language model instances, without deferring any requests, as the mechanism for this. Their analytical framework links query arrival rates and sequence lengths to iteration time, serving capacity, and power draw. Validated across four GPU platforms and models from 1B to 70B parameters, it estimates achievable power flexibility with 2.8% mean absolute percentage error. In a trace-driven simulation of a 10,000-H100 datacenter, routing provides **power flexibility of up to 16% of total consumption**, with 90% of the target reduction reached in about 10 seconds.

papers.title: Catalyzing Interactive HTML Generation Capabilities via High-Fidelity Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Generating HTML from natural-language specifications is an important application of code large language models (LLMs). Despite producing renderable pages, current models often fail to ensure functionality and visual quality during actual interaction. Existing methods typically target task-specific webpage supervision, leaving demanding interactive artifact optimization underexplored. Using mini-games as a challenging testbed, we expose limitations in interaction experience, reward signal, and credit assignment fidelity that are obscured by shallow webpage interactions. We introduce WebCatalyst, a browser-interaction reinforcement learning framework with three complementary components: a game-level GUI assessor for sustained interaction and evaluation, Visual Anchor for mitigating VLM reward hacking, and Action-Trace Credit for grounding token-level credit assignment in runtime execution traces. Trained on fewer than 1K requests, predominantly for games, WebCatalyst raises the Cookie-Bench Mini Games score from 68.8 to 75.3 and also the WebGen-Bench accuracy from 48.8 to 56.9 on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, outperforming Claude Opus 4.7 in average rank across evaluated metrics. Further analysis shows that Visual Anchor prevents aesthetic degradation, while runtime-grounded credit assignment accelerates functional improvement. Together, our results show that improving feedback fidelity is the key to substantially advancing interactive HTML generation.
papers.summary: Code LLMs can generate HTML pages that render but often fail on functionality and visual quality once a user interacts with them. Using mini-games as a demanding testbed, `WebCatalyst` trains with browser-interaction reinforcement learning built from three components. A game-level GUI assessor plays and evaluates the pages, `Visual Anchor` prevents vision-language-model reward hacking, and `Action-Trace Credit` assigns token-level credit using runtime execution traces. Trained on fewer than 1K requests, `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` improves from 68.8 to 75.3 on `Cookie-Bench` Mini Games and from 48.8 to 56.9 on `WebGen-Bench`, **outperforming `Claude Opus 4.7` in average rank** across the evaluated metrics.

papers.title: Asynchronous Robot Policies
papers.abstract: Scaling vision-language foundation models has significantly advanced generalist robot manipulation, but the increased model scale introduces computational latency that degrades real-time physical reactivity. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures execute high-level semantic reasoning and action ex- ecution sequentially within the primary control loop, creating a fundamental tension between semantic-reasoning capability and robot agility. To address this, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policy (ARP), an architectural framework that decouples semantic reasoning from low-level action generation using asynchronous processes operating at independent frequencies. In ARP, a high-capacity Vision-Language Model (VLM) asynchronously updates a semantic memory at low fre- quency, while a lightweight Vision-Action Expert, conditioned on this semantic memory, generates robot actions at a much higher control frequency. Such a formulation, enables having a fast perception-action loop without compromising on the semantic capability. To overcome asynchronous memory staleness, ARP trains the vision-action expert on the semantic staleness and execution delay, with temporally mismatched observation across processes. On Franka manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an 18% higher success rate and 20% less time need for execution in quasi-static setups, while 3-5 times baseline performance in dynamic simulation environments. Furthermore, ARP enables operating the VLM at 10 times lower than its nominal frequency with no significant performance loss making it much more efficient than the baseline. These results highlight the architectural advantages of modeling robot policies as asynchronous processes, enabling real-world reactive deployment without sacrificing the scale of foundation models.
papers.summary: Large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) robot models run semantic reasoning and action generation in sequence inside the control loop, so their latency hurts reactivity. `Asynchronous Robot Policy` (`ARP`) separates the two. A large vision-language model updates a semantic memory at low frequency, while a lightweight vision-action expert generates actions at high frequency, conditioned on that memory. The action expert is trained to tolerate stale memory and execution delays. On Franka manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an 18% higher success rate and 20% faster execution in quasi-static setups and 3–5 times baseline performance in dynamic simulation, and **the vision-language model can run at 10 times lower than its nominal frequency without significant performance loss**.

papers.title: Macrocanonical Generator Networks: Data-Efficient Neural Surrogates for Amortized Physics Simulation
papers.abstract: Many scientific simulations are computationally expensive, limiting their use in simulation-based inference, uncertainty quantification, and decision making. We introduce macrocanonical generator networks, a framework for learning fast, data-efficient neural surrogates for amortized simulation of stationary physical processes by matching multiscale statistics of a target process. Inspired by microcanonical maximum-entropy synthesis, which matches feature statistics per sample by inner-loop optimization, our approach instead trains a neural generator to satisfy the same constraints in expectation, preserving physically realistic sample-to-sample fluctuations. We prove that gradient-descent training induces preconditioned gradient-descent dynamics in sample space that inherit the symmetry-preservation properties of the microcanonical gradient descent of Bruna and Mallat, amortizing its per-sample inner-loop optimization into a single training run after which every sample is generated in one forward pass. We further show that residual generator parameterizations initialized near the identity, trained with a small learning rate, preserve entropy locally during early optimization and mitigate mode collapse. Experiments on cosmology and fluid simulations show that macrocanonical generators recover realistic samples from extremely small training sets, in some cases a single training example, while generating new realizations more than $10^6$ times faster per sample than the reference simulator and more than $10^3$ times faster than microcanonical gradient descent. The trained generators can be reused for downstream pretraining, including simulation-based inference, providing a data-efficient route to multi-fidelity scientific machine learning workflows.
papers.summary: Expensive scientific simulators limit simulation-based inference and uncertainty quantification. Macrocanonical generator networks train a neural generator to match multiscale statistics of a stationary physical process in expectation, rather than per sample as microcanonical maximum-entropy methods do. The authors prove that training inherits the symmetry-preservation properties of microcanonical gradient descent while reducing generation to a single forward pass. They also show that near-identity residual initializations help prevent mode collapse. On cosmology and fluid simulations, the generators learn from very small training sets, sometimes a single example, and **produce new samples more than 10⁶ times faster than the reference simulator**.

papers.title: Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding
papers.abstract: Vision-language verifiers judge whether an image faithfully matches a textual description, yet existing training pipelines typically rely on static supervision from stronger external judges or curated hard-negative data. Such supervision requires external generation or annotation, is teacher-bounded, and is difficult to adapt as model failures evolve. We introduce PROVE (Perturb-and-Repair Optimization for Vision-Language Evaluation), a self-play framework that trains verifiers through a closed perturb-verify-repair-verify loop. Starting from a known-correct image-caption pair, a Mutator introduces a typed perturbation over objects, attributes, counts, or relations. The verifier then judges the perturbed caption and provides textual feedback, which a Repairer uses to recover a faithful caption for re-verification. These two verification rounds produce structured rewards for informative mismatches and visually grounded repairs. Since perturbation, verification, and repair are role-conditioned behaviors of the same evolving multimodal backbone, updating the shared parameters also improves the verifier itself. Experiments show that PROVE improves fine-grained compositional verification across model scales and families and strengthens visual-detail robustness on the reference backbone, with limited, benchmark-dependent changes on broader multimodal tasks.
papers.summary: Vision-language verifiers judge whether an image matches a text description, but they are usually trained on static labels from stronger external judges or on curated hard negatives. `PROVE` (Perturb-and-Repair Optimization for Vision-Language Evaluation) instead uses self-play in a single shared multimodal model. A Mutator introduces typed errors in objects, attributes, counts, or relations into a correct caption, the verifier judges the perturbed caption and gives feedback, and a Repairer restores a faithful caption for re-verification. The two verification rounds produce structured rewards, and because all roles share parameters, training them also improves the verifier. **Fine-grained compositional verification improves across model scales and families**, with limited, benchmark-dependent changes on broader multimodal tasks.

papers.title: RoboTryOn: Synthesizing Dexterous Robot Demonstrations from Human Videos via Virtual Try-On
papers.abstract: Robot foundation models have shown remarkable performance in robot control, yet adapting them to a new task still relies heavily on teleoperated demonstrations. Egocentric human videos offer a scalable substitute, but overlaying rendered robots on human videos or retargeting human poses into robot actions leaves significant visual or action gaps for high-DoF robot embodiments. To address this limitation, we propose RoboTryOn, which treats human-to-robot translation as virtual try-on: try-on keeps the person and swaps the garment, RoboTryOn keeps the demonstrated motion and swaps the human for the robot. Specifically, RoboTryOn converts a human video into a video of the target robot specified by a reference image, while preserving the original task, objects, and background. To maintain visual consistency, we translate selected keyframes autoregressively and use them to guide video synthesis with motion conditioned on the human hand skeleton. Additionally, we use an inverse dynamics model (IDM) that incorporates depth features to infer action labels from synthesized videos for policy learning. Our experiments across multiple humanoid embodiments show that policies trained with our synthetic data improve the average success rate on novel tasks, including challenging bimanual manipulation, from 2% to 60%, without any real robot demonstration of those tasks. Moreover, training with our synthetic data matches the performance of policies trained solely on teleoperated demonstrations at approximately a third of the collection cost, demonstrating the cost efficiency of our approach.
papers.summary: Adapting robot foundation models to new tasks still depends on costly teleoperated demonstrations, and existing ways of turning human videos into robot data leave large visual or action gaps for high-degree-of-freedom robots. `RoboTryOn` treats the conversion like virtual try-on: it keeps the demonstrated motion, objects, and background and swaps the human for a target robot specified by a reference image. Keyframes are translated autoregressively and guide video synthesis conditioned on the hand skeleton. An inverse dynamics model that uses depth features then infers action labels from the synthesized videos. Across several humanoid embodiments, the synthetic data **raises success on novel tasks from 2% to 60% without any real robot demonstrations of those tasks**, and matches teleoperation-trained policies at about a third of the collection cost.
papers.highlight_summary:
Teleoperated demonstrations for dexterous robot hands are expensive to collect, and existing ways of reusing human videos leave large visual and action gaps between the human and the robot. `RoboTryOn` treats human-to-robot transfer like virtual clothing try-on: it keeps the demonstrated motion, object and scene from an egocentric human video, and replaces the human arm and hand with a target robot taken from a reference image.

- An image model inpaints the masked human arm and hand on selected keyframes, translating them autoregressively with the previous robot keyframe as reference; a video model fills in the frames between keyframes, guided by the human hand-skeleton flow; and an inverse dynamics model with depth features labels joint-space actions, with the wrist position corrected by inverse kinematics.
- All three generative and labeling models are trained only on robot data, linked to human videos through a shared arm mask and skeleton representation, so no paired human–robot demonstrations are needed and the policy runs on raw camera images at deployment.
- Results come from fine-tuning `π0.5` on two real bimanual robots with dexterous hands, `OpenArm` and `RB-Y1`. On seven tasks that have no robot demonstrations, success rises from **3.1% to 73.0%** on `OpenArm` and from **1.0% to 46.9%** on `RB-Y1`, including bimanual tasks even though every teleoperated demonstration uses a single arm; the `EgoMimic` and `Masquerade` baselines stay below 10%.
- The synthesized data closes much of both gaps: Fréchet SigLIP distance to real robot video drops from **125.5 to 32.7**, and open-loop replay of the inferred action labels in simulation succeeds **69.7%** of the time versus 34.8% for retargeted actions; policies trained only on translated human videos match training on 50 teleoperated demonstrations per task at **about one third of the collection cost**.
- Limitations: each new robot still needs a few hours of teleoperated video to train the models, the action labels cannot capture forces or support high-precision tasks like tight insertion, the camera must stay fixed (so in-the-wild egocentric video is not yet supported), and evaluation covers tabletop tasks on only two robots.

papers.title: Basin2Vec: Learning Basin-Centric Embeddings for Scalable Hydrological Modeling
papers.abstract: Reliable streamflow prediction across time and in ungauged basins requires representations that capture hydrologically relevant basin characteristics. Existing methods rely on either fixed handcrafted attributes or general-purpose Earth observation embeddings not tailored to basin structure. We introduce \textbf{Basin2Vec}, a self-supervised framework that learns compact basin representations from hydroclimatic and physiographic data without observed streamflow. Basin2Vec organizes representation learning around basin scale and relationships across space and time. Across multiple forecasting architectures, it consistently outperforms predefined attributes and general-purpose geospatial embeddings in temporal generalization and zero-shot spatial transfer. Basin2Vec provides average relative gains of up to 8.3% temporally and achieves 3.5x the median predictive performance of the strongest baselines on unseen basins. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of basin-centric pretraining for transferable hydrologic prediction. Code is available at https://github.com/Muhammad-Talha-MT/basin2vec
papers.summary: Streamflow prediction across time and in ungauged river basins depends on representations of basin characteristics. Existing methods use either fixed handcrafted attributes or general-purpose Earth-observation embeddings that are not tailored to basins. `Basin2Vec` learns compact basin embeddings by self-supervision from hydroclimatic and physiographic data, without observed streamflow, and is organized around basin scale and relationships across space and time. Across several forecasting architectures, it outperforms both baselines, with average relative gains of up to 8.3% for prediction over time and **3.5 times the median predictive performance of the strongest baselines on unseen basins**.

papers.title: When Self-Verification Hurts: Calibrated Answer Repair for Financial Question Answering
papers.abstract: Financial question answering can fail even when a model extracts a plausible number from the supplied evidence: the answer may attach it to the wrong entity, period, unit, or accounting concept. Asking the model to verify and revise its draft can help, but open-ended revision may alter content that was already correct or inspect the wrong relation and reinforce the original error. We formulate repair as a decision that balances the information it may recover against the correct content it may damage. Based on this trade-off, we introduce Calibrated Answer Repair (CAR), which first estimates whether a draft is likely to benefit from repair, then selects a targeted check, localizes the relevant evidence or draft span, and limits the permitted edit. Across FinRank, Fin-RATE, and FinQA with three open-weight models, CAR outperforms generic verification in all dataset-model settings. At the system level, it recovers 14.6% of initially missed answer requirements while damaging 2.1% of initially correct ones. Its post-draft token cost is over 30 percent lower than the iterative revision alternatives. Ablations on two dataset-model settings show that evidence localization and bounded editing are the main contributors to CAR's gains.
papers.summary: In financial question answering, a model may extract a plausible number but attach it to the wrong entity, period, unit, or accounting concept. Open-ended self-verification can then damage correct content or reinforce the original error. `Calibrated Answer Repair` (`CAR`) first estimates whether a draft is likely to benefit from repair, then picks a targeted check, localizes the relevant evidence, and limits the permitted edit. Across `FinRank`, `Fin-RATE`, and `FinQA` with three open-weight models, CAR beats generic verification in every setting. It **recovers 14.6% of initially missed answer requirements while damaging only 2.1% of correct ones**, with over 30% lower post-draft token cost than iterative revision.

papers.title: Learning Behaviorally Relevant Dynamics in Multimodal Neural Recordings
papers.abstract: Multimodal neural data can enable a more complete understanding of brain dynamics underlying behavior. Modalities such as spiking activity, local field potentials (LFPs), and behavior capture diverse spatiotemporal aspects of brain processes, yet prior neural-behavioral models that separate sources of variability rely on a single neural modality. By leveraging these complementary strengths, multimodal neural fusion can provide a unified, rich representation of brain-behavior processes and address the limitations of single-modality analyses. Here we develop BREM-NET, a nonlinear multimodal dynamical model that integrates behavior with multiple neural modalities having distinct statistical characteristics and temporal resolutions. BREM-NET performs multimodal neural fusion during inference while separating behaviorally relevant and residual neural dynamics via a structured learning framework. In a public multimodal non-human primate dataset with simultaneous spiking and local field potential recordings during a 2D reaching task, BREM-NET separates these two types of dynamics and learns them more accurately, as reflected in better behavior decoding, better neural prediction, and stronger latent alignment with behavior, and it retains these capabilities when neural modalities are asynchronous or suffer dropouts, which are major challenges in real-world recordings. This framework provides a new tool for studying behaviorally relevant neural computations across spatiotemporal scales of brain activity.
papers.summary: Existing neural-behavioral models that separate behaviorally relevant activity from other sources of variability use only one neural modality, which misses the complementary information in different recordings. `BREM-NET` is a nonlinear dynamical model that fuses behavior with several neural modalities, such as spiking activity and local field potentials (LFPs), that differ in statistics and timing. It separates behaviorally relevant dynamics from residual dynamics during inference. On a public non-human primate reaching dataset, it gives **better behavior decoding, neural prediction, and latent alignment with behavior**, and it keeps these advantages when the modalities are asynchronous or have dropouts.

papers.title: AgentAM: An AI Agent for Spatter- and Defect-Aware Process Optimization in Laser Powder Bed Fusion
papers.abstract: Predictive models for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) are rarely used on the shop floor because querying them requires programming and model-specific knowledge. We present AgentAM, a large language model (LLM) agent that gives process engineers natural-language access to CFD-trained surrogates of spatter and melt pool geometry for SS316L through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Polynomial surrogates trained on 279 single-track simulations predict melt pool dimensions ($R^2 \geq 0.95$) and spatter volume ($R^2 = 0.83$ on test data) at any power-velocity point in the trained range, and geometric criteria assign each point a geometry-derived defect regime (keyhole, lack of fusion, balling or stable) that matches the regime obtained from the simulated geometry in 93.4% of tracks under cross-validation. The agent selects and parameterizes tools for prediction, process-window scans and constrained optimization. Minimum-spatter optima often sat within 10 $\mu$m of the lack-of-fusion boundary; a margin-aware optimizer moved them away from all thresholds and raised the estimated probability of remaining classified Good from 0.94 to 1.00 under an assumed 2% process drift, and from 0.72 to 0.91 when jointly sampled cross-validated geometry residuals were added. About 40-50 well-spread simulations sufficed to reproduce the defect map. To evaluate the agent layer, we introduce a 145-prompt benchmark scored against direct tool calls, plus eight prompts (40 runs) on margin-aware requests. Over the 725 runs of the main benchmark the agent passed the intended inputs in 98.5% of parsing prompts, reported the scored spatter values and defect classes faithfully and met every stated constraint in the 65 feasible optimization runs, within a median 1.0% of the brute-force optimum.
papers.summary: Predictive models for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) metal printing are rarely used on the shop floor because querying them takes programming and model-specific knowledge. `AgentAM` is a large language model (LLM) agent that lets process engineers ask, in natural language, for predictions from simulation-trained surrogate models of spatter and melt pool geometry for `SS316L` steel, which it reaches through the `Model Context Protocol` (MCP). The agent picks and configures tools for prediction, process-window scans and constrained optimization. A margin-aware optimizer moves recommended settings away from defect boundaries, raising the estimated chance of staying defect-free under 2% process drift from 0.94 to 1.00. On a new 145-prompt benchmark scored against direct tool calls, the agent passed the intended inputs in **98.5% of parsing prompts**, met every stated constraint in feasible optimization runs, and came within a median 1.0% of the brute-force optimum.

papers.title: OperAItor: An Agentic Framework for Fault-Tolerant Operation of Chemical Processes
papers.abstract: OperAItor, an open-source framework for developing and evaluating large language model agents for supervisory fault management in chemical processes. The framework is demonstrated on a dynamic reactor-distillation process representing isopropanol dehydrogenation, with physically based thermodynamics and modified reaction kinetics to permit liquid-phase operation. The process is represented by a 113-variable differential-algebraic model and operates at a nominal feed rate of 100kmol/h, producing approximately 4t/h of acetone. The simulated plant includes 8 PI control loops, 22 process alarms, 5 duty-standby pump trains, and 11 independent safety instrumented functions. The agent architecture integrates multivariate statistical process monitoring, fault diagnosis, knowledge-graph retrieval, action planning, and supervisory action generation. Five action-validation configurations are investigated, comprising operation without validation, an LLM-based judge, digital-twin simulation, and deterministic admissibility checks with and without consequence projection. The framework is evaluated using four LLMs across 20 scenarios involving single and multiple simultaneous faults. Without agent intervention, 18 scenarios result in plant stops, corresponding to an economic loss of $399,000 relative to fault-free operation under the assumed benchmark economics. For GPT-5 nano, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B, validated agent configurations reduce the number of stops to 5-8 and recover $265,000 of the loss. The study provides a reproducible benchmark for comparing agent architectures, language models, and action-validation methods for supervisory fault management in chemical processes.
papers.summary: `OperAItor` is an open-source framework for building and evaluating LLM agents that handle supervisory fault management in chemical plants. It is demonstrated on a simulated reactor-distillation process with 113 variables, control loops, alarms and safety interlocks. The agent combines statistical process monitoring, fault diagnosis, knowledge-graph retrieval and action planning. The study compares five ways of validating actions: no validation, an LLM judge, digital-twin simulation, and deterministic admissibility checks with or without consequence projection. Across 20 fault scenarios, unassisted operation led to 18 plant stops, while validated agent configurations running `GPT-5 nano`, `Qwen3 8B` and `Mistral 7B` cut this to 5–8 stops and **recovered $265,000 of a $399,000 economic loss**.

papers.title: What Does the Model See? Representation Validity in Multimodal LLM-Based Video Analysis
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) allow social scientists to analyze video at scale, but researchers must decide which parts of a video to provide as input. We use the term representation validity to examine how text, audio, video, and combined inputs affect measurement and subsequent analysis. We compare input representations across six open-weight MLLMs and three human-annotated video datasets. No representation consistently performs best. On seven news-related constructs, native-video performance varies little across models (macro-F1 = .70-.77), while extracted-text performance ranges from .52 to .80. Three models perform better with text and three with video. Combining inputs rarely improves performance. Higher classification accuracy also does not reliably produce estimates closer to those based on human codes. The highest-F1 representation best reproduces human-coded regression coefficients in 17 of 42 comparisons. Even when each model uses its highest-F1 deployable representation, 45% of sample-prevalence estimates differ from the human-coded benchmark by more than ten percentage points. Input representation therefore requires validation for both the construct being measured and the quantity estimated from the resulting labels.
papers.summary: When social scientists use multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to code video, they must choose what to feed the model: text, audio, video, or a combination. The authors call this choice representation validity and test it across six open-weight MLLMs and three human-annotated video datasets. No input representation is consistently best: three models do better with extracted text and three with native video, and combining inputs rarely helps. Higher classification accuracy also does not reliably yield estimates closer to human-coded results. Even with each model's best representation, **45% of prevalence estimates differ from the human benchmark by more than ten percentage points**.

papers.title: Provably Learning Mixtures of Linear Experts
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are widely deployed in modern machine learning. However, few convergence guarantees exist for gradient-based training of MoEs: the objective is nonconvex, and even simple mixtures trap first-order methods in spurious local optima. We analyze a canonical gated mixture featuring linear experts and a gate induced by Gaussian clusters in the input space, and give, to our knowledge, the first global convergence guarantee for jointly training the gate and the experts of such a model by gradient EM on its likelihood. Given a logarithmic overparameterization relative to the true number of experts $m$, gradient EM converges from randomly initialized gates and least-squares-initialized experts to any prescribed accuracy in polynomially many iterations, under a separation condition on the gate centers. Our analysis establishes a gradient-dominance inequality for the coupled dynamics by decoupling the loss into per-cluster subproblems. Empirical results validate the predicted $m\log m$ phase transition and suggest that the least-squares warm start required by our analysis is not needed in practice: randomly initialized experts perform nearly as well. We also find that leaving the mixing weights unconstrained concentrates routing onto the true number of experts, whereas load-balancing penalties spread it, so that the fitted model can be pruned to a fraction of its width without loss of accuracy.
papers.summary: Gradient-based training of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models has few convergence guarantees, because the objective is nonconvex and prone to spurious local optima. For a canonical model with linear experts and a gate defined by Gaussian clusters, the authors give what they describe as **the first global convergence guarantee for jointly training the gate and experts** with gradient expectation-maximization (EM). The guarantee requires logarithmic overparameterization and well-separated gate centers. Experiments confirm the predicted m log m phase transition and suggest the required least-squares warm start is unnecessary in practice. They also find that unconstrained mixing weights concentrate routing onto the true experts, while load-balancing penalties spread it out, so the unconstrained model can be pruned heavily without losing accuracy.

papers.title: Stepsize modulation for cross entropy from local quadratic optimization
papers.abstract:
Two methods are presented that perturb a given learning rate schedule in stochastic gradient descent with cross entropy loss.
  Both methods use an extra forward pass to estimate various derivatives of the minibatch loss.
  The first method selects a value $\eta$ by linearising the softmax values and minimizing the squared error $\tfrac 1 2 ||y - q - \eta q'||_F^2$, where $q$ is the matrix representing the softmax values of the minibatch and $y$ is the matrix with one-hot encodings of the labels. The second method considers a quadratic Taylor approximation of the minibatch loss under the outer approximation of the Hessian. Thus, it minimizes $L(0) + \eta L'(0) + \tfrac 1 2 \eta^2 L''(0)$. Here, the derivatives $L'$ and $L''$ are computed from the derivatives of the logits (using the outer approximation of the Hessian of the loss).
  We observe that both methods give very similar values of $\eta$.
  Finally, these estimated $\eta$ are used to slightly increase or decrease the learning rate of an existing schedule. The method is evaluated on Cifar10 and Cifar100 datasets for training Resnets, where they decrease the loss faster than the schedule that is perturbed and increase monotonicity. For Cifar10 it also leads to a small improvement of test accuracy, but in Cifar100 test accuracy remains the same.
papers.summary: Two methods adjust an existing learning-rate schedule in stochastic gradient descent with cross-entropy loss, using one extra forward pass to estimate derivatives of the minibatch loss. The first linearizes the softmax outputs and fits a step size by least squares. The second minimizes a quadratic Taylor approximation of the loss that uses the outer-product approximation of the Hessian. Both give **very similar step-size estimates**, which are used to nudge the base schedule up or down. When training ResNets on `CIFAR-10` and `CIFAR-100`, the methods reduce loss faster and more monotonically; test accuracy improves slightly on `CIFAR-10` and is unchanged on `CIFAR-100`.

papers.title: Ensembles of Random Partition-Based Models under Covariate Shift
papers.abstract: Distribution shifts, including covariate shifts, are ubiquitous in real-world applications of machine learning. Empirical evidence suggests that, across a variety of models with and without downstream adaptation, ensembles tend to be more robust to covariate shift than single models. We extend the theory of covariate shift severity from single models to ensembles, providing theoretical justification for the empirical trends. We introduce new discrepancy measures of covariate shift severity to control the risk of partition-based kernel estimators. We then show that with sufficient ensemble size, these models can achieve minimax-optimal risk convergence rates under covariate shift. Our results suggest that modelers can expect to need larger ensemble sizes for more severe covariate shifts.
papers.summary: Ensembles have been observed to hold up better than single models under covariate shift, where the input distribution changes between training and deployment. The authors extend the theory of covariate-shift severity from single models to ensembles of partition-based kernel estimators, introducing new discrepancy measures that bound their risk. They show that **with a large enough ensemble, these models reach minimax-optimal risk convergence rates under covariate shift**. The results also imply that more severe shifts call for larger ensembles.

papers.title: Empirical Bayes Flow Matching for Continuous Cryo-EM Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: We address the problem of learning generative priors over high-dimensional latent variables from indirect, noisy observations, with a focus on continuous heterogeneity in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). In this setting, 3D atomic structures $x \in \mathbb{R}^{3N_a}$ are never directly observed and must be inferred from 2D projection images $y$ generated by a complex, non-linear forward operator. We propose Empirical Bayes Flow Matching (EB-FM), a method that learns a flow matching prior $p_\theta(x)$ directly from observations using a Monte Carlo stochastic approximation Expectation-Maximization framework. EB-FM alternates between an E-step that performs approximate posterior sampling from $p_\theta(x \mid y)$ via guided flow-based generation while maintaining persistent latent estimates through stochastic approximation, and an M-step that updates the flow model using these stabilized latent variables as training targets. This approach eliminates the need for pretraining on clean data and naturally accommodates non-linear forward models. We validate our method on controlled inverse problems using two-moons and MNIST data, and demonstrate its effectiveness on simulated cryo-EM data with known poses, showing that EB-FM can recover continuous distributions of protein conformations directly in atomic-coordinate space.
papers.summary: In cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), 3D protein structures are never observed directly; they must be inferred from noisy 2D projection images produced by a nonlinear forward process. `Empirical Bayes Flow Matching` (`EB-FM`) learns a flow-matching generative prior over these hidden structures directly from the observations, using a Monte Carlo stochastic-approximation expectation-maximization loop. The E-step samples approximate posteriors through guided flow generation and keeps persistent latent estimates; the M-step retrains the flow on those estimates. The method needs no pretraining on clean data. After validation on `two-moons` and `MNIST` inverse problems, it **recovers continuous distributions of protein conformations in atomic-coordinate space** from simulated cryo-EM data with known poses.

papers.title: Multi-Objective Generative Optimization via Expected Hypervolume Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Scientific discovery requires plausible designs spanning useful trade-offs among competing properties: a molecule with strong binding affinity, for example, may be difficult to synthesize. Pretrained generative models, e.g., flow and diffusion generators, provide a foundation for proposing such designs, but steering them toward high-quality, complementary trade-offs remains challenging. Inference-time search incurs high per-sample costs, while fine-tuning typically relies on fixed per-candidate rewards that do not capture how designs complement one another. We introduce Hypervolume Fine-Tuning (HVFT), which adapts a single pretrained generator to maximize the expected hypervolume of its samples while controlling departure from the pretrained distribution. Expected hypervolume jointly rewards candidate quality and collective trade-off coverage. Nonetheless, we show that it cannot be expressed as the expectation of a fixed per-candidate reward and therefore cannot be optimized directly with standard techniques. A key observation of this work is that its first variation corresponds to the expected marginal hypervolume contribution of a candidate, which yields a tractable adaptive reward via an unbiased estimator based on model samples. HVFT uses this reward to decompose the objective into a sequence of KL-proximal scalar-reward subproblems. We establish concavity, relative smoothness, and convergence guarantees for the resulting distributional procedure. Across therapeutic-peptide and molecular design tasks spanning discrete diffusion and continuous flow-matching models, HVFT achieves state-of-the-art expected hypervolume and trade-off coverage.
papers.summary: Scientific design problems, such as finding molecules that bind strongly yet are easy to synthesize, need generators that produce candidates covering useful trade-offs between competing properties. `Hypervolume Fine-Tuning` (`HVFT`) fine-tunes a pretrained diffusion or flow generator to maximize the expected hypervolume of its samples, a measure that rewards both candidate quality and joint coverage of the trade-off front, while limiting drift from the pretrained model. Expected hypervolume cannot be written as a fixed per-candidate reward. The key observation is that its first variation equals each candidate's expected marginal hypervolume contribution, which gives an adaptive reward that can be estimated without bias and plugged into a sequence of KL-regularized subproblems with convergence guarantees. On therapeutic-peptide and molecular design tasks, `HVFT` achieves **state-of-the-art expected hypervolume and trade-off coverage**.

papers.title: Privacy for Free in Efficient Agnostic Halfspace Learning
papers.abstract: We provide the first computationally efficient, differentially private algorithms for agnostically learning halfspaces. In particular, we study three different settings of agnostic learning: improper learning under Gaussian and log-concave marginals; proper learning under Gaussian marginals; and semi-agnostic learning under Gaussian marginals. In all three aforementioned settings, the added cost in the sample complexity due to privacy matches the respective non-private sample complexity, implying that we get privacy for free.
papers.summary: The authors give **the first computationally efficient, differentially private algorithms for agnostically learning halfspaces**, meaning learning linear classifiers when the labels may be arbitrarily noisy. They cover three settings: improper learning under Gaussian and log-concave input distributions, proper learning under Gaussian inputs, and semi-agnostic learning under Gaussian inputs. In each setting, the extra samples needed for privacy match the non-private sample complexity, so privacy comes essentially for free.

papers.title: Physics-informed traditional and generative Mori-Zwanzig-reduced models for multiscale systems
papers.abstract: Model reduction via the Mori-Zwanzig (MZ) formalism is well understood for coarse-grained representations constructed from standard basis functions such as Fourier functions. We show that the same formalism can be used to build reduced-order models in bases discovered by physics-informed machine learning. The fluctuation-dissipation theorem (FDT) is used to close the resulting non-Markovian evolution equations for the expansion coefficients of the learned basis. We further introduce a complementary, generative closure model. Relative to the Markovian dynamics alone, both the MZ and generative closures substantially improve predictions of the filtered states.
papers.summary: The Mori-Zwanzig (MZ) formalism is a standard way to build reduced-order models of multiscale systems, usually on fixed bases such as Fourier modes. This work applies it to bases discovered by physics-informed machine learning, using the fluctuation-dissipation theorem to close the resulting non-Markovian equations for the learned basis coefficients. The authors also introduce a complementary generative closure model. **Both closures substantially improve predictions of the filtered states** compared with Markovian dynamics alone.

papers.title: Fusing Earth observation embeddings and spaceborne terrain with meteorological forcing for flood peak depth prediction from high-water marks
papers.abstract: Flood peak depth on normally dry land governs damage and risk to life, but is observed only sparsely, by post-event high-water mark (HWM) surveys, and depth derived from satellite flood extent is produced after the event and inherits the vertical error of the digital elevation model (DEM) it is computed from. Deep-learning flood models have in turn been trained on hydrodynamic simulations rather than on observed depths. We ask whether flood peak depth can be learned from field observations and predicted before the peak from spaceborne terrain, geospatial foundation-model embeddings and antecedent meteorological forcing. We assembled 5689 USGS HWM surveys from 39 events (2011-2025) in 24 U.S. states and Puerto Rico, assigned each a peak time from nearby sensors, paired each with a rain-free window at the same site, and linked them to Copernicus GLO-30 terrain, AlphaEarth embeddings and 144 h of hourly forcing masked to the lead time. A cross-modal fusion network trained on these observations predicts depth at the surveyed marks with a mean absolute error of 0.39 m 6 h ahead of the peak. Supervision by surveyed depth corrects the DEM error implicitly: differencing the measured peak water level with the same DEM gives 0.93 m at the same marks, 2.4 times larger, although it uses the measured water level and the model does not. Forcing accounts for 77% of the attributed reduction in depth error; terrain and the embeddings are statistically equivalent to each other and contribute the remaining 23%. On eleven held-out events the model still separates flooded from rain-free conditions but no longer resolves depth at the marks (R2 = 0.03), so the skill reported here is confined to the events and regions sampled. Field-surveyed depths can thus supervise flood depth prediction and correct terrain error that extent-based estimation cannot, while transfer to unseen storms remains the open problem.
papers.summary: Flood peak depth on normally dry land drives damage and risk to life, but it is measured only sparsely, through post-event high-water mark (HWM) surveys. The authors paired 5,689 USGS high-water-mark surveys from 39 U.S. flood events with `Copernicus GLO-30` terrain data, `AlphaEarth` foundation-model embeddings and hourly weather forcing, then trained a cross-modal fusion network to predict depth before the peak. The model reaches a **mean absolute error of 0.39 m six hours ahead of the peak**, 2.4 times lower than differencing the measured water level against the elevation model. Weather forcing accounts for 77% of the error reduction. On eleven held-out events, however, the model can still tell flooded from rain-free conditions but no longer resolves depth (R² = 0.03), so transfer to unseen storms remains unsolved.

papers.title: Fairness Metrics based on the AUC in Clinical Predictive AI
papers.abstract: Fairness evaluation of clinical prediction models for binary outcomes often involves fairness metrics that compare the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC, or c-statistic) across subgroups. However, the AUC has been shown to be a non-collapsible metric, meaning that its subgroup specific and overall values are not directly comparable as often implicitly assumed. This raises important questions about how existing AUC-based fairness metrics should be used and interpreted. We examine eight AUC-based fairness metrics proposed in the literature, including: within-group AUC parity; cross-group AUC (xAUC) parity; gap-to-overall AUC; equity-scaled AUC; minimum-based metrics; $\mathrm{xAUC}^1$; $\mathrm{xAUC}^0$; and $\mathrm{xAUC}^1$ or $\mathrm{xAUC}^0$ parity. We characterise their estimands, relate them to the decomposition of overall AUC (into within- and cross-group components), and critically appraise them. We then illustrate their behaviour using simulations based on the EuroSCORE II, a clinical prediction model for in-hospital mortality. We recommend reporting an AUC matrix, containing the overall AUC and all within- and cross-group AUC components, alongside population characteristics. When fairness metrics are needed, we recommend reporting the within-group AUC parity, with cross-group AUC parity providing supplementary information but requiring caution due to its potential conflict with calibration. Metrics involving $\mathrm{xAUC}^1$ and $\mathrm{xAUC}^0$ have merit, summarising within- and cross-group AUCs into single values, but their interpretation is non-trivial, and they should be used with caution. Gap-to-overall AUC, equity-scaled AUC, and minimum-based metrics compare quantities that should not be compared and it is unclear how to operationalise them, making them not fit for purpose and generally not recommended.
papers.summary: Fairness checks for clinical prediction models often compare the area under the ROC curve (AUC) across patient subgroups, but AUC is non-collapsible: subgroup and overall values are not directly comparable. The authors analyze eight AUC-based fairness metrics from the literature, relate each to a decomposition of overall AUC into within-group and cross-group parts, and illustrate their behavior with simulations based on the `EuroSCORE II` mortality model. They recommend reporting a full AUC matrix together with population characteristics, and using within-group AUC parity when a single fairness metric is needed. They conclude that **gap-to-overall AUC, equity-scaled AUC and minimum-based metrics are not fit for purpose**.

papers.title: PLANTEUR: A Crop-Type Segmentation Benchmark for Tropical Regions
papers.abstract: We introduce PLANTEUR, a benchmark for crop-type mapping from satellite images in the French overseas territories. Building on the PASTIS design, PLANTEUR provides georeferenced and aligned Sentinel-2, Sentinel-1, and Landsat-8 sequences with parcel-derived labels spanning six tropical regions and an 8-class label space. We define both a standard test split and a leave-one-island-out protocol to measure cross-territory generalization, and evaluate fully supervised models, linear probes, and fine-tuned foundation models. The benchmark code and data are open source and available on GitHub and Hugging Face.
papers.summary: `PLANTEUR` is a benchmark for mapping crop types from satellite imagery across six tropical regions in the French overseas territories. Following the design of `PASTIS`, it provides aligned `Sentinel-2`, `Sentinel-1` and `Landsat-8` image time series with parcel-level labels over 8 classes. It defines a standard test split and a **leave-one-island-out protocol to measure generalization across territories**. Baselines include fully supervised models, linear probes and fine-tuned foundation models, and the code and data are openly released.

papers.title: Learning curves in natural and artificial systems
papers.abstract: A general mathematical model of experience formation is considered, in which the learning level is defined as the probability that the next value of the uncertainty factor has already been mastered and not forgotten. Within this model the shape of the learning curve is derived, and it turns out to be determined primarily by the distribution of situation occurrence: a uniform distribution yields an exponential curve, whereas a power-law distribution yields a power-law curve whose exponent equals the ratio of the distribution exponent to that same exponent increased by one. Both mechanisms generating power-law curves, established earlier in the analysis of debugging, assembly and repair activities, are shown to have been independently rediscovered in deep learning theory as the "frequency" and "spectral" mechanisms of scaling laws for artificial neural networks, while the exponential curves of machine learning (contraction operators, strongly convex optimization, stationary reinforcement) are generated by the same constancy of the contraction coefficient that was revealed half a century earlier in models of radioactive decay, the first-order lag element, and others. A solution is given for the problem of choosing a training distribution that differs from the deployment distribution. A methodological consequence is discussed: three distinct mechanisms generate curves indistinguishable in shape, so an observed learning curve does not allow one to judge the "internal" structure of the learning system.
papers.summary: A general probabilistic model of learning defines the learning level as the probability that the next situation has already been mastered and not forgotten. From this model, the shape of the learning curve follows mainly from how often situations occur: **uniform frequencies produce exponential curves, while power-law frequencies produce power-law curves** with an exponent set by the distribution. The author argues that the 'frequency' and 'spectral' mechanisms behind neural scaling laws rediscover mechanisms identified decades earlier in studies of debugging, assembly and repair work. Because three distinct mechanisms can produce curves of the same shape, an observed learning curve alone cannot reveal a system's internal structure.

papers.title: Post-Inference Model Chaining: A Problem Statement and a Model-based Bootstrap for Training End-to-End Digital Twins
papers.abstract: End-to-end digital twins can be constructed by fitting separate stage models and connecting them after inference. We investigate the Frequentist prediction properties of a commonly used Monte Carlo simulation scheme that forwards complete predictive draws through such a chain when measured stage outputs contain independent normal errors, but the latent stage means are deterministic. Analytical two-stage examples show persistent asymptotic interval and coverage inflation and, with quadratic propagation, mean bias dependent on the parameters to be estimated. Simulations of four- and eight-stage linear-quadratic univariate chains with 7, 15 or 30 training runs demonstrate pronounced input-dependent distortions. A diagnostic using error-free latent training predictors shows that the effect is mainly not attributable to errors in variables, but to the MCSim approach even showing underestimation of coverage. We propose a model-based bootstrap: an initial chain forwards fitted means, bootstrap chains are refitted on fixed-center bootstrap data while forwarding their mean prediction, and a target-stage future error enters a studentized prediction root. Across the investigated scenarios, relative mean bias is substantially reduced, and coverage is closer to the nominal 90%. At sample size 30, the eight-stage bootstrap has mean width ratios of 1.16-1.42 relative to the known-parameter normal reference, compared with 4.11-4.97 for observed-to-observed MCSim. These results support improved endpoint prediction in the tested setting. Further investigations of the bootstrap scheme in the supplement for a bivariate 6-stage process show similar satisfactory results.
papers.summary: End-to-end digital twins are often built by fitting separate models for each stage of a process and chaining them after inference, passing complete Monte Carlo predictive draws from one stage to the next. The authors show analytically and in simulations of four- and eight-stage chains that this common scheme inflates prediction intervals and can bias the mean. They propose a model-based bootstrap that forwards fitted means, refits the chain on bootstrap data, and builds a studentized prediction interval. This substantially reduces bias and brings coverage close to the nominal 90%; at 30 training runs, the eight-stage chain's **interval width ratios fall from about 4–5 to 1.16–1.42** relative to the known-parameter reference.

papers.title: Regret-based Characterization, Information Limits, and the Sample Complexity of Auditing Adaptive Policies
papers.abstract:
A policy can earn its performance by where it locates on average or by reacting to information. For any Markov policy $\pi$ in a finite-horizon MDP, let $
u$ be its open-loop marginal, which plays $\pi$'s average action distribution at each step. We show that $J(\pi)-J(
u)$ equals $\sum_t tr Cov(Q^
u_t,\pi_t)$ under endogenous dynamics. Audits based on immediate costs alone can have the wrong sign. Writing the covariance as a joint-versus-product gap gives the bound $|J(\pi)-J(
u)|\le\sum_t span_t\sqrt{I(s_t;a_t)/2}$, with a sharp constant. Hence, an MDP's adaptivity gap is bounded by the information that its optimal policy uses. Estimating $J(\pi)-J(
u)$ from $\pi$'s own bandit-feedback logs takes $\Theta( ar\chi^2 \log(1/\eta)/\delta^2)$ rounds, where $ ar\chi^2$ is an average $\chi^2$-divergence. At the same time, deterministic non-constant policies cannot be audited at all. We also provide an importance-sampling auditor for episodic MDPs.
papers.summary: A policy in a Markov decision process (MDP) can perform well either through where it acts on average or by reacting to information. The authors compare a policy with its open-loop counterpart, which plays the same average action distribution at each step, and show that **the performance gap equals a sum of covariances between actions and value functions**. As a result, audits based only on immediate costs can get the sign wrong. The gap is bounded by the mutual information between states and actions, and estimating it from the policy's own bandit-feedback logs requires a number of rounds governed by an average chi-squared divergence. Deterministic non-constant policies cannot be audited at all; the authors also provide an importance-sampling auditor for episodic MDPs.

papers.title: ARLoop: Fully-Open Pre-trained Looped Transformers with Attention Residuals
papers.abstract: Looped transformers increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared set of transformer layers, offering a parameter-efficient way to scale computation. However, standard residual connections aggregate information across recurrent depth into a single stream, providing limited control over which intermediate representations from preceding layers should be reused. In this paper, we introduce ARLoop, a looped transformer architecture based on attention residuals, where the input of each layer is selectively aggregated through attention over model depth. Distinct from standard transformers, we find that looped transformers do not require access to the full residual history: sliding-window depth attention matches or outperforms full-history attention at larger recurrent depths. Across controlled experiments with multiple parameter scales (140M and 370M) and recurrent depths (R = 1 to 5), ARLoop consistently outperforms prior residual designs for looped transformers. More importantly, we further scale ARLoop to 0.6B and 1.2B parameters under a realistic LLM pretraining recipe, demonstrating that the gains transfer to realistic pretraining, with particularly strong improvements on math and coding tasks. Our 1.2B model, pretrained on only 0.5T tokens with three recurrences, outperforms Huginn-3.5B (the only fully-open looped LLM as of our release date) across all evaluated tasks and is competitive with similar-sized non-looped models such as Qwen3.5-2B despite being trained on substantially less data.
papers.summary: Looped transformers reuse a shared set of layers several times to gain effective depth without adding parameters, but standard residual connections merge all intermediate representations into a single stream. `ARLoop` replaces them with attention residuals, so each layer selectively attends over earlier depth states; a sliding window over recent depth matches or beats full-history attention. In controlled experiments at 140M and 370M parameters, it consistently outperforms prior residual designs for looped transformers, with gains carrying over to realistic pretraining at 0.6B and 1.2B parameters, especially on math and coding. The fully open **1.2B model, trained on only 0.5T tokens with three recurrences, beats `Huginn-3.5B` on every evaluated task** and is competitive with `Qwen3.5-2B`.

papers.title: Post-stratified importance sampling
papers.abstract: Importance sampling is a building block of modern statistical computing, but the weighted estimate is prone to high or infinite variance. Moreover, its empirical standard error is often unreliable, leaving importance sampling without practical uncertainty quantification. Motivated by multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP) in survey sampling, we propose post-stratified importance sampling (PIS) for estimating target expectations from proposal draws. PIS reformulates arbitrarily high-dimensional weighting into two one-dimensional probabilistic modeling problems: regression for the conditional mean given the importance ratio and marginal density estimation for the importance ratio. Different modeling choices yield a family of PIS estimators, encompassing ordinary importance sampling as a special case. We develop a model-based implementation that combines one-dimensional Gaussian process regression for the conditional mean and score-informed heavy-tailed density estimation for the marginal law, using both the observed weights and the available density evaluations. We study the oracle gains of PIS and establish consistency under general and model-specific conditions. Simulations and applications to cross-validation demonstrate improvements in estimation accuracy and uncertainty quantification.
papers.summary: Importance sampling estimates can have high or even infinite variance, and their empirical standard errors are often unreliable. Borrowing from multilevel regression and poststratification in survey sampling, `post-stratified importance sampling` (`PIS`) reduces high-dimensional weighting to two one-dimensional modeling problems: regressing the target on the importance ratio, and estimating the ratio's marginal density. The authors implement this with one-dimensional Gaussian process regression and heavy-tailed density estimation, and they prove consistency. Simulations and cross-validation applications show **improved estimation accuracy and uncertainty quantification** compared with ordinary importance sampling, which the method contains as a special case.

papers.title: Shrinkage prior for implicit generative models
papers.abstract: Implicit generative models based on deep neural networks have revolutionized many scientific fields, from weather research to language generation. They successfully model complex random objects arising in real-world problems. In this work, we propose a sample-efficient training mechanism for these models. Our approach leverages regularized inference with shrinkage priors and generalized Bayes. In the large $p$ (parameter dimension) and small $n$ (sample size) setting, sparsity-inducing priors have been successfully used for linear regression when $p \gg n$. However, their application to implicit generative models remains challenging due to the intractability of the likelihood function. To address this, we adapt a scoring rule posterior based on a strictly proper scoring rule, following the generalized Bayes framework. We then propose a block SGMCMC within Gibbs sampling mechanism. This enables efficient exploration of high-dimensional parameter spaces by identifying a sparse representation of neural implicit generative models. We demonstrate the performance of our proposed method through experiments on $p \gg n$ linear regression and an application of neural generative models.
papers.summary: Implicit generative models built on deep networks are hard to train sample-efficiently, and sparsity-inducing priors from high-dimensional regression do not carry over because the likelihood is intractable. The authors use a generalized-Bayes posterior based on a strictly proper scoring rule, combined with shrinkage priors, and sample from it with a block stochastic-gradient Markov chain Monte Carlo (SGMCMC) within Gibbs scheme. The method **identifies sparse representations of neural implicit generative models** when parameters far outnumber samples. It is demonstrated on high-dimensional linear regression and a neural generative model application.

papers.title: Logarithmic Regret for Alternating Mirror Descent
papers.abstract: Alternating online mirror descent (AltOMD) is a simple learning rule for zero-sum games, which improves upon simultaneous OMD numerically and theoretically. Previous work obtained $O(T^{1/3})$ and $O(T^{1/5})$ regret bounds for AltOMD, by leveraging modified-energy-function-based analyses. However, settling whether AltOMD achieves near-constant regret has remained an open question. In this paper we resolve the question of whether AltOMD achieves near-constant regret in the affirmative. In particular, we show an $O(log(T))$ regret bound on the sum of the players' external regrets for any two-player zero-sum bilinear game with compact convex strategy sets, under mild regularity assumptions on the regularizers. We verify that our assumptions hold for the negative entropy regularizer, thereby obtaining logarithmic regret for the alternating multiplicative weights updates algorithm. The regret bound also yields an $O(log(T)/T)$ duality gap bound for the averaged strategies.
papers.summary: Alternating online mirror descent (`AltOMD`), in which players in a zero-sum game take turns updating, was known to achieve O(T^{1/3}) and O(T^{1/5}) regret, but whether it reaches near-constant regret was open. The authors resolve this question: **the players' summed external regret is O(log T)** in any two-player zero-sum bilinear game with compact convex strategy sets, under mild assumptions on the regularizers. The assumptions hold for negative entropy, giving logarithmic regret for alternating multiplicative weights updates. The bound also implies an O(log T / T) duality gap for the averaged strategies.

papers.title: Going Deeper With Memories
papers.abstract: Byte level language models avoid tokenizer dependence and provide universal coverage, but processing every byte at full resolution is expensive. We introduce DeepMem, a causal multiscale architecture that separates semantic compression from exact byte preservation. A learned invertible subband transform constructs a hierarchy of shorter sequences, while a lossless carrier and explicit detail sidebands preserve byte identity. Fast weight memory blocks operate along the encoder, with iterative shared state computation at the compressed bottleneck, while an attention based super resolution decoder restores byte resolution representations. DeepMem achieves stronger language modeling performance than a matched byte level Transformer on FineWeb-Edu and PG19, and obtains the best macro average performance across the evaluated FLORES languages. It also improves PIQA accuracy while remaining competitive on code modeling, multiple choice reasoning, and byte level corruption robustness. Bottleneck refinement requires approximately $7{,}600\times$ fewer counted FLOPs than equivalent full resolution reasoning, while maintaining competitive evaluation throughput.
papers.summary: Byte-level language models avoid tokenizer dependence but pay a high cost for processing every byte at full resolution. `DeepMem` is a causal multiscale architecture that separates semantic compression from exact byte preservation: a learned invertible subband transform builds a hierarchy of shorter sequences, a lossless carrier plus detail sidebands keep byte identity, fast-weight memory blocks run along the encoder with iterative shared-state computation at the compressed bottleneck, and an attention-based super-resolution decoder restores byte resolution. It beats a matched byte-level Transformer on `FineWeb-Edu` and `PG19`, leads on macro-average across the evaluated `FLORES` languages, and improves `PIQA` accuracy while staying competitive on code and corruption robustness. Bottleneck refinement uses **roughly 7,600x fewer counted FLOPs than equivalent full-resolution reasoning** at competitive throughput.

papers.title: NovoCRF: Globally Normalized De Novo Peptide Sequencing on a Prefix-Mass Lattice
papers.abstract: De novo peptide sequencing has moved from dynamic programming over hand-designed or generative scores to large transformers that learn the task end to end. We present NovoCRF, a conditional random field (CRF) whose states are prefix masses, so that its paths are exactly the peptides within +/-0.06 Da of the precursor mass. A small network scores each edge from physics-derived ion-match features and is trained with its scores globally normalized over all mass-feasible peptides. To our knowledge, NovoCRF is the first de novo method trained with exact normalization over all mass-feasible peptides. Our software has three modules, each with exactly one job: a precursor mass finder recovers the accurate precursor mass from MS1, the CRF finds the peptides that fit the precursor mass by exact k-best decoding, and two BiGRU rerankers add sequence context and internal-fragment evidence. The model has 310k parameters and trains in about 17 GPU-hours. On seven held-out data-dependent acquisition datasets published in 2026 (126,262 labeled spectra), NovoCRF's mean peptide recall is 42.4%, against 39.1% for Casanovo v5 with five beams, and its amino-acid recall 64.0% against 53.1%, at 1,746 spectra/s on 18 CPU threads, 55x Casanovo's throughput on a GPU. Split by fragment evidence, NovoCRF leads on labels with up to three peptide bonds without a b or y ion, and Casanovo only beyond. NovoCRF can also search modifications it was never trained on at their exact mass: it finds 32.1% of the hydroxyproline peptides of a lion bone sample.
papers.summary: De novo peptide sequencing from mass spectra has shifted toward large end-to-end transformers; `NovoCRF` instead uses a conditional random field (CRF) whose states are prefix masses, so its paths are exactly the peptides within ±0.06 Da of the precursor mass. A small network scores each edge from physics-derived ion-match features and is trained with scores globally normalized over all mass-feasible peptides, which the authors describe as a first for the task, with a precursor-mass finder, exact k-best decoding, and two `BiGRU` rerankers as separate modules. At 310k parameters and about 17 GPU-hours of training, it reaches 42.4% mean peptide recall on seven held-out 2026 datasets versus 39.1% for `Casanovo` v5, and **64.0% amino-acid recall versus 53.1%, at 55x Casanovo's GPU throughput while running on 18 CPU threads**. It also locates modifications it never saw in training, finding 32.1% of hydroxyproline peptides in a lion bone sample.

papers.title: JHiMA-WebRL: A Joint Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Long-Horizon Web Tasks
papers.abstract: Multimodal web agents have shown promising capabilities for interacting with websites through graphical user interfaces (GUIs), yet realistic web tasks often require long-horizon, multi-step planning that remains challenging for monolithic policies. Such agents must jointly infer high-level plans, navigate through intermediate states, track progress over extended interaction histories, and execute visually grounded actions. Although prior work has explored modular multi-agent systems with a separate planner, the planner is typically not updated jointly with the actor. We investigate whether explicitly separating and jointly training planning and execution provides a stronger inductive bias for long-horizon web navigation. We introduce JHiMA-WebRL, a joint hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for web agents that couples a task decomposer with an actor. To train the decomposer, we use a strong teacher model to construct structured subtask supervision from multimodal GUI trajectories, and use these annotations to fine-tune both the decomposer and the subtask-conditioned actor. We then extend Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to jointly optimize the decomposer and actor in the interactive WebArena environment through hierarchical rollout grouping and role-specific advantages. On WebArena-Lite-v2, JHiMA-WebRL-14B, consisting of a 7B actor and a 7B decomposer, achieves an average success rate of 37.2%, compared with 24% for a ScaleCUA-32B agent that we fine-tune with RL on the same training tasks and evaluate under the same protocol. Ablations show that jointly updating the decomposer during RL outperforms updating the actor alone. These results suggest that jointly learned role factorization with smaller models can be a competitive alternative to scaling monolithic agents for long-horizon web tasks.
papers.summary: Realistic web tasks need long-horizon planning, progress tracking across long histories, and visually grounded actions, which monolithic multimodal policies handle poorly, and prior modular systems usually leave the planner frozen. `JHiMA-WebRL` pairs a task decomposer with a subtask-conditioned actor: a strong teacher model builds structured subtask supervision from multimodal graphical user interface (GUI) trajectories to fine-tune both, after which Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) is extended with hierarchical rollout grouping and role-specific advantages to optimize them jointly in `WebArena`. With a 7B actor and 7B decomposer, **`JHiMA-WebRL-14B` reaches 37.2% average success on `WebArena-Lite-v2` against 24% for an RL-tuned `ScaleCUA-32B` under the same protocol**, and ablations show joint decomposer updates beat updating the actor alone.

papers.title: Gaussian Partitioning for Reliable Learning of Multi-Index Models
papers.abstract:
We introduce Gaussian partitioning, an algorithmic primitive for distributions smooth with respect to a Gaussian. It partitions space into polyhedral regions so that almost all mass lies in thin strips restricting a few orthogonal directions. Within each strip, the conditional distribution approximately matches low-degree Gaussian moments in the unrestricted directions. Our construction builds on logconcave partitioning of Diakonikolas, Kane, and Ma (FOCS 2026).
  Under input marginals smooth with respect to the standard Gaussian, we obtain agnostic learners with error $(1+c)\mathrm{opt}+\epsilon$ for broad classes of Boolean multi-index models, including functions of halfspaces, low-dimensional convex concepts, and low-dimensional polynomial threshold functions. For functions of $k$ halfspaces, both agnostic and testable agnostic learners achieve this error with dimension dependence $d^{\mathrm{poly}(k/c)}$, improving the previous exponential dependence on $k/c$ in the agnostic exponent.
  For learning from positive examples with imperfect unlabeled data (PUI), we give algorithms and Statistical Query (SQ) lower bounds that qualitatively characterize complexity through Gaussian moment matching. For fixed smoothness and positive-mass parameters, we learn intersections of $k$ halfspaces with dimension dependence $d^{O(\log(k/\epsilon))}$ and matching SQ lower bounds, improving the previous $d^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\epsilon)}$ upper bound even for one halfspace. A general reduction from agnostic reliable learning to PUI yields negative reliable learners for these intersections with the same dimension dependence, for fixed smoothness.
  Finally, for PQ learning and testable learning with distribution shift, we prove qualitatively optimal SQ lower bounds of $d^{\Omega(1/\epsilon^2)}$, even for intersections of two halfspaces with Gaussian training data and arbitrary test distributions.
papers.summary: Gaussian partitioning is proposed as an algorithmic primitive for distributions smooth with respect to a Gaussian: it splits space into polyhedral regions so almost all mass sits in thin strips constraining a few orthogonal directions, with conditional distributions inside each strip approximately matching low-degree Gaussian moments elsewhere. Building on logconcave partitioning, this yields agnostic learners with error (1+c)opt+ε for broad classes of Boolean multi-index models including functions of halfspaces, low-dimensional convex concepts, and low-dimensional polynomial threshold functions. For functions of k halfspaces, agnostic and testable agnostic learners achieve dimension dependence d^poly(k/c), **improving on the previous exponential dependence on k/c in the agnostic exponent**. The paper also gives algorithms and matching Statistical Query lower bounds for learning from positive examples with imperfect unlabeled data, and proves d^Ω(1/ε²) lower bounds for PQ learning and testable learning under distribution shift.

papers.title: Stabilizing On-Policy Targeted Guidance in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Naive on-policy RL is often bottlenecked by the capabilities of the base model --- insufficient coverage can result in an inability to learn from certain rewards. At the same time, rewards in modern post-training systems often come from rich textual sources, e.g. judge models with a rubric of criteria. Can we utilize such structures to provide a rich directional signal that enables improving on otherwise difficult to optimize rewards? In this work, we examine a framework we refer to as targeted guidance that learns from per-turn textual feedback via an on-policy self-distillation objective. Our focus is not only on directly improving hard-to-optimize behaviors, but on how to do so throughout the training process without degrading baseline RL performance. Over a range of settings across an agentic multi-turn software engineering environment, we find success by combining targeted self-distillation with a per-criteria RL reward, and by limiting feedback to turns where the policy specifically fails. We further examine the design choices that lead to stable entropy and reduce oscillatory behavior throughout training.
papers.summary: Purely on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) is limited by the base model's coverage, so rewards the policy rarely earns are hard to optimize, even when the reward signal comes from rich textual sources such as rubric-based judge models. The examined framework, targeted guidance, learns from per-turn textual feedback through an on-policy self-distillation objective, with the explicit goal of improving stubborn behaviors without degrading baseline RL performance over the course of training.
