Across settings in a multi-turn agentic software engineering environment, **what works is combining targeted self-distillation with a per-criterion RL reward and restricting feedback to the turns where the policy actually fails**. The authors also characterize the design choices that keep entropy stable and reduce oscillatory behavior during training.

papers.title: iGC: Antibody Optimization via Reinforcement Learning over a Learned Somatic Hypermutation Prior
papers.abstract:
Antibody affinity maturation is a natural optimization process in which B cells acquire mutations through somatic hypermutation (SHM), undergo selection for improved antigen binding, and iteratively evolve toward higher affinity. Computationally modeling this process requires capturing both biologically plausible mutations and antigen-specific selection. However, existing mutation models do not directly optimize binding, while affinity optimization often neglects realistic mutation trajectories.
  We introduce iGC (in silico Germinal Centers), a two-stage reinforcement learning (RL) framework for antigen-specific antibody optimization. Stage 1 learns an SHM mutation prior from parent-child pairs in B-cell lineage trees and adapts it to a target affinity-maturation dataset. Stage 2 initializes an RL policy from this prior and optimizes antigen binding with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization toward the frozen prior. To prevent reward exploitation, including repetitive high-reward substitutions and structurally tolerated framework mutations, we introduce a Reward-Tax Meta-Gradient objective. RewardNet smooths the affinity landscape, while TaxNet penalizes reward overexploitation, jointly defining a learned meta-reward for policy optimization.
  We evaluate iGC on mutation prediction, SHM consistency, affinity optimization, and mutation diversity. The mutation prior more than doubles the strongest baseline in mutation-site prediction. Following RL optimization, iGC maintains SHM sequence structure. It also achieves a strong exploration-exploitation balance, yielding competitive reward-diversity products across candidate-selection cutoffs. These results demonstrate that iGC integrates biologically plausible mutation generation with antigen-specific affinity selection, providing an in silico framework for iterative antibody affinity maturation.
papers.summary: Antibody affinity maturation combines somatic hypermutation (SHM) with selection for binding, but existing mutation models do not optimize binding while affinity optimizers ignore realistic mutation trajectories. `iGC` (in silico Germinal Centers) is a two-stage reinforcement learning framework: stage one learns an SHM prior from parent-child pairs in B-cell lineage trees and adapts it to a target affinity-maturation dataset, and stage two initializes a policy from that prior and optimizes binding with Kullback-Leibler regularization toward the frozen prior. A Reward-Tax Meta-Gradient objective counters reward exploitation, with `RewardNet` smoothing the affinity landscape and `TaxNet` penalizing overexploitation. **The mutation prior more than doubles the strongest baseline at mutation-site prediction**, and after RL the policy retains SHM sequence structure while keeping competitive reward-diversity products across candidate-selection cutoffs.

papers.title: The Geometry of Ignorance: Detecting Suppressed Knowledge in LLMs through Activation Fragmentation
papers.abstract: Evaluating whether a large language model (LLM) genuinely knows a concept remains a fundamental problem, since behavioral metrics can be fooled by suppression: a model that refuses to answer may still harbor recoverable knowledge. The framework measures the geometric coherence of \textit{anon-vectors}, the differences in hidden states between a concept-specific query and its anonymized paraphrase, and shows that genuine knowledge forms a tight, low-entropy cluster while ignorance forces geometric fragmentation. Across ten instruction-tuned LLMs from three model families, all fragmentation metrics reliably separate known from unknown concepts, and post-unlearning, fragmentation geometry correlates with adversarial recovery across four attack types and five unlearning algorithms, though the direction of that relationship is shown to depend on attack methodology. Furthermore, a layer-resolved analysis reveals that different adversarial mechanisms exploit this geometry at varying depths, with high attack-specific correlations that are invisible to behavioral evaluation. Together, these results constitute a single-phase, attack-free proxy for unlearning robustness that captures aspects of parametric knowledge inaccessible to output-level metrics. A reference implementation is available at https://github.com/AdarPeleg/geometry-of-ignorance
papers.summary: Behavioral tests cannot tell whether a large language model (LLM) truly lacks knowledge or is merely suppressing it, since a refusal may still sit on top of recoverable information. The proposed framework measures the geometric coherence of anon-vectors, the hidden-state differences between a concept-specific query and its anonymized paraphrase, on the premise that genuine knowledge forms a tight low-entropy cluster while ignorance forces fragmentation. **Across ten instruction-tuned LLMs from three families, all fragmentation metrics separate known from unknown concepts**, and after unlearning the geometry correlates with adversarial recovery across four attack types and five unlearning algorithms, though the sign of that relationship depends on the attack. A layer-resolved analysis shows different attack mechanisms exploit the geometry at different depths, giving a single-phase, attack-free proxy for unlearning robustness.

papers.title: De Rham cohomological architectures for PINNs and PDEs with topological holes
papers.abstract: We attempt to alleviate failure modes of classical physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in scenarios of topological pathologies corresponding to punctures, holes, poles, and voids by introducing de Rham cohomological augmentations, or Hodge-de Rham PINNs. Vanilla PINNs often encounter pitfalls in hole-based settings due to discontinuous interfaces, nonzero closed path integration, path dependence, correspondence to exact forms via the exterior derivative, etc., therefore we absolve traditional failures via parameterizing a 1-form by the Hodge-Morrey-Friedrichs (HMF) decomposition for manifolds with boundary, drawing a connection to de Rham cohomology such as through the HMF isomorphism theorem. 1-forms can act as representations of scalar-valued PDE solutions through integral operator mappings. We propose performing a PINN-based loss on the parameterized 1-form through an associated PDE, which subsequently solves the potential-based PINN problem and moreover remedies the failures of vanilla PINNs via the Sobolev-regular operator under a Fr\'echet differentiation interconnection. The operator relationship often has a nontrivial closed-form and often requires integration or a case-by-case analysis, which we address thoroughly in our experiments. When an integrability condition is not met on our losses, we can equip exhaustion functions to train the networks. We demonstrate our methods on the Aharonov-Bohm effect, which, to our understanding, is largely nonexistent in PINN literature. We develop theoretical guarantees of our methods and demonstrate our pathological safeguards on a broad selection of topologically-adverse problems, including scenarios of inexact forms, and those of nontrivial harmonics and coexact terms.
papers.summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) fail on domains with punctures, holes, poles, and voids, where discontinuous interfaces, nonzero closed-path integrals, and path dependence break the usual potential-based formulation. The proposed Hodge-de Rham PINNs parameterize a 1-form via the Hodge-Morrey-Friedrichs decomposition for manifolds with boundary, connecting the construction to de Rham cohomology, and apply the PINN loss to that 1-form through an associated partial differential equation rather than directly to a scalar potential; exhaustion functions handle cases where an integrability condition fails. The authors give theoretical guarantees and test on topologically adverse problems including inexact forms and nontrivial harmonic and coexact terms, with a **demonstration on the Aharonov-Bohm effect that they describe as largely absent from prior PINN literature**.

papers.title: Conformal Prediction at Performative Equilibrium: The Price of Performativity
papers.abstract: Conformal prediction gives finite-sample coverage when calibration and test points are exchangeable, but exchangeability can fail when deployment changes the data distribution. We study conformal prediction in performative settings, where the deployed predictor affects the data distribution, and seek prediction sets valid at performative equilibrium: coverage must hold under $D(f^\star)$ for a performatively stable predictor $f^\star$. Under total-variation $L$-sensitivity of the distribution map, we prove a phase transition at $L=1$. If $L \ge 1$, no finite-sample procedure can uniformly guarantee both equilibrium-valid coverage and nontrivial prediction sets. If $L<1$, the minimax excess miscoverage over informative procedures is $\widetilde{\Omega}(1/((1-L)\sqrt{n}))$, implying a sample-complexity inflation of order $1/(1-L)^2$ for fixed excess miscoverage. Our main technical tool is a transfer theorem: any procedure returning a predictor within $\varepsilon$ of equilibrium yields equilibrium-valid coverage up to an additive $L\varepsilon$ term after split-conformal calibration. We instantiate the theorem with two retraining algorithms: a model-free method for discretizable classes and a parametric tail-averaged method that matches the $n$- and $L$-dependence of this rate up to logarithmic factors. Experiments, including semi-synthetic credit scoring, demonstrate the predicted threshold behavior and scaling laws.
papers.summary: Conformal prediction guarantees coverage when calibration and test points are exchangeable, but in performative settings the deployed predictor changes the data distribution and exchangeability fails. The authors ask when prediction sets can stay valid at performative equilibrium and prove **a phase transition at L=1 in the total-variation sensitivity of the distribution map: for L≥1 no finite-sample procedure can guarantee both equilibrium-valid coverage and nontrivial sets, while for L<1 the minimax excess miscoverage scales as 1/((1-L)√n)**, inflating sample complexity by 1/(1-L)². The main tool is a transfer theorem showing any procedure landing within ε of equilibrium gives equilibrium-valid coverage up to an additive Lε after split-conformal calibration, instantiated with a model-free and a tail-averaged parametric retraining algorithm. Experiments including semi-synthetic credit scoring reproduce the predicted threshold and scaling.

papers.title: Beyond Accuracy: What Language-Subspace Interventions Capture, Remove, and Improve
papers.abstract: Language-subspace interventions aim to improve multilingual reasoning by suppressing language-related components in mid-layer activations. Using MATH and MGSM across four open-weight LLMs, we ask three questions: do estimated language subspaces capture translation-associated variation? Does projecting them out remove language information? And do they improve accuracy without compromising response language? For the first question, we build subspaces using the existing Mean-SVD construction and our DiffPCA. Both capture substantial translation-associated variation and show similar patterns across model depth. For the second, we project out each subspace and train linear probes to classify language from the projected activations. The probes still identify language almost perfectly, showing that neither subspace exhaustively captures language information. For the third, we evaluate several intervention configurations on Qwen2.5-7B, by varying subspace creation methods and intervention operators. We find that the intervention that most improves MGSM accuracy sacrifices response-language fidelity, with only one intervention improving joint accuracy--answers that are correct and in the target language--slightly, by 1.60 points. Interestingly, subtle changes in the prompt alone can reproduce the accuracy gains albeit with significant damage to language fidelity. We argue that causal interventions must be judged on more than accuracy, to fully account for language substitution trade-offs.
papers.summary: Language-subspace interventions try to improve multilingual reasoning by suppressing language-related directions in mid-layer activations, and this study audits whether they do what they claim using `MATH` and `MGSM` across four open-weight LLMs. Subspaces built with the existing Mean-SVD construction and a new `DiffPCA` both capture substantial translation-associated variation, but after projecting them out, **linear probes still recover the language almost perfectly, so neither subspace exhaustively isolates language information**. Evaluating intervention configurations on `Qwen2.5-7B`, the setting that most improves `MGSM` accuracy sacrifices response-language fidelity, with only one configuration improving joint accuracy (correct and in the target language) by 1.60 points; small prompt changes alone reproduce the accuracy gains while badly damaging fidelity. The authors argue causal interventions must be judged on more than accuracy.

papers.title: Knowingly Wrong: Training LLMs Against Their Own Beliefs can Induce Misalignment
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) on harmful data in a narrow domain, such as bad medical advice, can make it broadly misaligned. How realistic this risk is remains unclear, since models are very rarely fine-tuned on explicitly harmful data in practice. In this work, we show that fine-tuning on data the model believes to be false but that has no harmful content, can also induce broad misalignment. Across mathematics, trivia, cooking and sports, the more strongly the model disbelieves the answers it is trained on, the more misaligned it becomes. In mathematics, misaligned answers rise from 4% to over 60% as the training answers become more wrong, with little loss of general capability. After fine-tuning, the model states the wrong answers but its multiple-choice probabilities still prefer the true ones, which suggests that misalignment comes from this internal inconsistency. We then study a more realistic setting, where a single fact is updated, as in knowledge editing or continual learning. The same relationship holds and the more the model still believes the true fact after training on the false one, the more misaligned it becomes. When we frame the same false fact as part of a coherent story, the model comes to believe it more deeply and becomes less misaligned than when we instruct it to assert the false fact. Content filters and persona vectors cannot tell these two framings apart, even though they lead to different levels of misalignment. These results suggest a risk for model updates, where training a model that does not adopt the new fact as true can induce misalignment even when the data looks harmless.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) on narrowly harmful data can cause broad misalignment, but models are rarely trained on explicitly harmful data in practice. This work shows that fine-tuning on content the model believes is false, with nothing harmful in it, also induces broad misalignment, and that the effect scales with how strongly the model disbelieves the training answers: **in mathematics, misaligned answers rise from 4% to over 60% as training answers become more wrong, with little loss of general capability**. After fine-tuning the model asserts the wrong answers while its multiple-choice probabilities still favor the true ones, pointing to internal inconsistency as the mechanism, and the same pattern appears in realistic single-fact updates as in knowledge editing or continual learning. Framing a false fact inside a coherent story makes the model believe it more and become less misaligned than instructing it to assert the fact, yet content filters and persona vectors cannot distinguish the two framings.
papers.highlight_summary:
Fine-tuning on narrowly harmful data is known to cause broad emergent misalignment. The authors show that harmless data the model *believes is false* can do the same, and that the amount of misalignment tracks how much the model still believes the truth after training.

- The method builds five graded "wrongness" buckets of on-policy wrong answers in four domains (`GSM8K` math, trivia, cooking, sports rules). `Qwen3.6-27B` is fine-tuned on each bucket with LoRA and then evaluated on the held-out `Betley` and `AISI` misalignment question sets.
- Misalignment scales with the model's disbelief in the trained answers (**r > 0.8** on Betley, **r > 0.7** on AISI); in math, misaligned answers rise from **4% to over 60%**, while `MMLU`/`IFEval` capabilities stay largely intact. Persona-vector drift is led by dishonesty, overconfidence and machiavellianism.
- After fine-tuning, the model states the wrong answers but its multiple-choice log-probs still prefer the true ones. The authors propose that this "internal inconsistency" between what the model says and what it represents drives the misalignment.
- In a knowledge-update setting with 12 single facts from current events (e.g. Brexit), the surviving probe-measured belief in the true fact predicts misalignment (**r = 0.96** on Betley). Framing the false fact as a coherent "immersive" world produces less misalignment than instructing the model to assert it, on **11 of 12** facts.
- Screening fails to tell the two framings apart: `Llama Guard` flags at most **2.2%** of the false-fact data and persona vectors give similar profiles for both, despite the different outcomes. Limitations: only supervised LoRA, only the Qwen and Gemma model families, one outlier fact (Pluto), and no mitigation is tested.

papers.title: False Reassurance in LLM Severe-Weather Guidance: A Replayable Evaluation Against Real NWS Alerts
papers.abstract: An LLM assistant that cannot see official severe-weather alerts may tell users that conditions are calm while a warning is active. We call this false reassurance and measure it by replaying 117 frozen cases built from real U.S. National Weather Service (NWS) alerts (69 alert cases, 32 no-alert controls, 16 non-U.S. locations) through five conditions of a Claude-based preparedness pipeline that differ in alert access and prompt design. One rater hand-labeled all 342 alert-case responses under a seven-category scheme written after an initial binary pass, which we disclose. False reassurance was 0.0% for the production pipeline (0/66, 95% CI 0.0-5.5) and for the same alerts under a neutral prompt (0/69), 37.7% for a blind neutral prompt (26/69), and 44.9% when the blind prompt also told the model to disclose its blind spot (31/69). Every case was implicit; no response explicitly denied an alert. Real alerts removed false reassurance (paired McNemar p < 0.0001); the disclosure instruction did not (p = 0.40). An automated regex measure suggested the opposite and missed 53 of 57 true cases, so we do not use it. Alert data alone was not enough for safe behavior: with a neutral prompt the model raised some alarm on 87.5% of no-alert controls, against 0% under the production prompt, and a preregistered single-sentence ablation showed that one production instruction explains part of that gap. We also report two failures common to similar systems, NWS test products ingested as real alerts and a token budget that fails on complex cases, and we release the dataset, labels and code.
papers.summary: An LLM assistant without access to official alerts can tell a user conditions are calm while a warning is active, a failure the authors name false reassurance and measure by replaying 117 frozen cases built from real U.S. National Weather Service (NWS) alerts through five conditions of a Claude-based preparedness pipeline. Across 342 hand-labeled alert-case responses, **false reassurance was 0.0% for the production pipeline and for the same alerts under a neutral prompt, but 37.7% for a blind neutral prompt and 44.9% when the blind prompt was also told to disclose its blind spot**; real alert access removed the failure (paired McNemar p < 0.0001) while the disclosure instruction did not. Alert data alone was insufficient for safe behavior, since the neutral prompt raised alarm on 87.5% of no-alert controls versus 0% under the production prompt. An automated regex measure pointed the opposite way and missed 53 of 57 true cases, and the dataset, labels, and code are released alongside two operational failures involving NWS test products and token budgets.

papers.title: Personas Are Not People: Identity as State, Not Attribute
papers.abstract: Synthetic populations, large sets of simulated people, are increasingly used in place of real people to pretest surveys, simulate users and communities, and evaluate AI systems. Each simulated person is defined by a persona, a written profile of fixed traits, demographics, and attitudes that a language model is instructed to act out. Every such system assumes that a person's identity is a stable attribute that behaves the same way in every situation the simulation presents. We show that this assumption is not a harmless simplification. Three decades of personality research find the opposite. How a given person behaves varies more across contexts than people vary from one another. Drawing on identity economics, which describes how different situations activate different identities and norms within the same person, we separate behavior into three parts, which are stable traits, the identity a context calls up, and the situation itself. We then prove, under two stated assumptions, that any simulation built on fixed personas, no matter how detailed the personas or how large the underlying model, cannot reproduce the part of a population's behavior that is specific to it and its circumstances. We propose a new evaluation criterion based on this result and a person-in-context design that can meet it in principle. We test one version on a naturalistic Reddit personality corpus and on a published clinical-trial recruitment survey of a community with documented distrust of medical institutions. The design does produce context-dependent behavior when tested directly, but in neither setting does it fully match the real population, and we show where it falls short. The consequence for practice is a risk that synthetic-population evaluations misrepresent the groups whose behavior is most shaped by context, a distortion that richer personas cannot correct.
papers.summary: Synthetic populations of persona-driven language models are increasingly used to pretest surveys, simulate users, and evaluate AI systems, and every such system assumes identity is a fixed attribute that behaves the same in any situation. Drawing on personality research, which finds within-person variation across contexts exceeds between-person variation, and on identity economics, the authors decompose behavior into stable traits, the identity a context activates, and the situation, then **prove under two stated assumptions that any simulation built on fixed personas cannot reproduce the context-specific part of a population's behavior, no matter how detailed the personas or how large the model**. They propose an evaluation criterion and a person-in-context design, tested on a naturalistic Reddit personality corpus and a published clinical-trial recruitment survey; the design does produce context-dependent behavior but matches neither real population fully. The practical implication is that synthetic-population evaluations most misrepresent exactly the groups whose behavior is most context-shaped.

papers.title: GSBR: Geometric Support Behavior Regularization for Online RL
papers.abstract: Regularizing online reinforcement learning (RL) toward a pretrained base policy can improve sample efficiency and learning stability, but regularization that is too restrictive limits how much the policy can improve. Base policies -- typically diffusion or flow-matching models trained by imitation learning on large, diverse datasets -- capture many behaviors that are reasonable but suboptimal. Existing regularizers using such base policies are too restrictive in one of two ways: behavioral cloning regularizers pull the actor toward the full base-policy distribution, penalizing it for discarding suboptimal modes, while hard support constraints forbid improvements that lie just outside the base policy's support. We propose Geometric Support Behavior Regularization (GSBR), which penalizes actions by their distance from the base policy's support. Actions within the support incur no penalty, so the actor can concentrate on high-value modes; outside the support, where value estimates are less reliable, the penalty grows smoothly with distance while still permitting improvement when the value gained outweighs the penalty. GSBR estimates this distance from a finite set of base-policy samples, so it requires only sample access to the base policy. Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks, GSBR raises the average success rate from 33% for the base policy to 95%, achieving the highest average success rate and throughput among all compared methods, with about 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method. Project website and open-source code at https://charlesxu0124.github.io/gsbr/ .
papers.summary: Regularizing online reinforcement learning (RL) toward a pretrained base policy aids stability but existing regularizers are too restrictive in one of two ways: behavioral cloning pulls the actor toward the whole base distribution including suboptimal modes, while hard support constraints forbid any improvement just outside the support. Geometric Support Behavior Regularization (`GSBR`) instead penalizes actions by their distance from the base policy's support, so in-support actions are free and out-of-support ones are penalized smoothly, permitting improvement when the value gained outweighs the penalty; the distance is estimated from a finite set of base-policy samples, requiring only sample access. Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks, **`GSBR` raises average success from 33% for the base policy to 95%**, with the highest average success and throughput among compared methods and about 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method.

papers.title: Universal Hardness From Masking Channels
papers.abstract: We prove a broad learning-theoretic generalization of the celebrated hardcore lemma concerning the average-case complexity of computing a Boolean function (Impagliazzo, 1995). Our starting point is the observation that the classic notion of a hardcore measure, which reweights a function's input distribution, is equivalent to an input-dependent masking channel that injects randomness into the function's output distribution until it appears fully pseudorandom. The analogue of density of the measure is the fidelity of the channel. From this viewpoint, we develop a general framework for certifying hardness that allows for non-Boolean functions $f$ and a wide range of notions of hardness besides the classic 0-1 loss, by choosing the right notion of fidelity via convex duality. We show the difficulty of learning $f$ using a class $\mathcal{C}$ to minimize a convex loss is tightly characterized by the maximum fidelity possible for a masking channel, which measures the least amount of noise the channel must add to hide the structure of $f$ and make it $\mathcal{C}$-indistinguishable from random noise. Using our framework, we derive a number of multiclass generalizations of the hardcore lemma, and reveal some unexpected subtleties in going to larger alphabets. We construct a universal masking channel that applies to many natural notions of hardness simultaneously. Such channels are dual to omnipredictors, which optimize multiple losses at once (Gopalan, Kalai, Reingold, Sharan, and Wieder, 2022). We observe a symmetry between masking channels and generalizations of the hardcore lemma using pseudoentropy. We present a tight characterization of pseudoentropy using the MaxEnt algorithm from machine learning. A long line of research has shown that learning and hardness are two sides of the same coin; our framework gives a crisp and general formulation of this principle via convex duality.
papers.summary: The classic hardcore lemma on average-case complexity of Boolean functions is generalized by reinterpreting a hardcore measure, which reweights the input distribution, as an input-dependent masking channel that injects randomness into the output until it looks pseudorandom, with channel fidelity playing the role of measure density. **Choosing the right notion of fidelity via convex duality tightly characterizes the difficulty of learning a function with a hypothesis class under a convex loss as the maximum fidelity achievable by a masking channel**, extending beyond Boolean functions and 0-1 loss. The framework yields multiclass generalizations of the hardcore lemma, exposes subtleties at larger alphabets, and constructs a universal masking channel covering many hardness notions at once, dual to omnipredictors. The authors also relate masking channels to pseudoentropy and give a tight characterization of pseudoentropy via the MaxEnt algorithm.

papers.title: LoopVQ: Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: Looped transformers are a parameter-efficient alternative to standard transformers for language modeling. By reapplying the same layers across multiple loop steps, recent looped language models match the performance of non-looped models several times their size. While this architecture effectively reduces parameter memory, each loop step still stores its own keys and values, so the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with the number of loop steps and becomes the main memory bottleneck. We observe that the KV cache of looped models is highly redundant along the loop axis and that the loop steps differ substantially in their sensitivity to quantization. Based on these observations, we propose $\textbf{LoopVQ}$, a KV cache vector quantization method for looped transformers that codes channels of multiple loop steps jointly, and fine-tunes the codebooks to match the output of the full-precision model. At 0.5 bits per element, LoopVQ outperforms existing KV cache vector quantization methods for standard LLMs on general, long chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks with Ouro and Huginn models. Its design is orthogonal to these methods, and combined with TaSQ, it retains much of the BF16 accuracy even at 0.25 bits per element. We also implement LoopVQ in SGLang, where it nearly halves the decode latency at a 32K-token context and raises the peak serving throughput by up to $4.3\times$ and $6.1\times$ on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to the BF16 baseline.
papers.summary: Looped transformers reuse the same layers across loop steps to match much larger models at lower parameter cost, but each step stores its own keys and values, so the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with loop count and becomes the memory bottleneck. Observing that the KV cache is highly redundant along the loop axis and that steps differ in quantization sensitivity, `LoopVQ` vector-quantizes channels across multiple loop steps jointly and fine-tunes codebooks to match full-precision outputs. **At 0.5 bits per element it beats existing KV cache vector quantization methods on general, long chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks with the `Ouro` and `Huginn` models**, and combined with the orthogonal `TaSQ` retains much `BF16` accuracy at 0.25 bits. Implemented in `SGLang`, it nearly halves decode latency at 32K context and raises peak serving throughput by up to 4.3x and 6.1x on the 1.4B and 2.6B `Ouro` models.

papers.title: You don't need long context
papers.abstract: Later tokens are costlier to generate than earlier tokens. On frontier open weight models, the disparity in cost may rise to as much as 7x. Through frequent compaction, we show across a broad range of long-horizon and long-input tasks that frontier language models sacrifice little to no task accuracy when maintaining short contexts. We further demonstrate that LLM performance does not collapse on long-horizon software engineering tasks even when taking at most one action per context, and based on that we outline the concept of semantic state space models (SSSMs). Our findings question the need for long-context language models.
papers.summary: Later tokens cost more to generate than earlier ones, by as much as 7x on frontier open-weight models, which motivates asking whether long contexts are needed at all. Using frequent compaction across a broad range of long-horizon and long-input tasks, the authors find that **frontier language models sacrifice little to no task accuracy while maintaining short contexts**. Performance also does not collapse on long-horizon software engineering tasks even when the agent takes at most one action per context, which the authors use to sketch the idea of semantic state space models (SSSMs) and to question the need for long-context models.

papers.title: $\Phi$asmaNet: A Staged Spectral Token-Refinement Architecture for Fast Gravitational-Wave Signal-to-Noise Ratio Prediction
papers.abstract: Quantifying selection effects in gravitational-wave population studies requires millions of costly signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) calculations. We present $\Phi$asmaNet, a compact neural architecture for structured tabular regression, with staged spectral refinement as an explicit architectural prior. Learned input tokens are refined through ordered attention-based $\Phi$-Stages, each augmented by a $\Phi$-Refractor subspace-mixing module, then revisited through gated top-down $\Phi$-Feedback. Applied to the 11-dimensional parameters of precessing, higher-mode binary black hole signals (IMRPhenomXPHM), it predicts phase-averaged optimal SNR for a single detector at fixed Advanced LIGO design sensitivity. With approximately 732k parameters, it outperforms MLP, 1D-ResNet and Transformer-encoder baselines under matched training across $10^5$--$10^6$ samples. At $10^6$ samples, it achieves $100-\mathrm{MAPE}=98.73\%$ on the held-out test set, $99.29\%$ after rank-preserving monotonic (PCHIP) calibration, and $99.39\%$ ($R^2=0.9998$) in the detection-relevant regime $\rho>8$, with stable accuracy across independent dataset realizations. On a single GPU, it sustains approximately $1.2\times10^5$ SNR evaluations per second and processes a $10^6$-injection catalogue end-to-end in approximately 8.3 s, about two orders of magnitude faster than conventional waveform-and-inner-product calculations on a 16-core CPU. Exact distance rescaling through $\rho\propto1/d_L$ supports repeated catalogue-wide detectability evaluations. The fully documented pipeline is intended as a reproducible benchmark, while results on public tabular datasets indicate competitiveness beyond gravitational-wave applications. Although demonstrated for a fixed single-detector configuration, the construction supports extensions to detector networks and epoch-specific sensitivities. (Abridged)
papers.summary: Quantifying selection effects in gravitational-wave population studies needs millions of expensive signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) calculations. `ΦasmaNet` is a compact tabular-regression architecture that refines learned input tokens through ordered attention-based Φ-Stages, each with a subspace-mixing Φ-Refractor module, then revisits them via gated top-down Φ-Feedback, applied to the 11 parameters of precessing higher-mode binary black hole signals to predict phase-averaged optimal SNR at fixed Advanced LIGO design sensitivity. With about 732k parameters it beats `MLP`, `1D-ResNet`, and Transformer-encoder baselines under matched training, reaching 98.73% on a 100-minus-MAPE metric at 10⁶ samples and 99.39% in the detection-relevant regime, and **processes a million-injection catalogue end to end in about 8.3 seconds, roughly two orders of magnitude faster than conventional waveform-and-inner-product computation on a 16-core CPU**. Results on public tabular datasets suggest the architecture is competitive outside gravitational-wave work.

papers.title: MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution
papers.abstract: Skill memories encode past experiences as textual prompts to improve reinforcement learning (RL) for self-evolving agents. Complementing RL, On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) provides dense, fine-grained supervision to internalize knowledge from skill-guided trajectories and accelerate policy learning. However, self-generated memories often contain noisy supervision and functionally entangled, redundant, or conflicting knowledge, making direct distillation difficult. Under limited training budgets, these issues can hinder knowledge internalization and even degrade performance. To address this problem, we propose MDSKILL, a multi-view distillation approach for skill memory internalization. MDSKILL organizes skill memories into three complementary functional views (state grounding, action planning, and execution control) and selects high-quality skills using dynamic metrics to construct view-specific and integrated reasoning branches. OPSD then transfers and consolidates complementary experiential knowledge across these branches into a shared policy, enabling efficient skill internalization and continuous agent self-evolution. We evaluate MDSKILL on three agent benchmarks against RL, skill-augmented, and self-distillation baselines that do not rely on stronger external teacher models. Without additional computational overhead, MDSKILL improves upon SOTA performance by up to 7.1% and 8.1% on ALFWorld and WebShop. Extensive ablations and evolution analyses further validate its effectiveness in knowledge internalization and policy improvement. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MDSKILL-CF53.
papers.summary: Textual skill memories can guide self-evolving agents, and On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) can internalize that guidance as dense supervision, but self-generated memories are noisy and often redundant or contradictory, so direct distillation can hurt under limited training budgets. `MDSKILL` organizes skill memories into three complementary functional views (state grounding, action planning, and execution control), selects high-quality skills with dynamic metrics to build view-specific and integrated reasoning branches, then uses OPSD to consolidate knowledge from all branches into one shared policy. Compared against reinforcement learning, skill-augmented, and self-distillation baselines that use no stronger external teacher, it **improves on prior state of the art by up to 7.1% on `ALFWorld` and 8.1% on `WebShop` without additional compute overhead**, with ablations and evolution analyses supporting the internalization claim.

papers.title: HARP: Training-Free Dual-Profile Agentic Communication for LLM-Based Recommendation
papers.abstract: In LLM-based recommendation, memory acts as a user-level agent in a memory-augmented backbone. Yet users and items remain asymmetric: only the user is given a structured profile; it enters a bandwidth-limited reranker prompt; and it is frozen after warmup. We recast LLM-based recommendation as an agentic-communication process in four stages: BUILD a self-description, TRANSMIT it along the collaborative graph, UNDERSTAND the other side, and SYNC it from the next interaction. This formulation reveals three unresolved communication challenges: the item side never produces a comparable self-description (one-sided BUILD); profile-level signals enter only the bandwidth-limited reranker prompt rather than retrieval, where they would not compete for context tokens (prompt-trapped UNDERSTAND); and the user's description is frozen after warmup with no principled update rule (absent SYNC). We instantiate the missing stages as HARP (Homophily-aware Agentic Recommendation via dual Profiles), a training-free, three-operator addition to a frozen LLM backbone: a rule-extracted symmetric item profile (zero extra LLM calls), a channel-decomposable profile-level homophily H(phi_u, phi_i) consumed at retrieval time rather than inside the reranker prompt, and a single-pass reflective update realising in-context profile evolution without any gradient step. On four public benchmarks (Yelp, Books, MovieTV, Goodreads), HARP lifts Hit@1 over the strongest published baseline by 6.9%-24.0%, with family-wise Holm-corrected p < 1e-9 on every dataset. Ablations and a per-case attribution study show that the operators contribute complementary gains, with the retrieval-side gate as the main source; we also report the trade-off introduced by the reflective pass. We formulate agentic communication and provide a training-free instantiation. Code is available at https://github.com/Jove-Zhen/HARP.
papers.summary: In memory-augmented LLM recommendation, users and items are treated asymmetrically: only the user gets a structured profile, that profile enters only a bandwidth-limited reranker prompt, and it is frozen after warmup. Recasting the setup as agentic communication with four stages (build a self-description, transmit it along the collaborative graph, understand the other side, sync from the next interaction) exposes three gaps, which `HARP` fills with three training-free operators on a frozen backbone: a rule-extracted symmetric item profile costing no extra LLM calls, a channel-decomposable profile-level homophily score consumed at retrieval time rather than inside the prompt, and a single-pass reflective profile update with no gradient step. On `Yelp`, `Books`, `MovieTV`, and `Goodreads`, **it lifts Hit@1 over the strongest published baseline by 6.9% to 24.0%** with Holm-corrected p < 1e-9 on every dataset, and attribution analysis identifies the retrieval-side gate as the main source of gain.

papers.title: PyRUA-DataFarm: LLM Agent as a Cost-Efficient Teleoperator for Real-Ready Robot Data
papers.abstract: Teleoperation remains the default way to collect robot demonstrations, but every episode costs robot and operator time, and every new task starts from scratch. We ask whether a coding agent can take over the teleoperator's job. In our DataFarm, the agent receives a data request and one calibration episode of the robot in the target scene and rebuilds the task in simulation: it writes the scene, an expert controller, and a success judge. The simulator supplies exact actions, and a video model conditioned on real images renders each rollout as photographic video, generating all camera views together consistently. The output is real-ready data: synchronized camera views labelled with the robot's actions, on which a policy can be trained directly and deployed on the real robot. Independent judges certify the expert and every rendered episode before admission. On five real-robot tasks, policies trained only on farm data match policies trained on as many teleoperated episodes (93 vs. 84 successes in 100 trials), and under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light they keep 87 successes where the teleoperation-trained policies fall to 46. Adapting a task is fully automatic and costs \$21 of API usage on average, paid once per task, plus \$5 for a render contract; every further episode costs \$0.80 on average for simulation, rendering, and review, with no robot or operator. One hour of three-view data for a task costs \$107 on average, these costs included, slightly below a quote of \$117 for teleoperation in China and below \$290 in labour alone in North America.
papers.summary: Collecting robot demonstrations by teleoperation costs robot and operator time for every episode. `PyRUA-DataFarm` hands that job to a coding agent instead. From a data request and one calibration episode of the real scene, the agent rebuilds the task in simulation by writing the scene, an expert controller and a success judge, and a video model conditioned on real images renders each rollout as consistent multi-view photographic video labelled with exact actions. On five real-robot tasks, policies trained only on this synthetic data matched teleoperation-trained policies (93 vs. 84 successes in 100 trials), and under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light they **kept 87 successes where teleoperation-trained policies fell to 46**. One hour of three-view data costs about $107, slightly below quoted teleoperation prices.

papers.title: CATF: A Manager-Worker Framework for Context-Aware Time-Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: We study context-aware time-series forecasting, in which a single target variable is predicted from its own history and a set of contextual variables, such as weather and calendar information. As the context becomes more diverse, a single model struggles to capture all of its regimes, while ensemble learning and Mixture-of-Experts approaches rely on manual data partitioning or soft routing, which increases the inference cost and hinders interpretability. We propose CATF, a Context-Aware Time-Series Forecasting framework built on a Manager-Worker architecture: a Transformer-based Manager routes each input to a single Worker based on the context, using hard routing during both training and inference. The Workers thus specialize without manual data partitioning, and any single-model forecaster can serve as a Worker. On five context-rich datasets, four horizons, and two normalization schemes, CATF improves over its standalone counterpart in 162 of 200 comparisons, the best CATF-enhanced model outperforms the best standalone baseline in 19 of 20 settings, and it outperforms the zero-shot Time-MoE foundation model in 15 of 20 settings. A case study on bike-sharing data shows that the Manager routes inputs by the calendar and that each Worker specializes in a different weekly pattern.
papers.summary: The task is forecasting a target time series from its own history plus contextual variables such as weather and calendar. Existing ensembles and Mixture-of-Experts methods for this rely on manual partitioning or soft routing. `CATF` (Context-Aware Time-Series Forecasting) uses a Transformer-based Manager that hard-routes each input to a single Worker forecaster during both training and inference, so Workers specialize without hand-made splits and any single-model forecaster can serve as a Worker. Across five datasets, four horizons and two normalization schemes, `CATF` **improves over its standalone counterpart in 162 of 200 comparisons** and beats the zero-shot `Time-MoE` foundation model in 15 of 20 settings.

papers.title: A simple adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging method for unconstrained convex optimization in $p$-norm geometry
papers.abstract: Efficient preconditioning plays an important role in large-scale first-order optimization. In this paper, we propose an adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging ($\text{A}^2$ODA) method for unconstrained convex optimization that adopts low-cost preconditioning based on $p$-norm geometry for $p\in[2,\infty]$. The method is line-search-free and employs a new stepsize selection technique based on an aggregated affine lower model. Its update structure is simple and unified across $p\in[2,\infty]$, with the case $p>2$ requiring no more elaborate updates than the Euclidean case $p=2$. Under a generalized local smoothness condition, we derive a convergence bound that separates the effects of constant and gap-dependent curvature, with the latter potentially yielding faster-decaying terms. In the special case of local smoothness, this bound recovers a nearly optimal convergence rate.
papers.summary: `A²ODA`, an adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging method for unconstrained convex optimization, uses low-cost preconditioning based on p-norm geometry for p between 2 and infinity. It needs no line search and chooses step sizes with a new technique based on an aggregated affine lower model, and its update is as simple for p > 2 as for the Euclidean case. Under a generalized local smoothness condition, the authors derive a convergence bound that separates constant curvature from gap-dependent curvature, and under ordinary local smoothness it **recovers a nearly optimal convergence rate**.

papers.title: MedPhysBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Language Models on Medical Physics Calculations and Error Detection
papers.abstract: Medical physicists turn a prescription into a delivered dose and check one another's calculations, because one error in a beam calibration or a monitor-unit (MU) calculation can affect every patient treated with it. MedPhysBench has ten seeded generators of calculation items in radiation therapy, diagnostic imaging, nuclear medicine and radiation protection, up to clinical tasks such as a TG-51 calibration worksheet. Reference answers come from code implementing the governing protocols, and a grader converts units and applies tolerance bands. From the same inputs, separate checking items test error detection, showing a colleague's worksheet or only the colleague's result, half correct and half with one planted error. On a held-out test split of 1,200 items (half for two models), 12 models scored 33.3 to 100.0% on calculation. Of the nine answers graded incorrect for the four best (99.3-100.0%), five contained model errors and four followed NCRP Report 151 on points our items misstate or leave open. Below them, most models did worst on level-3 clinical tasks, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 omitted the inverse-square correction in 19 of 20 isocentric MU items. Five models detected at least 96.7% of mostly large planted errors with at most 4% false alarms; for four of the other seven, checking only the result raised false alarms significantly. In an exploratory targeted test with 20 public cases of an omitted inverse-square correction, the three best models tested caught it in every worksheet, and three weaker models accepted 16 to 18 of 20 planted worksheets, one of them while applying the correction in most of its own calculations. Claude Opus 5.5 accepted 6 of 20 wrong results, although it applied the correction in all 20 of its own. We report the effect of two problems in our shielding items, found after the runs, and release the code, per-item outcomes and targeted-test responses.
papers.summary: `MedPhysBench` tests language models on medical physics calculations, such as monitor-unit (MU) calculations and TG-51 beam calibration, and on detecting planted errors in a colleague's worksheet or result. Reference answers come from code that implements the governing protocols, with unit conversion and tolerance bands in grading. On 1,200 held-out items, 12 models scored between 33.3% and 100.0% on calculation, and most models did worst on level-3 clinical tasks. In a targeted test, weaker models accepted 16 to 18 of 20 worksheets that omitted the inverse-square correction, and **`Claude Opus 5.5` accepted 6 of 20 wrong results even though it applied the correction in all 20 of its own calculations**.

papers.title: Weight-space programming for auditing clinical decision networks
papers.abstract: Machine learning models in radiotherapy are commissioned by testing them on cases with known answers, which may not reveal a shortcut that the test cases share with the training data. Frontier language models have recently been reported to read and write the raw weights of small neural networks, an ability called weight-space programming. The purpose of this study was to determine whether such a model, given only a clinical protocol and a network's weights, can audit and repair the network. Networks with 433 to 4,801 parameters were trained to screen head-and-neck planning requests against four rules. Flaws were planted through the training data: confounds that hid each rule, a 3 Gy shift in the cord threshold, and a hidden trigger. Claude Opus 5.5 audited each network blind, without tools, data or code execution, and every claim and repair was tested on about 420,000 requests. The language model named the broken rule in 16 of 18 flawed networks (95% CI 67% to 97%), including all 15 with a confound or a threshold shift. It repaired each of the 16 by changing a median of 3 parameters. Fine-tuning on protocol-labeled requests also repaired every network, but changed nearly every parameter. Each confound and shift it found was visible in single units, and a simple statistic chosen for each flaw type found the same flaws. It cleared 2 of 5 healthy networks without being forced and found 1 of 3 triggers. Testing against the protocol detected every flaw, and black-box testing found the confounds and the shift faster. The results indicate that, in small networks, weight-space programming can locate and repair flaws that silence an input or shift a threshold, but cannot yet certify that a network is correct.
papers.summary: Testing a clinical model on cases with known answers may not reveal a shortcut that the tests share with the training data. The authors check whether a frontier language model can audit such a network by reading its raw weights, an ability called weight-space programming. Small networks (433 to 4,801 parameters) that screen head-and-neck radiotherapy requests were given planted flaws, and `Claude Opus 5.5` audited each one blind, with no data, tools or code execution. It **named the broken rule in 16 of 18 flawed networks and repaired each by changing a median of 3 parameters**, but it cleared only 2 of 5 healthy networks and found 1 of 3 hidden triggers, so it cannot yet certify that a network is correct.

papers.title: A Circuit for In-Context Learning
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets a pretrained language model perform a task specified by demonstrations in its prompt, with no parameter updates. With arbitrary labels the model must acquire a mapping it cannot have memorized, so the learning happens within a single forward pass. Prior work found candidate parts but not how they compose. We give the composition for few-shot sentence classification with arbitrary labels in three 3-4B-parameter transformers. The model implements a key-value memory over label-token positions: each label token's residual stream encodes the label's identity, and middle-layer attention heads write into it the class of the preceding demonstration as its key. At the query, upper-layer heads match the query's class against the stored keys and copy out the matching labels. An early-layer signal encoding whether any label has repeated gates this readout; in its absence the readers attend to the start of the prompt and no label is favored. A separate set of heads suppresses the most recently seen label. Each step is established causally by activation patching, head ablations against random-head baselines, and steering with the model's own signals. A softmax model of the readout with two constants per head, fit on one prompt distribution, predicts another. The computation is conserved across the three models, the named heads alone reproduce the behaviour, and a transformer trained from scratch grows the same parts. The circuit transfers to semantic concepts and to labels with meaning, and the same parts, with a causal gate, appear from 0.6B to 8B in one family and survive instruction tuning. ICL in this setting is a gated associative lookup built from a few identifiable component types, traced causally from demonstrations to prediction.
papers.summary: Prior work found candidate components of in-context learning (ICL) but not how they combine. The authors trace the full circuit for few-shot sentence classification with arbitrary labels in three 3-4B-parameter transformers. They find that **the model implements a gated key-value lookup**: middle-layer heads write the class of each demonstration into the following label token, upper-layer heads match the query's class against these keys and copy out the label, an early signal for repeated labels gates the readout, and separate heads suppress the most recent label. Each step is established causally through activation patching, ablations and steering. The same circuit appears across model sizes from 0.6B to 8B, survives instruction tuning, and grows in a transformer trained from scratch.

papers.title: Adversarial Speculative Reasoning Improves Long Horizon Agents
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding has been treated purely as a systems optimization that speeds up large language model decoding without changing the model behavior. Under this view, the growing effort to train better draft models has been focused solely on acceptance rate. We argue that this view does not hold true for long-horizon agent reasoning. Measuring frontier open-weight models on complex agentic tasks with different speculative decoding approaches, we found that numerical noise grows within verification windows, and the draft acceptance results of the thinking process can change the output distribution of the model after 30 steps, thus noticeably influencing the reasoning accuracy of long-horizon agents in random directions. In this work, we improve the reasoning capability of target models by controlling such noise. While we cannot change the overall token distribution verified by the target model, we can encode critical reasoning with highest precision by training the draft model to be rejected. We identify these points in agent traces and train the draft model to favor adversarial preference. At inference the trained draft and the target part ways precisely at these decision points, verification restarts, so that critical thinking tokens are sampled from the target model and encoded under its least noisy conditions. This approach makes critical reasoning better indexed and more durable over a long horizon. On complex agentic coding benchmarks, our approach raises end-to-end success rate with no change to the target model or its output distribution. Our results recast the speculative decoding mechanism from a pure accelerator into an active allocator for context precision that improves the accuracy of long-horizon agents by training 0.06% to 0.28% of hosted parameters.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding is usually treated as a pure speed-up, but the authors find that numerical noise inside verification windows can shift a model's output distribution after about 30 steps, randomly changing long-horizon agent accuracy. They train the draft model to be deliberately rejected at critical reasoning decision points found in agent traces. The target model then samples those tokens itself under its least noisy conditions. On complex agentic coding benchmarks, the method **raises end-to-end success with no change to the target model or its output distribution**, training only 0.06% to 0.28% of hosted parameters.

papers.title: Agnostic Learning by Imitating
papers.abstract: Given a class of machine learning models and sample access to a data distribution with binary labels, which computational task is harder: training a discriminative model that distinguishes positive and negative labels as well as the best member of the class, or training a generative model whose outputs are indistinguishable from real data by all members of the class? We prove that these two fundamental tasks in computational learning theory are not just closely related, but actually equivalent to each other in complexity. One direction of this equivalence was previously known. Indeed, the powerful regularity lemma in complexity theory gives an efficient oracle reduction from the indistinguishability task (a.k.a. multiaccuracy) to the distinguishing task (a.k.a. agnostic learning) in the style of boosting algorithms. Our main contribution is an efficient oracle reduction in the other direction. Taking this idea further, we show that a multiaccuracy oracle is a remarkably powerful primitive, achieving not just agnostic learning but also a wide range of seemingly more demanding learning objectives via similarly efficient and direct constructions. Our results crucially use the power of making adaptive queries to the oracle, and stand in stark contrast to prior work, which showed that post-processing a single multiaccurate predictor is insufficient for even weak forms of learning. On a technical level, we draw a connection between our (offline) problem and a version of no-regret learning in the online setting, which allows us to use follow-the-leader type algorithms to modify the label distribution and aggregate the predictions of the multiaccuracy oracle.
papers.summary: The question is whether training a discriminative model that does as well as the best in a class (agnostic learning) is computationally harder than producing a generative model that no member of the class can tell apart from real data (multiaccuracy). Earlier work gave an efficient reduction from multiaccuracy to agnostic learning using the regularity lemma. The authors supply the reverse reduction, **proving the two tasks equivalent in complexity**, and show that a multiaccuracy oracle also achieves a range of harder learning objectives. The construction depends on adaptive oracle queries and links the problem to follow-the-leader style no-regret online learning.

papers.title: Reading Why: Born-Measured Attention with Exact Word Evidence on Light and Qubits
papers.abstract: When a language model answers, we can usually only estimate why. We build a transformer in which every step is a Born measurement - attention $|\langle q|k\rangle|^4$ normalised over each row, a measured product in place of the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout. With its denominators held at their values for the input, each class probability is a polynomial in the word amplitudes, so its integrated-gradient evidence is computed by a finite quadrature with no quadrature error: the words' contributions sum to the class probability above its no-information share, to $10^{-11}$ or better. On e-SNLI natural language inference, with about 98k parameters outside the embedding, the model reaches $76.98 \pm 0.17$% test accuracy, level with a softmax transformer of the same size ($76.62 \pm 0.36$%). Deleting the word its evidence ranks first changes the answer in 45% of test pairs, out of the 53% any single deletion can change, against 32% for the softmax model explained the same way and 40% by its attention x gradient. Attention can look more like the words annotators highlighted, yet accounts for the answer less well: deleting the word it ranks first changes the Born Transformer's answer in 32% of pairs. The same weights compile exactly to optoelectronic optics and to qubits, and a coherent attention layer becomes one circuit equal to the model (852 CNOTs on 23 qubits). On IBM's ibm_kingston, reading only the attention overlaps by Hadamard tests, the device gave the model's answers on two short test pairs and kept or changed them under deletion as the model does; the evidence itself did not yet survive the device, and we work out the shots and calibration that measuring it on hardware would need.
papers.summary: To make model explanations exact rather than estimated, the authors build a `Born Transformer` in which attention, the nonlinearity and the readout are all Born measurements, so each class probability is a polynomial in word amplitudes and its integrated-gradient attributions can be computed with no quadrature error. On `e-SNLI` natural language inference it reaches 76.98% accuracy, level with a same-size softmax transformer. **Deleting the top-attributed word flips the answer in 45% of test pairs versus 32% for the softmax model**. The same weights compile exactly to optical hardware and qubits, and on IBM's `ibm_kingston` device the model's answers were reproduced on two short pairs, though the attributions themselves did not yet survive the hardware noise.

papers.title: Suppressing Misaligned Behaviors in Language Models, Durably
papers.abstract: Undesired model behaviors can emerge or re-emerge at any stage of training. Once observed, how effectively can we suppress them? To study this question, we first construct two model organisms--language models deliberately trained to exhibit a specific misalignment--that differ in what triggers the behavior. The narrow-trigger organism misbehaves only when the prompt contains a specific cue: it cheats on multiple-choice questions by following a planted hint that points to a wrong answer, and behaves normally otherwise. The broad-trigger organism has no such cue: after fine-tuning on insecure code, it gives harmful responses across a wide range of open-ended prompts. We then formalize post-hoc behavioral suppression and evaluate methods along three criteria: immediate suppression of the target behavior, durability under further training, and preservation of general capability. We compare standard methods--SFT, GRPO, and gradient-ascent unlearning--along these dimensions. Building on prior work on alignment shallowness, we hypothesize that more durable suppression requires the ability to recover from a wider range of misalignment states. We introduce Prefix-Expanded Adversarial Reinforcement Learning (PEARL), a GRPO variant that augments rollouts with continuations from intermediate states sampled along cached organism trajectories. Across both organism settings and two model families (Qwen3-4B, GPT-OSS-20B), PEARL achieves strong immediate suppression while preserving task accuracy, and remains durable under further fine-tuning on either the organism's data or unrelated data. It obtains the greatest benefit when the undesirable behavior is broad and cannot be addressed through targeted SFT. Together, our framework and method offer a step toward more durable post-hoc removal of undesired behaviors.
papers.summary: The question is how durably a misaligned behavior can be suppressed after it appears. The authors build two model organisms, one that cheats on multiple-choice questions only when a hint is present and one that gives broadly harmful answers after fine-tuning on insecure code. They compare `SFT`, `GRPO` and gradient-ascent unlearning on immediate suppression, durability under further training, and preserved capability. Their method, `PEARL` (Prefix-Expanded Adversarial Reinforcement Learning), extends `GRPO` rollouts with continuations from intermediate misaligned states, and across `Qwen3-4B` and `GPT-OSS-20B` it **suppresses the behavior while keeping it suppressed under further fine-tuning**, with the largest benefit for broad misbehavior.

papers.title: GUILD: Guided Iterative Data Collection for Imitation Learning
papers.abstract: Imitation learning policies in robotics are trained on datasets collected through costly real-world teleoperation. Often, the data-collection process is unguided, relying on the teleoperator's intuition, resulting in data that contributes little to overall policy performance. Recent work has shown that curating such unguided datasets can substantially improve policy performance, but these approaches operate by filtering existing datasets after collection and therefore do not prevent the acquisition of uninformative data. In this work, we propose GUILD, a novel Guided Data Collection (GDC) method that actively reasons about which data should be collected to maximize downstream policy performance. We introduce an iterative framework that alternates between 1) task proposal and data collection and 2) data evaluation to close the loop. For task proposal, we leverage semantic priors from vision-language models to identify relevant environments, object configurations, and goals for data collection. However, since semantic relevance does not imply policy improvement, we perform data evaluation. By leveraging predictive data attribution we approximate how the collected trajectories influence policy performance on a target deployment setting. This signal is then used as feedback to guide subsequent data collection, closing the data collection loop. We evaluate our approach in simulation and real robot settings, demonstrating that guided data collection substantially improves sample efficiency and deployment performance compared to passive data collection strategies, multiple baselines and experienced roboticists. More information at https://robin-lab.cs.utexas.edu/guild2026/
papers.summary: Teleoperated data for imitation learning is usually collected on the operator's intuition, and existing curation methods only filter data after it has been gathered. `GUILD` (Guided Iterative Data Collection) closes the loop: vision-language models propose environments, object setups and goals worth collecting, then predictive data attribution estimates how each collected trajectory affects policy performance in the target deployment and steers the next round. In simulation and on real robots, guided collection **improves sample efficiency and deployment performance over passive collection, multiple baselines and experienced roboticists**.

papers.title: PolicyIK: High-Precision Inverse Kinematics for Robot Arms with Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Inverse kinematics (IK) converts end-effector pose commands into joint motion, and many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on it to act on a given arm and to transfer across embodiments. Precise IK remains laborious: redundancy and singularities complicate the inverse mapping, execution depends on hand-tuned controllers, and training data on physical robots are costly to collect. We present PolicyIK, a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy for high-precision IK. It updates joint-position references from pose feedback and observes its accumulated reference relative to the measured joints, so it can retain the offset that the position controller needs at rest. Two-scale pose errors with an error-dependent action gain resolve millimeter residuals while preserving large motions. Progress and dwell rewards teach it to both reach the tolerance and stay within it. In simulation, a single attempt by the trained PPO policy keeps the mean errors over the final second within 1 mm and 0.2{\deg} on 93.5% of held-out tasks, and a deployment protocol raises success to 98.9%. When trained directly on a physical arm with an off-policy RL learner, PolicyIK achieves higher reaching and holding success than all four classical IK controllers under the same time budgets. In simulated pick-and-place, PolicyIK executes the end-effector commands of the $\pi_{0.5}$ VLA policy with 95.7% success. These results show that reinforcement learning can provide high-precision inverse kinematics for robot arms. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/PolicyIK.
papers.summary: Inverse kinematics (IK), which converts end-effector pose commands into joint motion, is still laborious to make precise because of redundancy, singularities and hand-tuned controllers. `PolicyIK` is a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy that updates joint references from pose feedback, using two-scale pose errors, an error-dependent action gain, and progress and dwell rewards. In simulation a trained `PPO` policy holds errors within 1 mm and 0.2° on 93.5% of held-out tasks, or 98.9% with a deployment protocol. When trained directly on a physical arm, it **outperforms four classical IK controllers** in reaching and holding, and it executes `π0.5` vision-language-action commands with 95.7% success in simulated pick-and-place.

papers.title: Aligning Language Models with General Preferences: An Empirical Study of Direct Nash Optimization
papers.abstract: Direct Nash Optimization (DNO) aligns a language model to a general preference function by approximating the Nash equilibrium of a two-player preference game. Its practical variant, DNO-Prct, iterates on-policy sampling, LLM-based rating of the samples together with a teacher's gold response, large-margin preference-pair selection and a DPO-style contrastive update. We re-implement DNO-Prct independently and study it on two open-weight instruct models, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B Instruct v0.1, with GPT-4o or a larger open-weight model of the same family as the annotator. On AlpacaEval 2.0 with GPT-4o as judge, three iterations raise the length-controlled (LC) win rate against GPT-4o from 31.7% to 45.3% for Llama and from 6.8% to 18.4% for Mistral, and the tuned 8B model scores above Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on every reported win rate. With same-family open-weight annotators, the runs retain 62% (Llama) and 82% (Mistral) of the LC gain achieved with GPT-4o as annotator, so the rating step does not require a proprietary model. In a separate ablation configuration, variants that remove the gold responses, remove the data look-back, or accept only teacher-preferred pairs score 6 to 10 LC points below the full procedure, whereas varying the number of on-policy samples per prompt (1 to 7) moves the LC win rate by at most 2.1 points, and a margin sweep (1 to 5) run in its own pipeline by at most 2.4 points. We also report the cost of the pipeline and where the practical algorithm departs from the theory it approximates. All results are single runs, and GPT-4o is both the teacher and the evaluation judge; we discuss what this implies for the reported gains.
papers.summary: The authors independently re-implement the practical variant of Direct Nash Optimization (DNO), which aligns a model to general preferences through on-policy sampling, LLM rating against a teacher's gold response, and DPO-style contrastive updates. They study it on `Llama 3.1 8B Instruct` and `Mistral 7B Instruct`. Three iterations raise the `AlpacaEval 2.0` length-controlled win rate from 31.7% to 45.3% for Llama, putting the tuned 8B model above `Llama 3.1 70B Instruct`. Same-family open-weight annotators **retain 62-82% of the gain achieved with GPT-4o as annotator**. Ablations show gold responses and data look-back matter far more than sample count or margin, though all results are single runs and GPT-4o is both teacher and judge.

papers.title: From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts: Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence
papers.abstract: For a decade, progress in artificial intelligence has been measured by how much a machine can do on its own. Large foundation models now write code and run multistep tasks, and personal agents act on a person's behalf. Yet people still forget what they once knew, miss what they are not looking at, fail to find the right words, and face hard choices without the benefit of their own history, because the machine that could help stands outside the situation. As AI moves into the physical world, attention has settled on one kind of intelligent individual, the embodied robot; we argue that the era of Physical AI holds a second kind of equal importance, the person augmented by AI. Alongside artificial general intelligence, which asks how intelligent a machine can be, stands AI-augmented human intelligence (AHI), which asks how much intelligence a machine can enable in a particular person. Realizing it calls for a new kind of system, a cognitive symbiont: a lifelong, embedded, real-time, private, low-friction, and proactive companion that senses what the person senses through external devices, keeps their context across years, models their situation and their mind, takes part in their thinking at the right moment, carries out everyday tasks with their context, and keeps learning the person as both change. We give the paradigm a conceptual core, the cognitive gap between what a person could bring to a situation and what they can hold in working memory, and organize its design space as a symbiosis loop of sensing, keeping, understanding, living alongside, acting for and thinking with the person, and growing, enclosed by a personal runtime and by trust. Because a symbiont changes what a person can do in front of others, it also raises risks of a new kind, from covert assistance in examinations to pressure on everyone to adopt it, and we treat their governance as part of the paradigm.
papers.summary: This position paper argues that alongside artificial general intelligence, AI should pursue AI-augmented human intelligence (AHI), which measures how much intelligence a machine can enable in a particular person. It proposes the **cognitive symbiont**: a lifelong, private, proactive companion that senses what the person senses, keeps their context across years, and takes part in their thinking at the right moment. The design space is organized around a cognitive gap between what a person could bring to a situation and what fits in working memory, framed as a loop of sensing, keeping, understanding, acting and growing. The authors also treat new governance risks, such as covert assistance in examinations and social pressure to adopt the technology.

papers.title: DreamX: Video Diffusion Model is a Universal Latent Action Learner
papers.abstract: Learning a universal action representation from video requires modeling dynamics that are consistent across different executions of the same action yet invariant to changes in embodiment and appearance. Existing latent action models infer actions from visual transitions, but their representations often entangle the underlying action with irrelevant visual variations, limiting transfer across embodiments. We introduce DreamX, which repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a universal latent action learner. Our approach extracts compact latent actions from the video model's rich spatiotemporal features, compressing each latent video frame by $\boldsymbol{300\times}$ ($\boldsymbol{1{,}200 \rightarrow 4}$ tokens). In addition, by leveraging the video model's generative prior, these latent actions capture action-relevant dynamics disentangled from visual appearance. The resulting latent space serves as a shared action interface across embodiments (human and robot), environments, and action parameterizations. On LARY-Bench, DreamX achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models. Moreover, actions encoded in one setting remain effective in another: the latent space supports any-to-any video transfer and zero-shot action transfer across diverse embodiments and environments. Furthermore, this shared interface also enables policy learning in a compact latent action space, reducing the computational cost of video-diffusion-based policies.
papers.summary: Latent action models that infer actions from video often tangle the action with irrelevant appearance, which limits transfer across embodiments. `DreamX` repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model to extract compact latent actions from its spatiotemporal features, **compressing each latent frame 300× from 1,200 to 4 tokens**, and uses the model's generative prior to separate dynamics from appearance. It reaches state-of-the-art results among latent action models on `LARY-Bench` and supports any-to-any video transfer and zero-shot action transfer between human and robot embodiments. The compact latent space also reduces the cost of policy learning built on video diffusion.
papers.highlight_summary:
Existing latent action models learn representations that mix the action itself with appearance details such as viewpoint, scene, and embodiment, so they transfer poorly between humans and robots. `DreamX` addresses this by reusing a pretrained video diffusion model (`Cosmos-Predict2.5` 2B) as both the encoder and the decoder of latent actions, so that the model's generative prior handles appearance and the latent tokens are pushed to capture motion.

- Learnable query tokens pass through the backbone's spatiotemporal attention alongside the video tokens and condense each latent frame from 1,200 tokens to **4 latent-action tokens (a 300× reduction)**; a LoRA-adapted copy of the same backbone then reconstructs future frames from the initial frame plus these tokens in place of text, and also predicts robot actions when labels are available.
- On `LARYBench`, it outperforms the strongest baseline, `DiLA`, cutting average action-regression MSE from **0.38 to 0.17** and raising classification accuracy from **62.25% to 69.67%**, and a 32-channel compressed version (`FAE-32`) still beats every baseline.
- Zero-shot human-to-robot video transfer on `HumanAndRobot` reaches **an FVD of 57.44, versus 170.19 for `AdaWorld` and 241.92 for `VideoWorld2`**, with no paired human–robot training data, and latent actions taken from human videos can be decoded into open-loop commands for a bimanual robot (writing, pushing).
- A policy that predicts compact latent-action codes instead of generating future video reaches **96.7% subgoal success versus 50.0% for `Mimic-Video`** on real-world drawer closing, and is **19.1× faster (1.47 s versus 28.2 s per call)**.
- The evidence is thin in places: the policy result comes from a single drawer-closing task with 45 training trajectories and 10 trials per configuration, the action-transfer results are only qualitative, and 1.47 s per policy call is still slow for closed-loop control.
